t.castello di racconigi@44.8,7.7:
Racconigi is a small town on the plain south of Turin, in Piedmont, surrounded by fields of maize and rice and lines of poplars. It is dominated by its castle, a grand residence of the House of Savoy, which ruled Piedmont and later Italy. Originally a medieval fortress, it was transformed over the centuries into a palace, with Baroque and neoclassical façades, and surrounded by a vast park with lakes, woods and a farm. The castle is part of the UNESCO-listed Residences of the Royal House of Savoy, inscribed in 1997.

The interiors of the castle are richly decorated, with apartments from the nineteenth century, when King Charles Albert made it his favourite summer residence. The last king of Italy, Umberto II, was born here in 1904. The park, laid out in the English style in the nineteenth century, is one of the largest in Piedmont, and it has greenhouses, a mock-Gothic farm and a lake. Visits to the interiors are generally guided.

Racconigi is also known for storks. A centre for the reintroduction of white storks and other wetland birds has been operating near the town for decades, and storks now nest on roofs and poles in the area. The nearby wetlands are home to many birds. Bra, a short ride south, is the birthplace of the Slow Food movement, and Pollenzo, nearby, has the University of Gastronomic Sciences in another Savoy residence.

The riding on the plain around Racconigi is flat and straight, through farmland and villages, with lots of traffic on the main roads. For better riding, head south into the Langhe and Roero, the hills famous for Barolo and Barbaresco wines, where the roads wind through vineyards and hilltop villages, with views of the Alps. The Langhe roads are among the best in Italy for motorcyclists, with endless curves and great food at the end. The Alps, with passes like the Colle della Maddalena, are within reach.

Racconigi has fuel and all services. Local food includes the cuisine of Piedmont: agnolotti, vitello tonnato, and the wines of the Langhe. Autumn, with the truffle season and the wine harvest, is the best time to visit.
t.canelli and asti spumante@44.7,8.2:
Under the streets of Canelli runs a second town, made of brick tunnels and vaulted galleries cut into the hillside, where for well over a century sparkling wine has rested in the cool and the dark. The locals call them the underground cathedrals, and they are the reason this small Piedmontese town is part of the UNESCO listing of the vineyard landscapes of Langhe-Roero and Monferrato. Canelli was one of the places where Italian sparkling wine was pioneered in the nineteenth century, using the local Moscato grape, and the town's big wine houses still welcome visitors into their cellars by appointment.

The landscape above ground is just as compelling. The vine rows march over steep hills in perfect lines, broken by hazelnut groves, little chapels and brick farmhouses, with castles and church towers on the ridges. The light here in late September and October, during the harvest, is soft and golden, and the air smells of crushed grapes. In spring, the hills turn an intense green and the views reach to the snow-capped Alps on clear days.

The roads are a pleasure. They follow the ridges and plunge into the valleys with a rhythm of tight bends and short straights, perfect for a relaxed but engaging ride. Santo Stefano Belbo, just a few kilometres away, is the birthplace of the writer Cesare Pavese, whose novels capture the rural life of these hills, and a road from there into the higher Langhe toward Cossano Belbo and beyond gets steeper and more rugged. Be mindful of slow tractors and wine trucks during harvest, gravel on minor lanes and the many cyclists who also love these hills.

Canelli, with nearly nine thousand people, has fuel stations and all the basic services, and Nizza Monferrato, home of Barbera wine, is just a short ride away. For food, you are in one of Italy's great kitchens. Look for vitello tonnato, agnolotti del plin, tajarin with butter and, in autumn, the white truffle that drives prices sky high in Alba. If you are riding on, enjoy the wine at dinner, not at lunch; the hills are steep and the roads unforgiving.
t.nakijin jo site@26.7,127.9:
On a hill on the Motobu peninsula in northern Okinawa, the long, curving walls of Nakijin castle follow the contours of the limestone like a stone dragon. In the fourteenth century, Okinawa was divided into three kingdoms, and Nakijin was the seat of the northern kingdom, Hokuzan, until it was conquered by the Chuzan kingdom in the early fifteenth century. The site is part of the UNESCO-listed Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu, which celebrates the unique culture of the Ryukyu islands, shaped by trade with China, Japan and Southeast Asia.

The walls are made of irregular limestone blocks, without mortar, and they wind for about 1.5 kilometres around the site. From the top, the views over the East China Sea and the islands are spectacular. In January and February, Nakijin is one of the first places in Japan where the cherry trees bloom, with deep pink flowers lining the paths, and the castle is lit up in the evening during the festival.

The Motobu peninsula is a beautiful place to ride. The roads wind along the coast, past beaches, coral reefs and small villages, and the bridges to the islands of Kouri and Sesoko offer spectacular views over turquoise water. Traffic can be heavy around the Churaumi Aquarium, one of the largest in the world, a short ride from Nakijin. Driving is on the left, speed limits are low, and summer brings heat, humidity and the occasional typhoon.

Nago, eleven kilometres away, is the main town in northern Okinawa, with fuel, shops and restaurants. Okinawan food is unique: try goya champuru, a stir-fry with bitter melon, soba with pork, and the local beer and awamori, a distilled spirit. The best times to visit are spring and autumn, when the weather is warm but not oppressive and the sea is perfect for swimming.
t.castello di govone@44.8,8.1:
Govone is a village of eight hundred people in the Roero, the hilly country on the left bank of the Tanaro across from the Langhe, and it is dominated by a palace far too grand for its size. The Castello di Govone was a residence of the House of Savoy, rebuilt in the baroque style in the eighteenth century, and it is one of the Residences of the Royal House of Savoy inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Inside are rooms decorated with Chinese wallpaper, and outside, terraced gardens look down over the valley.

The Savoy kings used Govone as a summer residence, and King Carlo Felice was particularly fond of it. Today the castle is owned by the municipality and serves as the town hall as well as a museum, which gives it a lived-in feel. Around Christmas, Govone hosts a popular festive event in the castle and the village. The surrounding Roero is a landscape of steep sandy hills, vineyards and woods, less famous than the Langhe across the river but just as beautiful, and its sandy cliffs, the rocche, are a striking feature.

The riding in the Roero and the Langhe is among the best in Piedmont. Narrow roads wind along the ridges and through the vineyards, climbing and descending constantly, with views over the hills to the Alps, which on clear days form a white wall on the horizon, with Monviso standing out. Surfaces vary, and the roads are narrow, so take care on blind bends. Traffic is light on weekdays but busier on weekends, especially in autumn during the truffle season. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Govone has a bar and basic services, but fuel is better found in Canale or Alba, the capital of the Langhe, thirteen kilometres away. Alba is famous for its white truffles, celebrated in a fair every autumn, and for Ferrero, whose chocolate factory is here. The wines of the Roero include Arneis, a fresh white, and Roero, a red made from Nebbiolo. Piedmontese food is superb: tajarin, thin egg pasta with butter and truffles, vitello tonnato and bagna cauda, a hot garlic and anchovy dip. From the castle gardens, the view across the Tanaro to the Langhe is lovely in the evening.
t.necropolis of istevene@40.2,9.3:
In Sardinian folklore, the little rock-cut tombs scattered across the island were the homes of janas, tiny fairies or witches who wove on golden looms and came out at night. Archaeologists call them domus de janas, fairy houses, and date them to the Neolithic and Copper Age, thousands of years before the famous nuraghi towers. The necropolis of Istevéne, near Mamoiada in the heart of the Barbagia, is a group of these chambers cut into the granite, some with carved details imitating the beams and doorways of real houses, and it belongs among the prehistoric Sardinian tombs that have gained UNESCO recognition.

Mamoiada itself is famous for its carnival, when the Mamuthones, men in dark wooden masks and sheepskins hung with heavy cowbells, move through the streets in a slow, rhythmic procession, a ritual that is ancient, haunting and very much alive. The village has a museum dedicated to Mediterranean masks, and it is also known for its Cannonau wine, made from vineyards on the granite slopes around the town. Nearby Orgosolo is famous for its political murals and its history of banditry.

The Barbagia is the wild heart of Sardinia, a land of granite hills, cork oaks, holm oaks and sheep. The roads are a delight for riders: winding, often empty, with good surfaces in places and broken, patched sections in others. Distances look short on the map but take time, and wandering sheep, goats, cattle and pigs are common hazards. Summer brings heat and the risk of forest fires, while winter can bring snow to the higher ground.

Mamoiada and Orgosolo are small towns with basic services, so for a sure supply of fuel and a wider choice, look to Oliena, about thirteen kilometres away, or Nuoro, the provincial capital. Local food is hearty and pastoral: roast suckling pig, lamb, pecorino cheese, carta da musica flatbread and culurgiones, stuffed pasta from the interior.

Spring, when the hills are green and the asphodel flowers, is the loveliest season, with autumn a close second. Visit Istevéne quietly, look into those small dark doorways cut into the rock, and remember that people buried their dead here long before Rome or even the nuraghi, in a land that still keeps many of its oldest rituals alive.
t.castello di pollenzo@44.7,7.9:
The village of Pollenzo was a Roman town, Pollentia, long before it was a Savoy estate, and in 402 a Roman army under Stilicho fought Alaric's Visigoths nearby in one of the last great battles of the Western Empire. Today the name means food. The castle and the neo-Gothic agricultural complex built around it by King Carlo Alberto in the nineteenth century, the Agenzia, now house the University of Gastronomic Sciences, founded by the Slow Food movement, which was born in nearby Bra. The estate is part of the UNESCO-listed Residences of the Royal House of Savoy.

The setting is the plain of the Tanaro river, at the meeting point of the Langhe and Roero hills. Across the river, the Langhe climb into the vineyards of Barolo and Barbaresco; on this side, the Roero's sandy hills grow Arneis and Nebbiolo. Verduno, on the ridge just above, is known for Pelaverga, a pale, peppery red. The air in autumn carries the smell of crushed grapes and, if you are lucky, a whiff of truffles, as Alba, the white truffle capital, is a short ride away.

The roads here are among the best in Piedmont for a rider who likes a mix of curves and food. The climbs into the Langhe are a delight, with tight hairpins through vineyards, ridge roads with views of the Alps and small medieval villages at every turn. The surfaces are generally good but narrow, and in autumn tractors and grape trailers share the road, often leaving mud and juice on the bends. Weekends bring car tourists in large numbers, while weekday mornings can be nearly empty. Fog in the valleys is common in late autumn and winter, adding a moody touch.

Bra is the nearby town for fuel and services, and it is worth a stop: an elegant baroque centre and a local speciality, salsiccia di Bra, a fine veal sausage that is traditionally eaten raw. The university complex at Pollenzo also has a wine bank in its old cellars and a restaurant, though opening times vary. If you are here for lunch, take your time; the region's cooking, from tajarin pasta to vitello tonnato, rewards patience. After the meal, a gentle ride along the Tanaro and a slow climb into the hills will settle everything.
t.necropolis of sant andrea priu@40.4,8.8:
Four or five thousand years ago, people on the high plateau of Campo di Santa Lucia in Sardinia carved a whole apartment of rooms into a cliff of soft volcanic rock, to house their dead. The Sardinians call these rock-cut tombs domus de janas, houses of the fairies, and Sant'Andrea Priu, near Bonorva, has some of the most remarkable. The largest, known as the Tomba del Capo, has a series of chambers whose walls and ceilings imitate the beams and pillars of a real house. Centuries later, in the early Christian and Byzantine period, it was converted into a church and its walls were painted with frescoes, some of which survive.

In 2025, UNESCO listed the funerary traditions of prehistoric Sardinia, with the domus de janas as its centrepiece. Sant'Andrea Priu is one of the best places to understand them. The plateau around it is wide and green in spring, golden in summer, with cork oaks, pastures and dry-stone walls. Sheep are everywhere, and their milk becomes pecorino sardo, the island's famous cheese. Near the tombs stands a large rock carved by nature into a shape that locals call the bull.

The riding in this part of Sardinia is rewarding and lonely. The SS131, the Carlo Felice, is the main north-south road, fast and busy, but leave it and the minor roads cross the plateaus and climb through hills with broad, open curves and very little traffic. The surfaces vary, and livestock may be on the road. Summer is hot and dry, with the mistral blowing strong, while winter can be cold and windy on the plateau. Spring is the best time, when the fields are green and covered with flowers.

Bonorva has fuel, shops and cafés; Macomer, nineteen kilometres away, is a larger town with more choice. Sardinian food is hearty: roast suckling pig, culurgiones, stuffed pasta, carta da musica, a thin crisp bread, and local cheeses. The nuraghe of Santu Antine, one of the finest Bronze Age towers on the island, is nearby at Torralba and worth a detour. When you visit the tombs, take time to let your eyes adjust to the darkness and look for the painted figures; they are faint, but still there after fifteen centuries.
t.necropolis of su crucifissu mannu@40.8,8:
Sardinians call them domus de janas, houses of the fairies, and when you crouch at the entrance of one you understand the name. They are tombs cut straight into the soft limestone by the island's Neolithic and Copper Age people, small chambers linked by low doorways, sometimes with carved false doors or bull horns on the walls. The necropolis of Su Crucifissu Mannu, just inland from Porto Torres, holds a couple of dozen of them scattered across a low rocky plateau among fields and scrub, one of the largest groups in the north of the island.

The site feels wonderfully unbothered. There are no crowds, just lizards, the scent of wild fennel and the drone of insects, and the openings in the rock look like the doors of a tiny underground village. Bring a torch if you want to peer inside. The people who carved them lived long before the nuraghi, the stone towers that are Sardinia's trademark, and their tombs are among the oldest monuments on the island.

Porto Torres, five minutes away, was the Roman colony of Turris Libisonis, and its remains include baths and a bridge. Its great treasure is the basilica of San Gavino, the largest Romanesque church in Sardinia, built of pale stone on the site of the martyrdom of three Roman soldiers. The town is also the port for ferries to the mainland and for boats to Asinara, the long island off the northwest tip that was a prison for decades and is now a national park famous for its little white donkeys.

The riding nearby is a mix. The SS131 dual carriageway links Porto Torres with Sassari and the south quickly but without charm. Much better is the road west towards Stintino, flat and fast along the coast past salt pans and lagoons, ending at La Pelosa, a beach with water so pale and clear it looks unreal; in summer access is limited and traffic heavy. Inland, the minor roads towards Sorso and the Nurra have gentle bends through vineyards and olive groves. The mistral blows hard on this coast, and can make the bike work.

Porto Torres has fuel, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat. Try the local seafood, or a plate of malloreddus, little ridged pasta. Spring and autumn are best for riding; midsummer brings heat and tourists in equal measure.
t.necropolis of mesu e montes@40.6,8.6:
Inland from Sassari, the Logudoro is a country of limestone ridges, small towns of honey-coloured stone and fields enclosed by dry walls, and in its folds lies the necropolis of Mesu 'e Montes, near the villages of Ossi, Muros and Florinas. It is a group of domus de janas, the rock-cut tombs of Sardinia's prehistoric farmers, some of them richly decorated with carved pillars, false doors and the stylised bull horns that seem to have been a symbol of protection or power.

The tombs were carved with stone tools into the hillside some five thousand years ago or more, and they were often reused for burials over many centuries. Standing inside one, with the cool rock around you, you feel how much effort went into shaping these spaces for the dead.

This part of Sardinia is also home to some of the island's finest Romanesque churches, built when Pisan and Genoese influences were strong in the twelfth century. The most famous is the Santissima Trinità di Saccargia, a short ride away near Codrongianos, with its striped walls of black basalt and white limestone and a tall bell tower rising from the fields. It looks as if it has been transported from Tuscany. There are several other similar churches in the area, many standing alone in the countryside.

The riding is good. The SS597 towards Olbia runs east from here through rolling hills and cork oak woods, with fast bends and good visibility. The minor roads that link the villages are narrower and more winding, with stone walls close to the edge, occasional potholes, and flocks of sheep moving between pastures. Sardinia is one of the great motorcycling islands of the Mediterranean, and even these unassuming inland roads show why: empty, flowing, with a new view at every crest.

The nearest towns with full services are Ossi and Sassari, a short ride away, both with fuel and shops; the smaller villages around have bars where you can get a coffee and perhaps a panino. Spring is the best time, when the fields are green and full of flowers; summer can be scorching. Look for pecorino sardo and the local carasau bread, thin and crisp, which shepherds once took with them on long trips to the pastures.
t.necropolis of sa pala larga@40.4,8.9:
Bonorva sits on the edge of a high plateau in central-northern Sardinia, a town of grey stone looking out over the plain of Santa Lucia. Around it, the land is dotted with prehistoric remains, and the necropolis of Sa Pala Larga is one of several groups of domus de janas cut into the rock in this area. The rock-cut tombs are older than the nuraghi, and many have intricate interiors.

The most spectacular nearby is Sant'Andrea Priu, a few kilometres east of Bonorva, a large domus de janas in a rock face that was later converted into a church in the early Christian and Byzantine period, with frescoes painted on the walls of the tomb chambers. The combination of a Neolithic tomb and a Christian chapel makes it one of the most unusual sites on the island.

A little to the north, near Torralba, is the Nuraghe Santu Antine, one of the most impressive nuraghi in Sardinia, with a tall central tower and a triangular bastion. The plain around is known as the Valle dei Nuraghi because of the many towers scattered across it. It is a landscape layered with history.

The riding around Bonorva is varied. The SS131, the main north-south road on the island, passes close by, fast and efficient. Better are the smaller roads that climb onto the Campeda plateau, a high, windswept tableland with cork oak woods, pastures and few houses, where the views stretch for miles. The roads here are generally quiet, with long straights and sweeping bends, though the wind can be strong and gusty. Heading west towards the coast, the roads drop through hills and valleys towards Bosa, a colourful town on the river Temo, and the coast road from Bosa to Alghero is one of the best rides in Sardinia.

Bonorva has fuel, shops and bars. The area is known for its cheeses, particularly pecorino, and for hearty mountain cooking, including roast suckling pig and lamb. The weather on the plateau can be cooler than on the coast, with fog in winter and strong winds at any time. Spring and early summer are ideal, when the fields are green and the air is fresh. Bring a torch to peer into the tombs, and take your time; this is a landscape that rewards patience.
t.sefa utaki@26.2,127.8:
For the people of the old Ryukyu Kingdom, there was no holier place than Sēfa-utaki, a grove of forest and rock on the southeastern tip of Okinawa island. An utaki is a sacred site in the Ryukyuan religion, often a grove, a rock or a spring, where gods are believed to descend, and this one was the most important of all. The kingdom's highest priestess, the Kikoe-ōkimi, usually a woman of the royal family, was inaugurated here, and for centuries men were not allowed to enter.

The path leads through dense subtropical forest to a series of shrines among the rocks. The most striking is Sangūi, where two massive rock slabs lean against each other to form a triangular passage. Walking through, you come to a small clearing where you can look out over the sea to Kudaka Island, a low, flat island believed to be where the creator goddess Amamikyu first descended to make the Ryukyu islands. The atmosphere is quiet and reverent, and visitors are asked to behave with respect. Sēfa-utaki is part of the UNESCO site of the Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu, listed in 2000.

The Ryukyu Kingdom was an independent maritime state for several centuries, trading with China, Japan and Southeast Asia, before being annexed by Japan in the nineteenth century. Its culture, language, music and cuisine are distinct from mainland Japan, and you will notice the difference everywhere: in the red-tiled roofs, the shisa lion-dog guardians on the houses, and the food, such as goya champuru, a stir-fry with bitter melon.

The riding in southern Okinawa is pleasant and relaxed. The roads along the coast near Sēfa-utaki have views of the turquoise sea and coral reefs, and the Niraikanai Bridge nearby sweeps down from the hills in a great curve towards the coast, with a spectacular view. Traffic can be heavy around Naha, but the rural roads in the south are quieter. Driving is on the left.

Fuel, food and supplies are easy to find in Nanjō and the surrounding towns. The weather is subtropical: warm all year, very hot and humid in summer, with typhoons possible from summer into autumn. Winter is mild and the best season for riding. Bring water and sun protection, and take your time in the grove.
t.zakimi jo site@26.4,127.7:
The walls of Zakimi gusuku curve across the top of a hill in Yomitan like a ribbon of pale limestone, following the contour of the land in graceful arcs rather than straight lines. Built in the early fifteenth century by Gosamaru, a celebrated castle builder of the Ryukyu Kingdom, the fortress is small but beautifully made. Its arched stone gateways, held in place by a wedge-shaped keystone, are among the oldest stone arches in Okinawa. Zakimi is part of the UNESCO site of the Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu, listed in 2000.

Gosamaru was a powerful lord who served the king in the period when the island was being unified. He later moved to Nakagusuku, where he built another fine fortress, and his story ended in tragedy, caught up in the struggles between rival lords. His walls at Zakimi have survived much: in the Second World War the Japanese army used the castle as an anti-aircraft position, and after the war the US military took over the site. It was later returned and restored.

From the top of the walls the views stretch over the surrounding countryside to the East China Sea. The site is quiet, with grass, trees and the sound of the wind. Nearby is the Yomitan pottery village, Yachimun no Sato, where potters work in traditional climbing kilns, and you can buy plates and cups in the distinctive Okinawan style. Cape Zanpa, a few minutes away, has a white lighthouse on dramatic coral cliffs.

The riding around Yomitan is easy and pleasant. The roads are mostly flat or gently rolling, through sugar cane fields and small villages, with occasional glimpses of the sea. Traffic is moderate, heavier on the main roads towards Naha. The coast road north along the west side of the island, towards the resorts of Onna and Nago, is scenic, with views of beaches and coral reefs.

Yomitan has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Try Okinawa soba, thick wheat noodles in broth with pork, or taco rice, an Okinawan invention combining Tex-Mex ingredients with rice. The weather is subtropical: hot and humid in summer, mild in winter, with typhoons possible from summer to autumn. Bring sun protection; the sun is fierce. Climb the walls late in the afternoon, when the light turns golden and the heat begins to ease.
t.necropolis of ispiluncas@40.2,8.9:
In central Sardinia, on a slope above the village of Sedilo, a cluster of rock-cut tombs opens into the hillside like a row of small dark doorways. These are domus de janas, "houses of the fairies" in the local language, burial chambers carved into the soft rock by the island's prehistoric inhabitants several thousand years ago. Ispiluncas is one of the larger groups, with tombs of varied plans, some with multiple chambers and carved details imitating the beams and doorframes of houses. In 2025 the domus de janas were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list, recognising one of the most distinctive funerary traditions in the Mediterranean.

Sedilo is best known for something much louder. Every July the village holds the Ardia, a wild horse race in honour of San Costantino, the Roman emperor Constantine, who is venerated locally as a saint. Riders gallop at breakneck speed around the sanctuary, protected by escorts firing blanks, and the whole thing is chaotic, dangerous and deeply rooted in local identity. The sanctuary of San Costantino stands on a ridge outside the village, overlooking Lake Omodeo, a large reservoir formed by damming the Tirso river.

The riding in this part of Sardinia is excellent. The roads around Lake Omodeo and up toward the plateau of Abbasanta and Macomer wind through cork oak woods, rocky outcrops and pasture, with long, flowing bends, light traffic and good surfaces in most places. Head east and the country rises into the Barbagia, with steeper climbs and tighter corners. Summer heat can be intense, with the air heavy with the smell of dry grass and myrtle, so ride early or late. Watch out for sheep, cattle and the occasional wild boar, especially at dusk.

Sedilo has a few bars and shops, but for fuel and more services, head for Ghilarza, Abbasanta or Macomer, which has around ten thousand inhabitants. Local food is hearty: roast suckling pig, pecorino, flatbread, and robust red wines. Park near the necropolis, walk among the tombs, and peer into the dark chambers, imagining the people who carved them with stone tools. Then ride down to the lake shore for a cool break before continuing your loop.
t.necropolis of anghelu ruju@40.6,8.3:
Not far from Alghero, on the flat land behind the coast, lies the largest group of domus de janas in Sardinia. Anghelu Ruju is a necropolis of more than thirty rock-cut tombs, dug into the sandstone with stone tools around five thousand years ago and later reused for burials into the Bronze Age. The site was found in 1903 when workers were preparing land for a vineyard, and excavations revealed chambers with carved bull's horns, false doorways and painted ochre, together with pottery, figurines and personal ornaments now displayed in museums in Sassari and Cagliari. The bull motifs are thought to have been linked to fertility and protection, and they give these dim chambers a surprisingly powerful presence.

Alghero itself is a delight, a walled port town with a strong Catalan heritage dating from the fourteenth century, when the Crown of Aragon took the city and repopulated it with settlers from Catalonia. A form of Catalan is still spoken by some locals, and street signs are often bilingual. The old town is a maze of narrow lanes, churches and sea walls, and the local cuisine is built on seafood, especially lobster, with good white wines from the surrounding vineyards.

The riding around Alghero is mixed but pleasant. The flat land inland, with its vineyards and olive groves, gives easy, relaxed cruising on straight roads, while the coast roads north toward Capo Caccia and the Grotta di Nettuno offer cliffs, curves and wide views over the sea. The road south to Bosa along the coast is one of the finest motorcycle roads in Sardinia, with endless bends carved into the cliffs, very little traffic outside summer and constant sea views. Watch for strong winds on exposed stretches, and expect heavy tourist traffic in July and August.

Alghero, about eight kilometres away, has plenty of fuel stations, cafés, restaurants and accommodation. Opening arrangements at the necropolis change with the season, so it is worth checking before you set off. Go in the morning, when the light is soft and the air still cool, walk among the tombs, and then head down to the coast for a swim or a long lunch. It is a gentle, rewarding stop on any ride through the northwest of the island.
t.petroglyph park b@40.5,8.7:
The Logudoro in northern Sardinia is a high, rolling country of basalt plateaus and the worn cones of extinct volcanoes, where cork oaks and wild olives stand in dry pasture and every second hill seems to have a ruined nuraghe on it. Petroglyph Park-b lies near the small villages of Cheremule, Giave and Torralba, in an area where the rock itself was used as an archive, carved into tombs and marked with symbols by people who lived here thousands of years before Rome.

The famous monuments around here are the domus de janas, the houses of the fairies, chamber tombs cut into rock outcrops in the Neolithic and Copper Age. Some have several rooms, false doors and carved details imitating wooden houses, and a few in this area show bull's horns in relief, a symbol of fertility and power that recurs across prehistoric Sardinia. The rides that pass here connect several of these sites, from Anghelu Ruju near Alghero to Mesu 'e Montes near Ossi, which together with others were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2025.

Torralba, a few kilometres away, is the base for Nuraghe Santu Antine, one of the most impressive nuraghi on the island, a Bronze Age tower complex built from huge blocks without mortar. The so called Valle dei Nuraghi stretches around it. Fill your water bottle before you explore; shade is scarce, and from June to September the sun is relentless, with temperatures that make a leather jacket a test of character.

The riding is a pleasure once you leave the SS131, the four-lane spine that runs from Cagliari to Porto Torres. The minor roads across the plateau curve between stone walls and cork woods, climb onto basalt tablelands with long views, and drop into small villages with steep, narrow centres. Surfaces vary, and grit, gravel and cattle are part of the deal. Spring, when the fields are green and full of flowers, is the finest season, and autumn is good too.

These are tiny villages, so do not count on fuel in each one. Stations line the SS131 and the bigger towns such as Ittiri, eighteen kilometres off, have reliable services. Food in the Logudoro is shepherd's food at its best: pecorino, roast lamb or piglet, and pane carasau, the thin crisp bread that keeps for weeks in a saddlebag.
t.necropolis of sos furrighesos@40.5,9.0:
In the Goceano hills of north-central Sardinia, a low cliff of pale volcanic rock above the village of Anela hides one of the island's more striking prehistoric cemeteries. Sos Furrighesos is a cluster of domus de janas, the rock-cut tombs whose Sardinian name means houses of the fairies, carved into the face of the stone by Neolithic farmers some five thousand years ago. Some of the chambers are simple niches; others open into several rooms, and a few still carry carved reliefs of bull horns, a symbol you meet again and again in Sardinian prehistory.

The name the locals gave such places tells you how later generations explained them. People who found small doorways cut into rock imagined tiny women living inside, sometimes weaving with golden looms, sometimes stealing children. Archaeologists credit the work to the culture of Ozieri, named after the town just to the north, whose people were skilled potters and clearly had a great deal of patience with stone tools.

Getting here is half the pleasure. The Goceano is quiet, rolling country between the Tirso valley and the higher ground of the Marghine, with cork oaks, pasture walled in dry stone, and small towns that close their shutters in the early afternoon. The roads that link Bono, Anela, Bultei and Burgos are narrow, mostly well surfaced and properly twisty, with blind bends where a herd of sheep can appear without warning. Above Burgos the ruin of the medieval Castello del Goceano sits on a rocky spike and makes a fine detour, with views over the whole district.

There is not much in the way of facilities at the necropolis itself, so treat it as a quiet stop rather than an outing. Bono is the nearest town with a decent range of shops and bars and a little over three thousand people; for a more certain choice of fuel stations, Ozieri, about twelve kilometres away, is the town to aim for. Carry water in summer, when the hills bake and the light turns everything the colour of straw.

Spring is the season to choose. In April and May the Goceano is green, the roadside verges explode with flowers, and the temperatures suit a riding jacket. The autumn months are almost as good, and you will share the roads with farm vehicles rather than tourists. Either way, stand for a while in front of those little doorways and think about who carved them, and why.
t.domus de janas of orto del beneficio par:
Most prehistoric tombs in Sardinia sit out in the countryside behind a gate and a dirt track. The domus de janas of Orto del Beneficio Parrocchiale are different: they are in Sennori itself, a few steps from the houses, carved into the soft limestone in what was once, as the name suggests, a garden belonging to the parish. A handful of chambers opens out of the rock, small rooms with low doorways, the work of Neolithic farmers who lived on this ridge thousands of years before anyone thought of building a church here.

Sennori and its neighbour Sorso sit on a balcony of hills just north of Sassari, looking across the Gulf of Asinara to the sea. The district is called the Romangia, and it is wine country. The sweet Moscato di Sorso-Sennori is the local speciality, along with robust reds from the surrounding vineyards, and the slopes falling toward the coast are striped with vines and olive groves. In late afternoon the light comes in low off the water and turns the stone of the villages honey-coloured.

The riding around here is relaxed rather than dramatic. From Sennori the road drops through bends to Sorso and on to the long sandy beach at Platamona, which fills with locals on summer weekends. Head east along the coast instead and you reach Castelsardo, a fortified old town stacked on a rock above the sea, with a castle at the top and women weaving baskets from dwarf palm in the doorways. The inland roads toward Osilo and the Anglona are quieter and more twisting, with good views back over the gulf.

Sennori is a town of nearly seven thousand people, so fuel, bars and small shops are all close at hand, and Sassari, eight kilometres away, has everything a traveller might need, including bigger workshops if the bike needs attention. Sassari has a reputation for its own food culture too: try fainè, a thin chickpea flatbread brought over by Ligurian traders, or a plate of snails in the autumn.

The tombs make a natural pairing with the larger necropolis of Anghelu Ruju near Alghero, which is on the same ride and gives you a sense of how widespread this way of burying the dead once was across the north-west of the island. Here, though, the charm is in the closeness: a prehistoric cemetery and a modern village sharing the same hillside, with nobody making a fuss about it.
t.vineyard landscape of piedmont langhe ro:
Barolo the village has a few hundred inhabitants and a castle; Barolo the wine has a worldwide reputation built on the Nebbiolo grape and on the peculiar soils and slopes of these hills south of Alba. Around the village, the Langhe rise in steep ridges striped with vineyards, each hill crowned with a village, a castle or a church tower: La Morra, Monforte d'Alba, Serralunga, Castiglione Falletto, Novello. In 2014 UNESCO listed the vineyard landscapes of the Langhe, Roero and Monferrato for the way centuries of winemaking have shaped every slope, every row, every cellar.

The castle of Barolo, once owned by the Falletti family, houses a wine museum, and the village streets are lined with enotecas offering tastings. Marchesa Giulia Falletti di Barolo is credited, along with Camillo Cavour, with helping to transform Barolo in the nineteenth century from a sweet wine into the dry, powerful red known today. Look across the valley from the belvedere of La Morra and you see the whole patchwork of vineyards, each with a name that wine lovers recite like poetry.

This is one of Italy's great riding regions. The roads follow the ridges and plunge into valleys, with tight bends, short climbs and views on every side. The surface is variable, sometimes patched, and tractors appear in the harvest season in September and October, along with tourists hunting for wine and truffles. In spring the vines are bright green; in autumn they turn red and gold, and morning mist fills the valleys while the hilltops stand in sunshine. The roads south of Monforte towards Dogliani and the Alta Langa climb higher into wilder country with hazelnut orchards and woods.

The food is legendary. Alba's white truffles are auctioned for fortunes in October and November, and shaved over plin, small pinched ravioli, or tajarin, thin egg pasta, they make one of the great dishes of Italy. Hazelnuts from the Langhe, the tonda gentile, are reputed among the finest in the world, and Alba is home to the Ferrero confectionery company.

For fuel, Alba, about twelve kilometres away, is the main town, and Monforte also has services. As for the wine: taste, buy a bottle, and open it at the hotel. The roads deserve a clear head.
Sardinia is covered in small rock-cut tombs called domus de janas, the houses of the fairies, or of the witches depending on who tells the story. They were carved into soft rock by the island's Neolithic and Copper Age communities, more than five thousand years ago, and there are thousands of them, from single chambers to complex underground houses for the dead. The necropolis of Monte Siseri, near the village of Putifigari in the hills behind Alghero, includes the tomb known as S'Incantu, the enchantment, one of the most elaborate on the island. Its chambers imitate the interior of a house, with carved details such as roof beams, pillars and doorways, and traces of red and black paint that once decorated the walls. The domus de janas have recently joined the UNESCO World Heritage list, a long-overdue recognition of Sardinian prehistory.

The landscape is the rolling, rocky interior of northwest Sardinia, with cork oaks, olive groves, Mediterranean scrub and pastures grazed by sheep. It smells of myrtle, cistus and wild fennel, especially after rain. Putifigari, Uri and Olmedo are small agricultural villages, quiet and welcoming.

Alghero, on the coast about eleven kilometres away, is a fortified town with an unusual history. It was conquered by the Crown of Aragon in the fourteenth century and repopulated with Catalans, and to this day a dialect of Catalan is spoken in its streets, with street signs in both languages. The old town, with its sea walls, towers and narrow lanes, is beautiful, and the seafood, especially lobster cooked Alghero style, is famous.

The riding in northwest Sardinia is varied and rewarding. The coast road from Alghero south to Bosa is one of the most spectacular in the Mediterranean, running high above the sea along cliffs, with long bends, few villages and views over a wild coastline. Inland, the roads through the hills are quieter, with gentle curves through cork forests and farmland. The wind, especially the mistral from the northwest, can be strong, and summer heat is intense.

Alghero has fuel and every service, and Uri and Olmedo have stations too. Try the local cheeses, pecorino in particular, and the pane carasau, the thin, crisp flatbread of Sardinian shepherds, with a glass of Cannonau, the island's red wine, in the evening.
t.genoa le strade nuove and the system of:
Genoa never tried to be pretty in the way Florence or Venice did. It tried to be rich, and succeeded, and the Strade Nuove, the new streets laid out in the sixteenth century, are the proof. The city's banking families, who financed the Spanish crown for decades, built palaces along Via Garibaldi, Via Balbi and Via Cairoli, and they did it on a steep, crowded slope where there was no room for gardens, so the grandeur is stacked into courtyards, loggias and monumental staircases. The palaces were registered in the Rolli, official lists that told the republic which houses should host visiting kings and cardinals, a bit like a medieval hotel guide for diplomats. UNESCO listed the system in 2006.

Three palaces on Via Garibaldi are museums, including the Palazzo Rosso and Palazzo Bianco, and Palazzo Tursi holds the violin of Paganini, a Genoese, which the city keeps as a treasure. Even if you skip the art, wander in through the open doors to look at a courtyard, because the best of Genoa is often behind a heavy door.

Genoa is a hard city for motorcycles in one way and a good one in another. The old centre is a maze of alleys called caruggi, closed to cars and often to bikes, but scooters and motorcycles are everywhere in the rest of town and parking is easier than for a car. Fuel is plentiful in the city of nearly six hundred thousand, and the Val Polcevera suburbs like Manesseno on the western side have pumps and cafes too. Traffic around the port and the elevated roads is heavy, with tunnels, merging lanes and aggressive timing, so treat it as an urban ride and keep your eyes up.

Leave early to get the better roads. Behind the city, the hills of the Apennines come close, and the old road over the Bocchetta pass above the Polcevera valley gives you proper bends after the stop-start of town. Eat focaccia for breakfast, farinata at lunch, and trofie with pesto in the evening, because pesto is Genoese and nowhere else does it better. Spring and autumn are best, when the light on the old stone is soft and the crowds are smaller.
t.northern part of okinawa island@26.7,128:
The northern third of Okinawa island is called Yanbaru, and it is nothing like the beach resorts and American bases the south is known for. It is forest, thick subtropical evergreen forest with giant ferns and trees dripping with moss, rolling over steep hills that drop straight into the East China Sea. It is also one of the richest places for wildlife in Japan, with species found nowhere else in the world, including the Okinawa rail, a flightless bird only found by scientists in 1981, and the Okinawa woodpecker. Together with Amami and a few other islands, the area was added to the UNESCO natural heritage list in 2021.

The road tells the story. From Nago, a city of nearly sixty thousand, Route 58 follows the coast northwards, with the sea shifting between turquoise and deep blue, small villages with concrete houses and hibiscus hedges, and long runs of fast curves. The surface is generally excellent, but the road gets quieter and narrower the further north you go. At the northern tip, Cape Hedo, wind blows hard and the coral cliffs are impressive, with the Pacific and the East China Sea meeting below.

Fuel is easy in Nago but scarce further north, where stations are few and close early, so fill the tank before you commit. There are small shops and roadside restaurants in villages, with Okinawan soba, a wheat noodle in pork broth, and bitter melon stir-fry as local staples. The weather is warm for most of the year, but rain falls often, humidity is high and typhoons in late summer and autumn can close roads.

The forest roads inland are the best fun, with tight bends, steep climbs and tunnel-like canopy, but they can be slippery with leaf litter and moss, and the wildlife matters. Slow down at night, because the rails and other animals are killed by traffic, and it is considered poor form to ignore the signs. Cross the narrow roads gently, and bear in mind that the habu, the local pit viper, is best admired at distance. The cool, dry months of November to March are the most comfortable for riding.
t.sao joao@0.1,6.6:
Sao Tomé is a green volcanic island on the equator, and for a century and a half it was a cocoa empire. The Portuguese planted vast estates called roças across the land, each one a small town with a manor, a hospital, a church, drying platforms and rows of workers' housing, and by 1900 the islands were one of the largest cocoa producers in the world. The labour was brutal. Workers contracted from Angola, Cape Verde and Mozambique worked in conditions little better than slavery, and the scandal broke in Europe in the early twentieth century, prompting boycotts by chocolate makers.

São João dos Angolares lies on the south-east side of the island, and it carries another story. The Angolares are the people who live in the south, said to be descendants of enslaved Africans who survived a shipwreck in the sixteenth century and made a life in the forest and the sea, fishing and farming separately from the plantation world. Their culture, language and cooking are distinct, and the village still has the smell of woodsmoke and fish.

The roça here is one of several, with its buildings in various states of grace, and it belongs to the group of roças listed with Colonia and Diogo Vaz in the ride titles. Many are now half-ruined, some are being restored and a few offer guided visits, so ask locally before you go. The island is small, and the town of São Tomé, with more than fifty thousand people, is the only place with real services, including fuel, so fill up there.

The road along the east coast is one of the island's best rides, though that is a relative term. The asphalt is patched, with potholes and sudden gaps, and the bends follow the coast between palms, beaches of black volcanic sand and villages where children wave. Rain comes hard and often, and the dry season, called gravana, from June to September, is the best time. Try fresh grilled fish, breadfruit and the island's chocolate, which is among the best in Africa, and remember that the equator itself, on the tiny Ilhéu das Rolas, is a short boat ride from the south coast.
t.la place forte de mont dauphin@44.7,6.6:
Vauban built this in a hurry, and you can feel the urgency in the plan. After the Duke of Savoy invaded Dauphiné in 1692, Louis XIV's great military engineer chose a spur of rock above the meeting of the Durance and the Guil rivers and laid out a fortified town on a strict grid, with ramparts, bastions and a parade ground. Mont-Dauphin was meant to close the Durance valley to any army coming from Italy, and it is one of the twelve groups of Vauban fortifications that UNESCO listed in 2008. The buildings are in a rosy-grey marble from the nearby quarries of Guillestre, and in evening light they glow like embers.

The fortress sits at about a thousand metres, on the road that leads into the Queyras, and the mountains rise on all sides, with snow on the highest peaks until early summer. It is a place of wind and swallows, with a few craft shops, a cafe or two and a lot of empty parade ground. Walk the ramparts and look south, where the Durance valley bends toward Embrun and the Lac de Serre-Ponçon. The streets were laid out for soldiers, not shoppers, so the town has a spare, geometric beauty.

For riders, Mont-Dauphin is a gate to some of the finest roads in the Alps. Guillestre, two kilometres away, is the start of the climb to the Col de Vars and the Col d'Izoard, and the road up the Guil through the Combe du Queyras has tunnels cut through the rock and hairpins above a gorge. The Col Agnel, which crosses to Italy at 2,744 metres, is another of the area's great passes. All of these high passes close for the winter, usually from about November until late spring, so check before you plan. Expect cyclists, motorhomes in summer and sudden thunderstorms in the afternoon.

Guillestre has fuel and a few supermarkets, and Embrun, sixteen kilometres downstream, is bigger. Fill the tank before heading into the Queyras, because the villages up the valley are small. Local specialities include walnut tart, mountain cheeses and a hearty tartiflette. The sun is strong at this altitude, so wear sunscreen, and carry a warm layer for the passes.
t.portovenere@44.1,9.7:
Portovenere is a pastel row of tall houses stacked along the water's edge, their backs forming a kind of sea wall, and at the end of the promontory a black-and-white striped church on a rock. The church of San Pietro, begun in the twelfth century in the Genoese Gothic style, stands on the foundations of an older sanctuary that was supposedly a temple of Venus, the goddess who gave the town its name, and the whole point of the place leans out into the Ligurian Sea. Across a narrow strait lie the islands of Palmaria, Tino and Tinetto, part of the same World Heritage listing that covers the Cinque Terre. Byron is said to have swum across the bay to visit Shelley at Lerici, and a cave below the church carries his name.

For centuries this was a Genoese stronghold against Pisa and the sea powers beyond, and the great Doria castle above the village still dominates the skyline. The tall narrow houses were built almost as a continuous defensive wall, with windows facing in and the seafront facing out, and the single main street, the Via Capellini, runs steeply from the gate to the point.

The approach from La Spezia is a coastal road with a few bends, some busy suburban stretches and views over the gulf, and the last kilometres are narrow, steep and congested in summer. Parking in Portovenere is a problem, so leave the bike in the car park at the entrance and walk down. Early morning or late evening is by far the best time, and in the off season you might have the lanes to yourself. The riding that makes this part of Liguria famous lies in the hills behind, where narrow, twisty roads climb between terraced hillsides and drop to tiny harbours.

Fuel is easy in La Spezia, a naval and port city with a big harbour. Portovenere itself offers small restaurants along the waterfront, with trofie pasta, anchovies, mussels from the gulf's farms, and focaccia, which is taken seriously here. Riomaggiore and the other Cinque Terre villages are close as the crow flies, but the roads linking them are narrow and often restricted, so many riders go by train or ferry instead.
t.monte cafe@0.3,6.6:
Sao Tome is a tiny island on the equator, in the Gulf of Guinea, and for over a century it was one of the biggest cocoa and coffee producers in the world. Monte Cafe, in the hills above the capital at about six hundred metres, was one of the great plantations, called rocas, that covered much of the island. The Portuguese began planting coffee here in the nineteenth century, and the estate grew to include a processing yard, drying terraces, a hospital, a church and rows of workers' housing, all in a cool, cloudy valley under thick forest. The roca system, built on forced and poorly paid labour, was harsh, and the buildings remain as a monument to both the island's wealth and its suffering.

Since independence in 1975, the rocas have declined, and many are now half-ruined, with trees growing through the roofs and families living in the old barracks. Monte Cafe has found a new life as a place that welcomes visitors, with a small museum of coffee and a working roasting operation, where you can taste coffee grown on the island, which is small-batch, aromatic and smooth. The surroundings are lush, with plantation shade trees, banana plants and flowering shrubs, and the air is fresh and damp.

The ride up from Sao Tome city is a short climb of around ten kilometres, through villages and forest on a road that has been improved in places and is rough in others. Potholes are frequent, especially after the heavy rains, and tight bends mean that trucks and minibuses often come around on the wrong side, so go carefully. The wet season, with the heaviest rain from October to May, makes the road slippery, and the gravana, a cooler dry season between June and September, is more comfortable. The island has only a few hundred kilometres of road and the traffic is light, which makes a day of riding quite relaxed.

Sao Tome is the only town of any size, about fifty thousand people, and the nearest source of fuel and supplies, so fill up before heading into the hills. The island's food is a blend of Portuguese and African cooking, with grilled fish, breadfruit and calulu, a stew of vegetables and fish or chicken.
t.tamaudun@26.2,127.7:
Tamaudun is the royal mausoleum of the Ryukyu kings, a walled complex of grey coral limestone at the foot of Shuri hill, and it feels a little like a stone ship, heavy, low and enclosed. King Sho Shin had it built in 1501 to house the remains of his father and later the kings of the Second Sho dynasty. The Ryukyu kingdom was an independent maritime state with ties to China, Japan and Southeast Asia, and its rulers were buried in a tradition that blended Chinese and Okinawan styles. The tombs have three chambers: one where the bones were laid, one where they were washed, and one for the remains of lesser royalty.

Much of the site was wrecked in the Battle of Okinawa in 1945, and the mausoleum was rebuilt after the war, along with the nearby Shuri Castle, which has itself burned and been restored more than once. The two together are part of the Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu, listed by UNESCO in 2000. Nearby lies Sefa-utaki, a sacred grove where the priestesses of the kingdom held ceremonies among tilted rocks and old trees.

Riding on Okinawa has its own character. Traffic keeps to the left, speeds are low, and roads in the south are busy with cars, buses and military traffic from the American bases. Heat and humidity are heavy from May to October, and typhoons between August and October can close roads and cancel ferries. Further north the roads are better for pleasure: the coast road from Naha to Cape Hedo passes beaches and cliffs, and the Yanbaru forest has curvy roads under dense green canopy. A light rain jacket is always useful.

Naha and its suburbs have all the fuel and food you could need, and Okinawa soba, goya champuru and awamori spirit are the local specialities. The mausoleum charges a small entry fee and is quiet and shaded, so it works well as an early stop. Watch for habu snakes if you walk off the path in the countryside, and avoid riding after dark in rural areas, where roads are unlit.
t.nakagusuku jo site@26.3,127.8:
On the ridge above Nakagusuku Bay the walls of an old castle follow the curve of the hill in a long ribbon of pale limestone, and the shapes are surprisingly sophisticated. Nakagusuku was built, probably in the fourteenth century and extended in the fifteenth, by the lord Gosamaru, who was respected as a master builder, and its walls use a technique of fitted, curved stones with no mortar, in a pattern the Okinawans call nunozumi, cloth-laying, and a more rugged style called aikatazumi, which looks like a jigsaw. Six enclosures step up along the ridge, with gateways, a well and the foundations of halls.

The castle's story ends in political tragedy: in 1458 the king's forces, who feared Gosamaru's growing power, attacked and he took his own life. Centuries later, in 1853, Commodore Perry's expedition passed through Okinawa and the officers admired the skilful masonry and the arches, which they believed to be a Western skill. The site is one of the Gusuku Sites of the Kingdom of Ryukyu on the UNESCO list, and from the highest enclosure the view takes in the Pacific on one side and the East China Sea on the other, a rare thing on an island so narrow.

The ride to the castle runs along Route 329 and local roads through Kitanakagusuku, with sugar cane fields and views of the bay. Traffic keeps left on Okinawa, speeds are modest, and military traffic and rental cars are common. The weather turns quickly, with sudden showers in the rainy season in May and June and strong typhoons in late summer and autumn. Summer is hot, with humidity above eighty per cent, so start early and drink a lot of water.

Chatan, a few kilometres away, is a lively seaside town of about twenty-eight thousand, with American Village, a shopping and entertainment area, as well as fuel stations and many restaurants. Try Okinawan soba, taco rice and sata andagi, a round fried doughnut. The castle has an entrance fee, a small visitor centre and good paths. Sunset from the walls, when the stones turn warm and the bay glows, is worth waiting for.
t.langa of barolo@44.6,8.0:
Fog is the word that gave the Langhe's great grape its name. Nebbiolo comes from nebbia, and in October the mist fills the valleys below Barolo so thoroughly that the village seems to float on a lake of cloud, with the hills of the Langhe rising out of it row after row. The vineyards here are among the most prized in Italy, and the countryside, with its hill-top villages, castles and terraced slopes, has been listed by UNESCO together with Roero and Monferrato. Barolo itself has fewer than five hundred people, a castle once held by the Falletti family and now home to a wine museum, and a main street that is entirely devoted to selling bottles.

The wine, a dark red made from Nebbiolo and aged for years before it is ready, has long been nicknamed the king of wines and the wine of kings. The villages around, La Morra, Monforte d'Alba and Serralunga, each give the grape a slightly different voice. Alba, to the north, is better known for white truffles, which are sold at a fair every autumn that fills the town with scent and visitors. Hazelnuts, grown on the same hills, end up in chocolate, and the sweet tooth of Piedmont is easily satisfied.

The riding is a pleasure, though it needs patience. Roads climb and fall over the ridges in tight bends, with steep gradients and gravel at the corners where tractors cross. In harvest season, in September and October, farm vehicles are everywhere and the surfaces are slippery with crushed grapes. Weekend cyclists are numerous, and views across to the Alps, when the haze clears, are superb. Alba, with about twenty-five thousand people, is the place for fuel and a serious meal. Barolo and the nearby villages have little beyond a few bars and enotecas.

Pasta with butter and sage, the little stuffed agnolotti, and braised beef cooked in Barolo itself are the local dishes. Spring brings green vines and soft light, and late autumn brings colour, mist and the smell of wood smoke. Summer is warm and hazy, and the cellar doors are open for tasting, so plan a rest stop rather than a long ride afterwards.
t.l enceinte urbaine@44.9,6.6:
Briançon sits at a height of more than thirteen hundred metres, which makes it the highest city in France, and it has the defences to match. The old town on its hilltop is ringed by walls built to the plans of Vauban, Louis XIV's military engineer, in the decades after 1700, and together with a fort across the valley they make a showpiece of the works that UNESCO listed in 2008. The walls are still intact, the gates still work, and from the ramparts the view over the meeting of valleys is spectacular.

The old town is steep, and the main street, the Grande Gargouille, has a stream of water that runs down its centre in a stone channel. Narrow lanes lead off it to small squares, workshops and cafes. The town has always been a gateway between France and Italy, and a place where armies were stopped, and the fortifications reflect that.

Briançon is a motorbike town. The great Alpine passes radiate from it: the Col du Lautaret to the west, with its views of the Meije and the Écrins glaciers; the Col du Montgenèvre to Italy, at around eighteen hundred and fifty metres; and the Col d'Izoard, with its lunar landscape, to the south. All are famous, all are open only in summer, and snow can close them from late autumn until well into spring, so check conditions before planning a route. The roads are well surfaced, with long climbs and a lot of hairpins, and in July and August they are shared with a large number of cyclists, caravans and other motorcyclists.

With nearly twelve thousand inhabitants, Briançon has everything a rider needs: fuel, repair shops, hotels and restaurants. Villar-Saint-Pancrace, just next door, is smaller but has a few cafes. Try tourte, a pie of local cheese and potato, or the local cheeses. The old town parking is limited and the streets are steep, so leave the bike at the foot of the hill and walk up.

The best months are June to September, when the passes are clear, the air is fresh and the days are long. Afternoon storms can build quickly over the high ground in summer, so start early.
t.chapitre@44.6,6.0:
Le Chapitre is a small name on a map of the southern Alps, in the Hautes-Alpes department, in the green trough of the Champsaur where the Drac river gathers itself before heading to Grenoble. Saint-Bonnet-en-Champsaur and La Roche-des-Arnauds are the nearest villages, each under two thousand people, and Gap, the departmental capital with forty-odd thousand, is about ten kilometres away.

This is the stretch where the Route Napoléon comes in. In March 1815 Bonaparte landed on the Riviera after escaping from Elba and marched north to Paris over these hills, and the road he followed is signposted all the way, the N85, climbing past Gap and over the Col Bayard, at about 1,250 metres, before dropping towards Grenoble. For a rider that means an excellent, wide, well-engineered road with long, readable curves, a modest gradient, and enough views of the Dévoluy cliffs to keep your eyes busy. The Champsaur side is quieter, with smaller departmental roads wandering up to hamlets where hay is still turned by hand.

Weather in the Hautes-Alpes is dry by Alpine standards, with something like three hundred days of sun in popular memory, but thunderstorms build quickly on summer afternoons and the high roads can be icy in March and November. Early morning is lovely, with mist in the valley and clear peaks above. Bees and walnut trees, lavender at lower altitude and larch at higher, make the air smell different from one bend to the next.

For practical needs, the usual rule applies: a hamlet like this has no station, so fill up in Gap or in Saint-Bonnet, where you will also find a bakery and a bar for a coffee. Gap has a big supermarket and plenty of restaurants, and its market is lively on Saturday mornings. The local cheese, bleu du Vercors-Sassenage and tomme, goes very well with the walnut bread. Carry water on warm days, because the villages are well spaced and fountains, though common, are not always drinkable.
t.cinque terre and portovenere@44.1,9.7:
Five villages cling to the cliffs of the Ligurian coast, Monterosso, Vernazza, Corniglia, Manarola and Riomaggiore, and a little further south the old harbour of Portovenere guards the entrance to the Gulf of La Spezia, often called the Gulf of Poets because Byron and Shelley both lived around it. The whole coast is a World Heritage Site, and what UNESCO honours is the work of generations of farmers who built stone terraces on slopes so steep that they are almost vertical, with thousands of kilometres of dry-stone walls holding vines and olives. The sweet Sciacchetrà wine from these terraces is rare and expensive.

The villages were isolated for centuries, reachable only by mule track or by sea, and each has its own harbour, tall pastel houses and a church on a rock. Portovenere has a striking black-and-white church of San Pietro on a headland, built on the ruins of a temple to Venus, and a sea cave known as Byron's Grotto, from which the poet is said to have swum across the gulf to visit Shelley. Along the coast, the Via dell'Amore, the path of love, is a famous walkway that has been closed in part for repairs, so check the status.

For a motorcyclist, this is a place to be careful. The villages themselves are closed or restricted to cars, and the roads that lead to them are narrow, steep and winding, with hairpins, blind bends and car parks perched high above the sea. The high road, the SP370, along the ridge above the coast gives stunning views, but the surface is patchy and the traffic can be heavy in summer, with buses and campers. Some stretches are subject to landslides after heavy rain. Park at the top and take the train, which runs between the villages in a few minutes, or walk the footpaths.

La Spezia, eight kilometres away, has about eighty-eight thousand people and is the sensible base for fuel, repairs and a bed, while the villages themselves have almost none of these. Eat anchovies, either salted or fried, focaccia from a bakery and trofie with pesto, which was born in nearby Genoa. Visit in April, May, late September or October, avoiding the high summer when the paths are crammed. The rewards are the colour of the houses against the blue sea and the smell of rosemary on the cliffs.
t.urnes stave church@61.3,7.3:
The oldest stave church in Norway still standing stands on a ledge above a fjord, and you reach it by ferry. Urnes is on the north shore of Lustrafjord, the innermost arm of the great Sognefjord, and a small ferry crosses from Solvorn on the opposite shore in a few minutes, running regularly in the summer season. From the landing you walk up a path through farm fields to the church, which dates from around 1130 and is made of pine timber, black with tar, its shingled roofs layered up like a pagoda. Urnes was listed by UNESCO in 1979, among the first sites to be inscribed.

The reason people travel to see it is the carving. On the north wall are fragments of an older church, reused when this one was built, including a doorway where slender, interlaced animals twine through ribbons of vine in a graceful curving pattern that gave its name to the Urnes style, the last flourish of Viking art. The beasts are stretched and elegant, a long-necked creature fighting a snake. Inside, the nave is dark, with massive posts, carved capitals and the smell of old wood and tar.

The ride to get here is among the best in Norway. From Sogndal, the regional town of around seven thousand, a road runs up the fjord to Gaupne and onward to the Sognefjellet road, which crosses a mountain plateau at over 1,400 metres, the highest mountain pass in northern Europe, with glaciers, tarns and snow patches beside the tarmac. It is closed in winter and often opens only in late spring, so check before you go. Expect bends, tunnels, waterfalls and tour buses, with plenty of speed cameras and strictly enforced limits. Fuel is available in Sogndal and in Gaupne, but not on the mountain, so top up before the climb.

The Jostedalsbreen glacier, the biggest on the European mainland, is nearby, with arms of ice you can reach by a short road and a short walk. Fruit orchards line the fjord shores, and in early summer the cherry and apple blossoms are a delight. Try a waffle with brown cheese and jam at a roadside cafe.

The best months are June to September, and the long light evenings of midsummer are magical. Rain is common, so pack waterproofs.
t.waypoint 3@44.1,6.6:
The Route des Grandes Alpes is a French invention of the early twentieth century, a line drawn from Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean to link the high passes, and at this point on it you are in the quiet southern part, Haute-Provence, where the Alps run out of height and begin to smell of thyme.

This corner of the Alps has its own character. Villages are built of pale stone with russet tiled roofs, lavender and sage run wild on south-facing slopes, and in summer the cicadas make a continuous rasping din. The little narrow-gauge railway from Nice to Digne, known as the Train des Pignes, threads the valleys here and is still worth a look for its viaducts and stations. Near Annot the rock turns to great sandstone boulders and rock corridors, a favourite with climbers, and the place feels oddly like a miniature Fontainebleau in the mountains.

The riding is wonderful: roads are narrow, quiet and generally well kept, with hairpins and long curves that follow the rivers up into the forests. Expect little traffic outside of summer holidays. Further north the great passes, such as Allos and Cayolle, rise well above two thousand metres, and are open only in summer, roughly June to October. Even here, though, you should be ready for rain on summer afternoons and cold air in the shade. Early autumn is clear and calm, and spring brings flowers but also rockfall and unreliable weather.

Fuel is the thing to plan. These are small places, with only a few pumps, and some close early or on Sundays, so top up whenever you pass a station. Annot, about fifteen kilometres away, has a handful of shops and cafes, and a stop for a coffee and a slice of tourte, the local savoury pie, never goes amiss. Carry water in summer, since the heat in the gorges can surprise you.
t.ajaccio@41.9,8.7:
Napoleon Bonaparte was born in Ajaccio in 1769, a year after France bought Corsica from Genoa, and the town has never let anyone forget it. His family house is now a museum, a statue of him on horseback stands in the main square, and street names, cafés and shops all carry his name. The old town is a cluster of tall ochre houses along the harbour, with a modest cathedral where he was baptised, and the best way to feel the place is to sit at a harbourside table with a coffee and watch the ferries and fishing boats come and go.

Ajaccio faces west, across a wide gulf of blue water, and at its mouth the Sanguinaires islands, a line of pink granite rocks, glow red at sunset. The town sits on the west coast of Corsica, a mountainous island in the Mediterranean that rises steeply from the sea to peaks of over two thousand metres, and the interior is covered in maquis, a dense scrub of myrtle, cistus, rosemary and wild herbs that gives the island a perfume that you smell as soon as the ferry doors open.

The D81 is the coast road north, one of the most scenic roads in France. It leaves Ajaccio and runs along the gulf, then climbs and falls along the shore through Sagone and Cargèse, a village founded by Greek refugees in the seventeenth century, before arriving at Piana, where the Calanques, red granite pinnacles that plunge to the sea, appear in the road's final stretch. The road is narrow and twisting, with tight bends, sheer drops, no guardrails in places and campervans in summer, so take it steadily. The tarmac is generally decent, but occasional rockfalls and wandering cows and pigs are part of the landscape.

July and August bring the heaviest traffic and heat, and the best months for riding are May, June and September, when the light is warm and the road is quiet. Ajaccio has everything for riders, from fuel to repair shops and restaurants, and stations farther north become sparser, so fill up before leaving. Try brocciu cheese, charcuterie and chestnut-flour specialities, which are typical of Corsica.
t.boulder@37.9,-111.4:
Boulder, Utah, was the last town in the United States to have its mail delivered by mule, and the arrangement lasted until 1940, since no road reached it. The village sits at about 2,000 metres on the edge of the Aquarius Plateau in south-central Utah, a tiny community of ranches, a few houses and a lodge, with red sandstone cliffs on one side and pine and aspen forest on the other. The nearest big towns are far away, and the village still has a feeling of being at the end of something, which for generations it was.

The surroundings are among the finest in the Southwest. The Anasazi State Park Museum here preserves the remains of a village of the Ancestral Puebloans, who farmed this high ground about nine hundred years ago, and displays pottery and tools found on the site. Nearby, Boulder Mountain, the high plateau forest, is dotted with lakes and trout streams, and below it the land drops through slickrock canyons toward the Escalante River, in the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, a wilderness of arches, domes and narrow slots cut in sandstone.

The road here is Scenic Byway 12, one of the great roads of the American West. South of Boulder it crosses the Hogback, a narrow ridge where the road runs along a crest with steep drops on both sides, and then dips toward Escalante through a landscape of white and orange rock. To the north, it climbs over Boulder Mountain through forest to Torrey and the red cliffs of Capitol Reef. Bends are long and open, the surface is generally excellent, and traffic is light, though the road can ice over at the top in winter and gets cold even in summer. Another route, the Burr Trail, heads east from Boulder through spectacular canyon country, partly paved and partly gravel.

Services are sparse. Boulder has a lodge and a couple of places to eat, and there is a little fuel, but it is wise to fill up in Escalante, about forty kilometres to the south-west, or Torrey, to the north. Distances are large and cell coverage is patchy. Spring and autumn offer the best weather, and the stars on a clear night are magnificent.
t.col d izoard@44.8,6.7:
The Col d'Izoard, at 2,360 metres, is one of the great passes of the French Alps, on the road between Briançon and the Queyras, and the south side is the part riders remember. A few kilometres below the summit the road passes through the Casse Déserte, a startling field of orange and grey scree and rock pinnacles, eroded into odd shapes, which looks more like the surface of another planet than the Alps. In front of it stands a monument to the cyclists Fausto Coppi and Louison Bobet, who both won here in the Tour de France, and the Tour has crossed the pass many times.

The north side, from Briançon, begins in the Guisane and Cerveyrette valleys, among larch forests and meadows, and climbs through the hamlet of Cervières before reaching the summit by a series of wide, easy bends. The south side drops through Arvieux into the Guil valley, with views over the Queyras, a region known for its sunny weather, its old wooden farmhouses and the fortified village of Mont-Dauphin below. Briançon, a town of about eleven thousand, is the highest city in France at some 1,326 metres, with Vauban's fortifications dominating the old town, a UNESCO site, and plenty of fuel and restaurants.

Riding it is a delight. The surface is generally excellent, the gradients are moderate, and the corners are open and flowing, which lets you relax and look at the scenery. In midsummer, traffic builds with cyclists, motorcyclists and campervans, and the best time is early morning or late afternoon, when the light is long and low on the rocks. At the top there is a small refuge-like café and a viewing table with a panorama of the surrounding peaks, though services are limited, so do not count on fuel.

Snow closes the pass from about November until late May or June, depending on the year, and the local authority publishes opening dates, so check before you set off. Even in July, the summit can be cold and windy, and sudden thunderstorms and hail are possible in the afternoon. A windproof layer and warm gloves are sensible, and bring water, as the south side is hot and dry in summer.
t.menton@43.8,7.5:
Menton is the last town in France before Italy, the finish of the Route des Grandes Alpes, and after seven hundred kilometres of mountains it feels like being tipped into a warm bath. The old town tumbles down a hill to the harbour in tones of ochre, apricot and cream, topped by the baroque Basilica of Saint Michael with its glowing facade. The climate is the mildest on the French Riviera, sheltered by the mountains behind, and the local lemons are famous, celebrated each February in the Fête du Citron, when huge sculptures made of fruit and flowers fill the gardens and people parade through the streets.

The town has a gentle, slightly faded elegance, a place where Victorian visitors came for their health and a gaggle of grand villas still look out over the water. Jean Cocteau, the writer and artist, decorated the registry office in the town hall, and a museum of his work stands on the seafront. A short walk away, the gardens of Garavan, planted with exotic trees and flowers, benefit from a warmth that few other places in France can match. The Italian border is just beyond, close enough to walk, and many people cross for lunch.

The final ride down the mountain is the real subject. Many riders arrive from the Col de la Bonette, at 2,715 metres the highest paved pass in France when including its extra loop, or from the Col de Vars, at 2,109 metres. The descent toward the coast winds through high pastures, then narrow gorges, then pine and chestnut forest, before finally dropping through olive groves and terraced hillsides toward the sea. Along the way, perched villages such as Sainte-Agnès, at about eight hundred metres the highest coastal village in Europe, cling to rocky crests above the bay, with narrow lanes and glorious views. The temperature climbs as the road falls, and a rider can go from a frosty morning to a hot afternoon in a few hours.

Practical matters are easy in a town of nearly thirty thousand. Fuel stations line the approach roads, and there are cafes and restaurants all along the seafront. Traffic along the coast is heavy in summer, and parking is tight, so look for a secure garage. Pastry shops sell tarte au citron, and the local speciality is socca, a thin chickpea pancake, or pissaladière, an onion tart. Treat yourself with a swim: it is the tradition at the end of this journey.
t.sisteron@44.2,5.9:
Sisteron is the gate of Provence, a town of seven and a half thousand on the Durance river, where the valley pinches into a narrow gap, the Clue de Sisteron, between two walls of tilted limestone.
