The great citadel, a fortress on the rock above the town, has watched over the passage since the Middle Ages, and the present walls date largely from the sixteenth century. Napoleon passed through on 5 March 1815, on his way from the Riviera to Grenoble, and the Route Napoléon is marked by signs and eagle plaques along the road, from here to the north.

The town clings to the hillside, with narrow lanes called andrônes running between tall houses, and a Romanesque cathedral, Notre-Dame-des-Pommiers, stands at the foot of the old town. The air has a clear, dry quality, and the light is a sign that you have arrived in the south: the town claims some three hundred days of sun a year. Lamb from Sisteron has a quality label and appears on every menu, roasted with herbs, and the lavender and honey sold in the shops come from the plateaus nearby.

Fuel and food are easy here, which makes it a natural stop on the Route Napoléon. The road north from Sisteron, the N85, climbs through the Gap country and the Col Bayard, with long, open bends and distant views of the Écrins, and there are splendid sections between Sisteron and Grenoble where the road passes lakes and gorges. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, and lorries are common on the main sections, but the quality of the road and the scenery make it worthwhile.

Parking for bikes is possible near the foot of the citadel, and the climb up the path to the fortress takes about twenty minutes, with a good view over the Durance. The weather is bright but the wind in the valley, the mistral's cousin, can be strong, particularly in spring, so be aware of gusts. Summer is hot, and in winter the high roads may be icy. Take water and sun protection, and enjoy the smell of thyme and lavender along the way.
t.andalsnes@62.6,7.7:
Åndalsnes is a small town at the head of the Romsdalsfjord, hemmed in by some of the most vertical mountains in Norway. The Romsdalshorn, a sharp pyramid of rock, rises above the valley to the south, and the Trollveggen, Europe's tallest vertical rock face at around a thousand metres, stands a short way up the valley. The town itself is modest, with a few thousand people, a railway terminus, a harbour and a handful of cafes, and its main business is welcoming people who come for the mountains.

The riding from here is world famous. Trollstigen, the Troll's Ladder, climbs from the valley in eleven hairpin bends to a high plateau, with a waterfall, Stigfossen, dropping beside the road. It was opened in 1936 after years of work and is still a feat of engineering, with stone walls and tight corners. The pass is closed in winter, usually from late autumn to May or June, depending on snow, so check before you plan. Beyond, the road continues toward Geiranger, with the fjord far below and ferries crossing in the summer months.

Trollstigen draws crowds, and in July and August the road is full of campervans, coaches and cars, with cyclists and other motorcyclists among them. Early mornings and evenings are quieter, and midweek is better than weekends. Rain and low cloud are common, and the cloud can drop to cover the hairpins, so ride carefully. A small visitor centre at the top has viewing platforms and a cafe, though prices are high.

The town has fuel, a supermarket and a handful of places to eat, and it is the last real service point before the pass. The nearest larger town is Molde, about thirty kilometres away along the fjord, with a good selection of shops and a jazz festival every July. Fill the tank here, as stations on the mountain roads are scarce.

Åndalsnes is also a place to take things slowly. The light on the fjord in the evening, with the mountains turning pink, makes it worth staying an extra night, and the river running through the village is full of salmon in season.
t.trollstigen viewpoint@62.5,7.7:
The Trollstigen Plateau is a bare, glacier-scoured saddle at 858 metres, ringed by peaks with names like Bispen, the Bishop, and Kongen, the King, and the viewing platform here, a sculptural structure of steel and concrete that hangs over the drop, is the best place to understand what the road does. Below, the Trollstigen, the Troll's Ladder, zigzags down the side of the valley in eleven hairpins, with the long white thread of the Stigfossen waterfall falling beside it, and beyond lies the broad green Isterdalen and the far peaks of Romsdalen.

The road opened in 1936, after twenty years of work, and King Haakon VII drove over it at the opening. It links Åndalsnes, twelve kilometres away, with Valldal and the fjords of Sunnmøre, and it is one of the most famous roads in Norway, so expect crowds in summer. The viewing platform, completed in the early 2010s, was designed to blend into the rock, and there is a visitor centre, a small cafe and toilets on the plateau. The weather is a major factor, since clouds often fill the valley and hide the view, and a clear day is a gift.

The riding is demanding but rewarding. The gradient is about ten percent, with tight, narrow hairpins, and the road is often crowded with campervans, tour buses and cyclists, so patience and care are essential. The surface is good, but the edges are unprotected in places, and rain makes the paving slippery. The road is closed in winter and usually opens in May, depending on the snow, so check the status before you go. Summer afternoons are busiest, and the best time is early morning or evening, when the crowds thin and the low sun lights the cliffs.

Fuel is a concern, and the pass has none, so fill in Åndalsnes, which has stations and shops, or in Valldal, on the other side. The cafe on the plateau serves waffles and coffee, with prices to match the view.

Spend a few minutes on the platform, look back at the road you have climbed, and notice the scale of the mountains. The Norwegians say that the weather here can change in minutes, and it is a good idea to wear a warm layer.
t.valldal@62.3,7.2:
Valldal is a small town at the head of the Norddalsfjord, in the green and orderly farmland that lies at the foot of the great Sunnmøre mountains, and it is the first proper settlement you reach after the long descent from the Trollstigen. Valldal is famous in Norway for its strawberries, which ripen in July in the long summer light and are sold in roadside stands, and the local people take a great deal of pride in them.

The fjord has a darker history. In 1934, a huge rockslide fell from the mountain above Tafjord, a neighbouring arm of the fjord, and the wave it created swept along the shore and killed dozens of people in the villages. The slopes above these fjords remain unstable, and the rock above is monitored today. A feeling of the scale of things, of vertical walls and deep water, is part of the experience of the place. Another part is the ferry between Eidsdal and Linge, which crosses the Norddalsfjord on the road to Geiranger, a short and pleasant crossing with fine views.

Riding here is some of the best in Norway. The road from the Trollstigen drops through forest and farmland, with wide bends and a long run down to the fjord, and from Valldal the climb to the Eagle's Road at Geiranger is a classic. The surface is mostly good, but the traffic in summer is heavy, with caravans and coaches, and the speed limits are low and strictly enforced. The weather is changeable, with rain common and mist hanging in the valleys, and the temperature can drop quickly with altitude. The Trollstigen and the Geiranger road are closed in winter, so check dates before planning.

It is a good place to refuel the bike and yourself, because the roads on either side are long and the next services are some way off. Stranda, sixteen kilometres away, is a larger town with more choices.

Eat strawberries in season, and cake and waffles year-round, and walk down to the quay to look up at the walls of rock. It is a quiet place that sits in the shadow of its famous neighbours.
t.trollstigen@62.5,7.7:
The Trollstigen is best understood from below. Coming up from Åndalsnes, the road leaves the broad floor of the Isterdalen and rises through birch woods into a narrow valley, where a wall of rock closes in, and then begins to climb in earnest. Eleven hairpins, each with a name or a number painted on the stone, carry it up the slope, and the Stigfossen waterfall, which falls over three hundred metres, crashes beside the road and under a stone bridge, spraying anyone who stops. It is one of the great Alpine-style roads of Scandinavia, and it was a wild feat of engineering for its time.

Construction began in 1916 and went on for twenty years, with workers building retaining walls by hand and blasting a route through the rock. Hairpin after hairpin is supported by dry stone walls, many of which still stand, and the road opened in 1936. Åndalsnes, at the head of the Romsdalsfjord, is the starting point, a small town of two thousand people with a railway, a harbour, shops and fuel. Just beyond it is Trollveggen, the Troll Wall, the tallest vertical mountain face in Europe, a sheer cliff of about a thousand metres that draws climbers and base jumpers from around the world.

The riding is steep and tight, with a gradient of up to ten percent and sharp hairpin bends where larger vehicles must swing wide. The surface is smooth, but the road is narrow and the drops are real, so it demands care and a calm attitude, especially in rain, when the stone walls are wet and the cloud closes in. Meeting a coach on a hairpin is common, and it is wise to give way early. Summer weekends are crowded, so aim for early morning or the evening. The road closes for winter, usually reopening in May.

This stop is the finish of the climb, and there is a small viewpoint above the hairpins with a long view over the valley. The last bends are the steepest, and as you leave them the wide plateau opens before you. Fuel is not available on the road, so fill up in Åndalsnes before starting, and bring a warm layer, because the weather at the top can be cold even in July.

Stop in the evening, if you can. The long Norwegian summer light turns the rock gold, and the waterfalls glitter as they plunge into shadow. It is hard to look at it without feeling very small.
t.eucla@-31.7,128.9:
Eucla is a tiny settlement on the Western Australian side of the Nullarbor, near the South Australian border, and it has a story that is out of proportion to its size. In the 1870s the telegraph line that connected Western Australia to the rest of the continent ran through here, and the Eucla Telegraph Station became an important link, with operators sending messages by Morse code to Adelaide and Perth. The old stone station building, now half buried in drifting sand dunes, is still there, and walking around it, with the wind whistling in the empty windows, is quietly moving.

Below the escarpment lies the Roe Plain, a flat expanse stretching toward the ocean, and just beyond the dunes the sea still rolls onto the beach where a long wooden jetty once stood. The ruins of the jetty are visible at low tide. Above, the highway climbs the escarpment on a gentle slope, with a lookout that gives a wide view across the plain, and in the right light the colours of the rock and sand are remarkable.

Eucla has a roadhouse with fuel, food and accommodation, but prices are high and hours are limited, so plan ahead and do not assume that anything will be open late at night. The nearest large town is a very long way off, and a breakdown can mean a long wait, so carry water, spare food and a way of calling for help, though mobile coverage is patchy. The locals are friendly and used to travellers, and a conversation over a coffee is often more useful than any guidebook.

A peculiarity of this area is the time. Eucla and the surrounding region follow an unofficial time zone, forty-five minutes ahead of the rest of Western Australia, which can lead to confusion if you are used to the clock on your phone. Also be aware that there are quarantine rules on fresh fruit, vegetables and honey at the border, and inspectors will check your luggage. Be honest, and eat your apples before you reach the line.
t.flagstaff@35.2,-111.6:
Flagstaff stands at about two thousand one hundred metres, in a ponderosa forest at the foot of the San Francisco Peaks, and the air has the thin, clean taste of altitude. Humphreys Peak, the tallest mountain in Arizona at over 3,800 metres, is the old volcano that looms over the town, and in winter its slopes are white while the desert below is warm. That contrast is what makes Flagstaff a favourite for riders heading to the Grand Canyon: they start in cool pines and end in a gorge a mile deep.

The town has always depended on movement. The railroad came through in the 1880s, and then Route 66 followed, and the old road is still the main street, lined with neon motels and diners that look the part. Lowell Observatory, on a hill above town, is where Pluto was found in 1930, and the dark skies that attracted astronomers are still a draw. Telescope nights are worth planning around if you stay over.

The riding out of town is good. The road to the Grand Canyon's South Rim runs north through pine forest and then across open high desert, with long straights, some gentle bends, and the Peaks rising behind you. Another option is the winding Oak Creek Canyon road toward Sedona, which falls through red cliffs in a series of hairpins. Weather changes quickly at this height, and snow can arrive as early as October and as late as May, so check the forecast. Afternoon thunderstorms in July and August are common and intense.

Flagstaff has seventy thousand people, so fuel, repair shops, outdoor stores and plenty of places to eat are easy to find. Local breweries and coffee roasters give the downtown a lively feel, and a pizza or a burger after a long day at altitude is just right. Elk and deer visit the edges of town at dusk, so keep an eye out on the outskirts. Nights are cold even in summer, so pack a warm layer.
t.grand canyon national park@36.1,-112.1:
The first thing the Grand Canyon does is refuse to make sense. You walk to the South Rim, a flat forest of pine and juniper at about two thousand one hundred metres, and the ground simply ends. Below is a gorge up to sixteen kilometres wide and a mile deep, a stack of red, buff and violet rock layers that record nearly two billion years, with the Colorado River a thin brown thread at the bottom. Photos flatten it, and nothing prepares you for the scale.

The rim road system is what a rider wants. The drive east to Desert View follows the canyon for about forty kilometres, with a string of pull-offs, and ends at the Watchtower, a stone tower designed by the architect Mary Colter and finished in 1932, built to look like an ancestral Puebloan structure. West of the village, Hermit Road is closed to private vehicles for much of the year and run by shuttle. Surfaces are good and speed limits low, and tourist traffic and elk on the road are bigger hazards than curves.

The park is also a living place. Ravens and ground squirrels work the viewpoints, and California condors, reintroduced after near extinction, sometimes ride the updrafts at the rim. Dawn and dusk are the best light, when the rock glows from within, and summer afternoons often bring storms that lace the canyon with rain and lightning. In winter the rim can be snowy and icy, so check conditions.

Practical points matter here. Fuel inside the park is limited, and the town of Tusayan, a few kilometres south of the entrance, has more services and motels, with Flagstaff, about ninety minutes away, as the main base. An entrance fee applies, and it is valid for several days. Water fountains are available near the village, and you will need it, because the dry air at this altitude takes a lot out of you. Leave plenty of time, since the main viewpoints are tempting enough to eat a whole afternoon.
t.madura@-31.9,127.0:
Madura stands at the foot of a wall. The Hampton escarpment, an old sea cliff that marks the edge of the Nullarbor Plain, drops here by a hundred metres or so to the Roe Plains, and the Eyre Highway tumbles down it at Madura Pass, with a lookout where you can see the land stretch away to the south, flat as a table and glittering with salt bush. It is a rare moment of relief in the long, level crossing between Eucla and Norseman.

The name Madura comes from a station established in the 1870s, a vast pastoral lease famous for breeding horses. The Waler, the tough Australian cavalry horse, was raised here and shipped to British India for the army, and the ruins of the old homestead area are part of local history. Today Madura is a roadhouse, with fuel, a restaurant and basic accommodation, set at the foot of the pass in a sea of low scrub. There are no other services for long distances either side, and fuel is expensive, because everything has to travel a long way, so fill up here and carry a small reserve.

The Nullarbor, a name taken from the Latin for no trees, is a vast limestone plain, a former sea floor lifted and left bare, and below it lie the world's longest caves. The vegetation is low, chiefly saltbush and bluebush, and the sky is enormous. Wedge-tailed eagles circle above carcasses on the roadside, and dingoes sometimes trot along the verge. The air is dry and clear, and at night the stars are thick.

The road is mostly a single straight ribbon of asphalt, broken by gentle curves and long, gradual rises. Road trains rumble along it, wide and fast, and overtaking them needs careful judgement and a long clear view. Wind is variable, and dust storms and sudden rain can occur. The temperature swings by twenty degrees between noon and dawn, so dress in layers.

Take care at dusk and at night, when kangaroos are active and difficult to see, and avoid riding after dark if possible. Carry at least a few litres of water, tell someone your plan, and enjoy the extraordinary sense of space. Norseman, the end of the road, lies about seven hundred kilometres west.
t.bastia@42.7,9.5:
Bastia has always been the working port of Corsica. Genoa made Bastia the island's capital for centuries, until 1791, and the town retains a busy, slightly rough charm that is quite unlike Calvi's polish or Ajaccio's grandeur.

The place is a hub: ferries arrive from Nice, Marseille, Toulon and Livorno, and the road north leads round the Cap Corse peninsula, one of the finest coastal rides in Europe. The town also has a good market, narrow streets and a big church, Saint-Jean-Baptiste, whose twin towers dominate the old port. In the evening, the quayside cafes fill with locals, and the smell of coffee and the sound of voices make it a fine place to sit.

For riders the key is how to get out. The road south along the east coast is straight and busy, and the best way to the west is across the island, either through the Col de Teghime to Saint-Florent or via Ponte Leccia and the Col de Vergio. The traffic around Bastia can be heavy, especially at ferry times and in summer, so an early start is worth it. The Calanche of Piana, a tangle of red granite cliffs above the Gulf of Porto, is far to the south-west and demands a long, twisty day, but it is a spectacular reward.

Fuel is no problem. Bastia has stations, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat, though it is wise to fill up before heading into the mountains, where stations are scarce. Local specialities include charcuterie, fiadone, a lemony cheesecake, and Cap Corse wine.

Linger an hour by the old port at the start or end of the day. Watch the boats come in, drink a coffee, and let the island's rhythm slow you down.
t.lom@61.8,8.6:
It has a few thousand people in its municipality, a river that tumbles through a gorge beside the main street and a wooden stave church that has stood for more than eight hundred years. The church, with its dragon-headed gables and dark tarred planks, is among the oldest in Norway, and its interior of carved pillars and painted pews is very fine.

The road from here is the Sognefjellet, Route 55, the highest mountain road in northern Europe, topping out at around 1,430 metres. It climbs through Bøverdalen, past the entrance to the Jotunheimen national park, where Galdhøpiggen, at 2,469 metres, is the highest peak in the north of Europe. The scenery is bare and wide, with glaciers, black lakes and snow patches even in July, and the bends are open and well banked, with a smooth surface. The road is closed in winter, typically opening in May and shutting in late October, depending on snow, and weather can be cold and wet at the top. Reindeer and sheep graze beside the road, so watch for them.

Lom has a quiet character, and its centre has an outdoor shop, a mountain centre with exhibits on the peaks and a bakery that is known throughout Norway, where travellers queue for cinnamon buns and sourdough bread. The surrounding valley farms keep goats and make cheese, and the old wooden storehouses on stilts, built to keep grain from rats, stand beside the farmhouses.

Fuel is available in Lom, and it is a good idea to fill up before the climb, since stations are sparse on the mountain road. Vågåmo, twenty-eight kilometres to the east, is the next village of size, and the west side of the pass drops towards Luster and the Sognefjord, with more services and the famous stave church at Urnes nearby.

Visit the church if it is open. The smell of old tar and wood is the smell of Norway's past.
t.sognefjellshytta@61.6,8.0:
At 1,434 metres, Sognefjellshytta is the high-water mark of the Sognefjell road, which carries Rv 55 across the roof of Jotunheimen and is usually described as the highest mountain pass in northern Europe. The lodge that gives the spot its name sits right beside the road, a long timber building that has been taking in walkers, skiers and passing riders for generations, and the plateau around it is nothing but bare rock, tarns, snow patches that survive well into July and a sky that seems to start at your boots.

Riding up from the Lom side, the road climbs through birch and then past the tree line into a landscape of grey boulders and low arctic plants, with the big Jotunheimen summits standing to the south. The corners are open and gentle on the plateau, the surface is good and the traffic is mostly caravans and other motorcyclists, so the pace is relaxed. The west side is the dramatic one, dropping in long descents toward Skjolden and the head of the Lustrafjord, where the climate changes from alpine to damp, green and mild within an hour. Dress in layers, because the temperature on top can be near freezing in a summer morning while the fjord is warm.

The road itself opened in the late 1930s and is closed over winter, typically from November until late spring when the snow is cleared, so check the road status before planning anything outside summer. Coffee and waffles at the lodge are a tradition, and the staff are used to cold, damp riders who want something hot.

Norway's two highest peaks, Galdhøpiggen and Glittertind, are within reach of this area, and the old trading routes that crossed these mountains were used by farmers and cattle drovers for centuries before cars. Sit outside if the weather allows. The wind carries a smell of cold stone and wet moss, and the silence on a calm day is a very rare thing in Europe.
t.turtagro@61.5,7.8:
Turtagrø is a small hotel at the foot of the Hurrungane, a cluster of sharp granite peaks that Norwegians call their Alps, and it is where Norwegian mountaineering was effectively born. English climbers arrived in the late nineteenth century, led by William Cecil Slingsby, who made first ascents here and wrote about them, and the local guides who worked with him started a tradition that still draws climbers each summer. The hotel has been a base for expeditions since 1888 and has the pleasant, old-fashioned feel of a place where boots by the door are normal.

The road that brings you here is the western ramp of Rv 55, climbing out of the Fortun valley in a series of tight hairpins that turn the ride into something of a set piece. The bends are tight enough to reward patience on a loaded bike, the surface is good, and between corners you see waterfalls, birch woods giving way to bare slopes and the high summits appearing and vanishing in cloud. The air changes quickly, and a sunny valley can become a cold wet plateau in twenty minutes, so keep waterproofs handy. The road is closed in winter, so this section is a summer and early autumn ride.

The hotel serves coffee, cake and proper meals, which makes it a natural stop, and the terrace looks toward Store Skagastølstind, the peak Slingsby first climbed in 1876 and the one that made the early fame of the range.

If you want to walk, the trail toward Skagastølsbu hut is a rewarding half day. The valley floor is boggy and the weather can turn quickly, but the scenery is the sort that lingers. Come in July or August for dependable weather, or in September when the light is lower and the birches turn gold. The road is much quieter then.
t.moustiers sainte marie@43.8,6.2:
Seen from below, Moustiers-Sainte-Marie looks like it has been wedged into a crack in the cliff. A pair of limestone crags rise above the village, and between them hangs a star on a long chain, a golden ornament that has been renewed many times since the legend of a knight who vowed to hang one there after returning safely from the Crusades. The story is probably more charming than historical, but it gives the place its signature image, and you can see the star glinting from the road on a bright day.

The village sits at the western doorway of the Gorges du Verdon, around six hundred metres up, with a stream running through the middle and stone houses stacked up the slope. It was famous long before tourists arrived for its faience, a tin-glazed pottery with delicate blue and green designs that was made here from the seventeenth century, and workshops and boutiques still crowd the lanes. A steep path of some two hundred and sixty steps climbs to the chapel of Notre-Dame de Beauvoir, which commands a wide view over the roofs and the plateau beyond.

Riding to Moustiers is one of the good things about Provence. From Riez the road across the plateau passes lavender fields and almond orchards, and then winds up into the narrow valley and the gorge country, with views over the turquoise Lac de Sainte-Croix nearby. The bends are quick, the surface mostly smooth, and the light in the early morning is superb, though the summer crowds of cars and campervans can slow everything to a crawl by mid-morning. Come in June or September and the village feels like itself again.

The big caveat is parking: the village is small, the car parks fill early in July and August, and the lanes are too narrow for anything but walking. Park at the edge and stroll in. There are plenty of cafes, ice-cream stalls and restaurants, many with terraces over the stream, and a plate of the local lamb or a simple salad and a glass of rosé can be had for a fair price outside peak times.

For fuel, do not rely on the village: Riez is the nearest town of any size, and Digne-les-Bains is the major centre in the district, so fill up before heading into the hills.
t.castellane food@43.8,6.5:
Castellane sits at the bottom of a bowl, with a huge limestone rock standing over it like a stopper. The rock, simply called le Roc, rises about a hundred and eighty metres above the old town, and a small pilgrimage chapel, Notre-Dame du Roc, perches on top, reached by a steep path through the pines. The town lies on the Verdon river a little upstream of the great canyon, and it has been a gateway to this country for as long as there have been roads.

The most famous traveller to pass through was Napoleon, who came this way in March 1815 on his march from Elba to Paris, along what is now the Route Napoléon. The N85 follows his route, and Castellane makes much of the connection. The town square, the Place Marcel Sauvaire, is a lively place with plane trees, a fountain and a number of cafes and restaurants that spill onto the pavement in summer, and it makes an excellent place to eat.

Expect Provençal basics done decently: soupe au pistou, grilled lamb, a salad with local goat's cheese, fougasse bread, and a glass of rosé. It is also a base for rafting and canoeing trips on the river, and in July and August the main street fills with people in wetsuits and flip-flops, which makes for a cheerful if slightly chaotic atmosphere. The town has about sixteen hundred permanent residents, but that number grows several times over in the high season.

The riding in and out is the highlight. The roads converge here from every direction: the Route Napoléon runs north and south through the hills, the great gorge road runs west, and the quiet lanes toward Annot and the Var valley climb over the pass. Surfaces are mostly good, bends are flowing, and gradients are manageable, though the mountain weather means sudden rain and cold fronts even in summer. Check your fuel before arriving, because there are stations in Castellane itself but the nearest large town, Draguignan, is a long way south.

At around seven hundred metres, Castellane is cooler than the coast, with a clear light and the smell of lavender and thyme drifting from the hills. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, when the traffic is thinner and the colours are rich.
t.verdon balcony road@43.8,6.4:
The Verdon is a canyon for people who thought they had seen canyons. The river has cut a gorge through the limestone of Haute Provence, some twenty-five kilometres long, with cliffs that rise as much as seven hundred metres above the green water at the bottom, and the roads that run along the rims give you ridiculous views. This stretch, between Castellane and the area of Point Sublime, runs along the northern edge, and the balcony viewpoints along the road look down into a crack in the earth that appears to have no floor.

The geology is simple and spectacular: the limestone was laid down under an ancient sea, and the river has spent millions of years sawing through it. The water is a vivid turquoise from fine mineral particles, and the rock is pale grey and ochre, with pines and box clinging on every ledge. Griffon vultures, reintroduced here some decades ago after disappearing, ride the thermals along the cliffs, and with a bit of luck you will see one pass at eye level, wings spread, as if inspecting you.

The riding is a mix of spectacle and caution. The road clings to the rim, sometimes with a modest wall and sometimes with nothing at all, and corners can be tight and blind, with sheer drops beyond the verge. The surface is mostly good, but sand and gravel gather in the bends, and the tourist traffic in summer is heavy, with campervans, hire cars and cyclists. Take it slowly and pull into the signed viewpoints rather than stopping on the road. Early morning is when the light is best and the road emptiest.

The canyon is a place for photographers, but be aware of the glare at midday and the heat that radiates from the rock. A few viewpoints have railings and small car parks, and some have short paths that lead to even better angles. In spring the hillsides are bright with broom and wild flowers, and in autumn the oak and maple turn gold.

For fuel and food, Castellane is the sensible base, with services in the town itself, while the small villages along the rim have cafes of varying quality and limited opening hours.
t.lake sainte croix@43.8,6.2:
This is where the Verdon stops being a canyon and becomes a lake. At the western end of the gorge, a dam was built in the early 1970s at Sainte-Croix-du-Verdon, and the water backed up through the valleys behind it to form the Lac de Sainte-Croix, a sheet of vivid turquoise about ten kilometres long that fills the end of the canyon and laps against the Valensole plateau. The village of Les Salles-sur-Verdon was drowned when the water rose, and the people were moved to a new settlement built higher on the shore; in very dry years, old walls and fields are said to emerge from the water.

The colour is the thing. The Verdon's water comes from the Alps and carries fine rock flour that gives it a milky blue-green tint, and in sunlight the lake is a strikingly bright shade against the pale cliffs and dark pines. The shoreline is a mix of small beaches, rocky coves and boat ramps, and in summer the lake is crowded with pedalos, kayaks and swimmers. The water is cool, even in August, which is a relief after a morning on a motorcycle in the Provençal heat.

For swimming, the villages of Bauduen, Les Salles and Sainte-Croix all have beaches and landing stages, with cafes and rental shops, and you can paddle out to quiet coves along the north shore. Riez, the nearest town, has Roman columns standing in a field, a remnant of a temple to Apollo.

The ride along the lake road is a mix of gentle curves and short climbs, with views through the pines to the water. The surface is generally good, though narrow, and traffic is heavy in July and August, especially at weekends. The wind can blow hard along the lake, and a sudden storm can bring cold and rain, even when the morning started clear.

For fuel, plan ahead, as the shoreline villages are small. Aups and Riez are modest towns, and Manosque is the larger centre to the west, around thirty kilometres away. Bring a towel, and be prepared to park on the verge.
t.nice@43.7,7.3:
Nice rises from a wide bay of pebbles and blue water, with a ridge of hills behind it, and it has been a seaside resort since the English began wintering here in the eighteenth century. The Promenade des Anglais, the seafront boulevard they paid for, still runs for several kilometres along the shore, lined with palms, pale hotels and deckchairs, and the old town, Vieux Nice, behind the Cours Saleya flower market, is a tangle of ochre and pink houses with laundry hanging out of windows. Castle Hill, a wooded bluff at the eastern end of the bay, gives a view over the whole sweep of the coast. Italian influence is strong, as the city only became French in 1860, and the food shows it. Try socca, a chickpea pancake, a pan bagnat sandwich or a proper salade niçoise.

The Grande Corniche starts from here, the highest of three roads that climb the cliffs between Nice and Menton. It follows the line of the Roman Via Julia Augusta, and at La Turbie, around five hundred metres above the sea, the ruins of the Trophy of Augustus, built in the first century BC to mark Roman control of the Alps, stand on a ridge with a view down to Monaco. The road then passes Èze and other perched villages, where the bends are tight, the views are huge and the sun glints off the Mediterranean far below.

Riding here needs a bit of planning. Nice is large and busy, with heavy traffic, one-way streets and scooters weaving at every light, and the road along the coast is slow at any hour. Parking for bikes is easier than for cars, but be careful of theft and use a secure garage if you are staying. Fuel is plentiful in a city of three hundred and thirty thousand, though some stations in the old centre are limited, so use the ones on the outskirts. The Grande Corniche itself is best ridden early on a weekday, before the tourist coaches and the cyclists, and it can be windy on the open stretches.

Spring and autumn are lovely here. In midsummer the heat and crowds make the coast tiring, but the light is spectacular at dawn.
t.eze@43.7,7.4:
Èze is a village built like an eagle's nest, perched on a sharp rock about four hundred and twenty metres above the Mediterranean, with the sea spread out below on three sides. A tangle of stone lanes, stepped passages and vaulted alleys climbs the rock to the summit, where the ruins of a medieval castle have been turned into an exotic garden full of cacti and succulents, with views that stretch along the coast from Cap Ferrat to the mountains of Italy on a clear day.

The village dates back to the Middle Ages, when it was fortified against pirates and rivals, and its streets were carefully designed to be defended and shaded. Today the old houses are filled with art galleries, craft shops and small restaurants, and a perfume factory offers free tours. A famous hotel occupies a clifftop castle, and the village has long been a magnet for artists and the wealthy, so prices are what you would expect.

Below the village, a steep footpath known as the Nietzsche Path winds down to the coast at Èze-sur-Mer. The German philosopher is said to have composed part of Thus Spoke Zarathustra while walking it in the 1880s, and the path takes around forty minutes to descend, with views through pines and aloes. The climb back is harder than it looks, so be sure you have the time and energy.

For the rider, Èze sits on the Moyenne Corniche, one of the three coast roads between Nice and Monaco, and the approach is a pleasure: wide curves above the sea, dramatic views of the coast and tunnels cut through the rock. The surface is generally excellent, but traffic is heavy in the summer months and tour coaches fill the village car parks by late morning. Early mornings and early evenings are the best times to visit, when the crowds thin and the light turns golden.

The old village is entirely pedestrian and the lanes are cobbled and steep, so wear sensible boots. There is parking at the entrance, but it fills quickly and is not cheap. For fuel, La Trinité, a few kilometres away, and the larger town of Beausoleil have stations, and there are none in the village itself.
t.la turbie@43.7,7.4:
Look up at La Turbie and you see a ruin standing over Monaco like a broken tooth. It is the Trophée des Alpes, a huge monument built by the Roman emperor Augustus in 6 BC to celebrate the conquest of the Alpine tribes, and it stands at the highest point of the Via Julia Augusta, the Roman road that connected Italy with Gaul. Once crowned with a statue of the emperor and inscribed with the names of the defeated peoples, the monument was partly dismantled and later used as a fortress and quarry, and what you see today was largely reconstructed in the twentieth century with funds from an American donor.

The village itself sits at roughly four hundred and eighty metres, on the Grande Corniche, with the Mediterranean spread out far below and Monaco's tower blocks looking like toys at the bottom of a cliff. The little old town has narrow lanes, a baroque church and a feeling of being tucked away from the glitz. The view from the terrace beside the trophy is one of the best on the coast, taking in the whole bay of Monaco and the sweep of the shoreline to Italy.

The Grande Corniche is the highest and oldest of the three roads that run along the coast, and it follows much of the line of the Roman route. The riding is a pleasure: broad, sweeping bends, fine views and a smooth surface, with less traffic than the lower roads, though the bus tours still crowd the car parks at midday. The wind can be fierce on the exposed sections, and there is sometimes fog or cloud when the coast below is in sunshine.

Monaco is just a few minutes down the hill, so a detour to see the harbour and the Grand Prix circuit is easy. The tiny principality is very strict on traffic and parking, so be aware of the rules, and do not expect to ride as quickly as the Grand Prix drivers do.

For practical needs, Beausoleil, a town of about thirteen thousand people, lies just below and has fuel, supermarkets and cafes. In the village, a small selection of restaurants and bars serve good coffee and decent lunches. Take a layer, since the breeze at the monument can be cool.
t.manosque@43.8,5.8:
Manosque is the gateway to the high country of Provence, a lively market town on the Durance river with old walls, two surviving medieval gates and a hilltop of tiled roofs. The writer Jean Giono was born here in 1895 and lived in the area nearly all his life, and his novels, in which hills, shepherds and wind take the leading roles, brought the landscape of Haute-Provence to a wide readership. The town is also the home of L'Occitane, the cosmetics company that grew out of a small workshop distilling lavender and rosemary in the 1970s, and you will see its fragrance in many shop windows.

The Valensole plateau, east of town, is the famous heart of lavender country. From late June to the end of July, the plateau turns violet and a smell of honey, hay and herbs carries on the wind, and the rows of lavender run in crisp lines to the horizon. Bees swarm in the flowers and roadside stalls sell honey and oils. The other bloom to look for is the sunflower, which follows in July and August. To the west, the limestone ridges of the Luberon, with their villages of golden stone, form the first great chunk of the ride.

The riding in this area is gentle and flowing, with wide, easy roads that sweep over the plateau and long views to the mountains. Surfaces are good and traffic is light, but it picks up in lavender season, when cars park along the verge and tourists wander into the road to take photographs, so watch for them. In summer the heat is intense, so start early and drink plenty of water. Wind can gust across the open plateau, particularly the mistral, which blows from the north and can be strong enough to move a bike sideways.

Manosque has over twenty-one thousand people, so fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés are easy to find, and the big market on Saturday morning is worth a look. Take a flask of coffee and a bag of the local almonds, and head out in the cool of the early morning. The light is soft and golden, and the fields are at their best.
t.valensole@43.8,6.0:
The Valensole plateau is the Provence of the posters, and in the right fortnight it lives up to them. Rows of lavender, planted in precise lines that follow the curves of the land, stretch across a high, wind-scoured tableland at around six hundred metres, between the Verdon gorge to the north and the valley of the Durance to the south, with the village of Valensole in the middle. In the second half of June and through July, the fields turn a deep violet, the air is loud with bees and the scent is so strong it seems to settle on your jacket.

A note of honesty: most of the purple you see is lavandin, a sturdier hybrid grown for perfume and soap, rather than true lavender, which grows at higher altitudes. The difference matters to growers and perfumers, but your camera will not mind. Harvesting begins in July and continues into August, so the best colour is usually before the cutters arrive. The plateau also grows wheat, sunflowers, olives and almonds, and Valensole is known for its almond groves, which turn white in February, and its honey, sold at roadside stalls throughout the summer.

Valensole itself is a small town of about two and a half thousand people, with a church, a village square shaded by plane trees and a few cafes. Riez, with its Roman columns, is just to the east, and the ride to Moustiers-Sainte-Marie and the canyon is a short step further. Gréoux-les-Bains, a spa town on the Verdon, lies to the south-west.

The riding is easy and enjoyable: broad, gently undulating roads, with long straights and wide curves, often lined with plane trees, and views of the lavender stretching to the horizon. The surface is generally good, but traffic in July is heavy, with tour buses and photographers stopping on the road, so be careful of people stepping out. The wind can blow hard across the plateau, and the sun is fierce, so carry water and wear light layers.

For fuel, Oraison and Manosque, the latter about sixteen kilometres away, have stations, and the village has little more than a few essentials. Early morning is the best moment for photographs, with soft light and fewer visitors.
t.gordes@43.9,5.2:
Gordes clings to the edge of a limestone cliff on the western side of the Luberon, its tiers of pale stone houses stacked beneath a castle like a nativity scene, and it has the kind of looks that make strangers stop their cars in the middle of the road. The view across the valley toward the Vaucluse mountains is wide and golden, and in the late afternoon the stone takes on a warm honey colour. It is a village of around two thousand, and for much of the year, it is overrun with visitors, so the experience improves dramatically if you arrive early or stay late.

Among its neighbours are some of the most photographed sights in Provence. The Abbaye de Sénanque, a Cistercian monastery founded in 1148 and tucked into a narrow valley a few kilometres away, is surrounded by lavender fields that bloom in late June and July, and monks still live there. Near the village, the Village des Bories is a cluster of ancient dry-stone huts, built without mortar, whose origins are debated, with some dating to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and others perhaps earlier. During the Second World War, Gordes was a centre of resistance and suffered reprisals from German troops, and artists including Marc Chagall and Victor Vasarely later settled in the region.

On a motorcycle, the village itself requires care. The streets are steep, narrow and cobbled, and in high season they are jammed with walkers, so most riders will find it better to park at the edge and walk up. The roads around Gordes, though, are among the most pleasant in the Luberon, with good surfaces, easy curves and views of vineyards and cherry orchards. The Sénanque road is narrow and can be crowded in lavender season. Do not count on fuel in the village itself, so fill up in Cavaillon or L'Isle-sur-la-Sorgue, a town with nearly seventeen thousand people and famous antiques markets, which lies about twelve kilometres away.

Finish the day with a drink on a terrace as the stone cools. From above, the valley fills with shadow and the first lights come on, and the whole place settles into a quiet that feels like it belongs to another century.
t.la bollene vesubie food@44.0,7.3:
Rally fans know the name Turini the way footballers know Wembley, and La Bollène-Vésubie is the village at the foot of that legend. It sits on a spur above the Vésubie, a small cluster of stone houses in the lower reaches of the Mercantour foothills, with the road to the Col de Turini leaving the valley right beside it. The Monte-Carlo Rally used to send its cars up here in the dark, and the night stage over the Turini, with fans lighting fires along the hairpins, became one of motorsport's great spectacles.

For a rider the connection is more than trivia. The climb that begins here is long, wooded and full of rhythm, with a hairpin every few hundred metres and the big larch and fir forest of Turini closing in higher up. The pass tops out at around sixteen hundred metres, so the temperature drops sharply, and in spring or after a cold night you can find slush and old snow in the shaded corners long after the coast is baking. The tarmac is generally good, though a little rough on the upper section, and cars with rally ambitions are a hazard on summer evenings.

As a food stop, be realistic. The village itself is tiny, and what you find will be a small bar or auberge with a short menu and limited hours, so check before relying on it. Lantosque and Roquebillière, a few kilometres down the valley, are larger and offer more choice, with bakeries, grocers and the sort of plain mountain cooking you expect here: ravioli with a meat or herb filling, daube, polenta, and a plate of the local cured meats. A coffee and something warm are the natural reward before the pass.

The Vésubie valley is one that bears scars. Storm Alex tore through it in October 2020, wrecking roads and bridges, and much has since been rebuilt, but it is worth checking local conditions before committing to the route, because repairs and temporary closures can still apply.

Fuel is the thing to watch. There is nothing you can count on in the village, and the nearest large town for supplies is Contes, a good twenty kilometres down the valley and out toward the coast, so arrive with a full tank and you will have all the range you need for the pass and the Roya valley beyond.
t.vesubie scenic roads@44.0,7.3:
Between Roquebillière and Saint-Martin-Vésubie, the valley road tightens and rises, and the scenery stops being merely pleasant. The river drops into a narrow gorge, the slopes steepen into dark chestnut and pine, and the villages that were built on spurs above the water start to look like they were fitted into the gaps. This is a landscape that rewards a rider who slows down, partly because the road demands it and partly because there is a great deal to look at.

One small detour is worth a lot. The hamlet of Venanson, perched on the slope above the road, has a little chapel dedicated to Saint Sebastian, whose walls are covered with late-fifteenth-century frescoes painted by Jean Canavesio, a painter from Piedmont. The pictures show scenes from the saint's life, vivid and a little rough, and they were meant to protect the village from the plague. The chapel is usually kept locked, so you may have to ask at the village or check the hours.

The road itself is a series of tight bends and short straights following the river, with a surface that varies from smooth to patched. After the floods of October 2020, parts of it were washed away and rebuilt, and some sections are newer than the rest. Rockfall and gravel in corners are common, particularly after rain, and there are narrow points where a tour coach can fill the whole lane, so keep to your own side and watch the mirrors on blind bends.

The air here carries the smell of chestnut leaves, wet stone and cold water, the sort of alpine freshness that makes the coast feel a long way away. In autumn, the chestnut woods turn the slopes gold and brown, and the local people go out to gather nuts. In summer the shade is welcome, and the river offers a few spots where a swim in cold, clear water is possible if you scramble down.

For fuel, do not rely on the valley. Roquebillière and Saint-Martin have little, and Contes, over twenty kilometres south, is the sure choice, so plan your tank accordingly before heading up.
t.cargese@42.1,8.6:
Cargèse has two churches facing each other across a small valley, one Roman Catholic and one Greek Orthodox, and that tells you almost everything about the town. In 1676, a group of Greek families from the Mani peninsula in the Peloponnese, fleeing Ottoman rule, were given land on this stretch of the Corsican coast by the Republic of Genoa. They built their village, held to their rite and language for generations, and for a long time the Greeks and the Corsicans lived side by side without mixing. The two churches, one Latin and one Greek, stand on either side of the village, and the Greek church, with its icons and painted interior, is a delight.

The town sits on a small headland above the sea, on Corsica's west coast, north of Ajaccio and south of the great red cliffs of Piana. It has a population of about a thousand, a handful of cafes, a few restaurants, a pretty harbour and a long view across the Gulf of Sagone. Behind it rise the maquis-covered hills, thick with myrtle, rock rose and wild lavender, whose smell, on a warm evening, is a thing of wonder. A Genoese tower, built to watch for raiders, stands on the headland nearby.

The D81, which runs north from here toward Piana, Porto and the Calanques, is among the greatest coast roads in Europe. It twists above the sea, with the red granite cliffs of the Calanques plunging down to blue water, tunnels cut into the rock and views at every bend. The surface is generally good, but the road is narrow and winding, with sheer drops and few barriers, and in summer it is clogged with tour buses and campervans. Leave early, or ride in May or September when the light is clearer and the traffic lighter.

Be prepared for the Corsican weather, which can shift quickly, and for the wind, which on the exposed sections can push a loaded bike off line. In summer, wildfire is a risk and the maquis is tinder dry, so no smoking at the roadside.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Cargèse is a small place, so fill up in Ajaccio, around twenty-seven kilometres south, or check whether the local station is open, and do not run low before the long stretch to Porto. There are plenty of places to eat, and grilled fish with a chilled glass of local rosé is the thing to order.
t.zonza@41.7,9.2:
The road from Porto-Vecchio to Zonza climbs out of the humid coast into another Corsica, one of chestnut and pine, granite and cold streams. Zonza lies at about eight hundred metres in the Alta Rocca, a small village of fewer than two thousand people scattered across a ridge, with the great granite needles of Bavella standing over it to the north. The coast is only twenty kilometres away, but the altitude, the air and the sense of space make it feel much further.

The Aiguilles de Bavella are a row of jagged granite pinnacles, bare and orange-brown in the late light, rising above the pass of the same name at around twelve hundred metres. They dominate the skyline for miles, and in the morning mist they appear and vanish like the spires of a drowned cathedral. The forests of laricio pine, the Corsican black pine, which grows tall and straight, cover the slopes, and the smell, resin and warm needles, is intoxicating. Wild mouflon, the shy mountain sheep of Corsica, live on the high ground, though you are more likely to see pigs and cows wandering on the road.

The riding is glorious. The road from Zonza to the pass is a narrow, winding climb through the forest, with tight bends, views over the valley and plenty of places to stop. The surface is generally good but uneven in places, and the road is often shared with free-roaming livestock, which have right of way in all but name. In summer, the traffic of campervans and hikers makes it slow, and in the early morning, it is magical. Weather in the mountains changes fast, so carry a waterproof.

The local food is the real treat. Corsican charcuterie, such as coppa, lonzu and figatellu, is cured in the mountain air, and a plate with a slice of brocciu, the fresh sheep's cheese, and a glass of local red is the perfect reward. Fire is the great danger here, and in dry summers the island is on high alert, so no smoking at the roadside.

Zonza has a few shops and restaurants and is the natural stop on this ride, but fuel is not something to count on, so the safest plan is to fill up in Porto-Vecchio, about twenty kilometres away.
t.porto vecchio@41.6,9.3:
Porto-Vecchio sits on a deep bay in the south-east of Corsica, and it is one of the island's most prosperous and cheerful towns. The Genoese founded it in 1539 on a hill above the sea, building a walled citadel to defend a harbour whose marshy shores bred malaria, and for centuries, it was a lonely, unhealthy outpost. Now the swamps are drained, the old town is lively with restaurants and shops, and the surrounding coast has some of the best beaches in the Mediterranean. Palombaggia and Santa Giulia, a short ride south, have white sand, turquoise water and pine trees, and they get very crowded in July and August.

The hinterland tells a different story. Corsica's famous maquis, the thick scrub of myrtle, arbutus, rock rose and wild herbs, covers the hills behind town, and in warm weather the whole island smells of it. Napoleon is said to have declared he could recognise Corsica blindfold by that scent. Cork oaks, stripped of bark every nine years or so, grow in the valleys, and the trunks, red where recently stripped, are a striking sight. Beyond them rise the granite peaks of the Bavella massif, with their jagged, needle-like pinnacles.

The Bavella route is the reason to be here. From Porto-Vecchio, the road runs inland through Zonza, a mountain village of about nineteen hundred people, and climbs to the Col de Bavella, at roughly 1,200 metres, where the Aiguilles de Bavella tower above the pass like a stone cathedral. Corners are tight, the surface can be rough with gravel and rockfall, and the road is narrow, so go slowly and be ready for pigs, cows and goats, which wander freely and do not give way. In July and August, the traffic is heavy and the road warm, so an early start is best. Snow can close the high section in winter.

Fuel is a point to remember. Porto-Vecchio has all you need, including several stations on the main road, but the mountains do not, so fill up before you leave and again as soon as you are back. A ferry connects the port with the French mainland, and the airport at Figari lies to the west. Take time for a drink on the old town's square, and try figatellu, a spicy Corsican sausage.
t.gorges@43.9,7.3:
North of Nice, the valley of the Paillon cuts up into the mountains, and Lucéram, Berre-les-Alpes and L'Escarène are small, stone-built villages along its length. The landscape is a little wilder than the coast, with olive terraces on the lower slopes giving way to pine forest and bare limestone higher up, and the air carries a scent of thyme and warm rock. The Paillon is a seasonal river, often almost dry in summer and surprisingly fierce after autumn storms.

The valley has a strong history. For centuries, the road through L'Escarène was part of the Route du Sel, the salt road that carried salt, olive oil and other goods between Nice and Piedmont, and mule trains used the old paved tracks that you can still find in the hills. L'Escarène has a large baroque church that shows how wealthy the trade made the village. Lucéram, perched on a hillside, is known for its collection of late medieval altarpieces, painted by artists of the Nice school, in its church, and its streets of narrow, vaulted lanes are good for a stroll. Local specialities include olive oil and a rustic bread.

For motorcyclists, this is a gateway to the Alpine Maritime backcountry. From Lucéram, the road climbs to the Col de Turini, a famous pass that features in the Monte Carlo Rally, and into the forests of the Mercantour. The corners are tight and technical, with hairpins and steep drops, and the surface is generally good. The valley road is also fun, with a rhythm of bends and tunnels. Fuel is scarce: Lucéram and Berre have little, so fill up in Contes, a town of nearly seven thousand people that has several stations, before you leave the coast.

Autumn is the best time, with clear air and quiet roads, though the first snow can fall high up in November. In winter, the Turini can be closed, so check before you go. The ride has taken you around the Verdon and over the mountains, and this valley feels like a calm last chapter, with the sea close at hand.
t.bedoin@44.1,5.2:
Bédoin is the village at the foot of Mont Ventoux, the white, bald summit that dominates Provence, and it is where the hardest and most famous approach starts. The mountain rises to 1,912 metres, and from far away it looks like it is covered in snow, though the whiteness is bare limestone scree. The ascent from Bédoin is about twenty-one kilometres, climbing through vineyards and cherry orchards and then through a dense forest of cedar and pine, before bursting out above the tree line at Chalet Reynard into a lunar landscape of pale stones, with a weather station and a radio mast on top. The Tour de France has crossed it many times, and the tiny memorial to the British cyclist Tom Simpson, who died near the summit in 1967, is a place of pilgrimage for cyclists.

Long before bikes, the poet Petrarch climbed Mont Ventoux in 1336 and wrote an account that many consider the first record of climbing a mountain for the sheer pleasure of the view. The wind has its own reputation, as the mistral, which blows down the Rhône valley, can gust here at over a hundred and fifty kilometres an hour, and the summit weather changes in minutes. The mountain is a biosphere reserve, with different climate zones from Mediterranean to alpine on its slopes, and it is rich in wild flowers and butterflies.

On a motorcycle, the climb is a delight: a steady, sinuous road with open bends and long views, though crowded with cyclists on summer mornings, so patience is needed on the lower slopes. The surface is generally good, and the upper part is exposed, with crosswinds and cold, so carry a warm layer even in July. The summit road is closed by snow from late autumn until spring, and sometimes at short notice, so check before you go. Bédoin, a village of about three thousand people, has fuel, cafés and bakeries, and Caromb and Mazan are close by with more.

The loop returns through the Gorges de la Nesque, a limestone canyon with a road cut into its walls and tunnels along the way, one of the great Provençal rides. Pack a picnic of local goat's cheese, bread and cherries, and sit above the gorge with your helmet off.
t.vassieux plateau meal@44.9,5.4:
Vassieux is a village that was wiped out in a matter of days in the summer of 1944. In July 1944, in the weeks after D-Day, German troops attacked the Vercors, where thousands of Resistance fighters had gathered in the mountain fortress, and gliders landed on the Vassieux plateau, carrying soldiers who overran the defences. The village was burned, its people killed, and the Resistance was crushed. Today Vassieux holds a memorial and a museum, and has been honoured as a Compagnon de la Libération, one of the few communities to receive the title.

The plateau itself is a high, open, windswept upland at around a thousand metres, with meadows, scattered farms and the long, grey wall of the Vercors cliffs to the east. In summer it is a green, peaceful pasture, and in winter it can be buried in snow. The sky is huge, the air thin and clear, and the sense of space is a pleasant change after the narrow valleys and cliffs of the Royans.

For a meal, the plateau has a few simple restaurants and farm inns, serving the hearty food of the mountains: gratins, trout, charcuterie, walnut cake and the blue cheese of the Vercors, the Bleu du Vercors-Sassenage, a mild, creamy cheese made from cow's milk that has its own protected name. Opening hours are short and tables are limited in the low season, so check ahead if you can, and expect the kitchen to close in the early afternoon.

The riding here is a pleasure: wide, sweeping roads across the plateau, with wide views and light traffic, and a good surface. The descent toward Die, over the Col de Rousset and through its tunnel, is a long, winding run with views over the Drôme valley. Weather can change quickly on the plateau, with fog, cold wind and sudden storms, so carry layers. In winter, the roads can be icy or closed.

Fuel is not available on the plateau in any reliable way, so fill up at Saint-Jean-en-Royans or in Die, about fifteen kilometres from here, and arrive with enough in the tank to reach the next supply.
t.granvin@60.5,6.7:
Everything in Granvin is measured in apples and water. The village sits at the head of a short fjord arm off the Hardangerfjord, with a calm river, a lake and a ring of steep hills that hold the orchards in a warm pocket. Fewer than five hundred people live in the centre, so this is a place of a church, a few houses and a handful of farm shops rather than anything urban.

Hardanger is Norway's fruit country, and the reason is a quirk of geography. The fjord keeps the climate mild, so apples, pears, plums and cherries ripen on terraces that cling to the slopes, and in May the blossom turns whole hillsides white and pink. Ulvik, a few kilometres along the fjord, is known for cider, and farm shops sell juice and fruit brandy from the same trees. The Hardanger fiddle, with its sympathetic strings that hum beneath the melody, comes from this region too, and you may hear it at a village festival if your timing is right.

For a rider, Granvin is a gateway. The big Hardanger Bridge, opened in 2013 with a main span of about 1,300 metres, is close by and sweeps the road across the fjord at a height that makes the heart skip. Beyond it the road continues towards Eidfjord and the high plateau of Hardangervidda, while the other way leads up the valley towards Voss. The roads here are a pleasant mix of fjord-side curves, tunnels and short climbs, and in fine weather the views from the bends are superb. Tunnels are long, cool and often damp, so keep your visor clean and your speed modest. There is a toll on the bridge, charged automatically.

On fuel, do not assume. Granvin is small, so the sensible larger stop is Voss, about twenty kilometres away, which has stations, supermarkets and every kind of cafe. Fill up there before you head along the fjord, because stations further into Hardanger are spread out and may close early.

Come in May for the blossom or in September for the fruit and the clear air. Summer is warm, though rain showers are never far away. Buy an apple from a roadside stall if you see one; it will be the best you have eaten for a while.
t.kristiansund@63.1,7.7:
Kristiansund is a town built on four islands, which means that getting anywhere in it involves a bridge, a tunnel or, if you are lucky, one of the little open Sundbåt ferries that have been shuttling people across the harbour for well over a century. It faces the open Atlantic on the Nordmøre coast, and for a long time it made its living from fish, specifically klippfisk, the salted and dried cod that was shipped out to Spain, Portugal and Brazil. The tradition has not died: bacalao, the dish the rest of the world cooks from that fish, is still something the town takes seriously, and a plate of it is a more honest welcome than any brochure.

The harbour is the heart of it, a natural horseshoe with painted wooden warehouses on the quays and the bigger, more modern town climbing the hills behind. There is a well-regarded opera tradition here too, which surprises everybody, with a house that claims a very long history as Norway's first. With sixteen thousand people, Kristiansund has everything a rider needs: several fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and lunch spots, and the sort of unhurried waterfront where it feels natural to sit for an hour with a coffee and watch the boats.

The reason most riders turn up here is what lies to the west. A tunnel under the sound carries you out to Averøy, and from there the road leads to the Atlantic Road, that short, famous run of bridges and causeways hopping from skerry to skerry. The best of it comes in a westerly gale, when waves climb the rocks beside the tarmac, but check the forecast first, since the road does get closed when the sea gets truly serious. Wind is the constant companion on this coast, so expect crosswinds on the bridges and dress for a cold sea breeze even in July.

Start the day here with a proper breakfast and a full tank. Light is best in the early morning and in the long evenings of summer, when the sun skims low across the water and turns the skerries gold. The road itself is smooth, and the fun is not in the twisties but in how close the open ocean feels.
t.finnegarden 1a 1b@60.4,5.3:
Finnegården is a name on the old wharf in Bergen, one of the properties in the long, gabled row of Bryggen, and it is worth stopping simply to understand what a property meant here. Each block was a tight cluster of wooden buildings running back from the quay, with storehouses, counting rooms and living quarters packed together, and each was owned and used by merchants from the Hanseatic League, the trading network of north German towns that dominated this coast.

The story of the timber is a story of fire. Bergen has burned many times, most dramatically in 1702, when most of the town was lost, and the houses were rebuilt on the same medieval pattern after each disaster. In 1955 another fire destroyed a section of the wharf. During the excavations that followed, archaeologists found hundreds of inscribed runic sticks, short messages that ranged from business notes to love declarations, and these are now displayed in the nearby museum. It is a lovely detail that ordinary merchants wrote ordinary things, and some of them survived eight hundred years in the mud.

Walk through the narrow passages between the buildings, and you will notice the floors slope and the walls lean. The ground beneath is soft and the wood is old, and conservation is a constant job. Workshops with craftspeople occupy some of the buildings, and the creaking, tarry smell of old timber stays with you.

Riding to Bergen is a matter of careful planning rather than speed. The city has a congestion charge and toll rings, and the centre is a tangle of one-way streets, tram lines and steep hills. It is best to park in a designated area and walk to the wharf. In wet weather the cobbles and painted road markings become slippery, so take your time. Bergen is one of the rainiest cities in Europe, so assume you will get wet at some point.

Fuel is available around the edges of the city, and the centre has plenty of cafes and fish restaurants. A fish soup or a cinnamon bun by the harbour is the traditional treat. Early morning is the quietest time at the wharf, before the cruise passengers arrive.
t.bryggen@60.4,5.3:
Bryggen is the face of Bergen, a row of narrow, tilting, brightly painted wooden gables along the north side of the harbour. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1979, and the postcards are accurate, though the reality is a little more interesting than the pictures because people still work and live in it.

The wharf was the centre of the Hanseatic League's Norwegian trade from the fourteenth century until the middle of the eighteenth. Merchants from Lübeck and other German towns lived there in strict, almost monastic communities, controlling the export of stockfish, the wind-dried cod from the Lofoten and Helgeland coasts that fed much of Catholic Europe on fast days. In return they brought grain, beer and cloth. The Norwegians who fished had little choice but to deal with them, and the resentments that built up are part of why the Hanseatic office closed in the end. Some of the old rules, such as bans on women and fire in the living quarters, sound extraordinary today.

Beside the wharf stands the Bergenhus fortress, with the stone Håkonshallen, a thirteenth-century royal hall, and the Rosenkrantz Tower. Behind the town rise seven hills, and a funicular runs up Fløyen for a view across the roofs and the harbour. On the opposite side the fish market sells smoked salmon, whale on occasion and sandwiches, and the whole waterfront smells of sea and frying.

Reaching Bergen on a motorbike is simple enough, since the roads from the east come down through tunnels and fjord valleys, but within the city you need patience. Tolls apply on the approaches, and parking in the centre is limited, so find a motorbike bay and walk. The cobbles can be slick when wet, which is most of the time, and the steep lanes behind the wharf are best left to those on foot.

For fuel, use a station on the outskirts; the old town has none. For food, there are many places by the harbour, from simple stands to serious seafood restaurants, with prices that match the view.

Go early in the morning or in the late evening, when the cruise crowds have gone and the light is low. Then the old gables look as they did to the German merchants, tall and watchful over the water.
t.bergen@60.4,5.3:
Bergen is the kind of city that makes you pack the waterproofs first and the camera second, and then makes you glad you did both. Seven hills stand around a sheltered harbour, the Atlantic sends in rain on most days of the year, and in between the showers the light comes through so cleanly that the painted houses on the slopes seem lit from inside. About two hundred thousand people live here, and it is a lively, slightly stubborn place that thinks of itself as the real capital of western Norway.

Tradition dates the founding to 1070, and for a time in the thirteenth century this was the seat of the Norwegian kings. Later came the Hanseatic merchants and the stockfish trade, and then the shipping and the offices that still define the economy. The composer Edvard Grieg was born here and lived out of town at Troldhaugen, where you can see his little composing hut by the water. A cable car climbs Ulriken, the highest of the seven mountains, and a funicular climbs Fløyen, and both are worth it on a clear evening.

As a starting point for a long motorcycle day, Bergen has its trials and its rewards. Getting out means using the tunnels and the toll ring, with traffic that thickens badly at rush hour, so leave early or late. Once clear, the E16 climbs towards Voss through a valley of lakes and waterfalls, with long bends, short tunnels and plenty of trucks. Then you are into the fjord country proper, where the roads follow water, cross on ferries and tunnel through mountains, and a day that looks short on the map turns out to be very long in the saddle.

Fuel and food are no problem in the city, with stations on all sides, and you should fill up before the long run east, since the villages beyond Voss are further apart. For breakfast try a cinnamon bun, called a skillingsbolle locally, and for the road take a thermos and a waterproof.

The weather is the real character. A morning can start with drizzle and clear by lunch, or the reverse, and the fjords can be wrapped in cloud and then reveal themselves all at once. May and June are often the driest and brightest months, while September brings clear light and fewer visitors. Whatever the forecast says, expect a shower, and carry on.
t.n r yfjord area@60.9,7.0:
The Nærøyfjord is narrow in a way that photographs struggle to show. Branching from the Aurlandsfjord, itself an arm of the great Sognefjord, it squeezes to about 250 metres across at its tightest, with mountain walls that climb to nearly 1,800 metres on either side and cast the water in shadow for much of the day. UNESCO listed it together with Geirangerfjord in 2005, and the setting at Gudvangen at its head is dramatic even by Norwegian standards, with waterfalls dropping from hanging valleys and snow patches lingering into summer.

What makes it special is how little has changed. Small farms on ledges high above the fjord, some abandoned and some still in use, speak of generations who lived with avalanches and falling rock. Nearby Undredal, a small village on the Aurlandsfjord, is known for its goat cheese, and you can often taste it at a farm or a shop. The old valley road once reached the plateau at Stalheim by a ferocious cobbled track, and the Stalheimskleiva, one of the steepest roads in northern Europe with thirteen hairpins, is still open in summer for the brave.

Riding here is a mix of tunnels and mountain views. The long Gudvanga tunnel, over eleven kilometres, takes the main road through the rock between Gudvangen and Flåm, and the older roads over the hills and along the fjord offer the real scenery. Surfaces are generally good, but tunnels are damp and cold, so a clean visor and a layer for warmth are wise. Expect tour buses in July and August, and be patient behind them on narrow bends. Weather can change quickly, with rain closing in even on a bright morning.

Fuel is the practical limit. This is remote country, and the nearest larger centres are Voss in one direction and Sogndal in the other, about thirty-five kilometres from this point. Stations in the smaller villages exist but close early, so do not count on them. Bring a snack, and fill up before you commit.

The fjord is best seen on the water. Small ferries and quiet electric boats run from Gudvangen and Flåm, and the silence gliding between the cliffs is remarkable. If you ride, aim for early morning or late evening, when the road is quiet, the water is still and the light pours down the cliffs.
t.west norwegian fjords geirangerfjord and:
Here is the other side of Geirangerfjord, the one the tour brochures skip. High above the water, on the mountain called Åkneset, a huge slab of rock is slowly sliding towards the fjord. Tens of millions of cubic metres of it are monitored day and night by sensors, because if it ever fell in one go it could send a wave through the narrow fjord and the village at its head. The danger is real, the monitoring is serious, and the local authorities have plans for evacuation. It is the sort of fact that puts the postcard in a different light.

The same geology made the view. The fjord is a drowned glacial valley, cut deep by ice during the cold ages and flooded as the sea rose, and its walls are bare gneiss streaked with waterfalls. Farms such as Skageflå were built on shelves where there is no real reason to build, and the paths that reached them were so steep that people used ladders. You can still see a few of the ruins from the water, which makes you wonder about the people who lived there.

For a rider, the roads in are famous. From the south the road climbs through a high bare plateau, then plunges down in tight bends to the village. From the north, the Eagle Road comes in with a series of hairpins and a view that makes motorists stop in a row. A ferry also connects the fjord with Hellesylt, and another crosses the Norddalsfjord, so planning around timetables is part of the day. The roads are usually closed by snow in winter, and open again around May, though high stretches may stay closed longer. Heavy traffic in July can slow you to a crawl on the narrow sections.

Services are limited. Stranda, about twenty-four kilometres away, is the nearest town with a proper choice of fuel and food, and Stryn is farther again. The village at the water has seasonal shops and cafes, but you should arrive with plenty in the tank and use the ferry stops to eat.

Aim for early morning, when the cruise ships are not yet in and the mist rises from the water. That is when the fjord feels as old as it is.
t.norheimsund@60.4,6.1:
Norheimsund is a quiet village on the north shore of the Hardangerfjord, the long, deep fjord that cuts into western Norway, and it is the capital of Norwegian fruit country. The climate here, tempered by the fjord, allows apples, plums, pears and cherries to ripen on terraces above the water, and in May the orchards bloom white and pink, with the Folgefonna glacier shining across the water. In autumn, farm stands sell apples, juice and cider, and the fjord road smells of ripe fruit.

The village itself is small, a cluster of white wooden houses, a harbor, a waterfront and a church, but it has a bustling air in summer, when cruise boats and cyclists arrive. Close by, the Steinsdalsfossen, a waterfall of about fifty meters, drops in a graceful veil, and a path leads behind it, so you can stand between rock and falling water. The Hardanger region is also known for its violin, the hardingfele, with sympathetic strings, and for a delicate form of embroidery.

The roads here are some of the loveliest in the country. Route 7 follows the fjord shore, with gentle bends, tunnels and views across water to the mountains, and a bit farther on, the Hardanger Bridge, a graceful suspension span opened in 2013, crosses the fjord in a single long arc. Ferries cross the fjord at several points, and side roads climb through orchards to high farms. The surface is excellent, but Norwegian speed limits are low and strictly enforced, with fixed and mobile cameras, so keep to them. Tunnels can be damp and long, and rain is frequent.

Norheimsund has fuel, a supermarket and cafes, and it is the main service point on this side of the fjord. Øystese, a few kilometers east, has a small museum and more shops. The best time is mid-May for blossom, or September for apples and clear light, though summer is also lovely, with long evenings. In winter, snow closes some mountain roads.
