The weather on the west coast is changeable, so pack waterproofs, and expect cloud over the peaks.
t.le trayas@43.5,6.9:
Le Trayas is the point where the Var gives way to the Alpes-Maritimes on the Corniche d'Or, and for a hamlet with very few buildings it carries a lot of weight in the memory of anyone who has ridden here. The little station on the coastal railway, the scatter of villas on the slopes and the tiny harbour bring a sleepy feel, and the main event is the scenery: red porphyry cliffs, dark green forest and a sea that shifts between turquoise and deep blue as the clouds move.

The Corniche d'Or is a road you ride with half your attention on the water. From Théoule-sur-Mer, the route climbs and falls along the side of the Esterel, passing viewpoints and little beaches, with plenty of curves to keep it lively. The pace is leisurely. In summer, the traffic can be heavy, and on weekends the lay-bys fill with cars and bicycles. Best to come in spring or autumn, or leave very early in the morning. In winter, the coast is quiet and the light is crisp, though some small cafés close.

Behind Le Trayas, the Esterel massif stretches inland, and its highest point, Mont Vinaigre, reaches just over six hundred metres. The hills are scented with cistus, rosemary and myrtle, and the contrast between red rock and green scrub is the signature look of this part of the Riviera. Wildfires have shaped the landscape, and in the hottest months the authorities often restrict access to parts of the forest, so respect any closures and never throw a cigarette from the saddle.

To the east lies Théoule-sur-Mer, where a small fortified castle on the shore, the Château de la Napoule, was restored in the twentieth century by an American sculptor, Henry Clews, and now hosts exhibitions. The town of Mandelieu-la-Napoule, about seven kilometres from Le Trayas, is the best bet for fuel, shopping and restaurants. Cannes lies beyond. A coffee at one of the small seaside cafés and a moment watching the water, with the red rock behind you, is a good reason to slow down. Bring a layer in case the sea breeze turns cool in the evening.
t.theoule sur mer@43.5,6.9:
Théoule-sur-Mer is a little town squeezed between the red rocks of the Esterel and the sea, and it looks like a painting from the early days of the French Riviera. The houses are pink and ochre, the harbour is small and crowded with boats, and the hills behind are covered with pines and cork oaks. A fortified château with round towers, dating from the fourteenth century and now used as the town hall, stands near the shore, and the old fishing quarter has narrow streets and small terraces. The population is only about thirteen hundred, though it swells in summer.

Just along the coast lies La Napoule, with a castle that was a ruin until 1918, when an American sculptor, Henry Clews, and his wife bought it and rebuilt it as a home and studio, filling it with his strange, brooding sculptures. It is now an arts foundation and open to visitors. Inland, the hills of the Tanneron are covered in mimosa trees, which flower bright yellow in January and February, and there is a mimosa route that runs through the forest in the depths of winter when the rest of Europe is grey.

At the end of the Corniche d'Or, the road changes character, passing from the wild Esterel into the busier coast of Cannes and Mandelieu. The final stretch is a sequence of bends and viewpoints, with small bays below where the water is clear enough to see the rocks on the bottom. Riders should be wary of tourists stepping out between parked cars, and the occasional scooter overtaking on the inside. Parking in summer is very difficult, so arrive early.

Théoule itself has a few shops, bakeries and cafés, but for fuel and larger stores, Mandelieu-la-Napoule, about four kilometres away, is the better bet. The beaches are small, rocky and lovely, and the sea is warm from July to September. The Esterel can burn in dry summers, so respect fire warnings and closures. The best time to be here is May or late September, when the weather is warm, the crowds are thin and the light on the red rocks is at its best. Order grilled sea bream, and watch the sun go down behind the headland.
t.monaco@43.7,7.4:
Monaco is small enough to fit inside a large park, and it has packed into two square kilometres more than most countries manage in two thousand. The rock above the harbour has been held by the Grimaldi family since 1297, when Francesco Grimaldi, disguised as a monk, took the fortress by surprise, and the same dynasty still rules the principality. The Prince's Palace stands on the rock, with a changing of the guard at midday, and the old town around it is a tangle of lanes. Across the harbour, the Monte-Carlo Casino, built in the 1860s and finished by the architect of the Paris Opera, Charles Garnier, is a wedding cake of a building that still draws high rollers and sightseers.

Every May, the streets of Monaco become the Grand Prix circuit, a race that has run since 1929 through the same narrow streets, tunnel and hairpin, and fans can walk the route when it is open. The Oceanographic Museum, a vast neo-baroque building built into the cliff, was directed by Jacques Cousteau for thirty years and has a fine aquarium. The harbour is full of yachts, the cars parked outside the hotels are exotic, and the mood is one of discreet and polished wealth.

For the rider, the Grande Corniche is the way in. The road was built along the line of the ancient Roman Via Julia Augusta and later improved on Napoleon's orders, and it runs high above the coast, with enormous views of the sea, villages and the principality below. At La Turbie, just above Monaco, stand the remains of the Trophy of Augustus, a vast monument built in 6 BC to celebrate the conquest of the Alpine tribes, with a small museum and a viewpoint over the whole coast. The riding is wide, gentle and scenic, with long bends and good surface, though the traffic is heavy at times.

Monaco itself is a place to be careful. Speed limits are low, police are numerous, and parking is expensive, so leave the bike in an underground car park, and bring your documents, though there is no formal border control. Fuel is available but the prices are not generous. The streets are steep, and the traffic is thick, so keep patient. Evening light on the harbour, with the lights of the palace and casino coming on, is memorable, and a coffee on the terrace is worth the price.
t.calanques de piana@42.2,8.6:
On the west coast of Corsica, the granite does something that granite is not supposed to do. In the Calanques de Piana, huge cliffs of red-orange rock, eroded into pillars, needles and strange faces, plunge a few hundred metres into the sea. The colour changes through the day, burning orange in the late afternoon and deep crimson at sunset, against a sea of dark blue. This is part of the Gulf of Porto, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 together with the nature reserve of Scandola, and nobody who has seen it has been disappointed.

The road through it, the D81, is a nineteenth-century coast road that clings to the cliffs between Piana and Porto, and it is one of the great motorcycle roads of the Mediterranean. It is narrow, twisting and slow, with tight hairpins, blind corners and sudden drops, and the stone parapets are not always high. Buses and campervans squeeze past each other with inches to spare, and pigs and goats wander across the road at will. Ride carefully, stay in your lane, and take the opportunity to pull into the signed viewpoints. In the middle of the day, the light is flat and the road crowded. Early morning or the hour before sunset gives the best colours and the least traffic.

The nearby village of Piana, which is one of the most beautiful villages in France, is a cluster of stone houses on a hillside above the gulf, and a good place for a coffee. Walking trails lead down into the calanques, including the old mule path called the Chemin des Muletiers, and on foot you can see the rocks close up, though the paths are steep and rough and need proper shoes. Capo d'Orto, a jagged peak, stands to the east, and the maquis, the dense, fragrant scrub of Corsica, covers the slopes with cistus, myrtle and wild herbs.

Fuel needs careful planning. Piana is small, Porto has limited services, and the bigger towns of Ajaccio, about thirty-seven kilometres away, and Calvi are the safer places to fill the tank. Corsican roads can be slow, and distances take longer than the map suggests, so allow plenty of time and enjoy it.
t.porto@42.3,8.7:
Porto, on Corsica's west coast, is a small harbour village at the head of a gulf, and almost all of its charm lies in what surrounds it. A sixteenth-century Genoese tower stands on a rocky headland above the marina, one of the many watchtowers the Genoese built around the island to warn of pirate raids. A long eucalyptus grove, planted in the last century, shades the road down to the water. Behind the village, red granite mountains climb steeply toward the interior, and the whole gulf is ringed by cliffs that fall into the water.

Boats leave from the marina for the Scandola nature reserve, a wild peninsula of volcanic rock accessible only by sea or on foot, and for the tiny fishing hamlet of Girolata, which has no road to it at all. The trips are the best way to understand the coast, with sea caves, ospreys and underwater life, and the water is clear and rich. The reserve was established in 1975, and the Gulf of Porto and Scandola together became a World Heritage Site in 1983.

For a rider, Porto is a hinge between two great roads. South, the D81 climbs through the Calanques de Piana in a series of hairpins and cliffs. North, it winds up and over the Col de Palmarella, with views of the Gulf of Girolata, before descending towards Calvi. Inland, a side road climbs from the village of Ota, a few kilometres up the valley, into the Spelunca gorge, where old Genoese stone bridges cross the stream, and on to the mountain village of Evisa and the Aïtone forest of tall Corsican pines. All these roads are narrow and slow, so budget time and expect to drive carefully. The best light is early morning or late afternoon, and summer is hot and crowded, so spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Services are limited but adequate for the area. Porto has restaurants, a few shops and cafés, and seafood is the thing to eat, with fresh fish grilled over a wood fire, and perhaps a plate of Corsican charcuterie and cheese. Fuel is the main uncertainty, so do not rely on small stations. Calvi, about thirty-four kilometres to the north, is the sure option, and Ajaccio lies to the south. A cold drink on the marina and a look at the evening light on the cliffs is a fine way to end a day.
t.col de la croix@42.3,8.7:
Corsica's west coast road north of Porto is a long conversation between rock and sea, and the Col de la Croix is a small word in it. At just 269 metres, it is hardly a mountain pass by Pyrenean standards, but on this island height means little. The D81 climbs from the shoreline, winds along a wall of red-brown rock, and crosses a low saddle with a view out to the gulf, before dropping again. It is a place to ease off the throttle and look around, and perhaps put a foot down to catch the light on the water.

The surrounding landscape is the wild Corsican coast at its best. The maquis, a thick tangle of cistus, myrtle, strawberry tree and wild herbs, covers the hillsides, and in spring the air is heavy with its scent. Below, the sea is a hard, clear blue, and tiny coves are cut into the cliffs, reachable only by boat or on foot. A short way to the south lies the headland of Scandola, a nature reserve of volcanic rock accessible only from the sea. Nearby, the fishing hamlet of Girolata has no road, and visitors reach it by boat or on a long walk down a mule path.

The road itself is a good one for riders who like to take their time. It is narrow, with frequent tight bends, short straights and the occasional hairpin, and there are no barriers on parts of the edge. Surface quality is variable, with patches of gravel and broken edges, and rock falls are possible after heavy rain. Pigs, goats, cows and sometimes horses wander across the road, particularly at the quiet times of day, and they have right of way in practice. Early morning is the best time, with cool air and light traffic, while in July and August the coaches and campers make progress slow. Spring, with flowers in the maquis, and early autumn, with warm sea and calm weather, are the most pleasant seasons.

There are no services at the col. The nearest big town is Calvi, about twenty-six kilometres away, with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and its old citadel is worth seeing if you have time. Porto, in the other direction, has limited services. Make sure you start with a full tank, carry water, and allow a lot more time than the distances suggest, since Corsican roads are never fast.
t.solenzara@41.9,9.4:
The Solenzara river rises in the granite heart of southern Corsica and falls to the east coast in a series of pools so clear and green that they look lit from below, and it is here, at the mouth, that the Bavella road begins. The coastal village of Sari-Solenzara is small and workaday, with a harbour, a long beach and a handful of restaurants, and it also has a military air base nearby whose jets occasionally tear across the sky. It is a quiet place by Corsican standards, a spot to fill the tank, buy a bottle of water and have a coffee before the mountains.

From the shore the road climbs inland through chestnut and cork oak, then pine, rising in long bends along the river gorge to the Col de Bavella, at about 1,200 metres, among some of the most dramatic mountain scenery in the Mediterranean. The Aiguilles de Bavella are a row of jagged granite spires, rising a thousand metres or more above the forest, and at dawn or dusk they turn orange and pink. At the pass a small chapel, Notre-Dame-des-Neiges, holds a statue of the Virgin in a shrine, a reminder that the weather up here can bring snow even when the coast is warm.

The road is the D268, narrow, patchy and twisting, with drops on one side and rock walls on the other, and the pace is slow because of both the bends and the animals. Pigs, cows and goats roam freely in the Corsican hills, and they treat the road as their own, often lying in the middle at blind corners. Give them space, because they will not give you any. The Corsican pine, the laricio, grows tall and straight here, its trunks silver in the sun, and mouflon, the wild mountain sheep, live on the high slopes.

Villages such as Zonza, in the hills, have places to eat and stay, with a rustic menu of wild boar stew, chestnut-flour dishes and cured ham, and a glass of local red. For fuel, Sari-Solenzara has pumps, and Porto-Vecchio, thirty-one kilometres to the south, has more, so top up before you climb. The weather in summer is hot at sea level and cool at the pass, while storms can build in the afternoon. In dry summers, forest fires are a real danger, and the authorities restrict access, so check the situation before you set out. Rivers are tempting for a swim, but the rocks are slippery, and currents can be strong after rain.
t.col de bavella@41.8,9.2:
The Aiguilles de Bavella are the teeth of southern Corsica, a ridge of jagged granite needles that rise above the pass like the spines of some enormous stone creature. The Col de Bavella, at 1,218 metres, lies in their shadow, a saddle of dark pine forest and boulders where the road from Zonza crosses the range on its way to the east coast. A small chapel stands at the pass, with a statue of the Madonna of the Snows, and in the early morning light, with mist in the valleys, the sight is almost unreal.

The road, the D268, is one of the island's finest. From Zonza, it climbs through chestnut and pine woods in a series of tight bends, with the needles growing larger ahead, and the surface is generally good but narrow, with few barriers. Beyond the col it winds down toward the east coast and Solenzara, through forests of Corsican laricio pine, which can grow to forty metres and are among the finest in the Mediterranean. Cows, pigs and even mouflon, the wild mountain sheep, wander across the road, and you must be prepared to stop for them. The road is slow, and a good rider will keep well within limits and enjoy it.

The Bavella is high enough for serious weather. Thunderstorms build on summer afternoons, fog can drop onto the pass in minutes, and snow can close the road in winter. It is cold in the early morning even in summer, so a warm layer is sensible. The best time to come is late spring, when wildflowers cover the maquis, or early autumn, when the heat has eased and the tourists have gone. At the pass, a few small restaurants and a snack bar sell hot drinks, sandwiches and Corsican charcuterie, and the view from the terrace is worth lingering over.

The surrounding forest, part of the regional nature park, is also a hiking centre, and a section of the long-distance GR20 trail, the famous route across the island, passes through the south. A short drive from Zonza, the Piscia di Gallo waterfall tumbles down a granite slope, a popular spot for walkers.

For fuel, do not rely on the villages. Porto-Vecchio, about twenty-three kilometres away, is the main town of the south with stations and supermarkets, and Solenzara on the east coast also has services. Fill up before you head up, and allow plenty of time.
t.mont ventoux summit@44.2,5.3:
Mont Ventoux rises alone from the plains of Provence, and the summit, at 1,909 metres, is a bald white dome of shattered limestone that looks from a distance like a snowfield even in July. Nothing else stands near it. This isolation is the key to its character, because the mistral, the cold northerly wind of the Rhône valley, hits it with full force, and the weather on top is often wild when the lowlands are warm and sunny. Gusts above a hundred kilometres per hour are not unusual, and the summit has a long record of cold, wind and fog.

The mountain has a history that few can match. The poet Petrarch climbed it in 1336 and wrote a famous letter about the experience, often cited as the first account of climbing a mountain for the view. In the twentieth century, the Tour de France made it a legend, and a memorial near the top marks the spot where the British rider Tom Simpson collapsed and died in 1967. Cyclists leave bottles, caps and messages there, and it is a quiet place to pause. The red-and-white weather station tower on the summit is a famous landmark, and you can see it from many kilometres away.

The riding is more serious than it first appears. From Bédoin, the classic approach, the road climbs for about twenty-two kilometres through forest of oak and pine, with a steady gradient, then emerges at the Chalet Reynard onto the bare moonscape of the upper slope, with long, exposed bends and no cover. From Malaucène on the north side, the road climbs in a similar way. The surface is generally good, but the wind can be dangerous for a motorcyclist, so watch the gusts near the exposed bends, and keep both hands on the bars. The upper road is closed in winter because of snow, usually from late autumn to spring, so check before you go. A cold layer is essential even on a hot day.

The mountain is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, with an unusual range of habitats from Mediterranean oak at the bottom to alpine plants on the summit. Cedar forests, planted in the nineteenth century, cover parts of the slope, and the view from the top, on a clear day, takes in the Alps to the east, the Rhône valley to the west and even the Mediterranean to the south.

On the summit, a small shop and kiosk sell drinks, snacks and souvenirs in season.
t.gorges de la nesque@44.1,5.3:
The Gorges de la Nesque is a road that cuts across the limestone rim of a canyon, with sheer cliffs on one side and a drop of several hundred metres on the other. The Nesque river, which flows from the Monts de Vaucluse, has carved a gorge about twenty kilometres long and as much as four hundred metres deep through the plateau, and the road, the D942, follows the cliffs high above the river, with a series of belvederes, short tunnels and long, clean bends. It runs between Villes-sur-Auzon, on the western side, and Sault, on the lavender plateau, and it is among the most beautiful drives in Provence.

The riding is pure pleasure. The road has a good surface, steady gradients and wide, open curves, with excellent visibility, and the tunnels are short and well lit. The only drawbacks are the summer traffic, with campervans and cyclists slowing the pace, and the occasional rockfall after storms. Early morning and late afternoon are the best times, when the light turns the cliffs golden and the air is cool. In spring the hillsides are green, in autumn the oaks turn bronze, and in summer the heat is intense, with the smell of thyme and baked rock rising from the slopes.

The most famous viewpoint is the Belvédère du Castelleras, high on the cliff, which looks across the gorge to the pale limestone of the opposite wall. Not far away, the Rocher du Cire, a sheer cliff of rock, is home to peregrine falcons and other raptors, and its name means Wax Rock. Wild boar, foxes and golden eagles live in the scrub and forest, though you will rarely see them from the road.

At the eastern end, the road climbs to Sault, where lavender fields cover the plateau and in July turn the land purple. The village sells lavender honey, nougat and essential oil. Sault has a handful of cafés and shops, and the view from the village over the plateau is lovely.

For fuel, do not count on the villages. Mazan, about fifteen kilometres from the gorge, has stations and supermarkets, and Carpentras, a larger town, is a short ride beyond. Start the day with a full tank, carry water, and enjoy a quiet lunch in Sault.
t.la spezia@44.1,9.8:
La Spezia is a naval city at the head of a deep bay, and it is not trying to charm you. About eighty-eight thousand people live here, the Italian navy has a major base on the waterfront, and the port handles container ships and ferries. That makes it a practical place: big enough for fuel, garages, banks and a proper supermarket, and the starting point for the Cinque Terre, which lie just along the coast to the west. Many travellers pass through here without stopping, but the town has a pleasant seafront promenade and a market with excellent produce.

The bay is called the Gulf of Poets, because Byron and Shelley both lived around it, and Shelley drowned off the coast near Lerici in 1822. Lord Byron swam from Portovenere across to Lerici in homage. Portovenere, at the western tip of the bay, has a Gothic church on a rock above the sea, and it is part of a UNESCO listing with the Cinque Terre. A short ride south from La Spezia, you can reach the headland and Le Grazie, a small village on the bay with a sheltered harbour and old monastery.

For a rider, La Spezia is the gateway to the Ligurian coast. The roads out of the city climb at once into steep hills covered in olive groves and terraced vineyards, and the views over the water are wide. The corners are tight, the roads often narrow, and the surface has patches. The coast is steep and rocky, and the old villages cling to cliffs above the sea, with little parking. In summer, traffic is heavy and parking is scarce, so ride early.

Eat here, if you can. Liguria has its own cuisine: trofie pasta with pesto, focaccia, farinata made of chickpea flour, and anchovies from the sea. Pesto was born here, in a region with fragrant basil and Ligurian olive oil. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the light is clear and the sea is calm, and an early start gives you the coast to yourself before the day-trippers appear. Fill the tank in town, as the coast beyond is thin on stations.
t.portovenere@44.1,9.8:
Portovenere stands at the tip of a rocky peninsula at the southern end of the Ligurian coast, where the cliffs finish in a narrow point facing the island of Palmaria. It is a village of tall, narrow houses painted in faded yellow, pink and ochre, with a fortified waterfront that looks like a wall of colour from the sea. At the end of the point, on a rock above the waves, stands the black-and-white church of San Pietro, a Gothic building from the late twelfth century, built on the site of an earlier temple. The name itself means Port of Venus, and the old goddess seems to have been on good terms with the sailors.

The gulf beyond is called the Gulf of Poets, because Byron and Shelley and many others wrote about it. Byron is said to have swum across the water from Portovenere to Lerici, a feat of endurance, and a grotto beneath the church carries his name. The village, together with the Cinque Terre and the islands, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. A Genoese castle stands on the hill above, with views over the gulf, and the narrow main street runs from the harbour gate up past shops and restaurants to the church.

The ride to get here is the SP530 from La Spezia, a winding coastal road through the village of Le Grazie, with the gulf on one side and olive-covered hills on the other. It is narrow and twisting, with traffic that grows heavy at weekends and in summer, and the final approach to the village is restricted. A large car park sits at the entrance, and in high season it fills up early, so aim to arrive in the morning or late in the day. The bends are tight and the walls close, but the sea views are constant, and the road is a good way to get out of the cities around La Spezia.

The harbour restaurants serve fresh seafood, including the local mussels, which are farmed in the gulf, and trofie al pesto, the Ligurian twisted pasta in basil sauce. Prices reflect the setting, so expect to pay a bit more than in La Spezia. The village is small enough to cover on foot in an hour, and the walk to the church and along the sea wall is a pleasure.

For fuel, La Spezia, about six kilometres away, is a proper city with plenty of stations, and it is best to fill there before you drive down. A boat service links the village with the Cinque Terre in summer, an easy way to see them without taking the bike.

The best light is in the late afternoon, when the sun warms the pastel houses and the water turns deep blue.
t.levanto@44.2,9.6:
Levanto is the quiet neighbour of the Cinque Terre, close enough to use as a base and far enough to avoid the worst of the crowds. It sits at the head of a small bay on the Ligurian coast, with a long, sandy beach, which is rare in this part of Italy, and a town of arcaded streets, a medieval loggia and a Gothic church striped in black and white stone. The hills behind are steep and green with olive groves, vines and chestnut woods, and the coast on either side is a series of rocky headlands. The town is relaxed, with a mix of residents and visitors, and in summer it has the easy atmosphere of a seaside resort without the glitz.

The Cinque Terre villages, to the south, are tucked into coves and clinging to cliffs, and are linked by trains and footpaths. Cars are not welcome in most of them, and the villages themselves are mostly closed to traffic, so the sensible approach for a rider is to park in Levanto and take the train, which takes just a few minutes to the first village. Meanwhile, the roads over the hills from Levanto are good riding in their own right. A steep, twisting road climbs to the heights above the coast, with views over the sea and the terraced slopes, and the longer road inland over the Bracco pass is a classic of the Ligurian hinterland, with long bends through forest.

The riding on the coast is slow, tight and often busy. The old Aurelia road and its successors run through the hills with many bends and little room to pass. In summer, the traffic is heavy with holidaymakers, so the best times are spring and autumn, or early in the morning. Roads can be slick when wet, and rockfall and landslides are a recurring hazard after heavy rain.

Levanto has the services you need, including fuel on the approach roads, supermarkets, bakeries and many places to eat. The food is Ligurian, so expect focaccia, pesto, anchovies and fresh fish, and a glass of the local white wine is a good accompaniment. The farinata, a flat chickpea pancake baked in a wood oven, is a cheap and filling snack.

The nearest larger town is Casarza Ligure, about seventeen kilometres away, though most riders will find what they need in Levanto itself or in La Spezia, further south. There is also a good surf beach, popular with local young people, and the water is relatively clean.

Evening is the best time, when the day-trippers have gone and the old town fills with locals having an aperitivo.
t.portofino@44.3,9.2:
Portofino is tiny, absurdly pretty and aware of it. The harbour is a horseshoe of tall, pastel-coloured houses facing a little square, with fishing boats and yachts rubbing shoulders at the quay, and a hillside of pine and cypress rising behind. The Romans called it Portus Delphini, the Port of the Dolphin, and the name has stuck in a modified form. For centuries it was a quiet fishing village, and then in the nineteenth century foreign visitors, especially the British, began to fall in love with it, and in the twentieth century film stars and millionaires made it fashionable. The permanent population is only a few hundred, but the summer crowds are many times that.

The village is surrounded by the Portofino regional park, a promontory of steep, wooded slopes and rocky coves that is rich in walking paths. A short walk takes you to the church of San Giorgio and the Castello Brown, a fortress turned villa, with a view over the harbour and out to sea, and further along the coast is the abbey of San Fruttuoso, hidden in a cove and reachable only on foot or by boat. The lighthouse at the tip of the headland is another good objective, and the sea beyond is a deep, clear blue.

The road to Portofino is a lovely, slow ride from Santa Margherita Ligure, about three and a half kilometres away. It is a narrow coastal road that winds around the bay with the sea on one side and villas and gardens on the other, with views of the cliffs and the water. It is not a place for speed. In summer, the road clogs with cars and taxis, and the parking in the village is limited and expensive, so you may be turned back or forced to pay for a space. Motorcycles often fare better than cars, and a small bike can find a spot where cars cannot, though the police are alert to illegal parking. Early morning or late evening is the best time, with mist on the water and the harbour almost empty.

Services in the village are plentiful and priced for the clientele. A coffee on the quay is an expensive pleasure, though the view justifies it, and the restaurants serve Ligurian classics such as trofie with pesto and fresh seafood. For fuel, you should fill in Santa Margherita Ligure or Rapallo before heading out, since there is none in the village itself.

The best time to come is in the shoulder season, April to June or September to October, when the weather is mild and the crowds are smaller. In midsummer, go at dawn or after sunset.
t.genoa@44.4,8.9:
Genoa is a city built on a slope, with a port at the bottom and neighbourhoods stacked above it like seats in a theatre. It has been a great maritime power since the Middle Ages, and the Republic of Genoa ruled trade routes across the Mediterranean, financed kings and sent Christopher Columbus, who was born here, to his voyages. The old town is one of the largest medieval centres in Europe, a maze of narrow lanes called caruggi, where sunlight rarely reaches the street and every doorway seems to hold a shrine, a shop or a bakery. With over 580,000 people, the city is a proper metropolis, with everything from fuel to repair shops.

Genoa's wealth is visible in the Strade Nuove and the Palazzi dei Rolli, a group of Renaissance and Baroque palaces that are listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Painted facades, marble stairs and gardens hide behind modest doors. The port has been renewed with the aquarium and the old harbour area, and the great lighthouse, the Lanterna, has stood since the twelfth century. Focaccia is eaten for breakfast here, dipped in a cappuccino if you want to be authentic.

For a rider, the city is an exercise in patience. Traffic is dense, roads are steep and narrow, scooters are everywhere, and the motorway and ring roads run on viaducts above the buildings. The Morandi bridge collapsed in 2018, and a new one, designed by Renzo Piano, replaced it. If you are arriving from La Spezia along the coast, you have the pleasure of a gradual approach, but the last hour is usually urban. Park carefully, ideally in a secure garage, as bike theft is a risk in any big port city.

At the finish, treat yourself to the local food. Trofie with pesto, stuffed vegetables, fried anchovies and a plate of farinata are hard to beat, and a sweet pandolce goes with coffee. Walk down to the old port in the evening, when the light turns golden on the water and the ferries to Sardinia and Corsica sit in the dock. Then sleep, because the steep streets make a long day.
t.san teodoro@40.8,9.7:
San Teodoro is a summer town on the north-east coast of Sardinia, a place that lives for the months between June and September and goes very quiet the rest of the year. It sits between the granite hills of Gallura and a lagoon where flamingos sometimes wade, and its reputation rests on a beach. La Cinta is a long strip of fine white sand that runs for kilometres between the sea and the lagoon, backed by dunes and juniper, and across the water the limestone bulk of the island of Tavolara rises like a ship's prow, fierce and grey, nearly six hundred metres high. The little island has a claim to be the world's smallest kingdom, a title once held by a family of shepherds and fishermen who were recognised by a king of Sardinia in the nineteenth century.

The beach is the draw, but the landscape behind is of interest too. The hills are covered in maquis, the scented scrub of myrtle, rock rose, wild olive and cork oak that smells wonderful on a hot afternoon, and the granite boulders are rounded into strange shapes by wind and rain. The lagoon is a protected wetland where egrets, herons and flamingos feed, and in spring and autumn migrating birds stop to rest.

The riding is a pleasure at the quieter times of the year. The state road, the SS125, runs south from here along the coast toward Budoni and Posada, with long, easy bends, hills and sea views. In summer, the traffic is heavy and slow, with holiday cars, camper vans and the sort of overtaking you would rather not witness, so go early. In the shoulder months, the road is empty and the air is clear. The surface is generally good, though some sections have been patched and rough, and goats and cows can wander onto the road in the quieter inland stretches.

The town has everything for visitors: restaurants, bars, shops, a few nightclubs and a good supply of fuel stations on the main road. Seafood is the local speciality, with grilled fish, spaghetti with clams and bottarga, the cured mullet roe of Sardinia, and for the sweet tooth, seadas, fried pastries filled with cheese and drizzled with honey. Olbia, about twenty-two kilometres to the north, is the nearest big town, with its ferry port and airport.

Visit in June or September if you can. The sea is warm, the beach is not packed, and the prices are lower.
t.orosei@40.4,9.7:
Orosei is a small old town on the Cedrino river, a short way inland from the long beaches of Sardinia's east coast, and it is one of those places that sits in the middle of a big story without making a fuss about it. Behind it, the white limestone mountains of the Supramonte rise, a wild and almost unvisited country of canyons and caves, and to the south the coast runs on toward the Gulf of Orosei, where cliffs and hidden beaches are reached by boat. The town was once a significant port and a seat of Spanish rule, and it still has a cluster of churches, an old watchtower and a medieval centre with some fine stone houses. It is known for its churches, of which there are many, and a few of them are very old.

The countryside is one of citrus orchards, irrigated fields and vineyards along the river plain, framed by the mountains, and the beach, a long sweep of sand backed by pines and dunes, is a short ride away. The marble quarried nearby, a pale stone sometimes compared with that of Carrara, has been used in buildings across the island. A little further, the great canyons and caves of the Supramonte and the beaches of Cala Gonone make good day trips for those with time.

For motorcyclists, Orosei lies on the SS125, the Orientale Sarda, one of the best-known roads in Sardinia, which runs the length of the east coast. Here it is a fast, open stretch with long bends and views of the mountains. To the south it climbs through the hills toward Dorgali, with a series of tunnels and ridge-top views over the sea, and the surface is generally good. In summer, the road is busy, with holiday traffic and heavy lorries, and the heat can be fierce on the plain. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with cooler air and clear light. Mountain roads inland are narrow and slow, with goats, cattle and sudden changes of surface.

The town has the services you need. There are fuel stations on the main road, supermarkets, restaurants and cafes, and small hotels and guesthouses. Local food leans toward the traditional, with roast suckling pig, handmade pasta called malloreddus and the wafer-thin carasau bread of the island, and the local cheeses are excellent. A glass of the red Cannonau wine, made from the local Grenache variety, is good with all of it.

The town is at its best in the early evening, when the sun lights the old stone and the mountains turn violet.
t.gaupne@61.4,7.3:
Gaupne sits at the head of the Lustrafjord, which is the innermost arm of the Sognefjord, and it is a small village in a very large landscape. The fjord here is narrow and deep, with steep mountainsides rising straight from the water and farms perched on the shelves above, and from the village you can see glimpses of the Jostedalsbreen glacier plateau to the north. Gaupne has just over a thousand people and the municipal centre of Luster, with shops, a petrol station and a few places to eat, and Sogndal, about twenty kilometres away, is the larger town if you need more.

The road you have been riding is the Sognefjellet, the highest mountain pass road in northern Europe, which crosses at about 1,430 metres between Lom in the east and the Lustrafjord in the west. It was built in the 1930s and it is a fine road, with wide curves, long views over bare rock and snowfields, and a surface that is generally excellent. The high section is closed in winter, usually from around November until May, and snow can remain beside the road well into summer. On the western descent, the road drops through a series of bends into the valley of the Jostedøla and then along the fjord.

The nearby Urnes stave church, on the opposite shore of the fjord, is one of the oldest of its kind, built in the twelfth century and listed by UNESCO. Its carvings of twisting animals and plants gave a name to the Urnes style, and the little ferry across the fjord from Solvorn is a pleasant crossing. In the village, orchards grow in the mild micro-climate, and the Lustrafjord is known for cherries and apples in late summer. The Norwegian Glacier Museum at Fjærland, on the other side of the mountain, is a trip for another day.

Practicalities are easy: fill up here before or after the pass, since fuel is thin in the mountains. Cafes serve waffles, coffee and open sandwiches, and local cider is available in season. Weather can change fast, from sunshine to rain, and the high road can be cold even in July, so wear layers. In the evening, when the light hits the fjord at a low angle, the water turns silver. It is a good place to pause at the end of the road.
t.monument valley@37.0,-110.1:
Everyone has seen this place before they arrive. Monument Valley, on the Utah-Arizona line inside the Navajo Nation, has been the backdrop for so many Westerns and car commercials that the first sight of the buttes feels like a memory. Mitten Buttes, Merrick Butte, the thin Totem Pole: great red sandstone towers left standing as the softer rock around them wore away, rising up to a thousand feet above a flat floor of sand and sage. The colour shifts through the day, orange at noon, then deep red and violet at dusk.

John Ford filmed here for decades, beginning with Stagecoach in 1939, after a trading post owner called Harry Goulding reportedly travelled to Hollywood to show photographs and persuade the studios that the valley was worth the journey. John Wayne became linked to the landscape. More recently, a stretch of US 163 north of the valley became famous as the place where Forrest Gump ends his cross-country run, and riders stop there to take photographs with the road running straight to the buttes.

This is Navajo land, a tribal park rather than a national one, and it is run by the Navajo people, who live in scattered homes and graze sheep on the valley floor. There is a seventeen-mile dirt loop that goes among the buttes, in bad condition at times, and local guides run tours in open vehicles. The Navajo Nation observes daylight saving time, unlike the rest of Arizona, so clocks can be confusing. Respect the land, stay on the roads, and ask before photographing people.

The ride in, along US 163, is spectacular, a straight ribbon of tarmac that runs between mesas and low desert, with long views and hardly any traffic. Wind can be fierce, and summer heat is extreme, so early starts are best. Fuel and supplies are available at Kayenta, about thirty-three kilometres south, and at Mexican Hat to the north, so fill up before you reach the valley. Dawn and dusk are the best times, with low light and long shadows, and you can pick a viewpoint and wait for the colours to change. Mutton stew and fry bread are the local dishes.
t.springdale@37.2,-113.0:
Springdale is a one-street town pressed against the walls of Zion Canyon, and its few thousand sandstone-coloured buildings, cafes, shops and motels all exist for the national park next door. Mormon pioneers founded the settlement in 1862, drawn by springs and the Virgin River, which cuts a narrow gorge through the red rock, and they farmed orchards and fields along it. Today the main road is lined with cottonwoods, and the huge cliffs of Zion rise above the rooftops, turning from pale pink to flaming red at sunset.

Zion's rocks are layers of ancient sand dunes, cemented and carved by water into towers, domes and slot canyons. The cliffs, mostly Navajo Sandstone, are streaked with desert varnish and show the curved lines of the old dunes. The Virgin River, small and muddy most of the year, is the cutting tool, and flash floods can roar down the canyons after storms. For much of the year, the scenic drive up the main canyon is closed to private vehicles, and visitors use a shuttle bus, but the Mount Carmel Highway, which leaves the canyon floor eastward, is open to traffic.

The ride begins by climbing out of the canyon in a series of switchbacks cut into the cliff, with spectacular views down to the valley floor, and then enters the Zion-Mount Carmel Tunnel, a mile long, blasted through the rock and finished in 1930. Windows were cut into the side of the tunnel to let in light and views, a pleasant touch. Because of the tunnel's size, larger vehicles must pay an extra fee and be escorted, and traffic is sometimes controlled, so be prepared for waits. On the east side, the road emerges onto a plateau of slickrock domes and striped hills.

Fuel is available in Springdale, though prices are high, and the bigger town of Hurricane, about twenty-six kilometres to the west, offers more choice. Food ranges from casual cafes to restaurants with patios facing the cliffs. The park is crowded from spring to autumn, so start early and try to be at the entrance before nine. Summer heat is intense, and winters can be cold, with occasional snow. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with comfortable temperatures and colourful cottonwoods.
t.zion canyon junction@37.2,-113.0:
Zion is an odd park, because its main road is closed to you. The Zion Canyon Scenic Drive, which runs up the Virgin River valley between towering sandstone cliffs, is generally given over to shuttle buses for most of the year, and the spot where it leaves Highway 9 is Canyon Junction. The shuttle stop is a few steps from the road, with the Watchman rising behind it, a blunt buttress of red rock. The motorcycle stays on Highway 9, which means the real ride starts here, up the switchbacks toward the east.

The Zion-Mount Carmel Highway is one of the most spectacular short roads in the western United States. It follows Pine Creek out of the main canyon in a series of six tight switchbacks, climbing through pale Navajo sandstone cliffs toward the famous tunnel. Behind you, the canyon opens, and the rock walls, in shades of cream, pink and red, lean overhead. The road was built in the late 1920s and opened in 1930, a major piece of engineering in its day, and the stonework on the walls and bridges still looks tidy.

Because Zion is one of the most visited parks in the country, the junction and the road are crowded in spring, summer and autumn. Plan around it by arriving early, ideally before eight, or in the evening, when the light is lovely. Summer afternoons can be fiercely hot and thundery, and flash flood warnings are common. Winter is quieter and cold, with the odd icy morning. The speed limit is low, and rangers enforce it, with good reason: tourists, cyclists and deer all share the road.

The entry fee is payable at the park gate in Springdale, and parking at the visitor centre fills early. Springdale, just outside the south entrance, has fuel, restaurants, supermarkets and a good choice of motels, though it is busy and prices reflect the view. Hurricane, further west, is a bigger town with more choice. Carry water, a hat and sunscreen even in cool weather, and treat the walls with respect.
t.zion mount carmel tunnel@37.2,-113.0:
The Zion-Mount Carmel Tunnel is a long, narrow bore through a cliff, a mile and a tenth from end to end, and it was one of the great engineering gambles of its time. Crews working in the late 1920s drilled it by hand and dynamite through solid sandstone, and carved a series of windows in the canyon-side wall to let in light and let out dust. Those openings are still there, glimpses of daylight and drop and sky that flash by as you ride, which is as close as you will come to being inside a cathedral on a motorcycle. The tunnel opened in 1930, and for a long time it was the only way across the plateau.

For riders, the tunnel is a unique experience. It is dark, with a low ceiling, cool air and a distinct smell of damp rock, and your headlight should be on. The bore is narrow, and the park service has long regulated large vehicles: they pay a fee and use the centre of the road, and traffic is stopped in the opposite direction while they pass. Motorcycles do not need an escort, but you may find yourself waiting for a motorhome, and the queue of idling engines in a tunnel is a good argument for patience. Stopping inside is forbidden.

The approach is up the Pine Creek switchbacks from Canyon Junction, six tight bends climbing steadily through gorgeous cream and pink rock. East of the tunnel the road emerges into open slickrock country, a gentle, rolling landscape of white domes and pine, very different from the canyon below. In winter, ice and snow can close the road, and spring and autumn are the pleasantest seasons for riding. Watch for bighorn sheep, which often graze near the road.

The nearest fuel is at Springdale on the west or at Mount Carmel Junction on the east, so fill up beforehand. Hildale and Colorado City are on the other side of the plateau, and Hurricane is the largest town nearby. There is no stopping at the tunnel, no services and no water, so plan your breaks before and after. The east side has a viewpoint and a few pull-outs, and the park charges an entry fee at the gate.
t.checkerboard mesa@37.2,-112.9:
Checkerboard Mesa looks as though someone has scored a giant loaf of bread with a ruler. The great dome of Navajo sandstone is crossed by two sets of lines, one set horizontal and curving, and the other vertical and straight, and the effect is a checkerboard pattern that runs the height of the rock. The horizontal lines are the ancient dunes, the sloping layers laid down by wind in a desert some 190 million years ago. The vertical cracks came later, as the rock shrank and the stone dried and split, and weathering has deepened both.

The pull-out is right beside the Zion-Mount Carmel Highway, a short distance east of the tunnel, and it is one of the easiest geology lessons you will ever get. You do not need to climb or walk; you can sit on the bike and look. The mesa is the first thing you see after the road exits the narrow canyon, and the sense of opening out is wonderful. On a clear day, in the right light, the sandstone turns from cream to peach to orange, and the shadows in the cracks pick out the pattern.

The riding here is the best bit of the highway. East of the tunnel, the road is rolling and open, with broad curves and good visibility across a landscape of white slickrock, juniper and pinyon pine. The speed limit is low, there are bighorn sheep and mule deer, and the sky is huge. Drive time to Mount Carmel Junction is relatively short. In the early morning there are few people, and in the afternoon the hot sun and wind can make the roadside feel exposed, so a layer and a water bottle both help.

The parking area is small and the access is easy, so it fills up fast on summer days. Mount Carmel Junction, about twenty minutes to the east, has a small fuel stop and cafes, and Kanab, further east, is a larger town with more choice. Springdale, on the west, has everything but is a long way back. Keep an eye out for livestock and sudden weather, particularly in thunderstorm season.
t.mount carmel junction@37.2,-112.7:
Mount Carmel Junction is hardly a settlement at all, just a crossroads on US 89 where the road from Zion comes out onto the high plateau, with a motel, a diner and a petrol pump or two. But after the narrow gorges and tunnels you have come through, its openness is a relief. The land is a wide, pale, sage-covered plateau, with low pink cliffs in the distance, and a big sky overhead.

The rock around here is Navajo Sandstone, the same formation that makes the great walls of Zion, but here it lies in broad, bare domes and ridges, with long arcs of cross-bedding that show where wind once piled up ancient sand dunes some hundred and ninety million years ago. The lines on the rock are the faces of those dunes, frozen in stone. Checkerboard Mesa, a short distance back toward the park, is a good example, with its pattern of grooves and cracks looking like a chessboard, and it is one of the most photographed features along the road.

For riders, the junction is a decision point. Turn north and US 89 runs toward Bryce Canyon, with its forest of orange spires, about an hour away. Turn south and you reach Kanab, a small town with a long film history, and the road to Lake Powell and the Arizona strip. To the south-west lie the Coral Pink Sand Dunes, a state park where wind has piled sand the colour of salmon. The riding on the plateau is relaxed, with long straights, gentle hills and little traffic.

Services at the junction itself are limited, so check your tank. Kanab, about twenty-four kilometres south, has more fuel, restaurants and motels, and Fredonia, just over the Arizona line, is also an option. Summer days are hot, but the plateau is high, at around five thousand feet, so nights are cool. Afternoon storms can come up quickly, and the colours after rain are intense. Bring water and sunscreen, and expect wind. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable times.
t.bryce canyon@37.6,-112.2:
Calling Bryce a canyon is generous, since it is really a series of enormous amphitheatres eaten into the edge of the Paunsaugunt Plateau, and what fills them is a forest of stone. The hoodoos, as these spires are called, stand in crowds of orange, pink, and cream, some as tall as a ten-storey building, all of them carved by frost. Water seeps into cracks in the soft limestone, freezes at night, thaws by day, and slowly prises the rock apart. The cycle happens on well over a hundred nights a year, which is why the place looks so unfinished.

The Paiute people had a story for it. They said the hoodoos were the Legend People, turned to stone by a trickster as punishment, and standing at the rim in the low light it is not hard to see why the idea took hold. The park takes its name from Ebenezer Bryce, a Mormon settler who ran cattle here in the 1870s and is said to have described it as a hell of a place to lose a cow. Whether he said exactly that or not, the line has lasted longer than his homestead.

The ride in is a spur off Utah Highway 12, heading south on Highway 63 and then onto the park road along the plateau rim. The road is smooth, with gentle gradients, and rises past pine and aspen to viewpoints at some eight to nine thousand feet. Altitude matters more than the road does: mornings are cold even in summer, and the air at the rim is thin enough to make a short walk feel longer than it should. Expect slow tourist traffic and plenty of pull-offs. Winter can bring snow, though the main road is usually kept clear.

Services are limited near the rim, though the lodge and a few shops nearby keep riders watered and fed. For fuel, Panguitch, about thirty kilometres north, is the safe choice, and the communities along Highway 12 are small. Go for sunrise if you can bear the early start; the light at the amphitheatre in the first hour of day is the reason this park has the reputation it does. Take a jacket, and walk at least a few steps below the rim, where the hoodoos close around you and the silence is complete.
t.kodachrome basin@37.5,-112.0:
The name is a piece of advertising that turned into geography. In 1948 a National Geographic expedition passed through this corner of southern Utah, struck by the colours of the rock, and named it after Kodachrome, the film that Kodak had made famous. The state later adopted the name for the park, and it has stuck, which tells you something about how intense the reds, pinks, and whites of the cliffs can look in good light.

What makes the basin unusual is not the colour but the stone pipes. Dozens of narrow, chimney-like columns stand scattered across the valley floor, ranging from a few metres to the height of a small building. They are sand pipes, formed when sediment filled ancient springs and then hardened, and as the surrounding softer rock eroded away, the pipes were left standing. There are said to be around sixty or so, and geologists still argue about exactly how they formed, which is oddly comforting.

The road to the park runs south from the village of Cannonville, roughly ten miles, and is paved and easy. It leaves Highway 12 and the crowds behind, and the basin itself is a quiet place with a campground, a few short trails, and views across to the cliffs of Grosvenor Arch country. A gentle road loops through the basin, and it is the sort of place where you cut the engine and listen to the wind. The ride on Highway 12 around it is better than most, with long, high-desert curves that climb through juniper and sagebrush and drop into red-walled valleys.

Do not look for fuel here. Cannonville and Tropic are small, and it is safer to fill the tank in Panguitch or Escalante, which is a good-sized stop on the byway and has stations and cafes. Water is available at the park, but carry your own on any walk, because the sun is fierce, particularly from June to August. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons, and a winter morning with a dusting of snow on the pipes can be astonishing. Afternoon storms in late summer bring flash floods in the washes, so keep an eye on the sky and stay out of the dry channels.
t.hogsback@37.8,-111.4:
The Hogsback is where Highway 12 stops being a road and becomes an experience. Between Escalante and Boulder, the road climbs onto a narrow ridge of Navajo sandstone, with a steep drop on both sides and the canyons of the Escalante River spread far below. For a mile or two there is no verge, no barrier worth the name, and nothing to look at but a lot of air. Nervous riders slow down; confident ones slow down more, because the view is worth it.

The land here is a maze of slickrock domes, canyons, and mesas, cut by the Escalante and its tributaries into one of the last river systems in the lower forty-eight to be mapped. It was so remote that it was the last part of the continental United States to be charted. The road itself is a story of stubbornness: Boulder was so isolated that mail arrived by mule until 1940, and the highway across the Hogsback was not paved until the 1980s. When it was, Boulder lost something of its seclusion and gained a steady stream of curious visitors.

The riding is the best on the byway for sheer drama. The corners are open, with big views, and the gradient is steady, though the road is narrow and the surface can have patches of gravel. There is little room for error, so stay in your lane, keep your speed modest, and take photographs from a pull-off rather than the saddle. Wind can blow across the ridge with real force, especially in spring, and in winter ice can form on the shaded slopes. Rain turns the red dust into mud, so check the forecast.

Services are far apart. Escalante, to the southwest, has fuel and food and is the most sensible place to fill up, and Boulder, to the northeast, has a few places to eat. Do not rely on anything on the ridge itself. The light is best in the morning or late afternoon, when the rock glows and the canyons fill with shadows, and the best time of year is spring or autumn, before the heat of midsummer or the cold of winter. The sense of space is something you do not forget.
t.boulder utah@37.9,-111.4:
Boulder is one of those small places whose story is almost better than the scenery, and the scenery is excellent. Tucked beneath the dark flanks of Boulder Mountain in south-central Utah, it was so remote that mail was carried in by mule until the 1940s, which made it the last community in the contiguous United States to get its post that way. The highway that now links it with Escalante, completed only in the mid-1980s, ended its isolation, and the village has absorbed visitors with good grace.

It sits at about 6,700 feet, in a small valley of red rock, aspen, and green pasture, with the Aquarius Plateau above it. The plateau is among the highest forested plateaus in North America, rising to more than eleven thousand feet, and holds dozens of lakes and cold streams. Nearby, an excavated Ancestral Puebloan village, now a small state museum, shows how people lived here a thousand years ago. Boulder also marks the start of the Burr Trail, a road that runs east through spectacular slickrock country toward Capitol Reef and Lake Powell, partly paved and partly dirt.

For a rider, Boulder is a satisfying end to the Hogsback section of Highway 12. From here the road climbs north over the mountain, with gradual bends and big views, and the surface is good. It is a mountain road, so the weather matters: snow can close the high part in winter, and summer thunderstorms can bring hail. The road across the plateau reaches over nine thousand feet, and it is much cooler than the desert below. Wildlife, including deer and cattle, can wander onto the road.

Fuel is a question. Boulder is small, and a station is not something to rely on, so plan to fill up in Escalante to the south or Torrey to the north before you commit to the mountain. There is good food in the village, from simple lunches to surprisingly inventive dinners that use local produce, and the pace of life is gentle. If the day is hot, a stop in the shade of the cottonwoods is welcome. Autumn is the season for aspen gold, while late spring brings green meadows and snow still lying on the high ground.
t.capitol reef@38.3,-111.3:
The name sounds like a Washington joke, but Capitol Reef is real, and so is the long wrinkle in the earth it protects. The Waterpocket Fold is a hundred-mile buckle in the crust, a monocline where the rocks on the west were lifted several thousand feet above those on the east, and then eroded into a maze of cliffs, domes, and canyons. Early travellers called the barrier a reef, like a reef in the sea, and the white domes of Navajo sandstone looked to them like the Capitol building. Hence the name.

The ride arrives at the little oasis of Fruita, where the Fremont River cuts through the fold and a group of Mormon pioneers planted orchards in the late nineteenth century. They are still there. The park maintains the apricot, cherry, apple and peach trees, and in season you can pick fruit in the orchards and pay by weight at the honour boxes. Nearby is a small historic homestead where they bake fruit pies, which people drive hours to eat. Petroglyphs left by the Fremont culture, who lived here a thousand years ago and more, are carved into a cliff beside the highway, and a boardwalk lets you stand under them.

On the bike, Highway 24 is a joy through the park, winding between red cliffs, with the road following the river and then rising through badlands. From the west, the Scenic Byway 12 comes over Boulder Mountain at nearly three thousand metres, with cold air and aspen forest, and drops into red-rock country. The surface is good and the corners are open and fast, with long views. Watch for deer and cattle on open range, and for gusty winds on the ridges. Summer is hot, with thunderstorms and flash floods in the canyons, and winter snow can close the high passes. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Services are limited. The nearest big fuel stop is in Torrey, about eleven miles west, and the park does not sell fuel, so top up before you come. Loa, a bit farther, is another option. The Fruita campground is a shaded place to rest, with deer wandering through the orchard at dusk.

Take a short drive on the park's scenic road in the late afternoon, when the sun slants low across the fold and every ledge turns to copper.
t.necropolis of puttu codinu@40.5,8.5:
Domus de janas means houses of the fairies, and that is what Sardinians called the small chambers cut into rock faces across the island, believing them to be the homes of tiny supernatural women. They are in fact tombs, carved out by the island's Neolithic and Copper Age people some five thousand years ago, often with rooms arranged like houses, carved doorways, false roof beams and symbols such as bulls' horns. The necropolis of Puttu Codinu, near Villanova Monteleone in north-west Sardinia, is a group of these tombs cut into a low limestone outcrop amid fields and scrub, one of thousands across the island.

The tombs are small and simple from outside, but crawl inside one and the care of the carving is striking, with the walls smoothed and the doorways framed. Some have been reused over thousands of years, and finds from them are in the archaeological museums at Sassari and Alghero. Look for the signs from the road, and take a torch.

Villanova Monteleone is a hill village of over two thousand people, with stone houses on a ridge between the Temo valley and the sea, and on a clear day you can see the coast and the Capo Caccia headland from the village. The road from here down to Alghero winds through cork oak forests, olive groves and pastures, a lovely ride with little traffic. Lake Temo, a reservoir to the east, is a quiet place surrounded by woods.

The great ride in this area is the coast road between Alghero and Bosa, the SP105, which runs along cliffs high above the sea for some forty kilometres, with almost no buildings, sweeping views and griffon vultures overhead. It is one of the finest coastal roads in Italy, and it can be windy. Fuel and supplies are available in Villanova Monteleone, Ittiri and Alghero, and the local food includes roast suckling pig, pecorino, and the seafood of Alghero, especially lobster. Spring and autumn are perfect, while summer brings heat and crowds on the coast.
t.hills of barbaresco@44.7,8.1:
Barbaresco is a hill, a village, a tower and a wine, and in the Langhe those things are hard to separate. The village sits on a ridge above the Tanaro river a few kilometres northeast of Alba, its medieval brick tower standing over rows of vines that roll off in every direction like a green sea frozen mid-swell. Together with the neighbouring Barolo country and the Roero and Monferrato, these hills form the vineyard landscape of Piedmont listed by UNESCO in 2014.

The grape is Nebbiolo, named, some say, after the autumn fog, the nebbia, that settles in the valleys at harvest time. Barbaresco wine is pale garnet, fragrant and firm, and the cellars of the village and of nearby Neive and Treiso welcome visitors, often with a tasting in a cool vaulted room. Neive, with its well preserved hilltop core, is one of the prettiest villages in Italy by any measure. And then there is Alba, famous for its white truffles; the international truffle fair runs on autumn weekends, and the whole town smells of them. Ferrero, the chocolate company behind Nutella, began here too.

For riding, the Langhe could have been designed by someone who loves motorcycles. Narrow roads climb and fall over ridges, linking villages with views of the Alps on the horizon, and every crest brings a new vista. The bends are endless, sometimes tight and steep, often lined by vines rather than barriers. Watch out for tractors at harvest, gravel washed onto the road after storms, cyclists and visitors driving slowly as they look for wineries. Spring and autumn are perfect, with October bringing golden vines and that famous fog in the mornings.

Alba has around twenty-five thousand people and plenty of fuel and services, and small towns nearby have petrol stations too. Food is part of the pilgrimage: vitello tonnato, tajarin pasta with butter and sage or truffle, and hazelnut cake made with the local nuts. If you plan to taste, arrange a stop for the night, because the hills around here deserve to be ridden with a clear head.
t.nizza monferrato and barbera@44.8,8.3:
Barbera is the everyday red of Piedmont, the wine on every trattoria table, and around Nizza Monferrato it has been raised to something more serious. The hills between Nizza, Vinchio, Castelnuovo Calcea and Mombercelli are covered in vines, planted in rows that follow the contours of the slopes, and the best wines from this area carry their own designation, Nizza DOCG, made from barbera alone. The vineyard landscapes of Langhe-Roero and Monferrato were listed by UNESCO in 2014, and this corner of the Asti hills is a fine example of what that means: a working landscape shaped by centuries of farming, with hilltop villages, brick churches, and small family wineries at the end of gravel tracks.

The riding is excellent, in a low-key way. The roads follow the ridges and dip into the valleys, with a constant series of bends, short climbs and descents, and views that open up across the vineyards to the distant Alps on clear days. The surfaces vary from smooth to rough, and some of the smaller roads are narrow and steep. Traffic is light outside the harvest season, when tractors and trailers loaded with grapes take over in September and October. Autumn is the most beautiful time to ride here, when the vines turn yellow and red and the morning fog fills the valleys, leaving the hilltops floating in the sunshine.

Vinchio is the home village of the writer and partisan Davide Lajolo, and the hills around it are protected as a small nature reserve, the Val Sarmassa, with woods and walking paths among the vines. Nizza Monferrato, about five kilometres away, is a lively market town of over eight thousand people, known for its arcaded streets and its local variety of cardoon, the cardo gobbo, which is grown bent over under soil to keep it pale and tender and is the classic accompaniment to bagna cauda, the warm garlic and anchovy dip of Piedmont.

Fuel and services are easy to find in Nizza and the larger villages. The local food is rich and seasonal, with truffles in autumn, hand-cut pasta, and hearty meat dishes. Many wineries offer tastings, but remember that you are riding: buy a few bottles and save them for the evening.
t.grinzane cavour castle@44.7,8.0:
Count Camillo Benso di Cavour, the man who more or less engineered the unification of Italy, spent years as mayor of this little Langhe village before he went on to bigger things, and the square brick castle on its knoll still carries his name. He experimented with winemaking here too, at a time when Barolo was still finding its modern form, so the building sits at a neat crossroads of Piedmontese politics and Piedmontese wine.

Today the castle houses a regional wine shop and museum, and every November it hosts the famous auction of Alba white truffles, when a few knobbly fungi change hands for sums that would buy a decent motorcycle. The rooms inside hold displays on truffle hunting, local crafts and Cavour himself, and the terrace gives a wide look over the rows of Nebbiolo vines folding away towards Barolo, La Morra and Serralunga. The vineyard landscapes of the Langhe, Roero and Monferrato were inscribed by UNESCO in 2014, and from up here you understand why.

As riding country the Langhe is a delight once you accept it is not fast. The roads climb from the Tanaro valley onto narrow ridges, snake through vineyards with tight hairpins and drop into villages where the street becomes a single lane between stone houses. Surfaces vary from fresh to patched, and in autumn you share them with tractors hauling grapes and with slow cars full of wine tourists. Late September and October are glorious, with the vines turning gold and red and fog lying in the valleys in the morning. Summer afternoons can be hot and hazy, and the light is best early or in the hour before sunset.

Alba is six kilometres away and has everything a rider needs: fuel on the ring roads, mechanics, and an old centre of towers and arcades where a plate of tajarin with butter, or with truffle if the season and your wallet allow, is close to compulsory. Hazelnuts are the other local obsession; Alba is the home town of Ferrero, and Piedmont's tonda gentile nuts turn up in cakes in every bar. If you are tasting wine, do it after you have parked the bike for the day.
t.katsuren jo site@26.3,127.9:
Katsuren castle stands on a limestone hill on the east coast of Okinawa, near the base of the Katsuren peninsula, and its curving walls step up the slope in a series of enclosures to a summit with sweeping views across the sea. It is one of the gusuku, the castles of the old Ryukyu kingdom and the warring lords who came before it, and it was inscribed in 2000 together with Nakijin, Zakimi, Nakagusuku, Shuri and several sacred groves.

The castle is associated with Amawari, a fifteenth-century lord who grew rich on trade and became powerful enough to challenge the king himself. In the Ryukyu court histories, he is cast as a villain who attacked a loyal rival and was destroyed for it, but in local tradition he is remembered as a popular hero who looked after his people. Excavations here have turned up Chinese porcelain and other foreign goods, a reminder that this little island was at the crossroads of trade routes linking China, Japan, Korea and Southeast Asia. The wall stones are fitted together with impressive precision, and the smooth curves are typical of Okinawan castle design.

From the top you can see the Kaichu-dōro, a long causeway road running straight out across the shallow sea to Henza island, and beyond it to Miyagi and Ikei islands. Riding it is a highlight of any trip to Okinawa: water on both sides, often turquoise, and the islands at the end with small villages, beaches and the odd sugar cane field. Wind can be strong on the causeway, and sudden tropical downpours are common.

Okinawa's roads are well kept and drive on the left, as in mainland Japan. Traffic around Okinawa City and Uruma can be heavy, and speed limits are low and carefully observed. Katsuren-haebaru and the surrounding towns are well served with fuel stations, convenience stores and restaurants. Try Okinawa soba, pork belly rafute, goya champuru, and the local Orion beer when you are done riding for the day. Typhoons hit between summer and autumn, so check forecasts.
t.necropolis of mandras@40.1,9.0:
Cut into a slope of volcanic rock above the valley of the Tirso, near the village of Ardauli in central Sardinia, the Necropolis of Mandras is a cluster of prehistoric tombs that the Sardinians call domus de janas, houses of the fairies or witches. They were carved out of the rock with stone tools by farming communities, mostly in the late Neolithic, and some of the chambers imitate the inside of a house, with carved beams, doorways and pillars. Folklore said they were built by tiny women who wove gold at night, and in a sense the name says more about how ancient they felt to later generations than any date could.

The tombs look out over Lake Omodeo, the largest artificial lake on the island, created in the 1920s by damming the Tirso. The rising water drowned the old village of Zuri, but its Romanesque church of San Pietro was taken down stone by stone and rebuilt on higher ground, where you can still see it today with its red and grey stone. The lake gives this area of the Barigadu a softer feel than much of inner Sardinia, with reed beds, herons and fishermen at the water's edge, and the hills around are covered with cork oak, holm oak and scrub.

The roads around the lake and up through Neoneli, Nughedu Santa Vittoria and Sorradile are a gift to riders: narrow, twisting and hilly, with little traffic and constant changes of view between water and wooded ridges. Surfaces are mostly decent but can be broken or gravelly in places, and sheep and goats appear without warning, especially in the morning and evening when they are moved. In summer the heat is fierce in the afternoons; spring, when the hills are green and full of flowers, is the ideal season.

The villages here are small, a few hundred people each, with a bar or two, a grocer and not much else. For fuel, head towards Ghilarza or Abbasanta on the main road to the west, or to Macomer, the nearest larger town. In the villages, ask at the bar about local food: pecorino, the flat crisp bread called carasau and roast suckling pig at festivals. The silence up at the tombs, broken only by bees and the occasional bell from a flock, is the real reward.
t.necropolis of brodu@40.3,9.2:
Barbagia is the rugged heart of Sardinia, a land of granite hills, shepherds and fiercely held traditions, and on its western edge, near the village of Oniferi, the rock-cut tombs of Brodu are among the most elaborate on the island. Like other domus de janas, these chambers were carved into the stone by the people of the Neolithic Ozieri culture and later, but here several of them have carved decoration inside: false doors, imitation roof beams and, in some, the curved horn motifs that are thought to represent the bull, a symbol of strength and fertility that appears again and again in Sardinian prehistory.

The area around Oniferi, Orotelli and Orani is a good place to see how deep those traditions run. Orotelli has its own carnival masks, the thurpos, men in dark cloaks with blackened faces who play out a strange ritual of ploughing and yoked oxen. Orani was the birthplace of the sculptor Costantino Nivola, and a museum dedicated to his work sits in the village. Nuoro, the provincial capital just to the east, gave the world Grazia Deledda, the novelist who won the Nobel Prize for literature in 1926, and her house there is open to visitors.

Riding here is excellent but asks for attention. The main SS131 dual carriageway between Abbasanta and Nuoro gets you in quickly, but the real pleasure is on the smaller roads that wind across the hills between the villages, with tight bends, short climbs, granite outcrops and wide views across valleys of cork oak and pasture. The surfaces are often rough, and there is always the possibility of livestock on the road. Up towards Monte Ortobene above Nuoro, the road climbs in a series of curves through pines to a statue of the Redeemer and views over the Barbagia.

Nuoro, about thirteen kilometres away, is the place for fuel, food, accommodation and workshops. The villages have small bars where you can get a coffee and a sandwich with local cheese, and in the right season you may be offered a glass of Cannonau, the dark red wine of the region. Spring and early autumn are the best times; in midsummer the heat on the open hillsides is intense, and the necropolis offers little shade beyond a few trees.
t.domus de janas of roccia dell elefante@4:
On the side of the main road below Castelsardo, in northern Sardinia, a huge reddish rock stands alone at a bend, and it really does look like an elephant, trunk lowered, as if about to drink. It is a block of volcanic trachyte that broke away from the hills above and was sculpted by wind and rain into its strange shape. What most passing drivers miss is that its base was used long before anyone thought of elephants: two prehistoric tombs, domus de janas, were cut into the rock in the Neolithic period, and in one of them carved horn shapes, the symbol of the bull, can still be made out.

The area around is called the Anglona, a region of low volcanic hills, cork oaks, pastures and small villages between the Gulf of Asinara and the Coghinas valley. Castelsardo, a few kilometres away, is one of the most striking towns in Sardinia: a medieval citadel piled on a rocky promontory above the sea, founded by the Genoese Doria family, later held by the Aragonese and named for them Castillo Aragonés before it took its present name. The castle houses a museum of woven baskets, a craft the town's women still practise, and you will see their work for sale in the lanes.

The roads here are a pleasure. The SS134 runs past the elephant and links up with the coast road, which runs along the gulf towards Valledoria and Isola Rossa, with sea views and quick, flowing bends. Inland, roads to Sedini, Bulzi and Perfugas twist through the hills, with small Romanesque churches standing alone in the countryside. The mistral, the strong north-west wind, can blow hard across the gulf and push you around on exposed stretches, and the coastal road gets busy in August.

There is a small parking area at the rock and usually someone selling local products in season, but no other facilities. Castelsardo has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants, and is the natural base; Sennori and Sorso, further west towards Sassari, are larger towns. Eat seafood in Castelsardo, perhaps lobster in the Catalan style, and if you have time, visit the beach at Lu Bagnu just below the town for a swim before riding on.
t.isola del tinetto@44.0,9.9:
