Three islands trail off the tip of the Porto Venere peninsula like stepping stones: Palmaria, the largest, then Tino, and finally the Tinetto, a bare rock with the ruins of an early medieval monastic settlement and a small lighthouse beacon. Together with Porto Venere and the Cinque Terre, they form a World Heritage Site, listed for the way people shaped this rugged coast with terraces, villages and fortifications. The Tinetto is home to a rare lizard found only on these islands, and the waters around are rich in marine life.

Porto Venere is a gem of a village, with tall, narrow, colourful houses lining the harbour, a Genoese castle above, and the church of San Pietro on a rocky point at the end of the peninsula, with views over the sea and the cliffs of the Cinque Terre. Byron's Grotto, a sea cave below the church, is named after the poet, who is said to have swum from here across the gulf to Lerici to visit Shelley.

The Gulf of La Spezia, also called the Gulf of Poets, was a favourite of the English Romantics. Shelley lived at San Terenzo, near Lerici, and drowned in a storm off the coast in 1822. Lerici, with its castle and harbour, is a lovely town across the gulf.

The road from La Spezia to Porto Venere follows the western shore of the gulf, through Le Grazie and Fezzano, narrow and winding with views over the water, and busy in summer. Parking in Porto Venere is very limited, and a bike is a great advantage. The road over the hills toward the Cinque Terre is twisting and dramatic, with steep drops to the sea. Boats run from Porto Venere around the islands, a great way to see the Tinetto up close.

Fuel is available in La Spezia and Lerici, eight kilometres away by sea but much further by road. Restaurants in Porto Venere serve fresh seafood, including mussels from the gulf, and the local pesto and focaccia. Summer is very busy; spring and autumn are calmer.
t.petroglyph park a@40.5,8.7:
The north-west of Sardinia is a country of low volcanic hills, pasture, cork oak and stone, and the villages of the Logudoro are small, quiet and far older than they look. This area, around Cheremule and Giave, is dotted with traces of a world that predates the Romans by a very long time. The island's prehistoric people carved tombs into soft rock, the domus de janas, which translates as fairy houses, and built round stone towers called nuraghi, of which there are thousands.

Around here, domus de janas are cut into rock faces and boulders, sometimes with painted or carved details in the chambers such as horned symbols and false doors, and they are thought to be several thousand years old. The best known of the nuraghi in the area, Santu Antine at Torralba, only a short ride away, is a huge three-lobed tower with a corridor and a stair, and it is worth the detour.

The riding is some of the best on Sardinia and almost nobody is on the roads. Smooth, curving two-lane routes cross the high plateau and drop into little valleys, with views over cork forests and open grassland dotted with sheep. The main arteries, the SS131 and SS597, are fast and easy, while the smaller roads can be rough with potholes, loose gravel and sleepy livestock, so keep an eye on the surface. Spring brings flowers and green hills, autumn is mellow, and August is hot and dry with wildfires an occasional risk.

Cheremule and Giave are very small, with a bar or two and not much else, and fuel is a concern. Ittiri, about eighteen kilometres away, is the closest sizeable town and has pumps, as does Thiesi and Bonorva, and it is wise to top up there before heading into the quiet country. Pecorino, flatbread and a strong red from the island are the right things to find in a village bar, and Sunday lunch is serious business in Sardinia, so do not expect a quick bite at two in the afternoon.
t.funerary tradition in the prehistory of:
The high country of central Sardinia, between the Tirso river and the hills of the Barbagia, is a landscape of basalt plateaus, cork forests, small stone villages and long, empty views. The nearest places on our list, Nughedu Santa Vittoria and Neoneli, are small villages with only a few hundred people each, and the town of Macomer is some twenty-five kilometres away. The prehistoric story here is about how the island's early people treated their dead, and the title reflects that.

Sardinia is full of tombs. The domus de janas, rock-cut chambers dug into stone outcrops from the fifth millennium BC onward, are the most common, and they are often carved to resemble houses, with roof beams, doorways and hearths cut in the rock. Later came the giants' tombs, long communal graves with a curved stone front, built by the Nuragic civilisation.

The roads are lovely and lightly used. The route along the Tirso valley and Lake Omodeo, one of the biggest artificial lakes in Italy, has smooth long bends and views over shining water, and the climbs into the hills offer short, tight sections with good surfaces. Livestock, loose stones, sunbaked tarmac and the occasional wild boar are the hazards. In spring the hillsides are green and yellow with broom, while summer is hot and dry, and autumn brings mushrooms and mist.

For something to see on the way, the Nuraghe Losa, near Abbasanta, is one of the best-preserved Nuragic towers on the island and well worth a stop. Ghilarza, a short run away, was the childhood home of Antonio Gramsci, and the house is now a small museum. Fuel can be hard to find in the small villages, so use the pumps at Macomer, Abbasanta or Ghilarza when you pass. Sardinian lunch is long and generous, with roast pork, sheep's cheese and carasau, the thin crisp bread, so plan your timing accordingly.
t.agua ize@0.2,6.7:
Agua Izé was once the grandest of São Tomé's roças, the great plantation estates that made this tiny island, just north of the equator, one of the world's leading cocoa producers in the early twentieth century. It lies on the southeast coast, about thirteen kilometres from the capital, and the buildings tell the story: a big administrative house, long workers' quarters, a hospital, storehouses and drying platforms, all now peeling and softened by tropical growth. Walls are flaking yellow and ochre, and roofs sag, but the scale is unmistakable.

Behind the architecture lies a hard history. The roças ran on contract labour brought from Angola, Cape Verde and Mozambique, under conditions that were bitterly criticised abroad. Portugal's rule ended in 1975, and the estates were later broken up, leaving communities of descendants who still live in the old quarters. People hang washing from the verandahs, children play on the drying platforms, and the plantation feels like a village built inside a ruin. Be respectful when you wander, and ask before photographing people.

The riding is slow and sensual. The coastal road is paved in places and punishing in others, pitted with potholes that fill with rain, and traffic is a mix of minibuses, motorbike taxis and pedestrians who stroll along the edge. Mountains of dense rainforest rise inland, and palm trees lean over the sea. The humidity is heavy, so you will be sweating within minutes, and sudden downpours can drench you, especially from October to May. The drier gravana season, roughly June to September, is easier.

Fuel and food come from São Tomé town, a place of about fifty thousand, so fill the tank there before heading out. Along the coast you will find small shops and a few simple eateries serving grilled fish, breadfruit and fried banana. Cocoa still grows in the shade of taller trees, and in the drying season you may smell fermenting beans, rich and sour. Dark chocolate from the island is sold in the capital and is worth carrying home.
t.diogo vaz@0.3,6.5:
Diogo Vaz is a roça, one of the old plantation estates that once covered most of São Tomé, the small island in the Gulf of Guinea that straddles the equator. The Portuguese found the island uninhabited in the fifteenth century, settled it with enslaved labour from the mainland and grew sugar, and later, in the nineteenth century, built an economy on cocoa and coffee. By the early twentieth century São Tomé was among the world's leading cocoa producers, and the roças, each with a manor house, a hospital, a drying yard and a village of workers, were small worlds of their own.

The legacy is painful. The labour was brutal, whether slave, contract or forced, and in 1953 colonial authorities carried out the Batepá massacre against islanders. After independence in 1975, the roças were taken over by the state and then fell into decay, and today many stand half empty, with peeling paint, rusting machinery and families still living in the old workers' quarters. Diogo Vaz, on the north-west coast, has the typical layout, with its drying platforms and buildings set among cocoa trees and palms, and it makes a haunting visit.

The island is a place of intense green, with volcanic peaks wrapped in cloud, steep forested slopes and black sand beaches, and the smell of fermenting cocoa beans, sweet and sour, hangs around the plantations. In recent years small producers have revived the quality chocolate trade, and some estates now offer tours, so you can taste the beans and see the process. Monte Café, the coffee roça in the hills, is the other stop on this ride.

The ring road around the north of the island has some good stretches and many potholes, with goats, chickens, children and the occasional taxi sharing the surface. The weather is warm and humid all year, and the main rainy season runs from September to May, which can make the dirt tracks to the estates slippery. The drier months from June to August are the most comfortable. São Tomé city, about twenty-six kilometres away, is the only place with reliable fuel and supplies, so fill the tank before you go. Roadside stalls sell grilled fish, fried banana and breadfruit, and the coffee is excellent.
t.isola del tino@44.0,9.9:
Isola del Tino is an island you are almost never allowed to visit. It lies just off the southern tip of the Ligurian coast, a short distance beyond Portovenere and the island of Palmaria, and it belongs to the Italian navy, which keeps it as a military zone. The one exception is the feast of San Venerio, on the thirteenth of September, when boats ferry visitors across and the public may walk on the island for the day. Venerius was a hermit who lived on the island, and the ruins of a medieval monastery built in his honour stand among the pines and rocks.

The scenery is the reward on the mainland side. Portovenere is a compact harbour village of tall, narrow, pastel houses facing the sea, crowned by a Genoese castle and the black and white striped church of San Pietro on a rock above the waves. Lord Byron is said to have swum across to Lerici from here, and the bay carries his name. The whole stretch, with the Cinque Terre next door, is a UNESCO site, though the islands carry a different flavour from the crowded villages to the north.

The ride in from La Spezia is short and charming. The road follows the western shore of the gulf, with views over the water to the marble mountains of Carrara, and then climbs and bends along the cliffs to Portovenere. It is narrow and busy in summer, and parking in the village is very limited, so go early or after the day-trippers leave. Fuel is in La Spezia, a naval city of nearly a hundred thousand people, rather than in the tiny villages of Le Grazie and Portovenere on the peninsula.

Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, when the air is clear and the sea is blue. You can watch the island from a harbour-side bar, with a plate of anchovies or a focaccia, and think about a hermit's life.
t.gusuku sites and related properties of t:
Okinawa was a kingdom of its own until the late nineteenth century, and the gusuku are what is left of its stone fortresses. The word means castle, but these are curving walls of pale coral limestone that follow the shape of a hill, with gateways like keyholes and view platforms over the sea. The Ryukyu Kingdom, which was unified under King Sho Hashi in 1429, traded between China, Japan, Korea and southeast Asia, and grew rich as a middle man, with Shuri as its capital. UNESCO listed the Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu in 2000, among them Shuri Castle, the royal burial place of Tamaudun and the garden of Shikinaen.

The castle at Shuri was largely destroyed in the Battle of Okinawa in 1945, rebuilt after the war, and then badly damaged by fire in October 2019, with reconstruction work continuing afterward. Even so, the walls and gates of the site and the surrounding streets still show the style of the kingdom, with red-tiled roofs, stone lions called shisa against evil spirits, and awamori distilleries in the old district. Further north, Nakagusuku is a different sort of castle, a ridge fortress with elegant curved walls, which the ride list reaches next.

For a rider, Okinawa is a pleasure. Traffic drives on the left, the island's roads are well kept, and speed limits are low, with police and cameras attentive, so patience is rewarded. The built-up area around Naha is slow and congested, with long lines of traffic, but the northern roads on the east coast and the coastal route up to Cape Hedo are delightful in good weather. The island has a subtropical climate. Typhoon season runs from summer to autumn, the rainy season in May and June is wet and humid, and the best months are March to April and October to November.

Fuel is easy in Naha, a city of over three hundred thousand, and in Tomigusuku, where the main roads are lined with stations. Food is a joy: Okinawa soba, goya champuru, a stir-fry of bitter melon, and a glass of awamori, the island's own rice spirit, for those not riding.

Look at the stone of the walls in late afternoon, when the coral limestone turns pale gold against the sky.
t.geiranger@62.1,7.2:
The Geirangerfjord is a narrow cut, around fifteen kilometres long, between cliffs that rise over a thousand metres from the water, and it is among the best-known sights in Norway. The village at its head, Geiranger, is tiny, with only a few hundred residents, but in summer, cruise ships anchor in the fjord one after another and the pier fills with people. UNESCO listed the fjord in 2005, along with Naeroyfjord, and a short walk along the shore brings you to the base of the Seven Sisters waterfall, which pours straight into the fjord from a high ledge.

For a rider, arriving in Geiranger is the best part of the trip. From Eidsdal in the north, the Eagle Road drops through eleven hairpins to the sea, with a grand view of the fjord from the top at Ornesvingen. From the south and east, the road comes down from the high plateau by Djupvatnet, past remote lakes and snow patches, and through a series of tight switchbacks. The Dalsnibba viewpoint, reached by a private toll road, takes you to about 1,500 metres, with a view straight down to the fjord. Roads here have narrow sections, steep gradients and plenty of campervans, so patience helps, and mountain roads usually open only from May to October, depending on snow.

The village itself is a good place for lunch or a waffle with brown cheese. Fuel is the thing to watch. Do not rely on finding it at every stop here, and plan to fill up in Stranda, about twenty-seven kilometres away, or in other larger towns on the route. Weather changes quickly, and a fjord can be sunny at the water and wet at the top.

There is also the ferry to Hellesylt, which carries motorcycles and gives you a different view of the cliffs from the water. Leave early in the morning, when the ships have not yet arrived, and the place feels much closer to what it was.
t.grasse@43.7,6.9:
Grasse smells of something before you can see it. The old perfume capital of France climbs a steep limestone hillside about a dozen kilometres from the Mediterranean, high enough above Cannes to catch a cooler, more mountain air, and for generations the fields of jasmine, rose and tuberose on the terraces around the town fed its distilleries. Perfume came here from the leather trade: glovemakers in the seventeenth century began scenting their gloves, and the business outgrew the leather. Today the town still has big perfume houses and a handful of working fields, and in May the rose harvest and in late summer the jasmine are the times to be around.

For a rider, Grasse is where the sea-level traffic and the real hills meet. A town of nearly fifty thousand people, it has ample petrol, supermarkets, bakeries and cafés, and it makes a sensible stop before heading up toward the Gorges du Verdon or down to the coast. The old centre is a knot of steep one-way lanes, steps, and tall ochre houses with shutters that peel in the sun, and driving through it on a big bike is more of an adventure than anyone needs; leave the machine at the edge and walk up to the Place aux Aires and the cathedral.

The roads around are another matter. Heading north on the D-roads toward the plateau, you climb into the Préalpes de Grasse, where the corners tighten, the pines thicken, and the air smells of thyme and dry earth. The surface is generally decent but narrow, with plenty of blind bends, cyclists in the early morning, and walkers' cars parked on the verges at weekends.

It is worth knowing that summer here is hot and the dust-dry hills are a fire risk, so some forest roads close on bad days. In winter the high ground can be icy even when the coast is warm, and the cold is sharper than you expect from the postcard. In spring the light is soft and the hillside terraces go quiet green.

Pick a table in the sun on one of the squares, get the tank topped up before the hills, and try a socca or a pissaladière if the bakery has them; both are Provençal ways of making a good lunch from almost nothing.
t.isola palmaria@44.0,9.8:
Isola Palmaria is the biggest of the three islands that lie just off the southern tip of the Ligurian coast near Porto Venere, the others being the tiny Tino and Tinetto. Together with the Cinque Terre and Porto Venere itself, they make up a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, and on a clear morning the sight of the cliffs plunging into the water, with pastel houses on the headland opposite, is as good as anything on the Italian coast. The Gulf of La Spezia was nicknamed the Gulf of Poets after the English writers who came here, including Byron, who is said to have swum across to Lerici from a grotto at Porto Venere that now carries his name.

You do not ride onto the island. A short ferry crosses from Porto Venere, and the island itself is a place of footpaths, abandoned military batteries, quarry scars and thick Mediterranean scrub. It was once quarried for Portoro marble, a black stone with golden veins that decorated churches and palaces across Europe. A few farmers and fishermen live on Palmaria, and the paths are rough in places, so wear proper shoes and take water.

What a rider will care about is the road to the water. The coast road from La Spezia to Porto Venere is a narrow, twisting ribbon with the sea close below and stone walls on the other side, a pleasure in spring and a trial in summer, when queues build and parking at the village is limited. Come early, leave the bike at the larger car parks on the approach, and walk the last stretch. Porto Venere has fewer than a thousand people and few services, so fuel is best found in La Spezia or Lerici, the latter a seaside town of nearly nine thousand, with a castle and a long promenade.

The village is worth the effort. The church of San Pietro stands on a rocky promontory where a Roman temple once stood, and its black and white striped stonework glows in late afternoon light, with waves breaking on rocks below. Seafood is the obvious choice for lunch, with mussels from the gulf, trofie with pesto, and farinata, a chickpea pancake baked in a wood oven. Sunset from the headland is a good reason to stay.
t.sonohyan utaki ishimon@26.2,127.7:
Naha is the capital of Okinawa, and the hill above it carries the story of the Ryukyu Kingdom. Sonohyan-utaki Ishimon is the stone gate in front of a small sacred grove at the foot of Shuri castle, and it was where the Ryukyuan kings said a prayer for safe travel before leaving the castle. Built in the early sixteenth century, it is a stone archway with a rounded top and a pair of wooden doors, set into a low wall with a stand of trees behind it. Behind the gate there is no building, only trees and a quiet space, because in Ryukyuan religion the divine presence lives in groves and rocks, not in constructed temples. These sacred places are called utaki, and they were tended by priestesses called noro, a tradition that has not entirely disappeared.

It is a UNESCO site, part of the Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu. The rest of the complex, including Shuri castle, was damaged by a fire in 2019, and reconstruction of the main buildings has been under way since, so it is worth checking what is open before travelling.

Okinawa is a good place to ride, though Naha itself is busy, with heavy traffic, lots of traffic lights and a limited monorail line that crosses the city. Driving is on the left, and drivers are generally polite, but lanes are narrow and parking is tight. Once you leave the city, the roads along the coast, particularly the road north toward Cape Hedo, are scenic, with sea views, sugar cane fields and sections of forest. In summer it is hot and humid, typhoons can arrive from July to October, and sudden squalls can make the road slippery.

Tomigusuku, a city of fifty-five thousand, and Naha, with three hundred thousand, offer fuel, shops, restaurants and everything else, and there is no shortage of petrol stations on the main roads. The local food is distinct from mainland Japan: goya champuru, a stir-fry with bitter melon, rafute, slow-cooked pork belly, Okinawa soba in a pork broth, and awamori, a strong rice spirit. Look out for the shisa, lion-dog statues perched on roofs to ward off evil spirits.

Walk the old stone-paved lane up to the castle if you can, and linger at the gate in the late afternoon, when the light filters through the trees.
t.shuri jo site@26.2,127.7:
Shuri Castle stood on a hill above Naha for roughly five hundred years as the seat of the Ryukyu Kings, and the stone foundations are all that survive of the earlier structures. The kingdom was independent until 1879, when Japan annexed it, and had a long history of trade between China, Japan, Korea and Southeast Asia, which gave the castle a distinctive style. The red-lacquered halls, with Chinese-style roofs, dragon pillars and gold decoration, looked unlike any castle on the Japanese mainland. The main hall burned down in October 2019 in a fire that shocked the island, and reconstruction has been under way since, with work visible to visitors and the date of reopening still to be confirmed.

Even without the main hall, the site is impressive. The great stone walls, curved like waves along the contours of the hill, are made of limestone fitted so tightly that they have withstood earthquakes, typhoons and the heavy fighting of the Second World War. Gateways open one after another as you climb, including the Shureimon, a two-tiered gate with a sign saying land of courtesy, and the stone paving of the old approach is worth walking. From the upper terraces, you can see Naha, the harbour and the sea beyond.

The castle site is part of the UNESCO listing of the Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu. For riders, Shuri is a hillside district on the edge of Naha, so the roads are steep and busy, with parking limited around the entrance. Check the car park rules for motorcycles, and leave early to avoid the tour buses. In the wet, the stone paving is slippery, and the sun in summer is fierce.

Naha and Tomigusuku provide every service, from fuel and supermarkets to small restaurants. For a local meal, try the soki soba, with tender pork ribs, or a plate of umi-budo, sea grapes, in season. The nearby Tamaudun, the royal mausoleum, and the old stone streets of Shuri, with their coral walls and shisa guardians, deserve an hour of your day.

October to May is a more comfortable time than the humid summer, though typhoon season runs into October.
t.shikinaen@26.2,127.7:
Shikinaen is a villa garden on the southern edge of Naha, built at the end of the eighteenth century as a second residence for the Ryukyu royal family. It was also used to host envoys sent from China, who came to invest each new king, and who were treated to feasts, music and walks through the grounds, in a ritual of diplomacy that kept the small kingdom on good terms with its powerful neighbour. The design blends Chinese and Japanese ideas with local ones, with a pond at the centre, a stone bridge, a pavilion and walkways laid out among trees.

The garden was heavily damaged during the Second World War and has been restored, and it is part of the UNESCO listing of the Ryukyu sites. The main building is a low house in the Okinawan style, with a tile roof, open verandas and sliding screens, and it faces the pond with a view of islands in the miniature landscape. The charm lies in the quiet details: stone lanterns, curved bridges, and the shade of old trees. It is a good place to sit for a while on a hot day, and a modest entrance fee is charged.

Riding in southern Okinawa is mostly urban or suburban, with Naha's dense roads and bridges. Traffic moves on the left, often slowly, with many traffic lights, and roadworks are common. In a city where the monorail runs overhead and large American military installations occupy chunks of land, the garden provides a sudden pocket of calm. Parking can be tight, so look for motorbike bays and leave the bike in the shade if possible. Tomigusuku and Naha have every service you might need, including fuel on nearly every main road, convenience stores and many restaurants.

The climate is subtropical, with hot, humid summers and a typhoon season that peaks between August and October. Winters are mild, with temperatures that are comfortable for riding, and the best time to visit is between November and April, when the air is dry and the light is clear.

Afterwards, try a bowl of Okinawan soba, a plate of goya champuru, and a glass of awamori, if you are not riding, or a cup of jasmine tea if you are.
t.col de vars@44.6,6.7:
The Col de Vars is the gentle one on the Route des Grandes Alpes, and it knows how to be pleasant. At 2,108 metres it separates the Guil valley from the valley of the Ubaye, linking Guillestre in the Hautes-Alpes to Barcelonnette on the other side, and from the top you look over rounded grassy slopes, scattered larches and a few farm buildings, with the jagged peaks of the Queyras and the Mercantour at a respectful distance. It lacks the savage edges of the higher passes, and is better for it on a warm day, when the grass smells of thyme and the cowbells carry on the wind.

The climb from Guillestre is long, steady and open, with sweeping bends and a few hairpins near the top, while the descent to Jausiers is a flowing run through larch forest and meadows with good surface and wide corners. On the way up you may pass the ski resort of Vars, a bit worn in summer, and the small chalets and mountain farms of the high pastures. Marmots whistle from the rocks near the road, and in early summer the hillsides are covered with alpine flowers. Because the pass is lower than many on this route, it opens earlier in spring, usually by late May, and stays open later in autumn, but snow can fall at any time of year.

Near Guillestre, at Mont-Dauphin, is the star-shaped fortress that Louis XIV's engineer Vauban built to guard the frontier, now on the UNESCO list with a dozen other Vauban sites. It is a reminder that these passes were once important military routes as well as trade routes. Barcelonnette, on the other side, has a surprising Mexican heritage, since many of its residents emigrated to Mexico in the nineteenth century, returning with fortunes and building colourful villas.

A small cafe or snack stand sometimes operates at the summit in season, but do not rely on it. The best time to ride is early morning or in the evening, when light is warm and traffic at its thinnest, though weekends in July and August are busy with cyclists, as it is a favourite of the Tour de France.
t.col de la bonette@44.3,6.8:
The Col de la Bonette is the high-altitude trophy of the Alps, and it is worth being clear about the statistics. The pass itself is at 2,715 metres, but a loop road branches off to circle the Cime de la Bonette at 2,802 metres, making it the highest paved through road in Europe, or so it is usually claimed. The road was built largely for military reasons in the 1930s, when France worried about its Italian border, and finished in its present form around 1960. Up here, on the border of the Mercantour National Park, the landscape is bare scree and rock, with patches of snow lingering into July, and nothing grows taller than a lichen.

From Jausiers in the north, the road climbs a long valley through larch forest, then opens above the tree line in an enormous bowl, with long, steady hairpins climbing the slope. The surface is generally good, but frost damage and loose gravel at the edges are common, and in places the road narrows. The pass is open from about June to October, and often closes at the first heavy snow, so do check. The descent toward Saint-Étienne-de-Tinée on the south side runs through the old barracks of Restefond, abandoned stone buildings that have been slowly crumbling since the Second World War, and then down a deep, wild valley.

At this altitude the air is thin, the sun fierce and the temperature can be ten degrees colder than in the valley, with fierce wind. Bring windproof layers and gloves even in August. Marmots and chamois are visible if you stop quietly, and ibex have been reintroduced in the area. The views from the summit loop are extensive: peaks stretching toward Italy and, on a clear day, the Mediterranean haze beyond.

Jausiers on the northern side and Saint-Étienne-de-Tinée on the southern side both have pumps, and Embrun, about thirty-seven kilometres away, is the nearest larger town. A small stand sometimes sells drinks at the top in season, but don't count on it. Go early, avoid afternoon storms, and take the loop to the very top, because the point of the exercise is to stand somewhere that most Alpine roads never reach.
t.col de turini@44.0,7.4:
Turini belongs to the Monte Carlo Rally more than to any map. For decades the rally's night stage over this pass has been one of the most famous in motorsport, the Nuit du Turini, when spectators light fires in the forest and cars appear out of the darkness with a wall of floodlights. At 1,607 metres, the col is not especially high, but it is wrapped in a dense forest of fir and larch, which is why the hairpins on both sides are so intimate, with rock walls and tree trunks flashing past close to your shoulder.

The pass links the Vésubie valley with the Bévéra and Roya valleys, a mountainous hinterland that is only an hour or so behind the glitz of Nice and Monaco but feels like a different country. The villages here are stone-built and perched, with names like La Bollène-Vésubie and Moulinet, and the roads between them follow narrow valleys that smell of resin and wet rock. Nearby, the Mercantour National Park protects wolves, chamois and golden eagles, though what you are more likely to see are cyclists and other bikers, who make this a popular loop on weekends.

The riding is technical rather than fast: tight, blind hairpins, a surface that varies from smooth to patched, and long shadows that keep patches of damp on the road well into the day. Cooler air at altitude also means that tyres may take longer to warm up in the morning. The road is generally open year-round, but snow and ice can close it in winter. On the descent toward Sospel and Menton, the air gets warmer and the vegetation changes to olive and lemon, which is a nice trick.

Lantosque and La Bollène-Vésubie in the Vésubie valley, and Breil-sur-Roya on the other side, have pumps, though hours can be short in the villages, and Nice is the sure bet for services. The nearby hotel-restaurants at the top are a pilgrimage for rally fans, with photos of drivers on the walls, and a plate of local daube or ravioli is a fine reward. In autumn the forest is quiet, with mushrooms and woodsmoke in the air.
t.kingman@35.2,-114.1:
Kingman is where Route 66 gets down to business in the Arizona desert. The town sits at about a thousand metres between the Hualapai and Cerbat mountains, with creosote flats stretching in all directions, and it has been a railway stop, a mining supply town and a highway halt in turn. Today it is a tidy, sun-bleached place of nearly thirty thousand people, with a long main street, Andy Devine Avenue, named after the gravelly-voiced Hollywood actor who grew up here. A small museum devoted to Route 66 occupies an old powerhouse, and a neon-lit downtown has diners, motels and murals that keep the mid-century atmosphere alive.

Kingman has a few celebrity footnotes. Clark Gable and Carole Lombard were married here in 1939, driving out from Los Angeles for a quiet ceremony away from the press, and the town has remembered it with pride ever since. Locomotive Park, a small public green near the old railway, displays a steam engine, and the surrounding streets have vintage signs and shops selling kitsch and memorabilia.

The ride out of town to the west is one of the best segments of old Route 66. The road climbs over the Black Mountains through Sitgreaves Pass, a twisty, narrow, steep stretch of old pavement with hairpins and cliff drops, built before modern engineering smoothed things out. The old gold-mining town of Oatman, on the other side, is home to wild burros that wander the main street, descendants of animals left by miners, and they are happy to be fed, though they can be pushy. The road is narrow, with no guardrails in places, and the surface is rough, so take it slowly. To the east, long, straight sections cross open desert toward Seligman and Peach Springs, with big skies and distant mesas.

Summer here is brutally hot, with temperatures regularly above forty degrees, so start early and carry plenty of water. Spring and autumn are better, though winter can bring cold nights and the occasional snow. Kingman has several fuel stations, supermarkets, motels and diners, and the next services can be far apart, so top up the tank and water bottles before heading out. A classic breakfast in a Route 66 diner, with eggs, hash browns and bottomless coffee, sets you up nicely for the day.
t.escalante@37.8,-111.6:
Escalante is a small town on the edge of nowhere, and it is proud of it. Mormon pioneers settled here in 1875, in a valley at about 1,770 metres, and named it for Silvestre Vélez de Escalante, the Franciscan friar who passed through the region with Spanish explorers in 1776 on a failed attempt to find a route to California. Today it has a few hundred inhabitants, a handful of motels and cafes, and the air of a place that exists mainly to serve those exploring the vast and strange landscape around it.

That landscape was among the last in the lower forty-eight states to be properly mapped. The Escalante River was the last river charted in the contiguous United States, and the nearby Henry Mountains were the last mountains. In 1996, much of the region was protected as the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, a roadless wilderness of slot canyons, sandstone domes, arches and petrified wood. Dinosaur fossils are still being found. The land is a patchwork of vivid colours, red, orange, pink and white, layered like a staircase from the Grand Canyon to Bryce.

For riders, Scenic Byway 12 is the draw, and it is one of the most spectacular roads in the United States. East of Escalante, the highway runs across slickrock country to the Boulder Mountain, passing the trailhead for the hike to Calf Creek Falls, a perennial waterfall in a narrow canyon. Then comes the Hogback, a narrow ridge where the road runs along a knife edge with steep drops on both sides and no room for error. The curves are smooth and the surface is good, but the drop-offs are real, and crosswinds can be strong, so ease off and enjoy it. Snow can close higher sections of Boulder Mountain in winter, and thunderstorms in summer afternoons bring flash flooding to the dry washes.

Escalante has fuel stations and a general store, but services are thin in the surrounding area, so fill up whenever you can. Boulder, a short way east, is smaller still. Carry water, because summer temperatures can climb above thirty-five degrees, and sun exposure is severe. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with cooler air and golden light on the cliffs. At night, with no light pollution, the stars are brilliant.
t.flagstaff@35.2,-111.7:
Flagstaff stands at about 2,100 metres, higher than most Alpine villages, and it feels it. The air is thin and dry, the sky is a deep blue, and the town is wrapped in the largest ponderosa pine forest in North America, with the San Francisco Peaks rising to the north. The tallest of them, Humphreys Peak, is 3,851 metres, the highest point in Arizona, and it holds snow into early summer. The peaks are volcanic, the remains of a huge cone that blew out long ago, and they are sacred to many Native nations, including the Hopi and Navajo.

Route 66 runs straight through town, along the railway, and the old motels with their neon signs are still there. Flagstaff grew up as a lumber and railroad town, and then as a stop for travellers on the highway, and a lively downtown of brick buildings, bookstores and brewpubs has survived beneath the mountains. Lowell Observatory sits on a hill above town, and it was here in 1930 that Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto, a fact the city still celebrates. In 2001 Flagstaff became the world's first International Dark Sky City, and the stars on a clear night are astonishing. Northern Arizona University gives the town a young, outdoorsy feel.

For riders this is a place of altitude and of choices. West along old Route 66, the road runs through pine forest to Williams, then drops into desert toward Seligman, a classic stretch. North, the road leads to the Grand Canyon, about a hundred and thirty kilometres away, and to the Painted Desert. Nearby, the black cinder cone of Sunset Crater and the cliff dwellings of Walnut Canyon are easy short trips. Weather needs respect: summer thunderstorms build over the peaks in the afternoon, winter brings heavy snow, and mornings can be near freezing even in spring, though the valley below is hot. Cold-engine starts feel different at this height.

Flagstaff has seventy thousand people, so fuel, repair shops, motels and a good range of restaurants are all plentiful. Parking is simple, and the old downtown rewards a short walk, with coffee shops and a Route 66 mural or two. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear skies and moderate temperatures, and the aspens on the peaks turn gold in late September.
t.winslow@35.0,-110.7:
Winslow, Arizona, is famous for a song. In 1972, the Eagles released Take It Easy, with the line about standing on a corner in Winslow, Arizona, and today a small park on the main street has a statue and a mural, and tourists line up to take their picture on the corner. The town sits on the old Route 66, on the high plateau of northern Arizona, beside the Little Colorado River, with a population of about nine and a half thousand, and a long railway history that shaped it.

The great building is La Posada, a hotel built in 1930 by the Santa Fe Railway and the Fred Harvey Company, and designed by the architect Mary Colter in the style of a Spanish hacienda. It was the last of the great Harvey House hotels, and after it closed in the 1950s it was nearly demolished, but it was rescued and restored by a private owner and reopened as a hotel with gardens, a restaurant and an art collection. Even if you are not staying, a walk through the gardens and lobby is a pleasure. Meteor Crater, a huge impact crater about fifty kilometres to the west, is almost a mile across and 550 feet deep, and the Petrified Forest National Park lies to the east.

The riding on the old road is long, straight and easy, with wide-open desert and few cars, and the surface is generally good, with some rough patches. The wind is a constant companion, and the heat in summer is strong, with thunderstorms in July and August, while winter brings cold and occasional snow. The best times are spring and autumn, when the light is clear and the temperatures mild. North of town the Navajo Nation begins, with high mesas and painted desert.

Fuel, food and coffee are easy in Winslow, which has many petrol stations, diners and motels along its main street. Holbrook, to the east, has the Wigwam Motel, where guests sleep in concrete tepees, and Flagstaff, to the west, is a larger mountain town. Diners serve burgers, green chile and Navajo tacos, a regional favourite on fry bread.

Take your photograph on the corner, have a coffee, and then walk to La Posada, where the quiet gardens and old rooms give a sense of how travel once felt.
t.seligman@35.3,-112.9:
Seligman is the town that saved Route 66. When the interstate bypassed it in 1978, the traffic that had kept the town alive simply disappeared, and the businesses along the main street faced ruin. A local barber, Angel Delgadillo, and his brother Juan began a campaign to preserve the old road, and in 1987 the Historic Route 66 Association of Arizona was founded here, launching a revival that spread along the whole route. The town is now full of neon, vintage cars and roadside kitsch, and the Delgadillo family's barbershop and the Snow Cap Drive-In, famous for its jokes and fake mustard bottles, are still going.

Seligman also inspired the town of Radiator Springs in the Pixar film Cars, whose creators visited the town and met Angel. The stretch of Route 66 west from here, from Seligman to Topock on the Colorado River, is the longest unbroken piece of the original road that survives, about 150 miles of two-lane highway across the high desert, through Peach Springs and Hackberry. The Grand Canyon Caverns, a huge cave system about forty kilometres west, are reached by an elevator that descends twenty-one storeys, and the Hualapai reservation at Peach Springs is the gateway to the western Grand Canyon.

The ride is wonderful. The old road runs through wide, open ranchland, with long straights and gentle curves, a view of a big sky and a line of telephone poles, and the traffic is light. The surface is generally good, with a few rough sections, and the wind can be strong. The town stands at over 5,000 feet, so summer is warm rather than hot, and winter nights are cold, and snow can fall. Watch for cattle and wildlife on the road, especially at dusk.

Fuel and food are limited but sufficient. Seligman has a few petrol stations, diners and motels, but beyond it the services are spaced far apart, so fill the tank and carry water before heading west. Look for a burger or a milkshake at one of the old drive-ins, and check the opening times.

Walk down the main street, read the signs and talk to the owners, who like to chat. It is a living piece of American history, kept alive by stubborn people who loved their road.
t.castellane@43.8,6.5:
Castellane sits at the bottom of a rock, and the rock is the point. The town, at a little over seven hundred metres in the valley of the Verdon, is overlooked by a limestone crag nearly two hundred metres high, with a small chapel on top, Notre-Dame du Roc, which has been a pilgrimage site for centuries. A steep path climbs to it in about half an hour, and the view over the town's red roofs, the river and the surrounding mountains is superb. The town itself is small, with about sixteen hundred people, but it feels bigger in summer, when visitors fill the cafés.

Napoleon passed through here on 2 March 1815, on his march from the coast at Golfe-Juan to Paris, and the town claims him as a guest. The road he took, now the N85, is called the Route Napoléon and is marked by little eagle signs. It is one of the great motorcycling roads of France, mostly smooth and well engineered, with long bends and fine views, and it is busy with riders in summer. Castellane, at its midpoint between the coast and Digne, is the natural place to stop.

The Gorges du Verdon begin a few kilometres to the west, a canyon of extraordinary beauty, with cliffs of up to seven hundred metres and a river of turquoise water. The roads that run along its rim are narrow and exciting, with tight bends and long drops, and they are best ridden in the early morning, before the crowds arrive. Lake Sainte-Croix, at the western end, has beaches and boats.

Fuel is available in Castellane, which has several stations, and it is wise to fill the tank here before heading into the mountains. Food is Provençal, with a good selection of restaurants and cafés around the main square, and a market on Wednesday and Saturday mornings. The town is busy in July and August, and quieter in spring and autumn, when the light is soft and the roads are almost empty. Nights are cool at this altitude, even in summer.
t.digne les bains@44.1,6.2:
Digne-les-Bains is a town of nineteen thousand people at the heart of the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, a place with an unusual mixture of attractions. It lies in a wide valley at the meeting of several rivers, surrounded by mountains, and its hot springs have drawn visitors since Roman times. The thermal baths are still open. The town is the capital of lavender country, and each August the Corso de la Lavande fills the streets with floats decorated with the flowers. The scent of lavender is everywhere in summer, from the fields that cover the plateaus around.

Digne's literary fame comes from Victor Hugo, who set the opening of Les Misérables here. The kindly bishop Myriel, who gives shelter and silver candlesticks to Jean Valjean, was modelled on a real bishop of Digne, and the town is proud of the association. The explorer and writer Alexandra David-Néel, the first European woman to reach Lhasa, spent her last decades here and died in 1969 at the age of one hundred, and her house is a museum of Tibetan art. The philosopher and astronomer Pierre Gassendi was born in a village nearby.

The geology is remarkable. The hills around Digne are full of fossils, and a slab of rock a few kilometres from town, covered with hundreds of giant ammonites, is one of the best sights of the region. The surrounding area, the Haute-Provence geological reserve, is one of the largest in Europe, and it has been recognised by UNESCO as a geopark. The Train des Pignes, the narrow-gauge railway to Nice, begins its journey here.

As the end of the Route Napoléon's ride, Digne is a good place to spend the night, with hotels, restaurants and shops in plenty, and all the fuel you might need. Napoleon stopped here on 4 March 1815, and the route continues north to Sisteron and Gap. The roads around the town are excellent for riding, with lovely scenery and little traffic outside the summer. Summer is hot and bright, and winter can bring snow to the heights. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.sospel@43.9,7.4:
Sospel lies in the deep valley of the Bévéra, a small river that cuts through limestone mountains about twelve kilometres inland from Menton, and it feels like a different country from the coast. The air is cooler, the light is softer, and the town has a pleasant, slightly sleepy character with colonnaded squares and painted houses. Its medieval bridge, the Pont-Vieux, carries a tower that was once used to collect tolls from the traders, and although it was blown up in the Second World War and rebuilt, it remains the town's postcard image. Rows of pale and ochre buildings crowd along the river.

For riders Sospel is a crossroads of famous roads. To the west the road climbs to the Col de Braus, a little over a thousand metres, in a long series of hairpins. To the north, the Col de Turini, at over sixteen hundred metres, is the legendary rally stage of Monte Carlo, with miles of tight bends through pine forest. To the east, the road drops along the Roya valley toward Breil-sur-Roya and Italy, passing small villages perched on rock. With about three thousand people, Sospel has fuel stations, bakeries, cafés and small supermarkets, so it is the natural place to fill the tank before heading into the high country.

The history is layered. The town was part of the County of Nice and later the Kingdom of Sardinia before joining France in 1860, and the baroque church of Saint-Michel with its arcaded square testifies to the wealth of the old trade routes. Above the valley, the Fort Saint-Roch, part of the Maginot Line of the 1930s, is now a museum and shows how this frontier was prepared for war. Menton, the nearest large town, is famed for its lemons and holds a lemon festival each winter.

Eat on the main square if the weather is fine, where plane trees give shade and the fountain adds a little noise. Because this is both start and finish for the loop, the evening is the better time to enjoy it, when the light fades on the valley walls and the day's riders gather over a beer. Winter can bring ice to the passes, so check conditions before committing to the high roads.
t.rnesvingen eagle road@62.1,7.2:
There is a bend in the road above the Geirangerfjord where the whole country seems to drop away in front of you. Ørnesvingen, the Eagle Bend, is a hairpin on the road from Eidsdal, and the viewpoint at its edge, at about six hundred and twenty metres, looks straight down onto the fjord, a long, narrow slot of green water between cliffs with waterfalls pouring from the rim. Ships look like toys at the village of Geiranger below, and the air smells of cold stone and wet moss.

The Geirangerfjord is part of the West Norwegian Fjords, a UNESCO World Heritage area, and it is one of the most visited places in Norway. The cliffs are nearly vertical, and several of the waterfalls have names, such as the Seven Sisters and the Suitor, which face each other across the water. Abandoned farms cling to ledges high on the slopes, reached in the old days by ladders and ropes, and the stories of the people who lived there are a reminder of how hard life was. In summer, cruise ships crowd the fjord, and in the shoulder seasons it is much quieter.

The road down is the Eagle Road, Rv63, with a series of hairpins that drop steeply toward the fjord. It is a wonderful ride, with a good surface, well-marked corners and views at nearly every bend, though in high season it is full of campervans and coaches, so patience is needed. The higher stretches of the road close in winter and reopen in spring, usually by May, and the toll road up to Dalsnibba, at about fifteen hundred metres, gives one of the greatest views in the country.

Fuel is not available at the viewpoint. Stranda, about twenty-five kilometres away, has stations and shops, and there are also places in Geiranger, though prices are high. Cafés at the viewpoint serve coffee and waffles. Take care on the hairpins, particularly in wet weather, when the road can be slick, and watch for oncoming buses that take the corners wide. Early morning, before the tour groups arrive, is the best time, and the light on the fjord is soft.
t.oatman@35.0,-114.4:
A donkey will probably block your way into Oatman, and you should let it. The wild burros that wander the main street are descendants of animals left behind by prospectors, and they are tame enough to take carrots from tourists and stubborn enough to hold up traffic. The town itself is a little gold-rush survivor of about a hundred people, with wooden boardwalks, saloons and gift shops, and staged gunfights in the street for the benefit of visitors. It is kitsch, certainly, but there is something genuine in the dust and the mountains behind it.

The road is the reason to come. Old Route 66 climbs out of the Mojave Desert over the Black Mountains, through Sitgreaves Pass at about 1,100 metres, in a series of tight switchbacks with no guardrails and some steep drops. It is narrow, twisting and sometimes rough, and it was bypassed in the 1950s when a new, easier road opened further south, which is why the town went quiet. Travellers in the 1930s often had to let passengers out to walk the steepest corners, with the car overheating and the brakes complaining. A motorcycle takes it all in its stride, and the views over the desert are superb.

The gold is gone, though in the early twentieth century this was one of the richest mining camps in Arizona. Clark Gable and Carole Lombard spent a night at the hotel on their wedding trip in 1939, and the room is still shown. Prospectors' shafts scar the hills around the town, and the old mine buildings can be seen from the road.

Practical details matter in the desert. Oatman has no reliable fuel, so take fuel at Kingman or Bullhead City, on the Colorado River, before the climb. The summers are brutally hot, with temperatures that can reach well over forty degrees Celsius, and the road should be done early in the morning or in spring and autumn. Carry plenty of water. Spring wildflowers, after wet winters, can cover the slopes.

Mind the burros. They are protected, they kick, and they do not understand traffic. Feeding them is allowed only with approved food sold in the shops, and they can be pushy, so keep your pannier lids closed.
t.gap@44.6,6.1:
Gap is the highest prefecture in France, sitting at about seven hundred and fifty metres in a wide, sunny basin in the Hautes-Alpes, with mountains on every side. People often ride through it without more than a glance, which is a pity, because the town, with some forty thousand people, makes a comfortable halt on a mountain route: fuel stations at every entrance, supermarkets, a pleasant old centre with a pedestrian core, and cafés where you can sit in the sun. The Alpine light is strong here and the air dry, with something like three hundred days of sunshine a year, a figure the town likes to repeat.

The Route Napoléon passes through. On 5 March 1815, after landing on the Riviera, Napoleon came into Gap with a small band of soldiers, on his way north to Paris, and was received warmly by the townspeople. The road he took, now the N85, climbs north to the Col Bayard, at about 1,250 metres, and then drops through the high valleys toward Grenoble, with good bends, alpine meadows and views over the Écrins massif to the east. Nearly every village on the way has a plaque or a statue of the emperor, and in the Matheysine the road passes the Prairie de la Rencontre, where he met a battalion sent to arrest him and bared his chest to them, as the story goes.

The riding on the Route Napoléon is a mixture of fast, open sweepers and tighter climbs, on generally good surfaces, with plenty of traffic in July and August. Early morning is best. Snow can linger on the Col Bayard into April and fresh falls are possible in October, so the road is a late-spring to early-autumn affair. Wind is frequent in the Gap basin, and thunderstorms build over the ridges on hot afternoons.

East of the town the road runs to the huge reservoir of Serre-Ponçon, a very bright blue lake among the mountains, and a worthwhile detour. In the town itself, the cathedral and the markets are worth a short walk, and local specialities include walnut cakes, lamb from the high pastures, and a flat bread called the pompe. Fill your tank before you head north, because the mountain villages are small.
t.sault@44.1,5.4:
On a hot July afternoon, Sault is the best place in Provence to understand why people write poems about lavender. The village sits on a rocky spur at about 750 metres, on the edge of the great plateau that runs between Mont Ventoux and the Luberon hills, and in the weeks of the bloom, from late June to late July, the fields around it turn violet in long, curved lines up to the horizon. The smell is overwhelming on warm days, sweet, resinous and slightly medicinal, and bees fill the air. The villagers hold a lavender festival every year on 15 August, with processions, markets and music.

The village itself is small, just over twelve hundred people, with a main street of stone houses, a church, a bakery and a few cafés looking out over the plain. It is known for its nougat, made with lavender honey and almonds, and for spelt, an ancient grain grown on the plateau and used in soups and bread. Mont Ventoux rises behind it to the north, a bald white summit of 1,912 metres, and the climb from Sault is the gentlest of the three classic routes to the top, through forest and then an open, moonlike slope.

The road to the west, the D942 through the Gorges de la Nesque, is one of the best in Provence. It winds along the edge of a deep limestone canyon, with tunnels, overhangs and balconies cut into the rock, and a lookout point over a tall cliff, and it ends at Villes-sur-Auzon in the plain. The surface is good and the bends are smooth, but traffic can be heavy in summer, and there are cyclists on every climb. Early morning is the best time, when the light is soft and the air cool.

The plateau is exposed and the wind can be fierce, especially the mistral. Spring and early autumn are quieter, with fewer crowds, though the lavender is then out of season. Come in July for the colour and early in the morning for the road.
t.dorgali@40.3,9.6:
Dorgali sits on the eastern flank of the Supramonte, the limestone massif that fills the middle of Sardinia's Nuoro province, and the town spreads over its slope with the mountains behind and the Gulf of Orosei somewhere in the haze ahead. Six thousand people live here, enough for fuel, banks and a proper choice of bars, which matters because the SS125 Orientale Sarda is a long road with long gaps. Fill the tank here and you will not think about it again until Baunei or Tortolì.

The Supramonte is a rough, dry country of white rock, holm oak and juniper, cut by deep gorges. The best known is Gola Su Gorropu, a canyon whose walls rise several hundred metres and which can be reached on foot from the road above, a walk that takes a few hours and is not for flip-flops. Not far away, the ruins of the nuragic village of Tiscali hide inside a collapsed limestone dome, a place where people lived in the Bronze and Iron Ages and, according to the story, retreated when Rome arrived. Sardinia is thick with nuraghi, those conical stone towers of the second and first millennia before Christ, and this part of the island has some of the best.

Dorgali itself has a reputation for craftsmanship, with leather, ceramics, carpets and filigree jewellery all made locally, and it is the centre of a wine area whose Cannonau reds are dark and strong, not shy at all. Cheese, sausages, honey and the thin, crisp bread called carasau come with every meal. A lunch here is slow, so allow time, and remember that shops often close in the early afternoon.

The riding from Dorgali is the reason most people come. South of the town, the SS125 climbs through the hills in tight, rhythmical bends, with cork oaks and lentisk on one side and a drop on the other, and then it descends toward the coast with sea views that appear and disappear. Surfaces are generally good, though patched in places, and goats occasionally wander across the road. The side road to Cala Gonone, through a long tunnel under Monte Bardia, drops to a small resort on the gulf, where boats run to sea caves, and it is a good detour if you want a swim. In summer, the heat is serious, and the best riding hours are before eleven and after six.
t.baunei@40.0,9.7:
Baunei hangs on a ledge of limestone above the Tyrrhenian sea, a town of two thousand people with the Supramonte of Baunei rising behind it and the coast far below. The SS125 comes through here on one of its most spectacular sections, climbing out of the valley from the south and then running along the face of the mountains with sea views opening on the left. The Gennargentu massif, Sardinia's highest ground, lies inland, and the whole district is one of the wildest corners of the island.

It is a place of shepherds, and a place of walkers. The Selvaggio Blu, a famous multi-day trek along the coast, starts near here and crosses terrain so steep and so remote that the walkers carry ropes. On the plateau above the town, the Golgo plateau holds a deep karst pit called Su Sterru and a small church amid the oaks, reached by a rough track, where the world feels very quiet. If you have a few hours, the road to the plateau is worth a look, though it is narrow and rough in places.

Down at the sea, Pedra Longa is a tall limestone needle that rises from the water beside a little harbour, and the road to it twists down from the main highway in a series of tight hairpins. Santa Maria Navarrese, a few kilometres south, has a pleasant beachfront with bars and restaurants, and a church said to have been founded by a shipwrecked Spanish princess from Navarre, with an ancient olive tree beside it. Beyond it lies Tortolì, the larger town of the Ogliastra district, with eight thousand inhabitants and everything a rider might need, including fuel, supermarkets and repair shops. Baunei has its own small stations, but it is sensible to treat Tortolì as the sure bet.

The riding on this stretch is of the kind that leaves a grin. Long bends follow short ones, the surface is mostly decent, and the views are dramatic. Be careful in summer, when the road is busy with cars and campervans, and look out for loose gravel on the outside of corners. Early morning is best, when the light is soft on the cliffs and the air smells of resin and wild herbs, and the sea is flat and silver.
t.eidfjord@60.5,7.1:
Eidfjord lies at the inner end of the Hardangerfjord, one of the longest fjords in Norway, and the village, with only a few hundred people, sits at the foot of steep cliffs, where waterfalls fall from the plateau above and the water below is dark green and still. The setting is dramatic. In the early morning, mist hangs on the fjord, and the mountains rise on every side, while orchards of apple and cherry trees on the lower slopes recall that the Hardanger region is Norway's fruit garden. In spring, when the trees blossom, the contrast with the snow on the peaks is striking.

Above the village lies the Hardangervidda, the largest mountain plateau in northern Europe, a wide, bare upland of lakes, bogs and rounded hills, which is home to the biggest herd of wild reindeer in the country. The road, Route 7, climbs from the fjord to the plateau through the Mabodalen valley, with a sequence of tunnels and hairpins and a view of Voringsfossen, a waterfall that drops about 180 metres in two stages into a deep gorge. The fall is one of the most visited in Norway, and the viewing platforms give a close look at the spray and the cliffs.

Eidfjord has a visitor centre, the Hardangervidda Nature Centre, with exhibits on the geology, wildlife and human history of the plateau, and a small hydroelectric industry nearby makes use of the water. The Hardanger Bridge, a suspension bridge that opened in 2013 and has a main span of about 1,310 metres, crosses the fjord just beyond the village, and the road across it is smooth, exposed and unforgettable. Wind can be strong on the bridge, so a firm grip is wise.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Eidfjord has a few services, but it is small, and pumps in rural Norway are often unmanned and take only cards. Ulvik and Granvin, the nearest villages, are also small, and the larger towns of Voss and Odda are about an hour away. Fill up beforehand, and keep a bank card with a PIN. Tolls on tunnels and bridges are charged automatically, and rental bikes usually have a tag. The riding season on the plateau runs from late May to October, and snow can fall in any month at height. Layers and waterproofs are essential, because the weather changes quickly.
t.trollstigen hairpins@62.5,7.7:
Trollstigen, the Troll's Ladder, climbs out of the Isterdalen valley in eleven hairpin bends, with a gradient of about one in ten, and the road is as steep and tight as it looks in photographs. It was opened in 1936, after years of work, by King Haakon VII, and it still has the narrow width and stone-walled edges of its era, with passing places on the bends. The Stigfossen waterfall plunges beside the road, and a bridge crosses it at one of the hairpins, so that you ride through the spray.

The mountains around are among the most dramatic in Norway. Across the valley rise the Trolltindene, a line of jagged peaks, and the Trollveggen, the Troll Wall, a vertical rock face about eleven hundred metres high, the tallest in Europe, which draws climbers and base jumpers from around the world. On a clear day, the colours are vivid: grey rock, white waterfalls, green meadow and blue sky. In cloud, the peaks vanish, and the hairpins climb into a white void, with water streaming down the rocks.

At the top, a modern visitor platform made of steel and glass hangs over the gorge, and a viewing path leads along the edge. The plateau is about 850 metres high, bare and rocky, with patches of snow lingering into summer. Because of the snow, the road is closed in winter, usually opening in May or even June, and closing in October. Traffic in July and August is heavy, with coaches, camper vans and cars, and the bends can be congested, so an early start, before nine, is a good idea.

Riding the Trollstigen demands attention. The hairpins are tight, with a steep climb and a sudden turn, and the surface can be wet from waterfalls. Coaches take the whole road, so stay on the inside of left-hand bends and keep well back. Fuel is available in Andalsnes, twelve kilometres below, which has two thousand people and shops, but not on the pass. The road continues over the plateau to Valldal and the Geiranger fjord, with a ferry crossing on the way. Carry waterproofs, because rain is common, and take your time. The reward is a ride you will remember for life.
t.valldal strawberry@62.3,7.3:
Valldal is a village at the head of the Norddalsfjord, and each July it becomes the strawberry capital of Norway. The south-facing slopes above the water, sheltered by mountains, catch long summer light, and the berries that ripen on them are small, deep red and very sweet, with a flavour more intense than the larger kinds. Growers sell them from roadside stands, in cardboard boxes or as soft ice cream, jam and cake, and the season is short, starting in early July and ending in a few weeks. A bowl of fresh strawberries with cream, eaten on a bench with the fjord below, is a very good reason to stop.

Valldal sits at the junction of two great roads. To the south, the road climbs the Eagle Road toward Geiranger, and to the north-east, the Trollstigen road leads across the plateau to Andalsnes. The ferry from Eidsdal to Linge, a short crossing, links the two. The fjord is deep and calm, with steep slopes of birch and spruce, and small farms clinging to ledges, and in the evening the mountains turn pink.

The village has about a thousand people, and a handful of shops, a campsite and a hotel. Strawberry farms offer pick-your-own, and cafes serve waffles with cream and jam. Fuel is available at a small station, but opening hours are limited and it is not always staffed, so it is best to arrive with a reasonably full tank. Stranda, about seventeen kilometres away, has about two and a half thousand people and a larger selection.

The road to Valldal is well surfaced, with a mix of fjord-side bends, tunnels and short climbs, and traffic is heavy in July, when tourists and strawberry buyers arrive. Take it slowly and enjoy the views. Rain is common, and the mountains often vanish in cloud, but the damp makes the green of the fields even greener. Evenings are long in summer, and you can ride in daylight until after ten. In winter, many roads are closed or icy, and Valldal is quiet. If you can, come in July.
t.eagle road viewpoint@62.1,7.2:
Ornesvingen, the Eagle Bend, is a hairpin on the road above the Geirangerfjord, and the viewpoint beside it gives the classic picture of the fjord: a long, narrow slot of green water, hemmed by cliffs and waterfalls, with the village of Geiranger at the far end and the white wakes of ships crossing. The road that leads to it, the Eagle Road, climbs from the fjord in eleven hairpins, and takes its name from the birds that sometimes soar here. The name suits the bend, which seems to hang in the air.

The Geirangerfjord is a UNESCO World Heritage site, shared with the Naeroyfjord, and it is among the most visited places in Norway. Its walls rise more than a thousand metres, and waterfalls tumble down them, including the Seven Sisters, a row of falls side by side, and the Suitor, which faces them across the water. According to the legend, the Suitor is a man trying to woo the sisters, and the Bridal Veil is another fall that looks like gauze. In summer, cruise ships fill the fjord, and the village is crowded.

Higher still lies Dalsnibba, a mountain with a toll road that climbs to about 1,500 metres, with a view down onto the fjord, and a stop there is worth the effort on a clear day. The old farms along the fjord, some abandoned, cling to impossible slopes, and a few can be visited. Walking trails lead between them, and the air smells of pine and wet rock.

As for practical matters, the nearest towns of any size, Stranda and Stryn, are twenty-five and thirty-four kilometres away, and fuel is available in Geiranger itself, though prices are high. Fill up in Stranda or Stryn if you can. The road is well surfaced but narrow, with tight bends, and it can be crowded with coaches, so approach with care. Weather changes quickly, with cloud and rain often hiding the view, so be patient, and wait for a break. Early morning is the quietest time, and in autumn the light is clear and the crowds thin. Be aware that the road is closed in winter.
t.la palud sur verdon@43.8,6.3:
La Palud-sur-Verdon is a small stone village of the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, perched on the north rim of the Verdon Gorge, and it is where riders usually decide how they are going to spend the rest of the day. Behind it are fields of lavender and thyme, in front of it is the biggest canyon in Europe, and the village has just enough cafés, shops and bakeries to keep a person fed while they work out the details. It sits at about nine hundred metres, so the air is clear and in the morning it can be properly cool.

The Gorges du Verdon, sometimes called the Grand Canyon of Europe, was carved by the turquoise river of that name through limestone plateaus, with sheer walls rising up to seven hundred metres above the water. For centuries it was almost unknown, an impassable ravine that shepherds avoided. Not until the explorer Édouard-Alfred Martel, the father of modern speleology, made his expedition in 1905 did the full depth of it become widely known. The rock is pale, the water improbably green, and from the viewpoints the cliffs seem to hold their breath.

The riding from here is some of the best in France. The D952 runs along the north rim from Castellane, with the Route des Crêtes branching off from La Palud itself as a one-way loop with a series of belvederes. The corners are tight, the surface is mostly good, and the road clings to the edge of the abyss in a way that makes you thankful for the crash barriers. In July and August, traffic is heavy, with campervans, coaches and cyclists, so start early or aim for spring and autumn, when the colours are best and the crowds are thin. In July, the lavender fields around Valensole, a short way to the west, turn the plateau purple.

Fuel is the one thing to plan for. La Palud is small, and the nearest sure source is Castellane to the north-east, or Draguignan, a much bigger town, to the south, so fill the tank before you commit to the gorge roads. Food is easy: soups, local goat cheese, lamb and honey, and a pastis or a glass of rosé are the appropriate rewards after the ride.
t.rougon@43.8,6.4:
Rougon is a handful of stone houses piled on a rock above the Verdon, with the shell of a medieval castle on top and a view that justifies the whole detour. You come to it on the D952, the north-rim road that climbs from Castellane, and the village sits just off the highway at about nine hundred metres, a short climb away from the traffic. Most visitors drive past on their way to the viewpoints. Those who stop find a quiet street, a small church, and cats asleep on warm walls.

The ruined keep above the village is worth the short, steep walk. From the top you look straight down on the point where the river leaves the open valley and enters the first real narrows of the gorge, with the water far below, the colour of a swimming pool in an old postcard. Wild thyme and juniper grow among the stones, and in warm weather the whole hillside smells of herbs. Griffon vultures, reintroduced to these cliffs in the 1990s, circle on the thermals, and if you are lucky you will watch one close enough to count its feathers.

The road between Castellane and Rougon is a good one, a series of long, flowing bends with the gorge appearing and vanishing on one side and pine woods on the other. Surfaces are reasonable but patched, and rock fall is a possibility after storms. Summer weekends bring crowds to the viewpoints, so the best riding is in the morning or in the shoulder seasons, when the light is clear and the air cool. Winter can bring snow and ice at this altitude, and the high roads may be closed for a time, so check before you set out in the cold months.

The village has a small café or two in season, but not much else, and the better places to eat are back in La Palud or Castellane. Rougon works best as a pause for a few minutes of silence before the road carries on towards the famous viewpoints a little further along.
t.point sublime@43.8,6.4:
Point Sublime is the viewpoint where the Verdon Gorge opens its mouth. Standing on the rail, you look down some two hundred and fifty metres into a narrow slot where the river runs a vivid green between pale cliffs, with the walls closing in toward the Couloir Samson, the first real pinch in the canyon. Édouard-Alfred Martel, the French explorer who first mapped the gorge in 1905, is credited with naming the spot, and no one has since suggested a better word for it.

The viewpoint lies a few kilometres west of Rougon on the D952, with a parking area, a small café in season and a stall or two selling postcards and local honey. A trail leads down from here to the river for those with the legs and the time, and from the viewpoint you can also see where walkers on the famous Sentier Martel finish a long day on the cliffs. The path is not for the unprepared, so unless you are properly equipped, simply enjoy the view and watch the rock climbers on the far wall, tiny figures on a vertical world.

The riding to Point Sublime from either direction is enjoyable, with the gorge barely visible through the trees and the road dipping and rising in gentle bends. It is not as tight as the Route des Crêtes, and that makes it a more relaxed ride, with room to look around. The surface is generally good, though in summer traffic can be very slow behind campervans, so patience is part of the equipment. Early morning offers the best light, when the sun hits the far wall and turns the limestone gold. Afternoon haze can flatten the view.

The limestone cliffs here are home to peregrine falcons, choughs and, in the summer, large soaring vultures, and the river below is a favourite of kayakers when water levels allow. Fuel is not available at the viewpoint, so fill up in Castellane or Draguignan beforehand, and bring water, as the heat in July and August can be severe. After the viewpoint, you can continue to La Palud-sur-Verdon, where food and drink are plentiful and the village is a good base for exploring.
t.route des cretes@43.8,6.4:
The Route des Crêtes is a road built to be looked out from. The D23 loops for about twenty-three kilometres around the northern side of the Verdon Gorge, carved in the 1970s along the very lip of the cliffs, with a string of belvederes where you can pull over and look straight down for several hundred metres to the green river below. It is a one-way route for much of its length, which makes the riding simpler: no oncoming traffic on the blind bends, only the question of whether the bike in front is going slowly because of the view.

And what a road it is. It leaves La Palud-sur-Verdon, climbs onto the rim, and winds through a landscape of bare rock and pine, with tight hairpins, short straights and sudden drops. The surface is good, although grit sometimes collects on the corners, and the barriers are low, which concentrates the mind. Names to look for on the signs include the Cirque de Vaumale, a vast bowl of rock, and the Falaises de l'Escalès, where cliffs of around four hundred metres plunge into the canyon. The mirrors on the other side of the bends are there for a reason: walk to the edge only where there is a fence.

Timing matters. In July and August the road is busy by mid-morning, with cyclists, coaches and tourists taking their time, so go early. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and good light, and in winter the road may be closed or icy. The viewpoints are small and fill up quickly. Take it slowly, because the corners come faster than expected and the drops are real.

This is wild limestone country, where the plateau has been cut by water over millions of years into a landscape of bare ridges and deep clefts. Box, holm oak and Aleppo pine cling to the rock, and the summer air is thick with the smell of thyme and resin. Cicadas buzz through the heat. Griffon vultures soar along the cliffs, and in the evening the rock walls glow orange.

La Palud has few services and Castellane is the safer place to fill up, with Draguignan the bigger town to the south. Pack water and a snack, and carry a warm layer if you plan to stay for the sunset.
t.antheor@43.4,6.9:
Anthéor is a tiny seaside hamlet on the Corniche d'Or, the coast road between Saint-Raphaël and Cannes, and it sits in a spot where the red rock of the Esterel meets the Mediterranean in a way that no guidebook has ever made seem exaggerated. The cliffs here are a volcanic rock, rust-red and purple, ancient lava that cooled around three hundred million years ago, and they plunge straight into water so blue it seems inked. Above the hamlet the peak of Cap Roux rises, a bare, rose-coloured crag over the sea.

The road itself, the N98, dates from the early twentieth century and was cut and blasted along the shoreline with a stubborn commitment to staying close to the water. It twists in and out of coves, dips under cliffs and runs past tiny beaches, with the railway line threading through the same landscape on stone viaducts. The Anthéor viaduct was blown up in the Second World War and rebuilt afterwards, a reminder that this lovely coast was once a front line. The riding is slow, rhythmic and beautiful rather than demanding, with plenty of bends and constant views, and the main danger is a lack of attention to the scenery rather than the road.

Traffic is the one drawback. In July and August the Corniche d'Or is packed, and the narrow road and lack of passing places make progress a crawl. Early mornings in May, June, September or October are the answer, when the light is clear and the tarmac nearly empty.
