Parking at the small beaches can be difficult in summer, and the surface is sometimes gritty where red sand blows across.

The Esterel massif behind the coast is a wild, low range of red rock covered in cork oak, maritime pine and aromatic scrub, and it has been shaped by fire repeatedly. Walking trails climb to viewpoints, but make sure you check fire restrictions, since access to the forest is sometimes closed in dry summers. Saint-Exupéry, the author of The Little Prince, is linked to this coast, since he lived near Agay, a few kilometres to the west.

Anthéor itself has little beyond a couple of beach cafés in season, so Saint-Raphaël, ten kilometres away, is where you will find fuel, supermarkets and a good range of restaurants.
t.stegastein@60.9,7.2:
Stegastein is a long timber platform pushed out from the mountainside, high above the Aurlandsfjord, and it is as much a piece of daring architecture as a viewpoint. It reaches about thirty metres out from the slope at around 650 metres above the water, and a thin glass wall at the end keeps you from the drop. It opened in 2006 as part of the Norwegian scenic routes programme and has become one of the best-known viewpoints in the country. From the end of the platform you look straight down onto the fjord, an arm of the Sognefjord, and watch cruise ships turning in the water, looking like toys.

The road that leads to it, the old route between Aurland and Lærdal, is called the Snow Road at its highest point. Below the platform, it climbs in a series of well-built bends, with a good surface and plenty of places to stop. It is a comfortable climb for a motorbike, not too steep, with long corners that open onto the view and then close again. Traffic includes coaches in summer, and caravans, so be patient and use the lay-bys. The road is steep on its fjord side, with stone walls and a barrier at the edge, but the fall beyond is a long one, so keep to your side of the road.

The Aurlandsfjord is narrow and deep, the sides sheer, and the water a dark green that turns silver in the right light. The fjord's best-known village is Flåm, at its head, where the famous steep railway climbs to Myrdal. Farms once clung to impossible ledges above the water, and some were reached only by boat or ladder, and many are now abandoned. They give a sense of how hard life was here, and why so many people left for America in the nineteenth century.

Stegastein has a car park and a toilet, and you can get a coffee and a snack in summer. Fuel is not available at the platform. Aurland, below, has a pump and a few shops, and Lærdalsøyri, on the far side of the mountain, has more, so fill up before you climb. Come in the morning if you can, before the tour buses arrive, and bring a windproof layer, because the platform stands in the breeze. In the evening, the light on the fjord is soft, and the colours are at their best.
t.mabodalen@60.4,7.2:
Måbødalen is a steep, narrow valley that drops from the edge of the Hardangervidda plateau down to the Eidfjord, and the main road, Rv7, comes down it in a series of tunnels and bends that were once among the most feared in Norway. The valley walls are sheer granite, scoured by ice, with waterfalls on both sides, and the floor is a thin green strip with a river and a few farms. The descent is about a thousand metres in a short distance, and you feel it in your brakes and your ears. In the old days, travellers came down on a narrow, hand-built road with hairpins, parts of which still exist as a walking and cycling path.

The modern road is a good one, wide and well surfaced, with tunnels that cut off the worst bends. It is not a hairpin road in the Alpine sense, but it is steep and long, and when trucks and caravans use it in summer, patience is needed. Use engine braking on the descent, and do not ride the brakes. In winter the road can be icy at the top, with snow on the plateau and a warmer, wetter valley below. A rider coming up from the fjord will feel the temperature fall as he rises, often by ten degrees or more.

Eidfjord, at the foot, lies at the head of a branch of the Hardangerfjord, and it is a small village of about five hundred people, with a good harbour and a feeling of depth and shelter. The surrounding slopes are planted with orchards, and in May the whole district blossoms, making a vivid contrast with the barren plateau above. Apples, plums and cherries are grown here and sold at roadside stalls in season, a fine reward for the cold of the road.

For fuel, Eidfjord has a pump, but options are limited, and the nearest large town in the other direction is Geilo, on the east side of the plateau. Fill up before you go either way, and take the weather seriously. The road is open all year, but in storms it can close, so check the traffic reports before a winter trip. Whatever the season, the contrast between the bare mountain and the green fjord is dramatic, and it is the best argument for coming down by the slow way.
t.voringsfossen@60.4,7.3:
Vøringsfossen is the great waterfall of Norway, with a total drop of about 180 metres, of which around 145 are a clean, free fall into the Måbødalen gorge. The river Bjoreio runs across the Hardangervidda plateau and comes to the edge in a rush, and then it simply drops, with a roar you can hear long before you see it. The spray rises in a cloud and the rocks around it are wet and bright with moss. The viewing platforms on the edge give you a view straight down into the gorge, and it is worth taking your time, because the scale does not register at once.

The waterfall has been a famous sight since the nineteenth century, when the first tourists came, often by boat up the fjord and then on horseback and foot. A grand hotel was built at the edge of the gorge in the 1890s to receive them, and it is still there, a big old wooden building in the dragon style. Painters and composers came to look, and Kaiser Wilhelm of Germany was among the visitors who made the journey. The waterfall was a marvel and a status symbol, and it appears in many old photographs and paintings.

The road to the falls is the Rv7, which at this point runs on the plateau edge before dropping into the valley, and it is a pleasant, easy ride. There are fast, long bends, a good surface and wide views over the mountains. The main trouble is crowds in summer, when buses and campervans fill the car park and the road, so aim for the morning or the evening. At the edge, take care: the rock is slippery, and the platforms are railed, but the drop is enormous.

Eidfjord is the nearest village, about fifteen minutes down the valley by road, and it has a pump and a few shops. At the fall there is a café and a shop. The best time is after rain or in the spring melt, when the flow is at its greatest, and the best light is in the middle of the day, when the sun reaches into the gorge and the spray is full of rainbows. Wear a waterproof, as the mist can soak you in minutes.
t.dyranut@60.4,7.5:
Dyranut stands at about 1,245 metres on the western edge of the Hardangervidda, the largest mountain plateau in Europe, and it is a mountain lodge in the old Norwegian tradition: a simple wooden building with a restaurant, beds and a view over an enormous bare country. The plateau is a high, rolling upland of stone, bog, small lakes and low scrub, with the occasional snow patch hanging on into July. There are no trees, and the sky is large. When the cloud lifts, the light can be extraordinarily clear, and the mountains seem close enough to touch.

The Hardangervidda holds the largest herd of wild reindeer in Europe, and the animals roam over the whole plateau, moving between summer and winter grazing. You may see them from the road, a dark line against the pale ground, and they are best seen early in the morning or in the evening. The plateau is also a national park, and its protected status keeps it free from building. In the distance, the long white back of the Hardangerjøkulen glacier can show on a clear day.

The riding on the Rv7 here is open and fast, with long, easy curves that follow the lie of the land. It is a high-speed, high-altitude road, and you feel the exposure. Wind is usually the main thing, and it can be strong enough to move a bike sideways on the straights. Rain and fog arrive without warning, and the temperature at 1,200 metres is far below what you left in the fjord, even in July. Dress warmly, carry waterproofs, and treat any sign of ice with respect, because it can appear in any month.

The lodge is a welcome stop, with hot food, coffee and a toilet, and it is open in the main season. Do not count on it in the shoulder months, and call ahead if you can. Eidfjord, at the foot of the descent, has a pump, and Geilo, on the east side of the plateau, has more services, so make sure you start the day with a full tank. A bowl of hot soup, waffles with jam and sour cream, and a seat at the window are exactly what the place is for.
t.halne fjellstugu@60.4,7.7:
Halne Fjellstugu stands at 1,135 metres on the Rv7, beside the lake of Halnefjorden, in the middle of the Hardangervidda, and its main virtue is that it is there at all. This is an enormous, empty country, with very few buildings, and a mountain lodge on the road is a landmark in its own right. The place is a classic Norwegian fjellstue, a timber lodge with a restaurant, rooms and a big stove, and it has been taking in travellers, walkers and skiers in a country where weather can turn at any time.

The landscape is low and open, with reindeer moss, rocks and water, and the colour is a mix of grey, green and brown, lit by a very clear northern light. In late summer the ground turns red and gold with dwarf birch and bilberry leaves, and the light has a pale, silvery softness that makes every ridge stand out. The lake is cold and deep, and in winter it freezes and the whole area becomes a playground for cross-country skiers, who come in large numbers from February to April.

The road between Geilo and Dyranut is one of the highest main roads in the country, and in good weather it is a joy, with long, gentle bends and fast, open straights. Be prepared for the opposite as well. Fog, rain and wind sweep across the plateau, and ice can form on the surface in any month. Visibility can drop to a few metres, and you should slow down and light up. In winter the road is often closed or open only in convoy behind a plough, so check conditions at the Norwegian road authority before you go.

Geilo, with a couple of thousand people, is the nearest town of any size and has fuel, shops and plenty of places to eat, so fill up there before you cross the plateau. The lodge itself offers food and drink in season, but check opening times in advance. In the middle of the plateau, cell coverage may be patchy, and there is little help around, so let someone know your plan. A cup of coffee at the window, with rain on the glass and a stove burning, is a small and solid pleasure that you remember long after the ride.
t.utsikten@61.3,6.5:
Utsikten means the view, and at Gaularfjellet that is exactly what you get: a cantilevered platform of steel and glass pushed out over the edge of a mountain, with the valley dropping away below. The viewing point stands on the road over the Gaularfjellet, the mountain that separates the Sognefjord from the Førde district, and it looks down over a vast, folded landscape of rock, forest and river, with the fjord somewhere in the haze beyond. Nearby, the water of the Gaula comes down in several falls, and the whole slope is cut by streams. Spray from the falls drifts across the road in spring.

The road over the mountain is a prize for a rider. On the Sogn side it climbs in a series of tight hairpins and long, graceful bends, on a good surface with views at every turn. Short tunnels, stone walls and white railings line the way, and the gradient is steady and well planned. The cars here are often caravans and tourist coaches, and the road is narrow in places, so take your time and use the pull-outs. Early mornings and weekdays are quiet. In wet weather the road is greasy, and on the exposed sections the wind is strong.

The Gaularfjellet road is one of the Norwegian scenic routes, and the viewing platform is one of the structures built to mark it. Architects were asked to design places where people could stop without spoiling the landscape, and the results are often daring. This one gives a view of the mountain as a living thing, shaped by ice and water over thousands of years. The cliffs here show the layered, twisted rock of an old mountain chain, worn smooth in places and sharp in others.

Balestrand and Høyanger, on the road to either side, are small, and Sogndal is the nearest town with a good choice of services, so start the day with a full tank. A kiosk or café may be open in summer, but check before you rely on it. The best light is in the late afternoon, when the sun slants down the valley and turns the rock gold. Take a warm layer, as the platform is exposed, and the wind can be cold even on a bright day.
t.gaularfjellet@61.3,6.5:
The summit of the Gaularfjellet road stands at about 748 metres, which is not high by Norwegian standards, but the character of the place is that of high mountains: a bare, windswept plateau of rock, lakes and heather, with no trees and few buildings. The mountain divides the Sognefjord from the valleys of the Førde district, and the road crosses it in a series of long climbs and descents. On the plateau, lakes lie in every hollow, and in the evening they hold the colour of the sky. Sheep graze on the hills in summer, and a few mountain farms survive.

The two sides of the mountain are different. The western side, towards Førde, is gentle and green, with forest and farms, while the eastern side drops steeply toward the Sognefjord in tight bends and falls. From the top, the views over the ranges are huge, and you can see for many kilometres on a clear day. The plateau is also a place where weather arrives suddenly. Low cloud can wrap the summit in minutes, and fog is common. Visibility drops, the temperature falls, and the road feels lonely.

It is a good ride, with a lot of variety. The surface is generally fine, and the bends are well laid out, which makes for a smooth, rhythmic climb. Be careful on the descent to the fjord, where the corners are tight and the road is narrow in places. Watch for sheep and the odd tourist coach. Winter closes the road for months, and it is usually open from late spring to autumn, though that depends on the snow. Check before planning a trip in the shoulder months, as an early or late snowfall can shut it.

Fuel is a real concern. There is nothing at the summit, and the villages on either side, Balestrand, Høyanger and others, are small, so the safe course is to fill up at Sogndal or at a larger town before you set out. Take food and a hot drink, as services are few. In late summer, a handful of cloudberries or bilberries by the road make a free snack. The silence on the top, with the wind in the grass, is what the ride is about.
t.voringfossen@60.4,7.3:
Most people see Vøringfossen from the front, standing at a railing and watching the whole river fall into the Måbødalen gorge. A bit of understanding makes the view better. The river is the Bjoreio, which flows across the Hardangervidda, a plateau shaped by glaciers, and meets a step in the land where the ice cut the valley deep. The water falls about 145 metres in a single drop, with a total fall of around 180 metres, and the gorge below is a long, steep U shape, the classic profile of a glacier valley. The rock is hard, old and grey, and the walls shine wet in the spray.

Hydropower has changed the river. Upstream, the Bjoreio is dammed for electricity, and the amount of water going over the fall is managed, with the flow stronger in summer. That is a detail worth knowing, because in a dry spell the fall is thinner than the postcards suggest. Go after rain, or in the early summer melt, and the roar fills the whole valley and the ground trembles underfoot.

For the rider, the ride up from Eidfjord to the falls is a short, steady climb on the Rv7, in a valley hung with smaller waterfalls and stone walls. The road passes through a few tunnels, with long, open bends between them. A few hairpins mark the old road, now a path. The surface is good, and the traffic can be heavy with buses in July, so avoid the middle of the day. The weather in this part of Hardanger can be wet, and the road can be slick with spray. Take a waterproof.

The Hardanger region is known for fruit, and from Eidfjord you can ride along the fjord past orchards of apple, cherry and plum. In May the blossom is a sight in its own right, and in autumn there are roadside stalls with fruit and cider. Hardanger cider has become a local product, made from the apples of the fjord farms. It is a good way to end a day, though not a good way to start the next one.

Eidfjord has a pump and a few shops, and the falls themselves have a café and a toilet. If you are heading up onto the plateau, check the weather and fuel before you go.
t.kinsarvik@60.4,6.7:
Kinsarvik is a quiet village on the east shore of the Sørfjord, a branch of the Hardangerfjord, and what matters about it is its position, between the fjord and the mountains, at the foot of a valley that leads to the plateau. A small stone church stands here that dates from the twelfth century, one of the oldest in Norway, and a visitor can still walk in and feel the age of the walls. The village used to be a trading post and a meeting point, and the stone church is a clue to how important it was. Rich farmers and the church once ruled this coast, and this is one of the places where you can feel it.

Behind the village a path climbs through Husedalen, a valley with four waterfalls in a row, a fine walk for those with time and strong legs. It starts a short distance from the centre, and takes a few hours to do properly. The falls are fed by snowmelt and rain, and in spring they are loud and white. If you don't want to walk, the view of the valley mouth from the road is enough.

The roads around Kinsarvik are among the best for a motorbike in the region. The Rv13 runs along the fjord's shore in long, easy bends, between steep slopes with orchards and old farms, with tunnels where the cliff comes down to the water. The surface is generally good. Traffic can be heavy in summer, with tourist buses, and the tunnels are long and often wet, so use your lights and watch for water on the road. The scenery changes from one hour to the next, with the light on the fjord reflecting in the surface and the snow of the Folgefonna glacier visible on clear days.

This is also fruit country, with apples, cherries and plums growing on the slopes. Cider and juice are made and sold locally, and you will find small stalls and farm shops in the season. A ferry crosses the fjord from Kinsarvik to Utne, a nice break in the ride, and a good way to see the water from below. Kinsarvik has a few shops, a pump and a café, and a bigger choice can be found in Odda, to the south, or in Voss, a long way to the north. Check ferry times, and fill the tank before you leave.
t.karvag@63.0,7.4:
Kårvåg is the village where the Atlantic Road starts if you come from Kristiansund, a small cluster of houses on the island of Averøy, looking out over a coast so battered by weather that it has a name of its own, Hustadvika. This is open ocean, with nothing between here and Greenland to take the force out of the waves, and in winter storms the waves can throw spray clean over the road. In calm weather it looks mild, grey-green and flat, with low islands and bright lichen on the rock. Do not trust that mood. The sea here has a short temper and a long memory.

The Atlantic Road itself, Atlanterhavsveien, is only about eight kilometres long, but it crosses a run of islets and skerries on eight bridges, and it is one of the most famous drives in the world. It was built in the 1980s and opened in 1989, after years of work interrupted by storms, and it was meant to be a local road linking Averøy with the mainland. Instead it became a sensation, with bridges that curve and rise and dip, and a road that seems to hop from rock to rock. Fishing anglers stand on the bridges with long rods, and a few daring souls stand on the walkways at storm time to feel the spray.

Averøy has another treat, and it has nothing to do with motorbikes. The old stave church at Kvernes, dating from around 1300 and set among farms, is one of the loveliest wooden churches in the region, with painted decoration inside. It is a short detour, and if the church is open, you can step in out of the wind and the smell of tar and old timber will surprise you.

On the road, the speed limit is low, there are many places to stop, and the traffic can be heavy in summer, with coaches and campervans. Take it slowly and enjoy it. Weather is the main variable, with wind and rain coming quickly, so wear waterproofs. In a big storm, parts of the road may close. Fuel is easy to get in Kristiansund, about twenty kilometres away, which is a proper town of seventeen thousand people with supermarkets and a good harbour. Eide, on the other side, is small, so fill up in Kristiansund or before you cross.
t.storseisundet bridge@63.0,7.4:
Storseisundet is the bridge everyone has seen, even if they do not know its name: the long, curving span on the Atlantic Road that seems from the front to rise up and end in the sky. It is the longest of the eight bridges, about 260 metres, and it climbs to a height of some twenty-three metres above the water, enough for the fishing boats to pass beneath. The way it is built, with a bend in the middle and a steep hump, makes it look from one angle as though the road ends in mid-air, and the optical illusion has made it a favourite with film crews, car advertisers and photographers.

The experience of riding it is better than the photograph. As you approach, you see the road rise and curve, and then you are up, with the sea on both sides and the land laid out below. On a clear day the horizon is wide and the light bright, and on a stormy one the sea thunders against the skerries and the rain hammers sideways. The best way to see the bridge is from the parking area on the rock beside it, from which you can walk to a viewpoint and look back along its curve. A short loop path leads out to the shore.

The weather is the big thing here. In winter, storms can be violent, and waves have been known to break over the road, but even in summer a strong wind can make a motorbike twitch on the high span. Hold the bars firmly and keep your speed down. Rain, fog and low cloud can all spoil the view, so be flexible and come back at another hour if you have the time. Evening and early morning are the best times for light and for fewer tourists.

The road around the bridge is well kept, with parking areas, toilets and a small café at one of the rest stops, where you can buy coffee and waffles when the season is on. Fuel is in Kristiansund, about twenty-one kilometres to the north-east, so make sure you start the day with a full tank. It is worth stopping to watch the birds: gulls, eiders and the odd white-tailed eagle all use the thermals around the skerries, and a patient visitor may see a seal.
t.vevang@63.0,7.3:
Vevang is the village at the southern end of the Atlantic Road, on the mainland side, where the road comes ashore after its dance across the skerries and the landscape shifts from sea to land. It is a small place, a scatter of farms and houses, with a harbour and a few boats. The coast here is rough and low, with bare rock, thin grass and bright lichen, and in the late evening the light turns the rock to copper. A short distance away, there is a rest area on a headland with a walkway and a platform where you can stand and watch the waves.

I like Vevang for what it tells you about the road. The Atlantic Road has a reputation as a tourist attraction, and it is one, but it is also a local road, linking small communities that live by the sea. Fishing and fish farming remain important, and the houses are low and tough, painted in strong colours, built to survive the weather. On an ordinary day you see trucks carrying fish and farm machinery, and locals going about their business among the visitors. That is a good thing, because it keeps the place honest.

The ride here is easier than it looks, with gentle bends and a good surface, but the traffic can be an issue. In summer, drivers slow down or stop suddenly for photographs, and cyclists and walkers share the road. Watch the mirror, signal early and be patient. The wind is a constant companion, and in a gale a motorbike can be pushed around, so stay alert. The road can close in storms, and signs warn when that is the case, so take them seriously.

Eide, the municipality's main village, is a short way inland, with a few shops, a school and some services. It is small, and the nearest big town is Kristiansund, about twenty-six kilometres away, which has all the fuel, food and repairs you could need. Molde lies in the other direction, a longer ride. A flask of coffee and a bag of buns are good companions here, and a place on the rocks out of the wind is a fine spot for lunch. Whatever the weather, a visit at dawn or dusk is rewarding, as the light on the sea is extraordinary.
t.dalsnibba junction@62.0,7.3:
Dalsnibba junction is where the Fv63 road above Geiranger meets the turn-off to the mountain of Dalsnibba, on a high, bare plateau around a thousand metres above the sea. It is a bleak, beautiful place, with dark lakes, patches of snow and low scrub, and the road crosses it on its way between Geiranger and Grotli. The mountain rises to about 1,500 metres, and a private toll road leads to the summit, where a viewing platform offers one of the highest views of a fjord in Norway, looking straight down over the Geirangerfjord. The toll road opens in the warm season, once the snow has been cleared, and closes in autumn.

If you take the toll road, you climb a few more kilometres on a narrow, well-surfaced road, with tight bends and a steep drop, and you arrive at a car park on the top. From the platform, the fjord is a thin dark line far below, with the village of Geiranger at its head and cruise ships looking like tiny white toys. It is cold and windy, even in July, and the cloud can come down in minutes, so be ready to turn back if the view vanishes. On a clear day it is among the finest views in the country.

The ride across the plateau is a pleasure in itself. The road is wide and well surfaced, with long bends and open views of the mountains, and traffic is moderate, though it is thicker in summer when coaches run to Geiranger. The altitude brings cold air, and snow can fall even in midsummer, so do not underestimate it. A good rain jacket and gloves are worth carrying. The road is open only in the warm season, usually from late May to October, because of the snow, so check before planning a trip.

Geiranger, down the hairpins, has a few services, but it is small, and Stryn and Stranda are the nearest towns with reliable fuel, so fill the tank before you climb. Food and coffee are available at the summit in summer, and in the village below, but prices are high. Early morning is the quietest time, with fewer buses and a soft light on the mountains. If the weather is poor, enjoy the plateau and save the summit for another day.
t.ornesvingen@62.1,7.2:
Ørnesvingen is the top bend of the Eagle Road, Ørnevegen, the road that climbs from Geiranger to Eidsdal in eleven hairpins, with a viewing point that looks back down on the Geirangerfjord. The road was opened in 1952, and its steep, tight bends are carved into the mountainside above the water, with a gradient of about ten per cent. It was a great improvement on the old route, and it made Geiranger accessible by road from the north. The name comes from the eagles said to circle the cliffs, though the best-known eagles here now are the ones on the road signs.

From the viewpoint at Ørnesvingen, you see the fjord laid out below, long and narrow, with dark water between steep walls, and waterfalls pouring down the cliffs. The most famous of them, the Seven Sisters, can be seen from the water but not from here. The farms along the shore, some of them abandoned, cling to ledges high above the water, and it is hard to believe that people lived and worked there. The view is wide and dramatic, and the viewpoint has a car park and a railing, so you can take your time.

Riding the Eagle Road is a joy for those who like hairpins. The bends are tight but well engineered, with good grip and safe margins, and the climb is steady. Going up from Geiranger, you look back at the fjord as it falls away, and the height grows with each turn. Coaches and campervans use the road in numbers, and they need the whole width at the tightest corners, so wait for them and take your time. In wet weather, the surface is slippery, and in late autumn ice can form in the shade.

Geiranger has a few shops and a pump, but supplies are limited and prices high, so it is wiser to fill up at Stranda or Stryn. From Eidsdal, a short ferry crosses the fjord to Linge, a pleasant break that lets you rest on the water. In summer, queues can be long. The Geirangerfjord is a World Heritage Site, valued for its beauty and its geology, and the road along it is among the most famous in the world. Go early in the day if you can, for the light and the peace.
t.gudbrandsjuvet@62.3,7.5:
Gudbrandsjuvet is a narrow gorge on the river Valldøla, a short way from the road on the way up to Trollstigen, where the water squeezes through a slot in the rock and thunders down in a series of pools and falls. The walls of the gorge are smooth and polished, hollowed out by the swirling water over thousands of years, and the sound is a constant roar. A set of walkways and platforms has been built over and beside the gorge, designed to give a close view without damaging the rock. They are light, simple and made of steel and timber, and they hang over the chasm like a sketch.

The name comes from a legend. A man called Gudbrand is said to have leapt across the gap, at a place where the gorge is just a few metres wide, to escape his pursuers, and the story has been told in the valley for generations. It is a popular tale, though few people would attempt the jump themselves. The gorge is not very deep by the standards of the region, about twenty metres, but the force of the water makes it feel more dangerous than it is. Stay on the walkways, and do not climb over the rails.

The road here is the Fv63, one of the best motorbike roads in Norway, with long, flowing bends along the river, through forest and meadow. The surface is good, and traffic is moderate, though it can be heavy in summer with coaches and campervans heading for Trollstigen. The approach from Valldal is a pleasure, and the road beyond the gorge begins to climb toward the hairpins. Rain and mist are frequent, so take care on wet corners. In autumn, the leaves on the road can be slippery.

The nearest places are Valldal, which is small, Stranda, and Åndalsnes, which has about two thousand people and a few more services. It is wise to fill the tank before you set out on the Trollstigen route, and to bring a snack. The best time to visit is in the morning, when the light is soft and the crowds few, or after rain, when the river is full and loud. A visit takes half an hour, and it is a good break on a day of riding.
t.valdresflye@61.4,8.8:
At 1,389 metres the Valdresflye is the roof of Fv51, a broad shoulder of bare mountain between Valdres and the Jotunheimen range, and the nearest thing southern Norway has to a lunar landscape. Nothing grows taller than your ankle. The ground is stone, lichen and cushions of moss, scattered with boulders left by the ice, and small lakes lie in the hollows, still holding snow at their edges well into summer. To the north rise the big peaks of Jotunheimen, the highest mountains in northern Europe, with Galdhøpiggen above 2,400 metres, and the line of them against the sky changes with every kilometre.

The road across is a scenic route, and a good one. It climbs from the south in a series of open bends, crosses the plateau in long, easy sections, and drops towards Gjendesheim and the lake in a more twisting way. The surface is smooth and the road is wide enough for relaxed riding, with plenty of pull-outs and viewpoints. It is open only in summer, usually from late May or June until autumn, because the snow is deep and the winters are long, so check the dates. Wind and cold are the main challenges, and rain, sleet and even snow can arrive in any month. Wear warm layers, and keep a spare pair of gloves.

There are pull-outs on the plateau where you can stop and get your bearings. Look for the cairns that mark old paths, and for the sheep that wander the high ground in summer. Reindeer live in the area too, and you may spot them in the distance.

The nearest places are Beitostølen to the south and Vågåmo to the north-east, and in between there is only a mountain lodge or two. Buy petrol before you set out and carry food and a hot drink. The silence in the high country is profound, broken only by wind and the cry of a bird, and if you can pick a calm, clear evening, the long light on the mountains is something to remember.
t.gjende@61.5,8.8:
Gjende is a long, narrow lake in the heart of Jotunheimen, lying at about 984 metres between steep ridges, and it is famous for its colour. The water is a vivid green, almost milky, because it carries rock flour ground fine by glaciers upstream, and in sunlight it glows like a cut gemstone. Standing at the shore at Gjendesheim, where the road ends and the paths begin, you look down the lake between steep slopes, with the dark outline of the ridge rising on one side.

That ridge is Besseggen, and it is the most famous mountain walk in Norway. A narrow crest runs between Gjende, green and deep on one side, and Bessvatnet, a blue lake on the other, about four hundred metres lower. Thousands of people walk it each summer, taking a boat across the lake one way and walking the ridge back, a long day that needs good shoes and a steady head. The writer Henrik Ibsen used the ridge in his play Peer Gynt, in which the hero rides along its edge on a reindeer buck, a story every Norwegian school child knows. The boat across the lake is a good way to see it if you do not fancy the climb.

The ride to Gjendesheim along Fv51 is a fine one, over the high plateau and then down in bends to the lake. It is a road with real mountain atmosphere, and the light changes constantly, from brilliant to grey and back. The road is open in the warm season only. Parking at the lodge is busy on summer mornings with walkers, so arrive early or expect to wait. Rain and wind are common, and the temperature at the lake can be low even in July.

The mountain lodge at Gjendesheim offers food, drink and rooms, and it is a pleasant place for a bowl of soup and a rest. Beitostølen, in the south, and Vågåmo or the Otta valley, to the north, are the places to find it. Wild reindeer live in the nearby mountains, and in late summer the slopes are bright with bilberry and dwarf birch. Carry waterproofs, and respect the mountains, which can turn dangerous quickly.
t.hite overlook@37.9,-110.4:
Out here the map is mostly blank and the horizon is mostly rock. Highway 95 crosses the southeast of Utah through country that feels deliberately unfinished: slickrock benches, red-and-cream canyon walls, thin stands of juniper, and a sky with nothing to do but stay enormous. Hite Overlook sits above the old crossing of the Colorado River, where the river, drowned by Lake Powell, widens into a flat green-grey arm among the cliffs. The name comes from Cass Hite, a prospector who worked the river sands for gold in the 1880s and helped lure a trickle of others into this remote country.

The Bicentennial Highway was built in the 1970s, which tells you how recently this was one of the most isolated corners in the lower forty-eight. Before it, you needed a ferry, a four-wheel-drive or a lot of patience to get from Hanksville to the southern side. Today the road is a pleasure on a motorcycle: wide, well-surfaced, with long, rolling curves, big views opening at every crest, and so little traffic that you can ride half an hour without seeing another headlight. The long distances are the real hazard. Wind can be fierce on the open benches, and summer heat on the pavement is serious, so carry more water than looks sensible.

Lake Powell itself is a story. The reservoir was created by Glen Canyon Dam in the 1960s, flooding a labyrinth of side canyons that some people still mourn, and its level rises and falls dramatically with drought and snowmelt. At the overlook you can see the pale bathtub rings along the walls, the high-water marks of earlier years. The view is the point: broad, still and slightly eerie, with the Henry Mountains standing far away to the north.

Plan your fuel and food well before you get here. Hanksville, to the north, has petrol, a few motels and a famous burger place, and Blanding and Bluff to the south have more. Mobile signal comes and goes, and help is a long way off, so tell somebody your route. Late afternoon, when the low sun lights the canyon walls orange, is the best hour to be standing here.
t.yaki point@36.1,-112.1:
Yaki Point is a small, slightly out-of-the-way balcony on the South Rim, and it is blessed with a fact that suits quiet people: the spur road is closed to private cars for most of the year, so you reach it by park shuttle instead. Which means that, strictly speaking, this is the one stop on Desert View Drive where the motorcycle waits in a car park and you do the last stretch sitting down. The view is worth the small indignity. Beneath you the canyon falls away in terraces and buttresses, with the great stone shapes that early explorers named after Hindu and Egyptian gods standing out in the middle distance.

The South Kaibab Trail starts here, dropping from the rim along a ridge that gives some of the finest views of any trail in the park. You do not need to go far to enjoy it. A hundred metres down, the horizon has already opened up, and the sound of the wind in the pinyons gives way to a profound hush. The geology is the star: the canyon is nearly a mile deep and 277 miles long, and the rock layers record close to two billion years of Earth history in their stripes.

Riding Desert View Drive itself is a gentle business. It follows the rim east from Grand Canyon Village for about 25 miles, through ponderosa pine and juniper, with a series of pull-outs on the canyon side and easy, rolling curves between them. The speed limit is low, and the park enforces it, as elk and tourists wander across without notice. Early morning, when the light picks out every ridge and the temperature is mild, is the best time. Summer afternoons can be hot at the rim and thundery, and winter brings ice and snow with sudden closures.

You pay a park entrance fee, and the rim is high, at roughly 2,100 metres, so nights can be cold even when the days are warm. Do not underestimate the altitude or the dry air, and drink more than you think necessary. Fuel is sold at Desert View, at the eastern end of the drive, though a petrol station at the other end of a long ride deserves some respect, and Grand Canyon Village and Tusayan outside the south gate have more. Eat in the village before you set off. Sunset here is a quiet, slow affair, and worth timing.
t.grandview point@36.0,-112.0:
Grandview Point earned its name the old-fashioned way, by being very obviously grand. At more than 2,200 metres on the South Rim, it was one of the first places where tourists were brought to look into the canyon, and in the late 1890s a prospector named Pete Berry built a hotel nearby, the Grandview, to take advantage of the traffic. The stagecoach road from Flagstaff ended here before the railway reached the Village in 1901 and pulled the business west. The old hotel is gone, but the view is the same, and the pull-out looks across an uninterrupted sweep of the canyon with the Colorado River glimmering far below.

What makes it special is the geology laid out like a diagram. The Grandview Trail drops steeply from the rim to Horseshoe Mesa, where Berry worked copper claims, and old mining relics still scatter the slopes. You do not have to be a hiker to enjoy the view, but you can take a few steps on the trail to feel the edge of the world fall away. Pinyon pine and juniper crouch along the rim, and ravens ride the updraughts so close that you can hear their wings.

The ride along Desert View Drive here is a series of calm, rolling curves with moderate gradients and long lines of sight through the forest. The road surface is mostly good, but the verges are soft, and elk and mule deer are a constant hazard. At 35 mph or less, the point of the ride is not speed but rhythm. Pull in at each viewpoint, take a minute to look, and then continue. Crowds are lighter than around the Village, particularly in the morning and in late afternoon. Winter brings snow, and the road can close for a few hours or days during storms.

There are no services at Grandview Point apart from toilets. Desert View, about 20 kilometres to the east, sells fuel, snacks and souvenirs, and Grand Canyon Village, about 16 kilometres west, has shops, restaurants and petrol, though it is busier. Tusayan, outside the south entrance, has more still. Bring water and sunscreen, and a windproof jacket in any season. The rim can be cold, and the wind comes up out of the canyon with a sharp edge.
t.lipan point@36.0,-111.9:
Lipan Point has the widest view on the South Rim, or at least the one that feels widest. It sits well east of the crowds, where the canyon bends and the Colorado River comes in sight in long stretches, and on a clear day you can follow the river as it slides between its walls, then disappears and returns in a different colour. Below you a broad green terrace sits beside the water, which is the Unkar Delta, where Ancestral Puebloan farmers once grew corn and squash on the flat ground by the river. Their stone traces still lie there, hard to see from the rim but real.

The rock layers are laid out here in a particularly clear way, and the point is a favourite with geologists and photographers. In the middle of the view, near the river, you can pick out the Great Unconformity, a boundary where much younger layers sit directly on far older tilted rocks, with an enormous gap in the geological record between them. You do not need to understand it to be moved by it. The rapids at Unkar can be heard, faintly, on still evenings. Sunset and sunrise are the hours when the colours flare, deep reds and oranges and long blue shadows.

The route is a quiet one. Desert View Drive, which brings you here, is a gentle, forested road with easy curves, slow speeds and a good surface, and from Lipan you are only a few miles from the end of the drive. Watch for elk at dawn and dusk, for the odd tour bus, and for gravel at the entrances to the pull-outs. The altitude is about 2,200 metres, so mornings are crisp. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons for riding, and winter brings snow and closures at short notice.

Fuel and food are available at Desert View, a few kilometres on, where the Watchtower, designed by architect Mary Colter and finished in 1932, rises above the rim in stone, with murals inside and a gift shop and a small store. If you are going on east, Cameron on US 89 has fuel and a historic trading post. The park charges an entry fee, and the facilities at Lipan are limited to a few parking bays and a small paved viewing area. Stay behind the walls, which are low in places, and remember that the drop is long.
t.passo del penice@44.8,9.3:
Passo del Penice is where Lombardy, Emilia and Liguria nearly meet, a pass of about 1,150 metres crossing the Apennines between the Oltrepò Pavese and the valley of Bobbio. It is not a snow-capped giant but a long, wooded ridge with grass slopes and views to the plains and the Alps on clear days. On the summit of Monte Penice stand radio and television masts, which are visible from many kilometres away, and a small sanctuary church sits close to the top. The Giro d'Italia has crossed it in the past, and local cyclists regard it as a rite of passage.

The road from the north climbs through Oltrepò Pavese, an area of vineyards and small villages, and it reaches the pass through beech and chestnut woods. The bends are open and the gradient steady, with enough variation to keep you alert but not so much that you need to fight the bike. The surface is generally good, and traffic is light except on summer weekends, when cyclists and motorcyclists from Milan arrive in numbers. The descent toward Bobbio is more intimate, with tighter bends and a feeling of leaving the bright plain for older, darker country.

The food of the area is excellent. Varzi, on the northern side, is famous for its salame, which has protected status and a delicate flavour from slow curing in cool cellars. In the valleys you will find Piacentine specialities such as pancetta, coppa and pasta dishes with ragù or mushrooms, all served in small trattorie that often close in the afternoon, so plan your meals. The Oltrepò wines, especially the red Bonarda and the sparkling whites, are worth a taste if you are not riding.

For fuel, Bobbio and Varzi are the nearest towns, but both are small, so top up before you begin the pass. A few cafés and restaurants open near the top in the season, though they may be closed midweek or in winter. A hot drink in a mountain café is a good way to enjoy the quiet.

Weather deserves attention. Fog and cloud often sit on the ridge, and in winter snow and ice can close the road for a short time. In summer, thunderstorms build quickly on the heights. Early morning is best, with clear air and almost no traffic, and the light on the vineyards below is lovely.
t.bobbio trebbia road@44.8,9.4:
Bobbio is a small town, with fewer than three thousand people, but it sits at the centre of a story that stretches back more than a thousand years. In 614 the Irish monk Columbanus founded an abbey here, in the valley of the Trebbia river, and the monastery became one of the great centres of learning in early medieval Europe, with a library said to have held hundreds of manuscripts. The abbey of San Colombano still stands, and the crypt and cloister are worth a visit. The town's stone lanes, arcades and the Ponte Gobbo, a crooked medieval bridge with irregular arches that crosses the river, have the look of a place that has hardly changed.

The Trebbia itself is one of the loveliest rivers in northern Italy, with clear water running over pale pebbles and pools of green. It also has a place in classical history, because Hannibal defeated a Roman army on its banks in 218 BC. In summer, locals and visitors swim and sunbathe on its gravel bars, and the surrounding hills are covered in oak, chestnut and pine.

The road along the valley is a joy. It follows the river in long, flowing curves, with the rock walls close on one side and the water on the other. The surface is mostly good, though the edges can be rough and gravel sometimes collects on bends. Traffic is light, although summer weekends bring cyclists and motorcyclists. On a warm evening the light on the water and the soft sound of the river make it easy to slow down and enjoy the ride.

Food is a draw. Piacenza province is known for pasta such as pisarei e fasò, small dumplings in a bean and tomato sauce, as well as cured meats such as coppa, salame and pancetta. Many trattorie in Bobbio serve these, and closing times are strict, so a late lunch can be hard to find. Bakeries and cafés in the town centre are good for a quick bite.

Fuel is available in Bobbio, but with only a few stations, it is worth topping up before heading deeper into the valley. Larger towns lie farther away. Park the bike near the centre and walk into the old town. The streets are narrow and the cobbles are uneven, so wear shoes you can walk in.
t.portofino coast@44.3,9.2:
Portofino is a harbour the size of a courtyard, ringed by tall painted houses in ochre, pink and rust, with yachts tied up in front like expensive furniture. It sits on a rocky peninsula east of Genoa, in a regional park of pine, olive and holm oak that falls steeply into a clear sea. The village has long been a retreat for the wealthy, and the prices in the cafés reflect it, but the setting is real. Walk up the lane to the small church of San Giorgio or to Castello Brown, a fortress turned villa, and the view back over the harbour explains the fuss.

The road to get here is the better part of the story. From Santa Margherita Ligure, the coastal road winds along the shore for a few kilometres, clinging to the cliffs, passing the bay of Paraggi, with its tiny beach, and dropping to the harbour. It is narrow and busy, and in season it can become a slow queue of cars, scooters and coaches. Access is sometimes restricted on peak days, and parking in the village is limited and pricey, so be prepared to leave the bike in a designated bay and walk the last stretch. An early start or an evening visit makes the whole thing far more pleasant.

Nature on this headland is remarkable for a coast so close to a big city. Paths lead through the park to San Fruttuoso, a medieval abbey in a hidden cove reached on foot or by boat, where a bronze statue of Christ stands underwater offshore. The sea here is protected, and divers come to see the fish and the seagrass beds. On land, the Mediterranean scrub smells of resin and wild herbs after warm rain, and the light on the water shifts from turquoise to deep blue.

Fuel is not available in Portofino itself, so fill up at Santa Margherita Ligure, about four kilometres away, or at Rapallo, a larger town with a long promenade and a castle on the sea. Liguria is also the home of pesto, focaccia and farinata, a thin chickpea pancake, and all three are easy to find in the bakeries along the coast. A slice of focaccia is a fine lunch if the restaurant prices are too steep.

The road surface is mostly good, but with a lot of traffic and tight bends, ride with patience. The reward is a coastline that looks as though it has been arranged by a painter with a taste for contrast.
t.norheimsund fjord@60.4,6.1:
Norheimsund is where the Hardangerfjord stops being a line on the map and becomes something you stand beside. The village lies on the northern shore, in the municipality of Kvam, with the water spread wide in front and the ice-capped bulk of the Folgefonna peninsula on the far side. Fruit is the local trade. The slopes around here carry apple, plum, pear and cherry orchards, planted in small terraces wherever the soil holds, and in mid-May the whole shore turns white and pink. If you can time one ride in Norway for blossom, this is the one.

Just outside the village the Steinsdalsfossen waterfall drops over a lip of rock, and a path runs behind the curtain of water so you can stand in the spray and look out at the valley through it. It is one of those attractions that looks like a tourist trap and turns out to be properly good. A stone's throw away are the roads that matter to a rider, narrow ribbons that follow the fjord edge through villages of white wooden houses and fruit stalls with honesty boxes. The surface is generally fine, the bends are easy and the traffic usually light, though in blossom week and at harvest time the tour coaches arrive, and then the pace is theirs.

Weather runs on its own clock. Rain comes in off the North Sea and drapes itself over the mountains, then lifts to give one of those luminous, rinsed afternoons that Norwegians live for. Carry a waterproof even if the morning is clear. The fjord is deep and cold, but on still days it turns into a mirror, and the reflections of the orchards in the water are the reason the photo kind of stop is listed here.

Norheimsund is a proper village with a few thousand people and the usual Norwegian services, so you can expect a fuel pump, a supermarket and a bakery or two. Many Norwegian pumps take cards only, so keep a chip card handy. Øystese, three kilometres away, has more shops. If you are heading inland, remember that Voss, the nearest real town, is over thirty kilometres off, and the road between climbs through forest and past lakes with few stops.

Buy fruit when it is in season. Hardanger cider is made from the same orchards, and a bottle makes a decent souvenir, although you may prefer a fresh cherry from a roadside box and a seat on the harbour wall.
t.utne ferry village@60.4,6.6:
Utne sits on the tongue of land where the Hardangerfjord splits into its two inner arms, the Sørfjord to the south and the Eidfjord to the east, and it has been a crossing point for centuries. The ferry quay is the centre of the village, and everything else seems to have gathered around it. White wooden houses climb the slope behind, orchards run down toward the water, and the boats come and go with the rhythm of a small town clock. Ferries link Utne with Kinsarvik across the water and with Kvanndal on the other side, and being the bridge on the old route between east and west gave the place importance out of proportion to its size.

The village carries its history lightly but visibly. An inn here has been taking guests since the early eighteenth century, which makes it one of the oldest in the country, and the open-air farm museum of Hardanger, with its collections of fiddles, boats and tools, tells the story of how people lived and farmed along the fjord. The Hardanger fiddle itself, a violin with sympathetic strings that ring under the melody, comes from this region, and in summer you may hear it played at a festival or in a café.

As a food stop it suits a rider well. You arrive, queue for the ferry, and usually have time to buy a waffle, a coffee or a bowl of fish soup while you wait. The local fruit juices and ciders are made from the orchards you ride through, and cheese and cured meats from the farms nearby turn up on plates. Prices are Norwegian, which means high, and portions are fair.

The ride to Utne follows the fjord edge on narrow, winding roads with tunnels cut through the headlands and views that change at every bend. The surface is mostly good, but the roads are single lane in places with passing bays, so watch for oncoming traffic and slow down at blind corners. Check the ferry timetable before you set out, because services run less often in the evening and in the shoulder seasons, and a missed boat can mean a long wait.

Fuel is not guaranteed in the village, and the nearest town of any size is Voss, about twenty-five kilometres away by road and a good way beyond the ferry, so fill up before you leave the main road. If rain sets in, the café on the quay is a warm place to wait it out.
t.atlantic road bridges@63.0,7.4:
The Atlantic Road is only about eight kilometres long, and it is famous worldwide. It hops from island to island across a skerry landscape on the Romsdal coast, using eight bridges, the best known of which, Storseisundet, curves upward in a way that makes cars look as if they are driving off into the sky. From the right angle the bridge seems to end in empty air, and the photographs of it go round every list of great roads. It opened in 1989 after about six years of construction, during which engineers fought storms that regularly interrupted work, and it carried a toll until the cost was paid off.

The setting matters as much as the engineering. The road crosses a low, bare archipelago of rock, grass and seaweed, with the open Norwegian Sea on one side and sheltered water on the other. In a calm, bright spell the colours are almost Mediterranean, with pale rock and turquoise water, but when a gale comes in, spray hits the bridges and waves break across the road. People sometimes come here deliberately in a storm to watch, which is a fair way to spend an afternoon but a poor one to ride in. Check the forecast, because wind and wet are the main hazards, and the surface can be slick with salt and spray.

Fishing is part of the picture. Anglers stand along the railings and rocks, and a few small platforms and rest areas let you stop without blocking the road. The Eldhusøya rest area is the main stop, with a walkway and a café, and it is the place to leave the bike and walk out to feel the wind. In summer light lasts almost all night, and a late evening here, with the sun low over the sea, is hard to beat.

Eide, Elnesvågen and Batnfjordsøra are smaller. Fill up before you go, because the coast between settlements is long, and many Norwegian pumps are unmanned.

Ride the bridges slowly. The crest of Storseisundet hides the road beyond, and the sight of the sea on both sides is better enjoyed at a gentle speed. Go early in the morning if you want the light and the place nearly to yourself.
t.unite d habitation marseille@43.3,5.4:
Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation, finished in 1952 and known locally as the Cité Radieuse, or sometimes, less kindly, as the maison du fada, the madman's house, is a long concrete slab on stilts, raised above a park on the Boulevard Michelet. It contains around 330 apartments of different sizes, interlocking in section like pieces of a puzzle, with internal streets, a small hotel, a restaurant and, on the roof, a terrace with a children's pool, a gym and a view over the city and the sea. It was meant as a vertical village, and people still live in it.

The concrete is rough, board-marked and painted in strong colours on the balconies. The proportions follow the Modulor, Le Corbusier's scale based on the human body. Architects come from all over the world to see it, and in 2016 it was added to the World Heritage list with other works by the architect. Visitors can usually see part of the building and the roof terrace, but check the opening hours first.

Marseille is not an easy city to ride, but it rewards the effort. Traffic is fierce, and the cobbled and tram-lined streets are slippery when wet. The mistral, the cold north wind, can blow hard enough to push a bike sideways, and when it does, the sky is a clean and brilliant blue. Heading for the Calanques, the limestone creeks to the south-east, is a fine day out, and you should go early to avoid the crowds and the heat.

Fuel is easy in the suburbs, and the parking is easy near the Unité, with a large public park beside it. Eat bouillabaisse at a place with a good reputation and be ready to pay for it, or choose a simpler dish of grilled fish, or panisse, chickpea fries. A pastis with water in a bar by the Old Port is the right way to end the day. Stay alert in the dense traffic, lock the bike carefully, and enjoy a city that is loud, lively and a little rough around the edges.
t.gulf of porto calanche of piana@42.3,8.6:
The Calanques of Piana are red. Not a polite pink, but a deep rust-orange, the granite eroded by wind and sea into spires, arches and strange figures that people have been naming for centuries, such as the heart, the dog's head and the bear. They rise hundreds of metres straight out of the sea along the western coast of Corsica, with the maquis, the dense scrub of strawberry tree, myrtle and rock rose, clinging to every ledge. The scent on a warm day is overwhelming, and the whole area is part of a UNESCO site that also covers the Gulf of Girolata and the Scandola reserve.

The D81, the coast road that threads through the calanques between Porto and Piana, is one of the great rides of the Mediterranean, and it is narrow. There are places where it is barely wide enough for two vehicles, with sheer drops and few barriers, and coaches that take the bends wide, so you will often need to stop and let them pass. Take it slowly, in daylight, and keep to your side. The best light is in the late afternoon, when the rocks glow, and the sunset from the Piana side is famous for good reason.

Corsican roads have other hazards. Cows, pigs and goats wander freely, and they love to lie on the warm tarmac around a blind bend. The mountain weather can change quickly, and in summer, wildfires are a real risk, so watch for local warnings. Fuel is scarce on this stretch, so fill up in Ajaccio before you leave, or at Porto if you are coming from the north, and do not assume that every village has a pump.

The villages here have good simple food, with charcuterie, chestnut flour cakes, goat cheese and brocciu, a fresh sheep's cheese, and you will find honest cooking in the little restaurants. Cargèse, to the south, has an interesting history, as it was settled by Greek refugees in the seventeenth century. Take a swim in the sea off the nearest cove, a cold, clear plunge, and be ready for slow, careful riding on the way back.
t.naha@26.2,127.7:
Naha is the capital of Okinawa, a low, bright, warm city at the southern end of a long, thin island that for centuries was the Ryukyu Kingdom, independent and rich from trade between China, Japan and Southeast Asia. Its royal seat was Shuri Castle, on a hill above the city, with red lacquered halls in a style that mixes Chinese and Japanese ideas. A fire destroyed the main buildings in October 2019, and reconstruction is under way, though the walls and gates and the view over the city remain. The castle site belongs to the Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu, listed by UNESCO in 2000.

Riding out from Naha toward the northern part of the island is one of the more relaxed motorcycling days in Japan. Route 58 runs up the west coast, partly through busy built-up areas around US military bases, then opens into easier shoreline with sugar cane, small beaches and views across the East China Sea. Beyond Nago the hills grow greener and the road starts to twist, with the Yanbaru forest to the north holding the Okinawa rail, a flightless bird found nowhere else. Rain can come suddenly, and the road surface becomes slippery in moments. The typhoon season, from roughly August to October, can ground travellers entirely.

Okinawa has its own food culture, quite different from the main islands. Goya champuru, a stir-fry of bitter melon, tofu and egg, soki soba with its pork rib topping, and awamori, the local rice spirit, are all worth trying. The Makishi public market near Kokusai-dori Street has stalls selling fresh fish and pork, with upstairs restaurants that will cook what you buy. Kokusai-dori itself is a long, busy street of shops and souvenir stands, a bit tacky and a lot of fun.

For practicalities, you are in a city of three hundred thousand with fuel everywhere, and the same applies up Route 58. Driving is on the left. The island's bike scene is friendly, and you will see other riders on rentals and on their own machines. Heat and humidity in July and August are heavy. Spring is a good time, mild and bright, with the sea at its best.
t.panguitch@37.8,-112.4:
Panguitch is a small, tidy Utah town of about fifteen hundred people on the high plateau, and it is the doorway to one of the great motorcycle roads in the American West. Scenic Byway 12 starts nearby, climbs through Red Canyon with its orange spires and tunnels, and then runs on through Bryce Canyon country, Grand Staircase-Escalante and over Boulder Mountain to Capitol Reef. The name Panguitch comes from a Paiute word usually translated as big fish, and the nearby lake does indeed have good trout.

The town sits at about two thousand metres, which means nights are cool even in summer, and winter is properly cold. For riders this matters. May and early June can still bring frost and snow flurries, while July and August have afternoon thunderstorms, and September and early October are often the finest weeks, with crisp air, clear light and golden aspens on the hills. The roads around are broad, well-surfaced and mostly gentle, with long climbs, open views and the odd tight bend, and wildlife such as deer and the occasional cow on the road is a real factor at dusk.

Panguitch has an interesting past. Mormon settlers founded it in the 1860s, abandoned it during conflicts, and then returned. A famous episode in its history, the so-called quilt walk of 1864, tells of settlers who crossed deep snow to fetch food by laying quilts on top of the crust, and the town still celebrates it. The main street is lined with old brick buildings from the late nineteenth century, and a number of historic motels still run with their neon signs, which gives the place a pleasant roadside feel. You will find cafes serving big breakfasts and pie, small shops, and a couple of places to eat steak or burgers in the evening.

On the practical side, Panguitch has fuel stations and basic repairs, and it is the last reliable supply point before the long, thinly populated sections of the byway to the east. Parowan, to the west, is larger, though far enough away that it is better to fill up here. Carry water, a warm layer and sunscreen, because altitude catches people out, and book a room in advance in peak season.
t.bryce canyon city@37.6,-112.2:
Bryce Canyon City is a small cluster of motels, restaurants and shops at the entrance to Bryce Canyon National Park, in the high desert of southern Utah, at an altitude well over two thousand metres. Panguitch, the nearest real town, lies about thirty kilometres to the west. Nothing here is old, as the village grew with the tourists, but the setting is the reason for everything.

The park is a landscape of hoodoos, tall spires of orange, pink and cream rock carved from the edge of the Paunsaugunt Plateau by frost and rain. Water seeps into cracks, freezes at night and thaws by day, widening the gaps, and the result is a crowded amphitheatre of stone pinnacles. The Paiute people told a story of the hoodoos as people turned to stone, and the name of the park comes from Ebenezer Bryce, a Mormon settler who ran cattle here in the 1870s. At sunrise and sunset, the rocks glow in shades that change by the minute.

Scenic Byway 12, the road that passes here, is one of the finest roads in the American West. It runs between Capitol Reef and Bryce through the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, crossing a ridge known as the Hogback, with steep drop-offs on both sides, and rising through aspen and pine forest on Boulder Mountain. The surface is good, the corners are open and the views are huge, though in summer traffic of RVs and cars can be heavy near the park. Wildlife, including mule deer and pronghorn, can cross the road, particularly at dusk.

The altitude matters. Nights are cold even in summer, and snow can fall in late spring and autumn, with ice on the road in winter. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in July and August, and the dry air makes the sun strong. Bring layers, water and sunscreen. The best months are May to October.

Services are limited. There is fuel at Bryce Canyon City, though prices are high, and a few places to eat and sleep that are often full in the high season. Panguitch has more stations and shops, and Tropic, a small town to the east, has some services. Beyond that, towns are small and distances are long, so keep the tank topped up.

Walk a short way down into the hoodoos if you can. The view from the rim is grand, but among the pillars, in the quiet and the red dust, the scale is easier to feel.
t.mercantour@43.6,7.7:
The Mercantour proper lies behind the coast, in the mountains north of Nice, and it is a different world: a national park created in 1979, with high peaks above three thousand metres, deep valleys and a border with Italy along its crest. Beside it, across the frontier, lies the Italian Alpi Marittime park, and the two together protect one of the richest areas of wildlife in the Alps.

The Mercantour's story includes the return of the wolf. In the early 1990s wolves crossed the Alps from Italy and settled in the park, the first in France for decades, and they have since spread across the country. Ibex, chamois and marmots are common on the high slopes, and golden eagles and bearded vultures soar overhead. The park also holds the Vallée des Merveilles, where thousands of rock engravings of horned animals, daggers and geometric symbols were scratched into the stone in the Bronze Age, about four thousand years ago.

For motorcyclists, the best-known road in this region is the Col de Turini, at 1,607 metres, which climbs from the Roya and Vésubie valleys in a long series of hairpins through forest, and has been a famous stage of the Monte Carlo Rally. The roads are narrow, twisty and beautiful, with sheer drops in places, and the surface is generally good but can be gravelly after storms. Snow closes the highest roads in winter, and the passes can be icy into spring. Early in the morning, with the sun slanting through the larch trees, there are few better places to ride in Europe.

Back on the coast, Bordighera, a town of about nine thousand people in Italy, has fuel and plenty of cafes, and the border crossing from France is usually uneventful. Italian fuel prices differ from French ones, so it is worth glancing at both. The air at the end of the day smells of salt, pine and lemon trees, and the light over the sea turns pink and gold. After a long mountain day, a plate of pasta with pesto, the Ligurian classic, and a cold drink on the seafront is a very good reward.
t.cabanon de le corbusier@43.8,7.5:
The cabin is smaller than you expect. Le Corbusier built his Cabanon in 1951 on a rocky shore at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, a single room of about three and a half metres square, panelled in pine and furnished with fitted beds, a table and a few shelves. It was a retreat, a place where one of the most famous architects of the century could work and swim, and he spent a part of every summer here for years. He died in 1965 swimming in the bay just below, at the age of seventy-seven.

Next to it stands E-1027, the white modernist house that the Irish designer Eileen Gray built for herself and her partner, and a small restaurant where Le Corbusier took his meals. The three buildings together form a quiet, peculiar corner of the Riviera, wedged between the railway line and the sea, and the entire group is on the UNESCO World Heritage list. Visits to the Cabanon are usually by guided tour, arranged in advance, so book before you turn up, as drop-ins are rarely possible.

The riding here is some of the best on the coast. The Moyenne Corniche, which runs between Nice and Menton at mid-height, offers views over Monaco and the sea from a road cut into the cliff, and the Grande Corniche above it, built by Napoleon, gives the same panorama from higher up. Roquebrune itself is a village of steep stone streets, a medieval castle, and olive trees clinging to the rock. The weather is mild most of the year, though July and August are busy, with traffic crawling and parking scarce. The best times are spring and autumn, when the air is clear and the crowds thin.

Roquebrune-Cap-Martin has around 12,000 people, and fuel is available in the town and across the border in Menton. The cape itself is a pleasant place to walk, with a coastal path under pines that leads along the water to Monaco, and a coffee in the village afterwards is a fine way to end the day.
t.marseille@43.3,5.4:
Marseille is France's oldest city, founded around 600 BC by Greek sailors from Phocaea, and it has never entirely lost its Mediterranean temper. The Vieux-Port, the old harbour, is the heart: a long rectangle of water lined with fishing boats and yachts, a market where fishermen sell the morning's catch, and the quays where restaurants serve bouillabaisse, the fish stew that is the city's pride. The district of Les Grands Carmes lies a little to the north, near the old port and the Joliette docks, where warehouses have been turned into offices and flats.

Above it all stands Notre-Dame de la Garde, a basilica topped with a gilded statue of the Virgin, which can be seen from almost everywhere in the city. It is a short ride up, with views that stretch from the islands in the bay to the white limestone hills of the Calanques, the steep sea inlets that run east toward Cassis. The old Panier quarter, a tangle of steep lanes with murals and small shops, is a pleasure to wander on foot.

Riding in Marseille is not for the faint-hearted. The traffic is dense and fast, and the tunnels and flyovers can be bewildering. Scooters and motorbikes are common, and drivers are used to them, but you need to stay alert. Fuel is plentiful, and parking for bikes is easier than for cars. The mistral, a cold northerly wind, can blow hard in winter and spring, and it clears the air so that the light is extraordinary, but it can make a motorbike hard to hold.

If you have the time, ride out along the Corniche Kennedy, the coast road that runs above the sea south of the Vieux-Port, with the islands and the sun low on the water. The city is loud, rough, generous and alive, and in the evening a plate of fish on the quay is the best answer to all of it.
t.alesund@62.5,6.2:
Ålesund spreads across a string of islands at the mouth of the fjords on Norway's north-west coast, and it looks unlike any other town in the country because a single night in January 1904 burned it down. A wind-whipped fire destroyed most of the wooden town, leaving thousands homeless, and the rebuilding took only a few years. The architects who did the work were young and fresh from study abroad, so the centre came out in stone and Art Nouveau, with towers, turrets and curling ornaments in every street. German Emperor Wilhelm, who had holidayed in the area, is remembered here for helping with relief supplies.

The best view is from Aksla, the hill behind the town, which you can reach by climbing a long flight of steps or, more sensibly in riding boots, by the road. From the top you see the islands laid out like a map, the harbour full of fishing boats, and the white edge of the Sunnmøre Alps to the east. The town lives off the sea, and salted and dried cod has been exported from here for generations, so the old warehouses and quays are part of the story rather than scenery.

Riding out of Ålesund involves tunnels and bridges, because the islands are linked by them, including an undersea tunnel that dips well below the water. They are well lit and well signed, but they can be damp and cool, and the long ones feel colder than you expect. Once you are out on the open roads toward the fjords the riding improves quickly, with mountain walls, ferry crossings and green valleys, though rain is common and the coast can be windy.

Fuel is plentiful in the city and in the towns nearby such as Hareid, so fill up before the long fjord roads. A bag of fresh shrimp from the quay is the sort of lunch that locals will recommend, and the cafes around the harbour are good places to wait out a shower.
t.geirangerfjord area@62.1,7.0:
Geirangerfjord is a narrow arm of the sea that cuts into the mountains for about fifteen kilometres, and its walls climb straight up out of the water. Waterfalls drop down the cliffs, the best known being the Seven Sisters, and abandoned mountain farms cling to ledges that seem impossible to reach. The whole area is on the World Heritage list, and the reason is easy to grasp the first time you come around a bend and see it. The village at the head is small and in summer is crowded by cruise ships, which dwarf the houses and give the place a strange scale.

Getting here is half the point. From the north the road comes down from Åndalsnes over the Eagle Road, Ørnevegen, with eleven hairpins dropping to the fjord, and from the south you can arrive over the road from Stryn or by the small ferry from Hellesylt. The tight bends are fun but need patience in a line of campervans, and the surfaces are generally good. The high road up to Dalsnibba, a viewpoint well over a thousand metres up, is a toll road and gives a vast view back down to the water. Like all the high roads here, these routes close in winter and may open late after a heavy snow year.

The weather rules everything. A bright morning can turn to rain by lunch, and the mist can hide the view completely, so it pays to be flexible and let the clouds clear. Early or late in the day the crowds thin and the light is kinder to the cliffs. The air in the fjord smells of wet rock and pine, and a cold wind comes down off the glaciers even in July.

Services are limited, and the nearest bigger places on your map are Stranda to the north-west and Stryn to the south, both some distance away, so top up the tank before the climb. The village has places to eat and drink, but prices are what you would expect in a tourist harbour. If you want a quiet moment, stop on one of the lay-bys above the water and just listen to the falls.
t.col de@43.9,7.5:
Sospel sits in a deep, green valley of the Bévéra river, in the hills behind Menton, and it is one of those Provençal towns that has been quietly pretty for centuries without making a fuss about it. A fortified bridge with a toll tower, dating from the eleventh century, crosses the river, and the old centre has arcaded houses painted in faded ochre and rose. It is a market town of about three thousand people, with several good bakeries and a calm, small-town rhythm, and the sea is only about twenty kilometres away.

Just beyond the border, in Italy, Airole is a tiny village in the Roya valley, and the whole area is a patchwork of languages and histories. The region was part of the County of Nice and the Kingdom of Sardinia until 1860, and later the border zone was heavily fortified. Near Sospel, you can visit forts of the Maginot Line, built in the 1930s to guard the Alpine frontier, and some are open to visitors. Menton, on the coast, is known for its lemons and the lemon festival held each February.

The ride's great moment is the Col de Turini, at 1,607 metres, a pass of dense forest and tight hairpins that has become legendary among rally fans. The Monte Carlo Rally has used it for decades, and the night stage, with crowds around bonfires and headlights flashing through the trees, is known as the Night of the Turini. For riders, the road is thrilling, with a good surface, steep drops and tight bends, and it is rewarding at an unhurried pace. Further north, the Mercantour National Park, created in 1979, protects a wild landscape of high peaks, lakes and valleys, and it is home to ibex, chamois and a small population of wolves. The Col de la Bonette, one of the highest paved roads in Europe, reaches 2,715 metres and is only open in summer.

From Sospel, the roads fan out in all directions. The Col de Braus and the Col de Castillon are lovely climbs, with a series of tight bends and fine views, and they are much quieter than the coastal motorway. In summer, mornings are the best time, before the heat and the traffic.

Fuel is easy in Sospel, and cafes serve local specialities like pissaladière and socca. Weather can change fast, and snow closes the high passes from about November to May.
t.golfe juan@43.6,7.1:
Napoleon came ashore here. On 1 March 1815 he landed at Golfe-Juan with around a thousand men after escaping from Elba, and this beach, now a yacht harbour and a row of seafront restaurants, is where the Hundred Days began. From here he set off up through Grasse, Castellane, Digne, Sisteron, Gap and Grenoble, on a route that became the Route Napoléon and is still marked with little eagle signs along the way.
