The bay is a calm and rather sheltered curve between Antibes to the east and Cannes to the west, with the Lérins islands visible off the coast. Vallauris, only two kilometres inland, is the pottery town where Picasso worked after the war, and the shops and workshops still sell ceramics, though quality varies. The coast road is usually congested, especially in July and August, and you should plan to be out of the Riviera by mid-morning. Early starts are not just advice here, they are the whole difference between a pleasant day and a long crawl through built-up areas.

Once you turn north and begin to climb, the air changes. Olive groves and pines give way to dry limestone hills, and the road becomes the familiar sequence of bends and steady gradients that make the Route Napoléon a riders' favourite. Surfaces are generally good, but gravel and loose chippings can collect in the corners after storms, and the traffic of motorhomes and holiday cars can slow things down on summer weekends.

Fuel is no problem in the first hour. Vallauris, Antibes and Le Cannet are all large towns with plenty of stations, and it is wise to fill up before climbing into the hills, where villages are small and stations less frequent. The seafront at Golfe-Juan has cafes and seafood restaurants if you want a proper breakfast, though prices reflect the view, and a bakery in Vallauris will serve you better if you are watching the budget.

Take a minute at the water's edge before you leave. A plaque and a small monument mark the landing, and the sea here, flat and blue in the early light, is a good reminder of why the road ahead was built.
t.route napoleon@43.8,7.6:
Palm trees are the first surprise. This is Italy's Riviera di Ponente, a narrow strip of terraced hills and sea, and it makes a gentle finish to a ride that started on the French side.

The town has a long connection with palms. According to local tradition, Bordighera has supplied the fronds for Palm Sunday in the Vatican since the sixteenth century, and the date palms that line its streets are a legacy of that trade. The place became a winter resort for British and other northern European visitors in the nineteenth century, and the old villas and gardens still carry a faint air of that era. Claude Monet came here in 1884 and painted the coastal light and the palm groves, and the town has been proud of it since.

Riding here is mostly a coastal affair. The old Via Aurelia hugs the shore, with bends, traffic lights and the slow flow of local cars, and the autostrada runs behind in tunnels and viaducts. It is not a road for speed, but the sea views are generous and the evening light is warm, and in the cooler months the traffic eases. In summer, plan to arrive early or late, since Italians and French cross the border in large numbers at weekends. The hills behind the town have narrow lanes up to villages like Apricale and Dolceacqua, steep, twisty and full of old stone, and they make a rewarding detour if you have time.

Fuel and food are no problem. Bordighera has a population of over nine thousand, plus Vallecrosia, and both have stations, supermarkets and plenty of cafes. A focaccia from a bakery, a coffee at a seafront bar, and a glass of local Rossese di Dolceacqua wine make a very good ending, though the wine is best saved for the evening.

Take your helmet off, find a bench on the promenade, and listen to the sea against the pebbles.
t.calvi@42.6,8.8:
Calvi announces itself from a long way off, with the Genoese citadel on its rock above the bay and the mountains of the Balagne rising behind, snow-capped in spring. It is the natural end, or start, for the west coast road, the D81, which runs south towards Galéria and Porto.

The riding from here is some of the finest on Corsica. The D81 follows the coast, climbing and dropping around headlands and across river valleys, with views of turquoise sea, red rock and maquis, the scented scrub of cistus and myrtle that covers the island. Bends are continuous, the road is narrow, and the surface is variable, with some rough patches and loose gravel. Traffic is light outside July and August, but in summer, buses and campervans can slow progress. Early morning and late afternoon give the best light and coolest temperatures, and a spring ride, with wildflowers on the hillsides, is hard to beat.

The citadel is the main historical sight. Genoa built it in the fifteenth century to control the island, and the town has a long, if slightly doubtful, claim to be the birthplace of Christopher Columbus, a claim promoted by local plaques. The French Foreign Legion's parachute regiment is based nearby, and its soldiers are often seen in the streets. The Calvi Jazz Festival and other summer events fill the squares with music.

Practical matters are simple. Fuel is available in Calvi, but the coastal road south to Porto has little, so fill the tank before you leave. Restaurants along the marina serve fish and local charcuterie, including figatellu, the Corsican liver sausage, and the bakeries open early. The small airport and the narrow-gauge railway to Bastia mean you can get here without a bike, though it is better with one.

Stand on the citadel walls for a moment and look at the long line of the coast you will ride. It is a good reminder of why you came.
t.alpine maritime@43.6,7.0:
Cannes means film to most of the world, but the working town is a different thing.

The riding is stop-start, with traffic lights, one-way streets and heavy summer crowds. Still, there is something to enjoy in the last hour: the descent from the hills gives views over the Lérins islands and the bay, and the coast road in early morning or late evening is pleasant. In July and August, avoid the afternoon altogether, because the roads around the Croisette are jammed and parking is difficult.

Le Cannet has its own story. The painter Pierre Bonnard moved here in the 1920s, and died here in 1947, and his house and the local museum in a nearby villa preserve his memory. The old town of Cannes, Le Suquet, sits on a hill above the harbour, and its narrow streets, church and medieval tower give a view across the bay. The film festival began in 1946, and its red carpet and palace are on the Croisette. The Lérins islands, a short boat ride away, hold a monastery founded in the fifth century and a fort where the Man in the Iron Mask is said to have been held.

Fuel and food are easy but not cheap. Large stations lie on the inland roads, and prices are usually lower at supermarket stations than on the seafront. For a meal, the market of Forville in Cannes has good fish and local produce, and the back streets offer cheaper pizza and socca, the chickpea pancake typical of the Riviera.

Park, take off your gloves, and walk down to the water. After a day in the mountains, the warm Mediterranean air is an easy reward.
t.olbia@40.9,9.5:
Olbia is the gateway to Sardinia for most people arriving by sea. Ferries from Genoa, Livorno and Civitavecchia dock in the long gulf, and an airport serves the Costa Smeralda, the glamorous strip of coast to the north, which the Aga Khan developed in the 1960s. The town itself is older than it looks. The Greeks called it Olbia, meaning happy, and the Romans used it as a major port; in the 1990s, when workers dug a tunnel under the harbour, they found the remains of more than twenty ancient ships. The Romanesque church of San Simplicio, in grey granite, is one of the oldest in Sardinia.

The area is Gallura, a land of granite, cork oak and low, scented scrub called macchia, with rounded boulders balanced on the hills like sculptures. Offshore, the limestone block of Tavolara island rises sheer from the sea, an eerie silhouette, and local food reflects the mix of land and sea, with seadas, fried pastries filled with cheese and drizzled with honey, and a glass of the local Vermentino white wine. Mirto, a liqueur made from myrtle berries, ends the meal.

The ride begins on the SS125, the Orientale Sarda, which runs south along the east coast through Orosei, Dorgali, Baunei and Tortolì toward Cagliari, with mountains on one side and a series of wild gulfs on the other. It is one of the great roads of the island, with some tight and rough sections, including the high pass of Genna 'e Silana at about a thousand metres, where fog can hide the road. The surface can be patchy, and goats and cows take their time. Weather is generally sunny, but a strong mistral can arrive and blow hard, particularly on exposed stretches.

With nearly forty-three thousand people, Olbia has fuel stations, supermarkets and repair shops, so top up fully before you leave. Fuel stations on the Orientale are fewer, and many close in the afternoon, so do not run it low. Summer traffic is heavy in July and August, when the road is full of holidaymakers, and spring and autumn are better. Leave early, and stop for a coffee in the first village.
t.geiranger fjord@62.1,7.2:
Geirangerfjord is one of those places where the photographs do not exaggerate. A narrow arm of the Storfjord, about fifteen kilometres long, it is squeezed between mountain walls that rise to well over a thousand metres, with waterfalls pouring down the cliffs. UNESCO listed it in 2005 along with the Nærøyfjord, and the tour ships that fill it in summer are a sign of how famous it has become.

The waterfalls have names, and the most famous are the Seven Sisters, a line of cascades on the south side, and the Suitor, which faces them across the water. Old farms, such as Skagehola and Knivsflå, cling to ledges high above the water, and it is hard to imagine how families once lived there, with children tethered by ropes so they would not fall. Most were abandoned in the twentieth century. The village at the head of the fjord is small and busy in season, and quiet when the ships leave.

The riding to get here is the real event. The road down from the north, the Eagle Road, drops through eleven hairpins with views of the fjord below, while the approach from the south crosses the mountain and descends in tight bends. A short toll road climbs from the village to Dalsnibba, a viewpoint at about 1,500 metres, which gives a huge panorama. Many of these roads close in winter because of snow, often from late autumn to around May, so check before you plan. Expect coaches and campervans in July, and be patient on narrow sections.

Fuel is a point to plan around. The village at the water is small, and the more reliable services lie further away, with Stranda about twenty-seven kilometres off and Stryn farther again, so arrive with a decent amount in the tank. The ferry between Hellesylt and Geiranger is a classic way to see the fjord, and a motorbike can ride onto it.

The best light comes in the early morning or late evening, when the crowds have thinned and the rock catches the sun low. Bring a waterproof, because mist and rain are part of the picture, and so is the smell of wet stone and spruce.
t.langevatn@62.0,7.3:
This is where the day begins and ends, in the lake and mountain country that lies between the Geirangerfjord and the highlands, a landscape of dark water, steep birch slopes and snow that lingers on the north faces well into July. The ride is a loop on one of Norway's Scenic Routes, linking Geiranger with Trollstigen, and the lake gives you a calm place to set off from before the fjord and the passes demand your full attention. Stryn and Stranda are the nearest towns of any size, and both have fuel, shops and a bakery.

The roads here are beautifully surfaced and carefully engineered, though that does not make them easy. The Scenic Route from Geiranger climbs in tight hairpins above the fjord, with waterfalls dropping beside the road and viewpoints perched over the drop, and the gradient is steep enough to test brakes on the way down. On the other side, the Trollstigen climbs and descends the mountain in eleven hairpins, at a gradient of around nine per cent, with a waterfall crashing beside the road. Speed limits are low and enforced, camper vans and tour buses clog the road in July, and a slow rider is a happy rider. Mornings and evenings offer the best light and the emptiest tarmac, and rain is always a possibility, so bring waterproofs even on a clear day.

The high mountain roads close in winter, usually from late autumn to late spring, and the opening date depends on snow, so check road status before you plan the loop. Many of the farms in this region were once tiny, perched high above the fjords on steep slopes, with families raising goats and sheep in summer pastures, and some of them still operate as farms and cafes. The rock around here is a very old gneiss, scraped and carved by glaciers that left the fjords, lakes and U-shaped valleys.

The air here is clean and cool, with a smell of wet rock and pine, and the silence is rich after a day of engine noise. Reindeer sometimes wander across the high plateaus, and eagles patrol the cliffs. In summer, the sun barely sets, and the evening light can last for hours.

Take fuel in the larger villages before you leave, since stations are far apart. Pack warm gloves, a spare layer and snacks, because the climbs are cold even in July.
t.eidsdal@62.3,7.1:
Eidsdal is a farming village on the eastern shore of the Norddalsfjord, and the thing that matters to a rider is the ferry. A short crossing links Eidsdal with Linge on the other side, and on a sunny day it is one of the nicest breaks on the whole Scenic Route: you roll the bike onto the deck, switch off the engine, and spend a few minutes with salt air, gulls and a wall of green mountains rising from the water. Departures are frequent, and the village has a small ferry quay, a church and a handful of farms.

The road toward Geiranger climbs away from the fjord edge and over a high shoulder of mountain, then drops through the tight bends known as the Eagle Road, Ornesvingen, with views straight down to the water of the Geirangerfjord. Going the other way, the road leads toward Valldal and the beginning of the Trollstigen climb. The surface is smooth, the corners are sharp and the traffic can be heavy in midsummer, with camper vans, coaches and cyclists sharing the same ribbon of asphalt. Take your time and stop at the viewpoints, since the scenery changes with each bend. The best weather is usually in June and early September.

The district has a history of small-scale survival. Farms here are cut into steep slopes, with narrow fields, stone walls and wooden barns, and for centuries the fjord was the only road. Many farms are abandoned now, but a few are still operated, and some offer a coffee and a waffle to passing riders. The old church in the village, a plain white wooden building, has served the community for generations. Rockfalls and avalanches are a part of life, and warning signs are taken seriously.

Nature is dramatic. The fjord is deep, dark and cold, hemmed by steep walls of rock, and in spring snowmelt turns the cliffs into a curtain of waterfalls. Fulmars and kittiwakes nest on the ledges, and porpoises sometimes show up in the water. The smell of the place is damp rock, cut grass and the faint tang of seaweed.

Stranda has fuel and shops, and the larger villages along the route have petrol stations, so top up before the mountain sections. Carry a layer for the cold ferry deck, buy a ticket at the quay or on board, and enjoy the crossing.
t.valldal@62.3,7.3:
Valldal sits at the head of the Norddalsfjord, where a green valley of farms and orchards meets the foot of the mountains, and it is known across Norway for one thing: strawberries. The valley has a microclimate sheltered from wind and warmed by long summer days, and the berries that ripen here in July are small, sweet and intensely fragrant, sold from roadside stalls and baked into cakes and ice cream. Even outside the season, the village has a quiet, agricultural feel that makes a pleasant contrast to the drama of the surrounding peaks.

Practically, Valldal is useful. It has a petrol station, a grocery store, a cafe or two and a few places to stay, and it is the last real supply point before the Trollstigen climb. From here the road runs up the valley toward the mountain, past waterfalls and farms, and soon begins the ascent of the famous hairpins. Going the other way, it leads back to the ferry at Eidsdal and on to Geiranger. The tarmac is good, the bends are generous in the valley and tighter on the climb, and traffic is busy in summer. Opening dates for the mountain road depend on snow, and in winter it is closed, so check before you set out. The best riding is on a quiet weekday morning in June or September.

The area has a darker side in its history. In 1934, a huge rockslide fell into the Tafjord, a nearby arm of the fjord, and the wave it created swept through the villages along the shore, killing dozens of people, one of the most serious natural disasters in modern Norwegian history. Tafjord, a short ride from Valldal, still stands as a quiet memorial to that day. Rockfall remains a real hazard in these mountains, and the authorities monitor unstable slopes carefully. The people here are practical and cheerful, used to winter isolation and summer crowds.

Nature is lush in the valley and wild above. The slopes are covered with birch and spruce, while higher up the landscape turns to bare rock and snowfields, and rivers pour down in white torrents. The air smells of strawberries in July, and of cut hay in August. Eagles nest on the cliffs, and goats and sheep graze the hillsides.

Buy fuel here, grab a coffee and pick up a punnet of strawberries if it is the season. Pack waterproofs and a warm layer, since the weather on the pass can differ sharply from the valley.
t.aiguines@43.8,6.2:
Aiguines has four pepper-pot towers and a very good view. The village sits on the southern rim of the Verdon Gorge, in Provence, and its château, a seventeenth-century country house with a square plan and four corner turrets topped with coloured glazed tiles, looks like something from a children's book. It is private, but the façade can be seen from the village. Aiguines was once known for the turning of boxwood, with local craftsmen making wooden balls and other pieces on lathes, and the old workshop traditions are remembered in a small museum.

Below the village, the Verdon cuts the largest canyon in Europe, a slot up to seven hundred metres deep and as little as six metres wide in places, with limestone cliffs of cream and grey. The river is a startling emerald and turquoise, the colour coming from fine rock flour and minerals, and it empties into the Lac de Sainte-Croix, a reservoir whose colour is even more intense. Climbers, kayakers and walkers come in numbers, and from the road you can watch them as tiny dots on the rock face.

The riding here is some of the best in France. The Route des Crêtes, a one-way loop along the northern rim, runs through a series of viewpoints, and the Corniche Sublime, built in the 1940s on the southern side, hugs the cliff above the gorge, with tight bends, walls of rock and drops that can make your stomach turn. Both are narrow and need your attention; the surface is generally good, but it can be gritty and there are many cyclists and campervans. Visit early or late in summer to avoid the crowds, and keep your speed low on the blind bends.

Fuel is not in the village, so you must plan. Riez, thirteen kilometres away, and Draguignan, thirty-two, are the nearest options, and it is best to leave with a full tank. In July the plateau is purple with lavender, and the scent drifts into the road, while in autumn the light is clear and the crowds disappear. Summer afternoons can be fiercely hot, and thunderstorms occasionally break over the gorge, so watch the sky. Order a tapenade and a glass of rosé in the village, and enjoy the view while it lasts.
t.saint raphael@43.4,6.8:
Saint-Raphaël is the starting point of one of the most colourful roads in France, and the colour is its subject. The Esterel massif, a low range of volcanic rock behind the town, is made of red porphyry, which glows an almost unreal brick-red against the blue Mediterranean and the dark green of the pines. The town itself is a relaxed seaside resort of about thirty-five thousand people, with a promenade, a casino, a harbour and a handsome church in Neo-Byzantine style, Notre-Dame-de-la-Victoire, built in the nineteenth century.

History is thick here. Napoleon landed at Saint-Raphaël in October 1799, returning from Egypt, and left from the same shore for exile on Elba in 1814, so the town considers itself a footnote to imperial history. The neighbouring town, Fréjus, has Roman ruins, including an arena and an aqueduct, left from the days when it was a naval base of Julius Caesar. In the nineteenth century, the rise of the Riviera as a winter retreat brought writers and wealthy invalids, and Saint-Raphaël grew with them.

The Corniche d'Or, the Golden Corniche, runs southwest along the Esterel coast for about thirty kilometres to Théoule-sur-Mer, and it was built in the early twentieth century as one of the first tourist roads in France. The road clings to the cliffs, with the red rock on one side and the sea on the other, and it winds in and out of small coves, with views of rocks that rise from the water like carved sculptures. The bends are gentle and constant, the surface is good, and the pace is slow, because of the scenery and the traffic.

In July and August the Corniche can be clogged with cars, so ride early in the morning or in the shoulder seasons, and be careful about summer wildfires, which sometimes close the roads in the Esterel. Fuel, restaurants and bike shops are easy in Saint-Raphaël, so prepare there. The beaches along the coast are small and rocky, with clear water good for a swim, but the parking is limited. A plate of grilled fish and a chilled glass of Provence rosé in the old harbour will complete the picture.
t.aurland@60.9,7.2:
Aurland is a village at the head of the Aurlandsfjord, a branch of the great Sognefjord, and it is one of the most scenic spots in western Norway. Fewer than two thousand people live in the municipality, and the village has a harbour, a few shops and a long tradition of farming, goat cheese and fishing. The Aurlandsfjord is narrow and deep, with steep mountains rising above, and the neighbouring Nærøyfjord, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is a short distance away. Lærdalsøyri and Sogndal are the nearest towns, so fill the tank here before you set off.

The road you take from Aurland is the old mountain route to Lærdal, known as the Snow Road, which climbs over the Aurlandsfjellet plateau to about 1,300 metres. It is a National Tourist Route, and one of the great roads of Norway, with a viewing platform at Stegastein, a curved wooden-and-glass walkway that juts out 30 metres from the mountainside, 650 metres above the fjord. The view from the end, down the fjord and across to the far cliffs, is superb, and the structure is designed to feel as if it floats in the air.

Above the tree line, the road crosses a bare plateau of rock, snow patches and small lakes, and the atmosphere is stark and quiet. The surface is good, though narrow in places, and the gradients are steady. Weather is the main factor. The plateau is closed in winter, normally from late autumn to late spring, because of heavy snow, and snowdrifts can line the road well into June. In summer, fog and rain are possible, and even in July, it can be cold at the top.

The village is known for its brown cheese and for the Flåm Railway, a famous mountain railway that runs from Flåm, a few kilometres away, to Myrdal, one of the steepest standard-gauge railways in the world. Tourists arrive by cruise ships, so the summer days are busy, and the best time for riding is early in the morning. In the evening, when the crowds go, the fjord is calm and the light turns soft. A plate of fresh trout or a waffle with brown cheese makes a good start.
t.laerdalsoyri@61.1,7.5:
Lærdalsøyri is a small, perfectly preserved wooden town on the shore of the Sognefjord, and it feels as if the twentieth century only partly arrived. The old town, with its white clapboard houses from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, is a protected area, and the streets are narrow and quiet. About a thousand people live here. The Lærdal river, famous for its salmon, flows into the fjord beside the village, and a salmon centre tells the story of the fish and the people who have fished for them for centuries. Årdalstangen and Sogndal are the nearest larger towns, so this is a good spot to buy fuel and food.

The old road from Aurland ends here after descending from the plateau, and the last section is a long, winding descent through forest and farmland, with views of the fjord. The surface is good, the curves are gentle and the gradient steady, and you drop from bare rock to birch forest and then to orchards. The Lærdal tunnel, which opened in 2000, is the longest road tunnel in the world at about 24.5 kilometres, and it bypasses the mountain pass for most traffic. It has blue-lit caverns to break the monotony, and riders can choose between the tunnel and the old road.

Lærdalsøyri was an important trading post, where goods were exchanged between the fjord and the mountains, and the old customs house and warehouses recall that role. The Norwegian Wild Salmon Centre is a modern museum with an aquarium, and the nearby Borgund stave church, one of the best preserved in Norway, dates from around 1180. Its dragon heads and shingled roofs look like something from a Viking tale. It is a short ride up the valley and well worth the detour.

For food, try smoked or grilled salmon, local cheese and lefse, a thin flatbread. The old town has a few cafes and a small hotel, and there is a fuel station by the main road. The best time is summer, when the days are long and warm, but the village is attractive in autumn, with golden leaves. Take a walk through the old quarter in the evening, when the light falls softly on the white boards, and listen to the quiet.
t.haugastol@60.5,7.9:
Haugastøl is a mountain hamlet on the Hardangervidda plateau, and it feels exactly like the edge of the world's largest high-altitude plain in northern Europe. The Hardangervidda is a vast, treeless plateau of about 8,000 square kilometres, with an average height of around 1,100 metres, covered in lakes, bogs, heather and low mountains. It is a national park, home to Europe's largest herd of wild reindeer, and the weather is often harsh, with fog, wind and snow even in summer. Haugastøl sits on the northern edge, at about 1,000 metres, with a hotel, a few cabins and a railway station on the Bergen line, and Geilo, nearly twenty kilometres away, is the nearest town.

The road across the plateau is a National Tourist Route, and it is a quiet, wide, open ride. The surface is smooth, and the curves are long and gentle, with views across lakes and low ridges that seem to go on forever. You rarely see a tree, and the horizon is huge. The Hardangervidda has been used for centuries by herders and travellers, and old trails cross the plateau. In summer, the plateau is a hikers' paradise, with huts and trails, and in winter, it is a place for cross-country skiing. Roald Amundsen and Fridtjof Nansen trained on the Vidda before their polar expeditions.

Weather is the main point to consider. Even in July, the temperature can be close to freezing, and sudden storms or fog are common. Keep warm layers and waterproofs handy, and be prepared for strong winds. In winter, snow closes the road at times, and drifts are common into May. The road is not busy, but trucks and campers use it in summer, and reindeer sometimes cross, so keep an eye out.

Fuel is available in Geilo, but not on the plateau, and it is wise to fill the tank before you set off. Haugastøl has a hotel and cafe, where you can eat a simple meal of soup, bread and coffee. The air is clear and cold, with a smell of heather and wet stone. The huge sky and long light make this a place for slow riding and for being very small.
t.balestrand@61.2,6.5:
Balestrand is a village on the north shore of the Sognefjord, and it has one of the best settings in Norway: a wide, calm stretch of the fjord with mountains reaching up on all sides, orchards at the water's edge and a quiet, old-fashioned atmosphere. It has fewer than eight hundred inhabitants, and in the nineteenth century it became a destination for British and German tourists, who came by steamer to stay in the large wooden hotels. The Kviknes Hotel, a grand dragon-style building from 1877, is still in operation, and the English church of St Olaf, built by an Englishwoman who married a local painter, stands nearby. Vik and Hermansverk are the nearest towns of any size.

The painter Hans Dahl made his home here and painted romantic scenes of fjords and farms, and Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany visited regularly, which brought more fame to the village. His statue of Fridtjof the Bold stands on a hill above the fjord, a gift from the Kaiser, while the legend of Fridtjof's saga is set around here. The lanes are lined with old wooden houses, apple trees and flowers, and the mood is peaceful.

The ride from Balestrand starts with a fjord road and then climbs into the Gaularfjellet, a mountain pass. The road follows the Sognefjord for a while, then turns inland, with a series of bends and a rise through birch forest to an open plateau. The surface is generally very good, and the gradient is moderate. On the way, waterfalls, such as Hellefossen and Likholefossen, spill over cliffs beside the road. In spring, meltwater makes them roar.

Fuel is available at a small station in the village, but supplies are limited, so it is safer to fill up in Vik or Sogndal. A ferry connects Balestrand with Hella and Dragsvik, which is an enjoyable way to cross the fjord. There are cafes and shops serving the usual coffee and cinnamon buns, and local fruit and cider are sold in summer. The best time to ride is June to September, when the days are long, and the village is an easy, relaxing place to begin.
t.moskog@61.4,5.9:
Moskog is a small settlement in Sunnfjord, and it sits on the edge of Førde, the main town of the area, where the Gaularfjellet road comes to its quiet end. The countryside here is gentle compared with the high mountains behind: green farmland, birch woods and small lakes, with the Jølstravatnet lake and the Førdefjord nearby. Førde, with about eight and a half thousand people, is a modern regional centre, with fuel, shops, restaurants and a hospital, and it is only about seven kilometres away. Moskog itself is a scatter of farms and houses.

The Gaularfjellet road, which you have just ridden, is a National Tourist Route, and one of the most dramatic in western Norway. It climbs from the Sognefjord to a plateau at about 700 metres, then drops through a series of tight hairpins to the valley of the Gaula river, with a view of the Haukedalen valley and a famous viewing platform at Utsikten, which juts out above the bends. The road is narrow in places, with sharp bends and steep gradients, and the surface is generally good but can be damp. Rain is frequent, as the mountains catch the weather from the North Sea.

Sunnfjord has a long tradition of farming and fishing, and the district is known for its berries, apples and cheese. The Gaula river is a good salmon river, and anglers come from across Europe. The coast nearby has islands and skerries, and the sea is rich in fish. Among the local attractions is the Sunnfjord Museum, an open-air collection of old farm buildings near Førde, which gives a picture of rural life in past centuries.

Moskog lacks services, so use Førde for fuel, food and supplies. The town has bakeries and cafes, and a lively music festival in July, which attracts folk and world music artists. The weather is often wet, so waterproofs are wise, but when the sun appears, the green hills are dazzling. The late afternoon is a good time to arrive, when the light softens and the day's climb is behind you.
t.odda@60.1,6.5:
Odda sits at the southern tip of the Sørfjord, a branch of the Hardangerfjord, and it is an industrial town in one of the most beautiful settings in Norway. About five thousand people live here, in a flat, green valley between steep mountains, with the Folgefonna glacier above and the Låtefossen waterfall nearby. The town grew in the early twentieth century around a carbide and fertiliser industry, using hydropower, and the factories left a mark on the landscape and the fjord. Today, the industry has shrunk, and the town is a base for outdoor activities, with a few cafes, hotels and shops.

The big draw nearby is Trolltunga, a rock ledge that juts out horizontally about 700 metres above Ringedalsvatnet lake, and attracts hikers from around the world. The walk takes the best part of a day, and is not for riders in boots, but the trailhead is only a short ride from town. The Buarbreen glacier arm, part of Folgefonna, can be reached by a shorter walk, and Låtefossen is a double waterfall that thunders beside the road. The Folgefonna National Park protects the third largest glacier in mainland Norway.

The ride to Odda along the Hardanger route is a delight. The road follows the fjord for a long way, passing through orchards of apples, cherries and plums, which bloom in May and make the shore a sea of blossom. The Hardanger region is known for its fruit and cider, and farms sell fresh produce at roadside stalls in summer. The surface is generally good, with many tunnels and bridges, and the bends are moderate. Traffic can be heavy in summer, particularly with tourists heading for the hiking trails.

Fuel is available in Odda, and there are supermarkets and restaurants, which makes it a convenient finish. Try the local cider, but save it for after riding, and the cherries, if it is the season. The weather in Hardanger is mild, though rain is possible at any time, and the evening light, with the fjord turning to silver, is beautiful. Spend an hour by the water and listen to the stillness before you move on.
t.bud@62.9,6.9:
Bud is a tiny fishing village on the coast of Møre og Romsdal, and it has a big place in Norwegian history. The old fishing hamlet sits on a low, rocky shore, facing the open Atlantic, with a harbour, a few houses and a church. In the sixteenth century, it was one of the largest fishing stations on the coast, and in 1533, the Norwegian nobility gathered here to choose a new king, in a failed attempt to hold off Danish control. During the Second World War, the Germans built a coastal fortress here, the Ergan Coastal Fortress, which can still be visited, with guns, bunkers and tunnels. Molde, the nearest town of size, is over twenty kilometres away.

The reason most riders come is the Atlantic Road, the Atlanterhavsveien, a short stretch of road that hops across a string of small islands and skerries on eight bridges, including the curving Storseisundet Bridge, which seems to end in the air from one angle. It was opened in 1989 and has become a classic, with the sea crashing against the rocks in storms and waves occasionally washing over the road. The road is only about eight kilometres long, and on a calm day, it is a gentle ride with fishing anglers standing on the bridges. On a stormy day, it is thrilling, though also dangerous.

The surface is excellent and the curves are smooth, but wind is a big factor, and crosswinds on the bridges can be strong. Rain and spray reduce grip, so take care. In summer, the road is busy with tourists, so ride early or late. In winter, storms can close it. The nearby fishing villages have simple restaurants where you can eat fresh fish, including fish soup and fried cod, and there are small shops selling coffee and cakes.

Fuel is available at Elnesvågen and Molde, but not at Bud, so fill up in advance. The area is rich in birds, and whales and seals are occasionally spotted from the shore. The light, in the evening, is soft and golden, and the sea changes colour with every cloud. Bud is a calm place to finish a ride, with the sound of the sea in your ears.
t.langevatnet@62.0,7.3:
Langevatnet is a mountain lake in Møre og Romsdal, on the high road between the Geirangerfjord and the Trollstigen, and it sits in a bleak, beautiful landscape of rock, snow and water. The lake lies at about 1,000 metres, in a bowl surrounded by peaks, and the surface is often still, mirroring the mountains. The nearest towns, Stryn and Stranda, are over thirty kilometres away, so this is a remote place, and the tree line is far below. In summer, the water is glacial blue, and in spring, snowdrifts linger on the banks.

The road you follow is the Geiranger-Trollstigen route, one of the most famous in Norway, running from the Geirangerfjord, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, over the high plateau and down the Trollstigen, the Troll's Ladder. The road climbs from the fjord with eleven hairpins known as the Eagle Road, Ørnesvingen, and then continues over the mountains, passing lakes and snowfields. Most of the road is narrow and winding, with sheer drops and few barriers in places, and the surface is generally good. Tour buses are frequent in summer, so ride early or late.

The weather can be extreme. Even in July, the temperature at the lake can be a few degrees above freezing, and rain, fog and wind are common. In winter, the road is closed by snow, typically from October to May, and the date of opening depends on the avalanche risk and the clearing of the drifts. Keep warm layers close, and be careful of wet, slippery surfaces. In the thick fog, the road can disappear, so slow down.

The area is also rich in nature. Golden eagles and ptarmigan live in the high country, and in some seasons, you may see reindeer or mountain hares. Wildflowers bloom for a short time in July, with a surprising range of colours. There are no services at the lake, so fuel must be taken in advance at Stryn or Stranda, and food and drink are best brought along. A small kiosk may open in summer, but do not count on it. The silence, interrupted only by the wind, is an experience in itself.
t.sogge bridge@62.5,7.7:
The Sogge Bridge crosses the Rauma river just outside Åndalsnes, and it is the last landmark of a long day on the Geiranger-Trollstigen route. Behind it, the valley of Romsdalen is a deep, steep-sided trench, with the Romsdalshorn, a pyramid of grey rock, rising to about 1,550 metres, and the Trollveggen, the Troll Wall, Europe's tallest vertical mountain face, nearly a kilometre of overhanging rock. Åndalsnes, about three kilometres away, is a small town of two thousand people at the head of the Romsdalsfjord, with fuel, shops, a railway station and a harbour. Climbers have come here for over a century, and BASE jumpers jump from the Troll Wall in summer.

You have just come down the Trollstigen, the Troll's Ladder, which drops from the plateau in eleven hairpins, with waterfalls pouring beside the road, including Stigfossen, which the road crosses on a stone bridge. It was opened in 1936 after many years of work, and it is one of the most famous roads in the world. At the top, a modern viewing platform of steel and glass hangs over the valley. The gradient is about one in ten, and the hairpins are tight, with narrow lanes where two buses can barely pass. Wet weather makes the surface slick, and fog can hide the bends.

The road is closed in winter, usually from October to May, and the date depends on the snow. Even in summer, snowdrifts may remain beside the road. In the valley, the weather is milder, but rain is frequent, since the mountains catch the clouds from the sea. Early morning and evening are the best times to avoid the tour coaches, which arrive in big numbers from the cruise ships at Geiranger and Molde.

At Åndalsnes, the Rauma Railway, one of the great scenic lines of Norway, runs through the valley to Dombås, passing tunnels, bridges and the Kylling Bridge, a stone arch high above the river. The valley is also known for its salmon river, and anglers cast from the banks. The town has a handful of cafes and restaurants, where you can have a waffle, fish soup or a plate of local cheese. Fill the tank here, relax by the water, and look back at the wall of mountains you have just crossed.
t.garli@61.2,8.9:
Garli is a remote spot on the Valdresflye, the high plateau road between Valdres and Gudbrandsdalen, and it sits in a landscape of bare mountain, lake and marsh at about 1,000 metres. The Valdresflye is a National Tourist Route, and the road crosses the plateau through the Jotunheimen and Jotunheimen-adjacent country, with views of the great peaks to the north, including the Besseggen ridge and the Gjende lake. The road was built in the 1930s as a tourist route, and it is surprisingly smooth, with long gentle curves and a clear sense of space. Fagernes, over thirty kilometres away, is the nearest town, with fuel and services.

The country is the home of the Jotunheimen mountains, whose name means the home of the giants, and which contain Norway's highest peaks, including Galdhøpiggen at 2,469 metres. The plateau itself is covered in low vegetation, lichen, moss and dwarf birch, and in summer, there are wildflowers. Sheep and cattle graze, and farmers used to bring their animals here for the summer. Old summer farms, seters, are scattered along the road. The area is popular with hikers, and in winter, with cross-country skiers.

The weather is an essential factor. The Valdresflye often has fog, rain and strong wind, even in July, and temperatures can drop sharply. The road can be closed in winter, from about November to May, and snow can remain in June. Carry warm clothing and waterproofs, and do not underestimate the cold. When the sun appears, the plateau lights up, and the lakes turn blue.

Along the road are several viewpoints and rest areas, including a small stone and timber shelter designed to blend into the landscape, and the Gjendebu lake view, one of the most famous in Norway. A bit further on, Bygdin lake is a long, narrow mountain lake with an old steamer, the Bitihorn, which ran in summer. There is little in the way of services at Garli, so fill the tank in Fagernes before setting out, and take food and drink. A hot coffee from a flask on the plateau, with a view of the great peaks, is a fine reward.
t.vagamo@61.9,9.1:
Vågåmo is a village in the Gudbrandsdalen valley, in the middle of Norway's mountain heartland, and it sits beside the river Otta, with the Jotunheimen range to the west. The village has about fifteen hundred people, a church, a school, shops and a fuel station, and it is the place where the Valdresflye road comes down to meet the main valley. The Vågåvatnet lake lies just beside the village, and the farms stretch in lines along the hillsides. The name is thought to derive from an old word for a bay or inlet, and the lake was once much larger.

The village is known for the Vågå church, an old wooden building from 1625 with carved decorations. The area is also known for its long tradition of folk music and of the dance halling, a lively male solo dance, and the district is the home of the fiddle tradition. Peer Gynt, the hero of Ibsen's play, is said to have been based on a real person from the area, Peer Gynt of Vågå, and the Peer Gynt trail in nearby Gudbrandsdalen was named for him. Sagas and folktales are woven into the landscape, and old farmsteads, some of them hundreds of years old, can be seen on the hillside.

The ride down from the Valdresflye is a gentle descent, with views of the valley and the river, and the road passes through woodland and farmland. The surface is good, the bends are easy, and traffic increases as you come down to the main road. In summer, the valley is warm and bright, with fields of hay and barley, and in autumn, the birches turn yellow. Rain showers are common, and the temperature changes with altitude.

For services, Vågåmo is a convenient place to stop. Fuel, a bakery, a supermarket and a cafe are available, and the local specialities include trout from the lake, rømmegrøt, a sour cream porridge served with cured meats, and strong cheese. The village is a good base for visits to the Jotunheimen mountains, and the road to Lom and the Sognefjellet starts nearby. Before you leave, take a walk by the lake, and enjoy the quiet.
t.hanksville@38.4,-110.7:
Hanksville is a crossroads, and nothing more is required of it. A few dozen buildings, a gas station or two, a motel, a diner, and a long view of pale hills in south-central Utah, where the highways meet at the edge of some of the emptiest country in the lower forty-eight. The land is red, grey and pink, with eroded badlands, buttes and domes, and the sky is huge. Summer days are fiercely hot, nights are cool, and the silence is part of the attraction.

Hanksville has a long association with outlaws. The nearby Robbers Roost, a maze of canyons north of the town, was a hideout for Butch Cassidy and his Wild Bunch in the 1890s, and the rugged terrain made pursuit very difficult. To the south, the Henry Mountains rise to over eleven thousand feet, the last mountain range in the lower forty-eight to be mapped by the US government, and today the home of one of the continent's few free-roaming herds of bison. Capitol Reef National Park is to the west, with its multi-coloured cliffs, and the strange Goblin Valley lies to the north-west.

The Bicentennial Highway, Utah 95, heads south from here across the dry plateau and through the canyon country of the Colorado Plateau, passing Glen Canyon and the long fingers of Lake Powell where the road crosses the Colorado River, before arriving at Natural Bridges National Monument. Along the way it passes through scrub and sandstone, with long climbs, open views and almost no traffic. The road is paved and fairly fast, with big curves, but it is remote, and a breakdown can leave you waiting for hours.

Take the fuel question seriously. Hanksville has fuel, but the next supplies are a long way off, so fill the tank, and carry water. Phone coverage is patchy to absent along the route. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with warm days and cool nights, and the late afternoon light turns the rock to fire. Summer heat can top forty degrees Celsius, and flash floods are a danger in the washes during thunderstorms. At night, the stars are so thick that they seem to hang just above the road.
t.grand canyon village@36.1,-112.1:
Grand Canyon Village is the hub of the South Rim, a small, odd community of lodges, shops, a railway station and a clinic perched at about sixty-eight hundred feet on the edge of the biggest hole in the ground most people will ever see. The gorge is two hundred and seventy-seven miles long, up to eighteen miles wide, and over a mile deep, and it was carved by the Colorado River over millions of years, exposing layer upon layer of rock that records nearly two billion years of the planet's history.

The village grew with the railway, which arrived from the main line in 1901 and ended the stagecoach era. The Fred Harvey Company, which ran hotels and restaurants along the Santa Fe line, built the El Tovar hotel in 1905 as a log-and-stone lodge on the rim, and hired the architect Mary Colter to design a series of buildings that borrowed from Native American styles, including the Hopi House, which is still a shop. Many of these historic structures are still in use and are worth a look before you head out.

Desert View Drive starts here and runs east along the South Rim for about twenty-five miles, with a string of viewpoints just off the road. It is a gentle, flowing road in pine and juniper forest, with plenty of places to pull over, and it is far more peaceful than the busy village. The curves are easy and the surface is good, but speed limits are low, and elk, deer and tourists wander across the road. Early morning is best, with soft light on the rock and little traffic.

At this altitude the air can be crisp, with frost in spring and autumn, and thunderstorms in July and August. The sun at the rim is strong, and the dry air will dehydrate you, so carry water. Visitors are warned never to go beyond the guard rails, because every year there are accidents. Fuel is available inside the park, though it is worth confirming in season, and at Tusayan, just outside the south entrance. Food ranges from cafeterias to the historic hotel dining rooms, and you may want to book ahead in summer.
t.desert view@36.0,-111.8:
Desert View is where the canyon seems to change its character. At the eastern end of the South Rim road, the walls are lower, the river is visible as a green-brown ribbon far below, and the view opens to the north and east across the Painted Desert, a country of banded red and lilac mesas that fades away toward the horizon. The rim here is around seventy-five hundred feet, and the air is thin, dry and bright.

The landmark is the Watchtower, a seventy-foot stone tower finished in 1932 and designed by Mary Colter, who modelled it on the ancestral Puebloan towers of the Southwest. Inside, the walls are painted with murals by Hopi artist Fred Kabotie, and a spiral stair climbs to a window with a splendid view. It is a remarkable building to find on the edge of a precipice, and it deserves a few minutes, even if you have already had your fill of viewpoints. Next to it, a trading post sells Native American crafts and snacks.

The road that brings you here, Desert View Drive, runs for around twenty-five miles from the village, through pine forest, past one viewpoint after another, with the canyon opening up and closing again through the trees. It is a leisurely ride, easy on the bike and the nerves, but heavy with tourist traffic in summer, when cars slow down to look. Late afternoon, with low light and the rock turning orange and rose, is one of the best times to be at this end of the park. Beyond the east gate, the road drops to the Navajo Nation and the high desert.

The Navajo craft stalls just outside the gate are good for jewellery and pottery. Temperatures at the rim are mild for the desert, though still hot in July, and winter nights are cold, with snow possible. The sunsets are famously beautiful, with colour changing every few minutes, and the stars after dark are extraordinary.
t.briancon@44.9,6.6:
Briançon calls itself the highest city in France, and at around 1,326 metres, it has a good case. It sits in the upper Durance valley in the Hautes-Alpes, where several rivers and several passes meet, and for centuries that made it both a trading post and a fortress. Roads climb from here to the Col du Galibier and the Lautaret in one direction, to the Col d'Izoard and the Queyras in another, and to Montgenèvre and Italy in a third. A rider arrives from any of them in much the same mood: pleased to be somewhere with a restaurant.

The old town, the Cité Vauban, sits on a hill above the modern town, enclosed by walls and ramparts. Louis XIV's great military engineer, Vauban, redesigned the defences in the late seventeenth century, and the result, with its forts, bastions and gates, is now on the UNESCO World Heritage list. The steep cobbled main street, the Grande Gargouille, has a stream running down the middle in a stone channel, and shops, bakeries and small restaurants line the sides. It is a pleasure to walk, though cobbles and riding boots are not natural friends.

The riding around Briançon is some of the best in the Alps. The road up toward the Lautaret and Galibier follows the Guisane valley in a long, steady climb, with larch forest, snow peaks and the dramatic scenery that cyclists crowd to see each summer in the Tour de France. The mountain passes here open in late spring or early summer, and the high ones close in winter, so check conditions before planning an early or late-season ride. Mornings are often clear, with cloud building in the afternoon and occasional thunderstorms.

As a stop, Briançon is excellent. With over eleven thousand inhabitants, it has fuel stations, supermarkets, bike shops, banks, hotels and plenty of cafes, and it is a natural place to refill both tank and stomach. Try the local cheeses and a tourte, or a hearty plate of gratin dauphinois, and drink a coffee on a sunny terrace. The air is clean and dry, and the sun is strong, which is why the town has long had a reputation as a place for health cures and recuperation.
t.gorges du verdon point 1@43.8,6.3:
Where the Verdon canyon is at its deepest, the walls fall away on the south rim in cliffs of pale limestone that plunge several hundred metres to a river the colour of a green bottle. La Palud-sur-Verdon, on the northern edge, is the little hub for the Route des Crêtes, the one-way loop that runs along the rim of the gorge, and this stretch of road is its starting ground. Castellane is to the east and Aups to the west, each seventeen kilometres or so by road.

The Route des Crêtes is a ride that needs a calm approach. It is a narrow, winding loop of about twenty-three kilometres, with long drops, blind curves, and pull-offs at every belvedere where visitors park half on the road. The surface is mostly good but the bends are tight, so a gentle pace suits the scenery better than speed. Early in the morning you can have the road to yourself, and the light on the rock is a soft honey colour. In the afternoon coaches and cars clog the viewpoints, and the heat radiates off the stone.

The gorge was carved by the Verdon river through a limestone plateau, and it is often called the grand canyon of Europe, though it is a good deal smaller than its American cousin. It has been a magnet for climbers since the 1970s, and from the belvederes you can sometimes see tiny figures on the vertical walls. Griffon vultures were reintroduced in the area and now soar along the cliffs, riding the thermals with barely a wing beat. The air smells of thyme and hot rock.

Fuel is the thing to plan: La Palud is a small village and its services are limited, so fill the tank in Castellane or Aups before you start the loop. There are cafes and a few restaurants in the village, and a picnic from a bakery is a good idea. The road can be closed in winter after snow or ice, usually for short periods, and in summer the heat is intense by midday, so carry water and start early.
t.sognefjellet point 1@61.6,7.7:
Fortunsdalen is the quiet side of Jotunheimen, the valley that leads up from the Lustrafjord toward the high mountains. The road climbs steadily through birch woods and farmland past the village of Fortun and on to Turtagrø, a mountain hotel at the foot of the Hurrungane range, a cluster of jagged peaks including Store Skagastølstind, which rises to over two thousand four hundred metres. The hotel was a base for the first generation of Norwegian climbers in the nineteenth century, and a climbing club still has a hut there. Gaupne and Farnes are far down the fjord and the nearest settlements of any size.

The ride is a gradual one. Leaving the fjord the road works its way up a wooded valley with a fast, clear river, and the surface is generally smooth, with long bends and gentle gradients. The mountains grow closer as you climb, and the trees thin out into bare slopes, with waterfalls dropping from the cliffs. Early morning is lovely, with mist in the valley and sun on the high peaks. The road is also used by local traffic, hikers and cyclists, so keep to a steady pace.

This part of Norway was shaped by glaciers, and the valley is a classic U-shape with steep sides and a flat floor. The Hurrungane mountains are made of hard gabbro, a dark rock that climbers love for its grip, and they are among the most dramatic in the country. Wild reindeer roam the high plateaus, and golden eagles hunt over the ridges. In summer the meadows are full of wildflowers, and the air smells of cut grass and river water.

Fuel is not available in the valley, so fill up at the larger villages on the fjord, and carry on to Lom if you are heading the other way. Turtagrø has a restaurant where you can have coffee and waffles, and the setting is a fine one. The road over Sognefjellet is closed in winter, usually from late October until late May, and snow can fall at any time in the high parts. Pack warm gear even in summer, as the temperature at altitude can drop quickly.
t.sognefjellet point 2@61.6,7.9:
Sognefjellet is the highest mountain road in northern Europe, crossing the roof of Norway at 1,434 metres between the fjords of the west and the valley of Lom in the east. In this part of the ride, high on the mountain, the landscape is bare rock, tarns, snow patches and the glaciers of the Jotunheimen range. Trees give out long before the top, replaced by moss, lichen and low willow. The nearest villages, Farnes and Gaupne, are far below on the fjord, which gives you an idea of the isolation.

The road dates from the 1930s, and it is a long, slow ribbon over the plateau with smooth bends and a good surface. At this height there is a lot of sky, and the views are wide, with glaciers hanging from the peaks. Snow poles line the verge, ready for the winter, when the road is closed, and in summer you will sometimes see patches of snow beside the tarmac even in July. The temperature can be ten degrees colder than in the valley, and a fog bank can blow in within minutes, so keep a warm layer to hand.

The mountains here are the Smørstabbtindane and their neighbours, with a number of peaks above two thousand metres, and glaciers feeding the milky green lakes beside the road. Wild reindeer graze on the plateau, and The tundra flowers are small and bright in the short summer. The air is thin and clear, and the silence is broken only by the wind and the occasional whistling of a ptarmigan.

A mountain lodge near the top serves meals and coffee in season. The road is closed from about late October to May, and opens when the snowploughs have cleared it, with the walls of snow beside the road sometimes taller than a bike. Check conditions before you set off, since the weather up here is serious.
t.sognefjellet point 3@61.6,8.1:
The eastern side of Sognefjellet is where the mountains show their best. The road drops from the high plateau to the valley of Bøverdalen, with views of the Jotunheimen peaks, including the Galdhøpiggen, the highest mountain in northern Europe at 2,469 metres, in the distance. Lom, the nearest town, is a village of about two and a half thousand people at the foot of the valley, with a famous stave church from the twelfth century and a long tradition of mountain hospitality.

For a rider the descent is a delight. The road winds down the hillside in long bends, with a river alongside and the valley opening out below, and the surface is smooth. The views are wide and the road is well graded, so you can relax and enjoy the scenery. Be aware of cyclists, who like to ride up from Lom, and tour buses that take the road slowly, and take your time.

Lom is a good place to rest, with a few cafes, a mountain museum, a bakery that people drive a long way to visit, and a stave church of dark pine, tarred against the weather and carved with dragon heads. The church is one of the largest of its kind in Norway. The valley farms still graze cattle and sheep in summer on the high pastures, and in the autumn you may see them driven down. The glaciers feed the river, which runs a milky grey-green with rock flour.

Fuel is available at Lom, which is a proper centre for the valley, with a petrol station and a supermarket, and it is the place to fill up before climbing over Sognefjellet. The road is closed in winter, normally from late October to late May, so check conditions in spring and autumn. The weather in the high mountains can change quickly, and the cold can arrive even in July, so be prepared. In the evening, the light on the mountains is soft, and the river sounds loud in the quiet.
t.zion mount carmel highway point 1@37.2,-:
Springdale lies at the mouth of Zion Canyon, and the effect of arriving is rather like walking into a cathedral. Red and cream cliffs rise on every side, thousands of feet high, with the Virgin River winding below them and cottonwoods lining its banks. The village itself is small, a single main street running along the base of the walls, with cafes, galleries, motels and outfitters, and a grand view of the Watchman, a peak that stands guard over the entrance.

Zion's story is one of water and stone. The Virgin River has carved the canyon out of Navajo sandstone, a rock formed from vast sand dunes about 180 million years ago, and the cliffs still show the flowing lines of the old dunes in their cross-bedding. The Paiute people lived here for centuries, and Mormon settlers arrived in the 1860s, calling the canyon Zion, a place of refuge. The area was made a national park in 1919.

For riders, this is the starting point of the highway that connects the canyon with the plateau to the east. The road in from Hurricane and La Verkin follows the river, with long, gentle bends through red country, and the approach from the west is easy and scenic. Traffic can be heavy in spring and summer, and parking in Springdale is limited, so arrive early. The town has a free shuttle that runs along the main street to the park entrance.

Fuel is available in town, though it is more expensive than in Hurricane, about twenty-six kilometres to the west, where there are supermarkets, motels and several stations. Restaurants in Springdale serve everything from burgers to fine dining, and there are bakeries for early starts. A pass is required to enter the park, and motorcycle rates are lower than for cars.

The best season is spring and autumn, when the days are warm and the nights cool. In summer, the heat in the canyon can reach well over a hundred degrees Fahrenheit, with afternoon thunderstorms that cause flash floods, which can be dangerous in narrow canyons. Winter is quiet, with occasional snow on the high plateau.

Take time to look up. The cliffs change colour through the day, from pink at dawn to gold and red in the late afternoon, and the light is worth waiting for.
t.zion mount carmel highway point 2@37.2,-:
At Canyon Junction the traffic splits, and the choice reveals how Zion works. Turn left, and you enter the Zion Canyon Scenic Drive, a six-mile dead-end road that runs up the canyon floor to the Temple of Sinawava. In most of the year, private vehicles are not allowed on it, and the park runs a free shuttle instead. Turn right, and you are on the Zion-Mount Carmel Highway, a different road in every sense, built to lift travellers out of the canyon and across the plateau to the east.

The road you are about to take is a feat of engineering. It was built in the 1920s and opened in 1930, designed to give access to the park from the north rim and to the other national parks of southern Utah. Its crowning feature is a tunnel one point one miles long, blasted through the sandstone, with windows cut in the rock so that drivers could see out. The six switchbacks that lead up to the tunnel are cut into the cliff, and the road climbs about 800 feet in a short distance.

Riders should know that the tunnel has rules. Large vehicles must be escorted and pay a fee, and traffic may be stopped in one direction while they pass. Motorcycles can go through without escort, but the tunnel is narrow, dark and unlit in places, so use your headlight, remove sunglasses and keep to the right. Expect delays in summer, when queues of cars wait at each end.

The park entrance station at the south end of town charges a fee, and the visitor centre nearby has maps, water and information about road conditions. Fuel is not available in the park, and the nearest stations are in Springdale and Hurricane. The shuttle stops here for those who want to leave the bike and explore the canyon on foot.

The morning light is the best, with soft colours on the cliffs and relatively few people. Spring brings waterfalls from the cliffs after rain, and autumn gives golden cottonwoods in the canyon. In summer, start early, since heat builds fast, and carry plenty of water.
t.zion mount carmel highway point 3@37.2,-:
Six switchbacks stack up the side of Pine Creek canyon here, and for a few minutes the road feels more like an alpine pass than a desert highway. The Great Arch of Zion, a huge scoop in the cliff face, sits above the road, and the sheer white face of the East Temple rises across the canyon.

The road was designed to make this climb possible. Engineers in the 1920s cut the shelf into the rock and built retaining walls of local stone, and the work was done largely with hand tools, dynamite and mules. At the top, the road enters the tunnel, a bore with arched windows that give flashes of the canyon below. It was one of the longest tunnels in the country when it opened in 1930, and it remains a landmark of national park engineering.

For a rider, this is the best part of the ride. The bends are tight but well built, with a good surface and a moderate grade, and the views change with each turn. Traffic can be slow, especially in summer, but with a steady hand and an eye on the lane, you can enjoy the rhythm. Gravel and sand collect on the inside of the turns, so take care, and watch for sightseers who stop abruptly or step out of their cars for photographs. The parking areas along the road fill up quickly, and the pull-outs have limited space.

Fill up before the climb, and bring water, since the walls hold heat and the air can be dry. Wildlife is part of the scene. Bighorn sheep are sometimes seen on the cliffs near the tunnel, and peregrine falcons nest in the high walls, so a quick look up may be rewarded.

Light is dramatic in the early morning and the late afternoon. The cliffs turn from pink to orange, and the shadows add depth to the canyon. In winter the road may be icy on the upper switchbacks, and chains may be required in heavy snow. Spring and autumn are the best times to ride, and the park is quieter on weekdays.
t.zion mount carmel highway point 4@37.2,-:
Checkerboard Mesa looks like something a giant has scratched into a loaf of bread. The great dome of cream Navajo sandstone stands just beside the road east of the tunnel, patterned with a grid of vertical and horizontal cracks that form a regular chessboard of blocks. The vertical lines are the remains of the original dune layers, and the horizontal ones come from weathering, as water seeps into the rock and freezes and thaws. The result is one of the best-known formations in the park, and one of the easiest to photograph from the roadside.

East of the tunnel the landscape changes completely. The tight canyon gives way to a high plateau of slickrock domes, pine and juniper, with a feeling of open space that contrasts with the narrow valley behind. The rock is white and pale pink, polished by wind and water into smooth bumps and hollows. The road runs through this broken country in a series of long, fluid bends, with turnouts every mile or so, and good views over the domes toward the horizon.

Riding here is a pleasure in good weather. The surface is smooth and the curves are open and predictable, and the speed limit, around 35 miles an hour in the park, suits the scenery. Wind can be strong on the plateau, and sudden showers are possible in the afternoon. In winter, patches of ice can linger on the shaded stretches, and it is wise to check the road report before leaving. The turnouts are small, so use them carefully.

Springdale lies about thirty-six kilometres behind, and Mount Carmel Junction, outside the park to the east, has a small station and a cafe. Take water, as it can be hot, and carry a spare layer for the evening.

Pull out at the small parking area near the mesa, and walk up the slickrock for a few minutes. The rock is rough and grippy, and the view over the domes is a long one, with the pale cliffs on the horizon. Desert varnish, a dark patina made by bacteria, streaks the walls, and tiny pockets in the rock hold water after rain, with a brief life of tadpole shrimp and other creatures. Treat the area with care, and stay on the rock to avoid damaging the fragile soil crust.
t.zion mount carmel highway point 5@37.2,-:
Mount Carmel Junction is not much of a place, and that is part of its charm. A handful of buildings stand at the meeting of Utah 9 and US 89, on a high sagebrush plateau at around 5,200 feet, with the pale cliffs of the Vermilion range to the south and the long, low line of the Moquith Mountains beyond. The settlement was founded by Mormon families in the 1870s, as part of the United Order, an experiment in communal living, and the name comes from the biblical mountain.

The junction is a crossroads of the great national parks. North on US 89 lies Bryce Canyon, about an hour and a half away, with its forest of orange hoodoos, and on the way the highway passes through the red rock country of Long Valley. South on the same road is Kanab, a town known for its role as a film set for hundreds of Western movies, and beyond it the Arizona Strip, the Vermilion Cliffs and the road to the north rim of the Grand Canyon. Lake Powell and Glen Canyon are within reach.

For a rider, this is a place for a breath. The road from the park comes down in long, open bends and levels out into easy straights, with pale cliffs on either side and a view of sagebrush and juniper. Wind is common, and storms can arrive quickly from the south in summer. The surface is generally good, though frost heaves can appear after winter. Traffic is moderate, but tourist buses and RVs on US 89 can slow progress.

There is a small gas station at the junction, together with a motel and a cafe, so you can fill up, buy a cold drink and ask local advice. Kanab, about twenty-four kilometres to the south, has more of everything, including stations, supermarkets, motels and restaurants, and a small museum of the area's film history. Mount Carmel Junction can be closed for services in winter, so plan ahead.

The air is dry and clear, and the sky at night is extraordinarily dark. The stars are bright, and the Milky Way is easy to see. Mornings are cool, even in summer, and the altitude gives a sharp edge to the air. Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Summer can be hot, with thunderstorms in July and August. Whichever way you head from here, the road ahead holds some of the best scenery in the American West.
t.geiranger trollstigen norwegian scenic r:
High above the Geirangerfjord, where the mountains flatten out into a bare plateau of lakes and bare rock, the road feels less like a fjord route and more like a journey across the roof of Norway. This point lies on that upland ground south of the fjord, on the approach to the descent into Geiranger, in country where trees give up and the snow often lingers well into June. The nearest sizeable villages, Stryn and Stranda, are both more than thirty kilometres away, and nothing in between sells fuel, so arrive with a full tank.

The riding up here is open and fast by Norwegian standards, with long straights and gentle curves between the lakes, and the air is thin enough and cool enough that you will feel it through your jacket even in midsummer. The edges of the road are marked with tall poles that the snow ploughs use as guides, and that tells you how serious the winter is. The pass is usually closed from late autumn until spring, so check before you go outside the summer season, and expect patches of mist and cold rain at any time.

What makes this stretch worth knowing is the geology and the view it prepares you for. These mountains are old, hard rocks ground down by ice into rounded domes, and the fjord below is a glacial trench that was later flooded by the sea. A short side road leads up to a high lookout above the fjord, which is a toll road and is open in the season, and the view from there, straight down to the water and the tiny ferries, is the one that explains why the area is on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

The best time to ride is on a clear morning in July or August, when the road is dry and the light low enough to pick out the folds of the hills. Pull over at one of the little lay-bys, turn off the engine and listen; the quiet is remarkable, broken only by water running off the snow. Then carry on down toward the water, with fresh brakes and a low gear, because the next part is steep.

Geiranger is a village of a few hundred people that receives more than a hundred times that number of visitors in a summer day, mostly off cruise ships that anchor in the fjord. It sits at the very head of the Geirangerfjord, at the bottom of a steep amphitheatre of mountains, and the arrival from above is one of the best things you can do on two wheels in Norway: a series of tight hairpins dropping through forest and rock with the water coming into view bend by bend.

The road in is the famous one, the Ørnevegen or Eagle Road, with eleven hairpins and views over the fjord and its waterfalls. It is steep, so use engine braking and keep your speed down on the descent, especially on a loaded bike; I have smelled more than one set of brake pads on the way down. In summer it is busy, with coaches, camper vans and other riders sharing the road, so patience is part of the deal. On a sunny day the whole fjord is green and silver, and the waterfalls, among them the Seven Sisters across the water, are at their best in early summer when the snowmelt is heavy.

The village has fuel, groceries and plenty of places to eat and drink, though prices are high by any standard because everything arrives by road or sea. A café on the waterfront is the obvious place to sit and watch the ships come in. Some of the cruise vessels are larger than the village itself, and the contrast is half the entertainment. The fjord was listed as a World Heritage site in 2005 for its landscapes, and you can see why from the quay: sheer walls, abandoned mountain farms perched high above the water, and a surface so still that the cliffs are doubled in the reflection.

The abandoned farms deserve a thought. Families once lived and farmed on tiny ledges here, climbing ladders and chains to reach their land, and children were reportedly tethered to stop them falling. It is a reminder of how hard life was in a landscape that now appears so serene. Stay for the evening if you can, when the ships leave and the village exhales.
t.sognefjellet norwegian scenic route poin:
At the top of the Sognefjellet you are standing on the highest mountain road in northern Europe, and you will feel it. The point lies on the high plateau near the pass, at a little under fourteen hundred metres, where trees disappeared kilometres ago and the landscape is a mix of bare rock, tiny tarns, snow patches and low arctic vegetation. It feels more like the far north than southern Norway, and the weather matches: even in July, you can meet mist, sleet and a wind that cuts through a summer jacket.

The road across the top is wide and open, with long sections of fast, gentle riding, and the great attraction is the scale of the country around you. On one side are the glaciers and peaks of the Jotunheimen national park, among them some of the highest mountains in Norway. On the other are the wild, treeless slopes that run down toward the Sognefjord. A small lodge near the pass offers coffee and food in season, and there are lay-bys where you can pull off and take in the view.

Fuel is the thing to remember. There is none up here, and the nearest stations are a long way off, at Lom on one side and in the Lustrafjord villages on the other. If you are on a smaller tank, plan accordingly. The road is usually open from late May or June until October, but heavy snow can close it at short notice at either end of the season, and in summer you will see snow still lying beside the tarmac.

Mountain people have crossed this plateau for centuries, driving cattle and carrying goods between the Gudbrandsdal and the fjord country; before there was a road, it was a hard walking route. The modern road was built in the 1930s as a work project and has been improved many times since. Stop for a moment away from the traffic. The silence is huge, the air thin and clean, and the light changes the colour of the rock every few minutes. Then zip up, and prepare for the long descent.

Beyond the high plateau the Sognefjellet starts to drop, and this point lies in the zone where the descent begins to feel serious. It is a stretch of the road in wild mountain country on the west side, near the Turtagrø area, which has been a climbers' base for well over a century and sits below the Hurrungane, a cluster of sharp peaks including Store Skagastølstind, one of the most coveted climbs in Norway. Even if you never intend to touch a rope, the setting is magnificent.

The riding here is quite different from the top. The road narrows, the bends tighten, and the gradient increases as you head down toward the valley, so you will use engine braking and a steady hand. The surface is good, but the edges can be rough, and there are places where meltwater runs across the tarmac. Tunnels are few, but there are some short ones, and the temperature changes sharply when you pass in and out of the shade. Take it easy, particularly on a loaded bike or two-up, and be ready to meet vehicles in the middle of the road.

The nearest places with services lie down in the valley, at Fortun and further on at Gaupne, so check the gauge before you start the descent. A small hotel and hut in the area serve food in season, but they are not open all year. Water is plentiful, running off the mountains in streams you can often drink from, though it is wise to be cautious.

The geology is exceptional. The rock is hard, ancient gneiss and granite, carved by glaciers into steep walls and sharp ridges, and the valley has the characteristic U-shape of ice-cut terrain. In the evening, the peaks catch the last of the sun and glow pink for a few minutes. Late afternoon is a good time to be here, with fewer coaches and softer light, but remember that the sun sets over the western ridges earlier than you might think. Wear an extra layer and be careful with your pace as the temperature drops.
t.verdon gorge route point 4@43.8,6.3:
La Palud-sur-Verdon is the main village on the north rim of the gorge, and it exists to let you see it. About three hundred people live here, at an altitude of nearly a thousand metres, on a plateau of pasture and lavender, and in summer many times that number pass through, on foot, on bikes and in cars. There is a church with a stone bell tower, a handful of cafes, shops selling local honey and lavender, and climbing guides who work in the gorge.

The village is the start of the Route des Crêtes, a one-way loop of about twenty-three kilometres that follows the edge of the cliffs on the north side, with a series of viewpoints, or belvédères, where you can stop and look into the abyss. Each viewpoint has its own character. Some look straight down to the river, hundreds of metres below. Others look across the gorge to the opposite wall. The road is narrow and winding, with several tight bends, and it takes time, because you want to stop often.

The riding on the Route des Crêtes is unforgettable, but it asks for care. The road is narrow, and in places it has no barrier on the cliff side. Surfaces can be loose in places, with gravel on the bends, and coaches and cars sometimes park on the road. It runs one way, so you cannot turn back if you change your mind, and the road is closed in winter. In high summer, with the crowds, it is slow, and early morning or evening is better.
