The surrounding country is a limestone plateau, where the thin soil supports box, juniper and oak, and in June the lavender fields are in bloom, filling the air with scent. The gorge itself cuts a dark green line through it all. At night the sky is brilliantly clear, with very little light pollution, and the stars are spectacular.

La Palud is small, but it has what a village on the route must have: cafes, a bakery and basic shops. Fuel, though, is not something to expect in a village of three hundred, so fill up in Castellane or Riez before coming, and bring water.
t.corsica west coast d81 point 4@42.3,8.7:
Porto sits at the head of a deep gulf, where the mountains come down to the sea in a great amphitheatre, and it is the base for exploring the whole of this part of the coast. It is a small place, a marina and a few hotels and restaurants around a shingle beach, with a Genoese tower of the sixteenth century on a rock at the end of the bay and a row of eucalyptus trees along the road. The inland village, Ota, climbs the hillside behind and is older and more authentic.

Behind Porto lies the Spelunca gorge, a narrow, winding valley with old Genoese stone bridges, where the river runs between granite walls, and above it the high peaks of the interior. Walkers come for the paths, and swimmers for the cold green pools. Boats leave from the marina for the Scandola reserve, a wild, volcanic headland where the rocks plunge into the sea in red and black cliffs, and which is inaccessible by road. Scandola is a protected area, a UNESCO listing, and the home of ospreys, cormorants and rare marine life.

For a rider, Porto is the heart of the D81. The road runs from the Calanche of Piana down towards the gulf, with views of the bay and the sea, and then continues north over the Col de Palmarella. In summer it is busy, but the combination of sea, cliffs and bends is among the best in Europe, and it rewards patience. The surface is good, though tight and narrow in places, with little room for error. The most important thing is to keep to your side, to be careful on the blind bends and to give way to the large coaches.

Porto is small, but it has fuel, a few shops and several restaurants, which makes it a useful stop on this route. It is also the place to eat well. Corsican cooking is hearty, with wild boar stew, chestnut-flour cakes, strong cheeses such as brocciu, and sausages. Fresh fish is served at the quay.

The evening light on the gulf is memorable. As the sun sets, the cliffs behind the bay turn red and then purple, and the sea goes dark.
t.corsica west coast d81 point 5@42.3,8.7:
The climb out of Porto towards the north brings you to the Col de Palmarella, one of the finest viewpoints on the coast. The pass is not high, but it hangs above the sea, and from the roadside you look down on the Gulf of Girolata, a wide curve of blue water bounded by the dark promontory of Scandola.

Girolata, down at the water's edge, is a tiny hamlet that cannot be reached by road. There are a few houses, a Genoese tower on a rock, and a handful of boats in the harbour, and visitors arrive by sea or on a long walking path. It is a place that has changed little in decades, and the tower, one of many built by the Genoese to guard against Barbary pirates, is still in good condition.

The land is steep and covered in maquis, with fragrant cistus, myrtle and tree heather, and in spring the hillsides are bright with flowers. Where the maquis is cut away, red rocks show, the same granite and volcanic stone that make the coast so dramatic. Birds of prey ride the air above the gulf, and on clear days you may see Capo Rosso and the headlands to the south.

The D81 north of Porto is quieter than the section through the Calanche, and it is a delightful ride. The road climbs and descends in a series of long bends, hugging the slope above the sea, with few villages and little traffic. The surface is mostly good, but the road is narrow, and in a few places the edge is crumbling, so keep your attention on the road, not just the view. In the evening, the light on the water is magical.

A small snack stall sometimes operates at the viewpoint in summer, but it is not a reliable stop. Calvi, about twenty-six kilometres to the north, is the next large town, and Porto lies behind you, so the sensible plan is to make sure your tank is full before you leave.
t.norwegian scenic route gamle strynefjell:
The old Strynefjell road is a piece of nineteenth-century ambition that still works. It was finished in 1894 and for the first time gave the Nordfjord country a proper road across the mountains toward the east, a feat of hand labour and dry-stone masonry that astonished people at the time. The surface was meant for carts and carriages, not engines, and the road reflects that: narrow, winding and following the shape of the land rather than cutting through it. Stone retaining walls, built without mortar, still hold the edge in places where the mountain drops away.

This high country is bleak in the most beautiful way. The ground is bare rock, boulder fields and small lakes, with moss and low willow in the hollows, and the peaks of Jostedalsbreen's region stand along the horizon. Snow lingers well into summer, and in some years the old road is not clear until June. The air is thin and clean, and when the cloud lifts the visibility is almost unreal, with distant ridges standing out sharply in the clear light. When the cloud sits down, the road disappears into grey and the temperature drops, so be ready for either.

For a motorcyclist, the old road is slower and more interesting than the modern one that replaced it. The bends are tight, sometimes blind, and the width is limited, with cyclists and campers sharing the tarmac. Surfaces can be rough or patched, with frost heave and gravel at the edges, so ride with respect and keep your speed low. It is not a road for racing, but for taking in the landscape, with the engine ticking over and your eyes on the view.

Up here the settlements are far away. Stryn, thirty kilometres off, is the nearest village of any size in the Nordfjord direction, so arrive with fuel, water and something to eat. The road is normally open from early summer to autumn, but the date depends on snow, and the weather can turn quickly, so carry a spare layer. If the sky is clear, stop at a bend and look for the snow patches on the far ridges.

Where the old Strynefjell road crosses the open mountain, the landscape feels as if it has been scraped clean. The glaciers that once covered this country have left rounded rock, scattered boulders and lakes in every dip, and the soil is so thin that the vegetation seems to cling on by habit. Mosses and lichens colour the stone in rust and grey, and in the damp hollows cotton grass nods in the wind. Mountain streams cross the road in small culverts, loud with melt in early summer and almost silent by autumn.

The Strynefjell was the place where the old trading lines between the fjord valleys and eastern Norway met the mountain. People crossed on foot or with horses long before any road was built, carrying fish, grain, wool and other goods, and the paths are still visible in places as worn lines across the rock. Summer farms, called setrar in Norwegian, stood on the pastures at the edge of the high ground, where cattle and goats were brought from the valleys to graze for a few weeks in summer. Many of the buildings are now empty, but their stone footings still stand in the green patches.

A rider crossing here is aware of the sky more than anything else. The road follows the shape of the land, with long, slow bends and slight climbs, and every few minutes the view changes: a new lake, a new ridge, a new patch of snow. Wind is common, and rain showers can pass in minutes, so the ride is a succession of bright and dark moments. In good light the lakes turn deep blue, and the snow gleams. Stay alert for sheep and for walkers, who often cross without looking.

Facilities on the mountain are few, and the nearest village of any size is Stryn, about twenty-seven kilometres away. A hotel and a small shop near the pass may open in season, but do not rely on them, and carry food and water as a matter of habit. Late afternoon, when the sun is low and the shadows lengthen, is the best time to cross, and the colours are at their richest.

This high crossing was one of the major links between Nordfjord and the Gudbrandsdal valley long before cars existed. The road's builders worked by hand through the 1880s and 1890s, blasting rock with black powder and laying walls without mortar, and their work was not just practical but also a statement that this remote part of the country could be connected to the rest. Travellers soon followed, and the first grand mountain hotels grew up along the route to serve the carriages. Some of those buildings are still open as places to stay, with an air of Victorian mountain holidays.

The geology of the road is a lesson in ice. The great ice sheets ground the rock into rounded humps, called roches moutonnées, and left long lakes in the hollows, and the Jostedalsbreen glacier, the largest on the European mainland, lies not far to the south. Around the pass a small ski centre has operated on a patch of glacier for summer skiing, and on a warm day in July you may see skiers on a white strip above the road while you ride in a T-shirt. It is one of those contrasts that is easy to take for granted in Norway.

For riding, this section is an easy and pleasant one. The old road is narrow but generally in decent condition, with gentle gradients and mostly slow bends, and the views are open in all directions. There is usually little traffic apart from cyclists, a few cars and the occasional camper van, and it is easy to find a place to pull in and look at the view. In wet weather the stone walls are slippery with moss, and in fog the edges of the road can disappear, so slow down.

There are few services at this height, and the nearest settlement of real size is Stryn, about twenty-seven kilometres away. Fill up beforehand and bring food and drink. It is worth taking a small detour to the old hotel for a coffee if it is open. The best time is a clear morning in July or August, when the air is sharp and the distances are enormous.
t.norwegian scenic route geiranger trollst:
This is the road to Dalsnibba, a mountain with the cheerful reputation of having the highest fjord view in Europe, at about 1,500 metres above Geirangerfjord. The side road is a toll road that climbs from the high plateau at Djupvasshytta in a series of bends to a car park and a viewing platform on the summit. The surface is paved, though the road is narrow and exposed, and it is generally open only in the snow-free months, from about late spring to early autumn. The summit can be in cloud even when the valley is clear, so be ready to turn back if the view is lost.

The plateau itself, near the head of the Geiranger road, is wild country, a bare upland of rock, snow patches and small lakes at about a thousand metres, with sheep drifting over the grass and the peaks standing round like a crowd. Even in July you can see old snow beside the road. The lake near the hut is cold and clear, and the air has a sharpness you do not notice in the fjord below. It is a place where the weather can change in minutes, with cloud, hail, sun and rain taking turns.

The road from Grotli across the plateau is a lovely ride in its own right, with wide curves, long views and little traffic outside the summer weekends. The surface is generally good, and there are plenty of places to pull in. After the stark upland the descent to Geiranger will feel like a different country: hairpins, waterfalls and deep green forest, with the fjord appearing far below. Brakes and engine braking will both be useful.

There are no towns up here. Stryn, about thirty-two kilometres away, and Stranda, about thirty-five, are the nearest larger places, so make sure you have fuel and food before you start. The hut at Djupvasshytta offers refreshments in season. Bring a warm jacket and gloves, and if the sky is clear, take the time to walk to the edge of the platform and look down at a very small, very distant ship.

From the summit of Dalsnibba you look straight down on the Geirangerfjord, and the first reaction is usually silence. The fjord lies about fifteen hundred metres below as a thin, dark, winding groove between the mountains, with a ship the size of a toy at the quay and the village a handful of roofs. It is one of the finest fjords in the world, and together with the Nærøyfjord it carries a UNESCO listing. The sides rise nearly vertical, and the waterfalls that pour from the rim have names that have gone round the world: the Seven Sisters, the Suitor opposite them, and the Bridal Veil.

The fjord was cut by glaciers and then drowned by the sea, which is why it is so deep and narrow. Old mountain farms cling to ledges high above the water, so steep that, according to the stories, farmers tied their children with ropes so they would not fall. Skageflå and Knivsflå are two of the best known, long abandoned and now visited as part of the cultural landscape. Seen from above, they make it easy to understand why people left.

The viewing platform at the top has a car park and a small café building, and on a clear day the whole fjord and the surrounding peaks are in view, with snow on the highest. The wind can be cold and strong, and the light changes quickly, so patience is rewarded: the cloud often clears in a few minutes, and the view comes and goes like a stage curtain. In bad weather the summit can be wrapped in mist, so it is better to check the cloud base before starting up.

This is a short toll road off the main route, and it is only open in the snow-free season. The bends are tight, the surface is paved, and other visitors are generally careful but sometimes distracted. The nearest large villages are Stryn and Stranda, each more than thirty kilometres away, so keep your fuel and supplies in mind. Early morning is the best time for clear air and a quiet summit, before the cruise-ship crowds arrive.

Geiranger is a small village at the head of the fjord, with a harbour, a church, a few shops and a number of hotels, and for a place with so few permanent residents it handles an astonishing number of visitors. In summer several cruise ships may be anchored at once, each one far larger than the village itself, and a stream of coaches and cars winds down the hairpins to see it. Despite this, Geiranger has a calm, almost domestic feel when the ships have gone, and the evening light on the water is lovely.

The setting is the point. The mountains rise steeply on both sides, and the village sits on a small delta where a river meets the fjord. Opposite the harbour, the Seven Sisters waterfall pours down the cliff in seven separate streams, and boat trips from the quay go out to look at it and at the old abandoned farms. There is also a ferry that runs along the fjord to Hellesylt, a good way to see the cliffs from below, and a small fjord centre with exhibitions about the landscape and its people.

The roads in and out are among the most famous in Norway. From the south the road drops from the high plateau in tight hairpins with views of the fjord; from the north the road rises in a series of bends known as the Eagle Road. Both demand attention, with steep gradients and plenty of tourist traffic, and in wet weather the surface can be slick. The best time to ride is early morning or late evening, when the ships and coaches are fewer and the light is soft.

Geiranger is a small place, so for a larger choice of shops, fuel and services, Stranda, about twenty-seven kilometres away, is the nearest town. Park near the harbour, walk along the shore and sit with a coffee. The sound of waterfalls drifts across the water, and on a still evening the reflections of the mountains are as good as any picture.

The Eagle Road, Ørnevegen, is the one that leaves Geiranger to the north, and the viewpoint at Ørnesvingen is where it earns its name. At this bend the road swings round the edge of a steep slope with the whole Geirangerfjord laid out below, the village at its head and the mountains stepping away on both sides. It was built in the middle of the twentieth century, and the eleven hairpins that climb out of the valley are a fine piece of mountain engineering, with the gradient kept steady enough for the cars and buses of the day.

At the viewpoint a platform juts out over the drop, and from it you can see the Seven Sisters waterfall, the fjord and the road snaking up from the water. The cruise ships look like toys, and the villages tiny. In clear weather the sight is magnificent, but even in mist it is strangely dramatic, with the cloud rolling up the valley and the sound of water echoing from the cliffs.

On a motorcycle this is a satisfying bit of road. The hairpins are tight but well surfaced, and they come in a rhythm that is easy to learn after the first few. The danger is the traffic, because tour buses and campervans take the bends slowly and sometimes wide, and tourists walk around the viewpoint with cameras. Ride with patience, brake before the bends rather than in them, and keep to your own side. In the wet, the painted lines and the metal covers can be slippery.

Eagle Road leads on toward Eidsdal and the ferry across the Norddalsfjord, and from there to Valldal and the Trollstigen. For fuel and supplies the nearest larger place is Stranda, about twenty-four kilometres away, so be sure to have what you need. A short stop at the viewpoint is almost obligatory, and the early morning, with the light low and the ships still asleep, is when the place feels best.
t.norwegian scenic route sognefjellet poin:
The top of the Sognefjellet has the air of another planet, and I mean the cold, bare, magnificent kind. At about 1,430 metres it is the highest mountain road in northern Europe, and here the vegetation has given up entirely. What is left is rock, lichen, patches of old snow even in summer, and small black lakes that reflect the sky like pieces of slate. The mountains of Jotunheimen ring the horizon, and some of them wear glaciers that glint in the sun.

The riding is wide open. The surface is generally good, the gradients are steady, and the bends are broad enough that you can enjoy the scenery without worrying about the next hairpin. Wind is the real challenge. On a gusty day the plateau exposes you completely, and rain or low cloud can turn a pleasant ride into a cold slog in minutes. Even in July, temperatures can hover close to freezing, so keep warm layers handy.

There is a long history of crossing these mountains. For centuries, farmers, traders and cattle drovers moved between the fjord country and the valley of Gudbrandsdalen over high passes like this, long before a road was built. The modern route owes much to the twentieth century, and it is now one of Norway's national tourist roads, which is a polite way of saying that the views are officially recommended.

Nature rules here. Reindeer wander the high ground, and with luck you might spot one from the saddle. The smell is of cold stone and thin air, and the quiet on a still morning is almost loud. Photographers should aim for early or late in the day when the low sun lights the peaks from the side.

A small mountain lodge and a few simple stopping places exist near the top, but this is no place to expect a full range of services. Lom to the east and the valley settlements to the west are where you will find a proper meal and a bed. The road closes in winter, normally from late autumn to late spring, so be careful with dates.

The descent from the high plateau into the western valleys is the part of the Sognefjellet that riders remember longest, because the landscape changes so fast. One moment you are looking across bare rock and snowfields, and a few kilometres later you are among birches, alder and the first farms, with a roaring river beside the tarmac and waterfalls leaping from the cliffs. This is the upper end of the Fortundalen side, in the mountains above Luster.

The road drops in a series of long bends and tighter hairpins, and brakes get a proper workout, so engine braking in a low gear is your friend. Lean angles are gentle and the surface is mostly sound, but watch for gravel washed onto the corners after a storm and for the occasional camper van wandering across the middle. In summer the light can be sublime, with sun lancing through the gaps and lighting up the spray from the falls.

Climbers and walkers love this region. A little further up the valley lies one of Norway's oldest climbing centres, a lodge that has hosted mountaineers for well over a century, and the great ridges of the Skagastølstindane rise above it. Utladalen, the deep valley nearby, holds Vettisfossen, one of the tallest free-falling waterfalls in the country, though it needs a decent hike on foot to reach.

In terms of nature, you pass from alpine tundra down to subalpine birch forest in less than half an hour, and the temperature climbs with every hairpin. Reindeer sometimes graze higher up, and in the lower valley there are roe deer and the occasional moose. The smell of wet moss, juniper and glacial water is distinctive and stays with you.

There is no big town on this stretch, so carry some food and water. Sogndal and Årdalstangen are the larger places in the region, and Gaupne lies further down the road. Pick a dry day if you can, because wet conditions and cold fingers make this descent more demanding.
t.norwegian scenic route valdresflye point:
Bygdin is a long, narrow mountain lake lying like a blade between steep slopes, and the Valdresflye road runs along part of its edge. At roughly 1,060 metres above the sea it is already in the zone where the trees thin out and the weather takes over, and on a calm day the surface reflects the peaks so cleanly that you have to look twice to see which way up the world is.

The riding here is some of the best in southern Norway. The road follows the contours with long, easy bends and sudden views, and it then climbs toward the plateau with surprising grace. Gradients are modest, and the surface is generally in good condition, though frost heave can leave soft spots in spring. The wind across the lake can be strong, and in cloud the temperature drops so quickly that gloves and a warm layer are no luxury.

An old steamer-style boat has carried passengers on Bygdin for generations, a reminder that for much of history water was the highway of these mountains, long before the road came. A traditional mountain hotel stands near the water, and the area has long drawn painters, walkers and anglers who came for the trout and the quiet.

Nature in the area is stern but beautiful. The vegetation is low, with dwarf birch, heather and crowberry covering the slopes, and at the right time of year the moors turn red and gold. Reindeer graze in the high country, and the air is thin, cold and clean enough that you can taste it. If the cloud lifts, the snowfields of the Jotunheimen glow in the distance.

The area is sparsely served, with a few mountain lodges and stopping places, and Beitostølen to the south and Fagernes beyond are the places for proper supplies. The Valdresflye road is a seasonal route, usually open from late spring to autumn, so check the dates. Go in the morning, when the lake is stillest and the light flat and silvery.

Gjendesheim is the place where Norwegian mountain romance meets Norwegian mountain reality. The long, green lake of Gjende lies below, coloured by glacial flour into a shade that looks like it came from a paint chart for a particular kind of dream, and above it rises the Besseggen ridge, one of the most famous walks in the country. Ibsen sent his hero Peer Gynt riding across it on the back of a reindeer, and generations of schoolchildren have never quite forgiven him for making it sound easy.

The riding here is a pleasure. The road approaches from the Bygdin side through open country, with the surface mostly smooth and the bends sweeping rather than sharp, and it climbs gently toward the highest section of the Valdresflye. The summit is at roughly 1,390 metres, so the air is brisk and the wind can bite. There are viewpoints where you can look down onto Gjende and its steep sides, and the contrast of the green water with the grey rock is the image that sells the whole route.

The area is part of the Jotunheimen National Park, and the walking is serious. Besseggen is a full day for most people, using a boat across the lake for one leg, and the weather can change fast. If you are riding rather than walking, the best plan is to stop, look, and take in the scale. The place gives a good sense of how the glaciers carved these valleys, and in the rock walls you can see the layers and scratches left by ice.

Gjendesheim is a mountain lodge and trailhead, so a simple meal and coffee are often available in the season, but do not count on a wide choice. Beitostølen to the south is the nearest place for any real resupply. Parking is busy on summer weekends, and the best hours are early morning or late afternoon, when the day-walkers are away and the light is low and warm.
t.aursjovegen point 1@62.5,8.2:
The Aursjøvegen starts where the tarmac gets thin, and nobody has ever complained about that. It climbs out of the Sunndalen valley in a series of stone-lined hairpins, over bare mountainside and into a country of dammed lakes and wide views, with the peaks of Trollheimen and Dovrefjell on either side. Aursjøen itself is a reservoir, a long strip of dark water held by a dam, and the landscape around it has the stern, open quality of Norway's highest ground.

This part of the road lies close to the lake, with the surface a mix of old asphalt, gravel and patched sections that keep you honest. It is a mountain road in the proper sense, narrow and sometimes steep, with sheep on the surface and drainage ditches that can bite a front wheel. Speeds are low and the scenery repays slow progress, with long views across the plateau and the occasional glimpse of snow even in midsummer.

The road itself was built to serve the hydropower works in the mountains, and it is a reminder that much of Norwegian wealth rests on water falling from a height. Today it is a seasonal tourist road and usually requires a toll, opening in early summer once the snow has cleared and closing again in autumn. Dates vary from year to year, so look at the current information before you go.

Nature is a feature of this ride. The area borders the Dovrefjell national park, where musk oxen roam on the high ground, and the air is thin and cold even in July. Reindeer move over the plateau, and dwarf birch, lichens and mosses cover the stones. On a clear day the light is so strong that every rock throws a hard shadow.

There are no towns on the plateau, so carry water and snacks, and dress for conditions that can change fast. Åndalsnes lies far to the west, and Sunndalsøra, in the valley below, is the bigger centre for supplies. Start early and choose a dry day.
t.cap d ail@43.7,7.4:
Cap-d'Ail is the last French town before Monaco, and you can feel the principality pressing against it. The Basse Corniche winds in from Èze and Beaulieu between villas and pines, the rocks drop to clear water below, and then, almost without warning, you are among the towers of Fontvieille. Cap-d'Ail itself is quieter than its neighbour: a scatter of Belle Époque villas, gardens and newer apartments on the slopes above a small cape with coves and a little beach.

The best thing here is on foot. The sentier du littoral, the coastal path, runs around the cape from the Plage Mala, a tiny pebble cove under the cliffs, past old villas and gardens and along the rocks. Early in the morning or late in the day, with the sea glittering and the scent of pine and salt, it is one of the loveliest short walks on the Riviera. Park the bike, change your boots if you can, and give it an hour.

The riding around here is about choosing the right Corniche. The Basse Corniche along the coast is slow and congested, with lights, scooters, buses and Monaco commuters. The Moyenne Corniche higher up offers grander views, tunnels and smoother curves past Èze. The Grande Corniche, highest of all, follows the line of the Roman Via Julia Augusta and passes La Turbie, where the Trophy of Augustus, a huge Roman monument from the first century BC, still stands above Monaco. These rides head inland toward the Col de Turini and the Route Napoléon, so you will climb through La Turbie or Sospel and quickly leave the coast behind for gorges and hairpins.

Traffic is the main hazard. Weekday mornings and evenings fill the roads with workers driving into Monaco, summer adds tourist traffic and the Grand Prix weekend in May brings chaos. Be careful with the many speed cameras, and with sudden queues in the tunnels. The best time to ride the corniches is early on a weekday or in the evening light, outside July and August.

There are cafes, bakeries and restaurants in Cap-d'Ail, and the beach bars by the water are pleasant in summer. For fuel, Monaco and the larger towns along the coast are close. Whatever you plan, look up and back once as you climb out of town: the view of the cape and Monaco from the corniches above is one of the most striking pictures on the whole coast.
t.ospedaletti@43.8,7.7:
Palms, pastel houses and a bay that faces due south: Ospedaletti is the Riviera dei Fiori at its most relaxed, a small Ligurian town tucked between Sanremo and Bordighera with its feet in the sea and terraced hills behind it. The old coast railway has been moved inland into a tunnel, and its former line along the shore is now a cycle and walking path, so the seafront is quieter than you might expect on such a crowded coast.

The name comes from a hospice, an ospedaletto, that the Knights of Rhodes are said to have founded here for pilgrims and travellers in the Middle Ages, and the town later became a winter resort for wealthy northern Europeans who came for the mild climate. For anyone with petrol in the blood, though, Ospedaletti means racing. In the years after the Second World War, the streets of the town formed a road circuit that hosted car Grands Prix and motorcycle races, a fast, dangerous loop through the villas and along the corniche above the sea. Ride the Corso Regina Margherita and you are on part of the old course.

The Via Aurelia, the old Roman road along the coast, runs through the town and is the main way in, slow and often congested in summer, with buses, scooters and cyclists. The more interesting riding lies in the hills: narrow roads climb steeply through olive groves and greenhouses to villages like Seborga, a tiny hilltop village that half-jokingly calls itself an independent principality, and Vallebona, with its flower terraces. These lanes are tight, sometimes broken, and very steep in places, with superb views back over the sea.

The rides from here head west and north into France, toward the Mercantour and the Col de Turini, through Ventimiglia and up the Roya valley or over to Sospel. It is a quick change of scene: within an hour the palms and flowers give way to gorges, chestnut woods and hairpins climbing toward the high Alps. Plan the crossing for early morning, before the coast traffic builds up.

Ospedaletti has cafes, bars and seafront restaurants, and Ligurian food is a pleasure: focaccia, farinata made from chickpea flour, pesto and local olive oil from the Taggiasca olives grown in the hills. The beach is pebbly and the water clear, so a swim at the end of the ride is easy in summer. For fuel and a wider choice of shops, Bordighera and Sanremo are each a few minutes along the coast.
t.antibes@43.6,7.1:
Old ramparts rise straight from the sea at Antibes, and behind them a tight knot of lanes, markets and ochre houses climbs toward a castle on the shore. The town sits between Nice and Cannes on the bay of the same name, facing the snowy line of the Alps on clear winter days, with the long wooded peninsula of Cap d'Antibes to the south and the jazz town of Juan-les-Pins on its western flank.

The Greeks founded a trading post here called Antipolis, and for centuries Antibes was a frontier fortress facing Nice, which belonged to Savoy until 1860. The star-shaped Fort Carré, reworked by Vauban, still guards the entrance to Port Vauban, one of the largest yacht harbours in the Mediterranean, where superyachts line the outer quay. In 1946 Picasso was given rooms in the Château Grimaldi on the seafront to use as a studio, and the works he produced there in a burst of energy now form the heart of the Picasso Museum. The Marché Provençal in the old town is busy every morning with flowers, olives, cheese and socca, the chickpea pancake of the coast.

The ride around Cap d'Antibes is short and lovely, a narrow road past villas, pines and rocky coves, though the traffic in summer can be dreadful. For serious riding you head inland. The Mercantour and Col de Turini rides go northeast, up the Var valley or through Nice and into the mountains, where the hairpins of the Turini are famous from the Monte Carlo Rally. The Verdon ride goes northwest via Grasse, the perfume town, and the Route Napoléon to Castellane and the Gorges du Verdon, where the road follows the rim of a canyon several hundred metres deep before descending to the turquoise Lac de Sainte-Croix for a swim.

Riding out of Antibes takes patience. The coast is densely built up, the roads are congested for much of the year, and speed cameras are common. Leave early in the morning, especially in July and August, and you will reach the hills before the heat and the crowds.

Fuel, food and services are everywhere in and around Antibes, and the old town is a fine place for an evening meal when you return. Parking for bikes is easier than for cars, but keep valuables with you. A walk along the ramparts at sunset, with the Alps turning pink across the bay, is the right way to end a day.
t.near castellane@43.8,6.4:
West of Castellane, the Verdon river disappears into the earth. Or that is how it looks from the road: the D952 climbs away from the town along the river, through a valley of pale limestone, and then the river plunges into the Grand Canyon du Verdon, a gorge up to seven hundred metres deep, while the road clings to the northern rim above. This spot lies on that rim, near Point Sublime and the village of Rougon, where the view down into the gorge is one of the most famous in France.

Point Sublime is a short walk from a car park beside the road, and from the edge you look straight down into the mouth of the gorge, where the river runs green and cold between cliffs of white and grey limestone. Vultures, reintroduced into the area in the late twentieth century, often circle above the cliffs, and climbers dangle from ropes on the walls. Nearby, the Couloir Samson, a narrow slot where the river enters the gorge, can be explored on foot, and the classic hiking trail through the bottom of the canyon starts not far away.

The riding is extraordinary. The D952 is narrow, winding and exposed, with tight bends, low walls and sheer drops, and in summer it is crowded with camper vans, cars and coaches, so expect to slow down often. To the south, the Route des Crêtes, the D23, makes a loop out of La Palud-sur-Verdon along the very edge of the cliffs, with overlooks one after another; parts of it are one-way and it is closed in winter. On the south rim, the Corniche Sublime is equally spectacular. Early morning in June or September is the best time.

Castellane, about eleven kilometres east, is a lively little town at the foot of a huge rock with a chapel on top, and it has fuel, cafes, restaurants and shops. There is no reliable service on the rim roads themselves except in the small villages, so fill up in Castellane before heading out.

The Verdon country is dry, hot and fragrant in summer, smelling of thyme, lavender and pine, and the cicadas buzz relentlessly in the heat. Bring water, take your time, and stop often: every bend seems to reveal a better view than the last.
t.near riez@43.8,6.2:
On the eastern side of Riez, the Valensole plateau starts to tip down toward the Verdon, and this point lies in that open country between Riez, Moustiers-Sainte-Marie and the great turquoise reservoir of the Lac de Sainte-Croix. It is a land of wide fields and big skies, where in June and July the lavender fields bloom in long purple rows, filling the air with a scent so strong you can smell it through your helmet.

Riez is a small, old town with a surprising past. It was a Roman settlement, and four tall granite columns from a Roman temple still stand in a field on its edge, looking oddly out of place among the vines. The town also has a rare early Christian baptistery, one of the oldest buildings of its kind in France. The old town is a maze of narrow streets and faded houses, quiet most of the year.

Moustiers-Sainte-Marie, a few kilometres east, ranks high on any list of Provençal villages, clinging to a gap in the cliffs at the edge of the Verdon gorges. A golden star hangs on a long chain stretched across the gap high above the village, and legend says it was put there by a knight returning from the Crusades. Moustiers is also famous for its decorated earthenware, faience, made here since the seventeenth century.

The riding around here is a delight in a quieter way than the gorge itself. The roads across the plateau, such as the D952 and D11, are open, fast and flowing, with long views over the fields to the mountains. Down toward the lake, the roads twist through oak scrub and limestone, and the D957 crosses the lake on a bridge at the mouth of the gorge, with views of the turquoise water and cliffs. In July and August, traffic is heavy, and lavender season brings crowds of photographers parking on the verges.

Riez has a few cafes, shops and a fuel station, and Moustiers has restaurants and cafes. The nearest larger town is Digne-les-Bains, about thirty kilometres north. In summer, the lake is perfect for a swim, with beaches and clear water, so pack your swimsuit.
t.near eide@63.0,7.4:
The Atlantic Road was built to connect fishing villages on islands that had been linked only by boat, and it does so with a kind of reckless grace: a sequence of causeways, low bridges and short stretches of road that hop from skerry to skerry across the open edge of the Norwegian Sea. This point lies near Eide, on the mainland end of the route, between the fjord country and the coast, on the Romsdal peninsula between Molde and Kristiansund.

The Atlanterhavsvegen opened in 1989 after years of construction, often in brutal weather; workers faced twelve hurricane-force storms during the building. It is only about eight kilometres long, but it is one of the most photographed roads in the world, especially the Storseisundet bridge, which rises and curves so sharply that from some angles it seems to end in mid-air. On a calm summer day the sea is blue and glassy, with eider ducks and cormorants on the rocks. In autumn storms, waves crash over the road, and people drive out on purpose to watch.

The coast around here, Hustadvika, has a fearsome reputation among sailors, with shallow reefs and violent seas. Old fishing villages like Bud and the island community of Averøy survived on cod and herring, and the region is still known for klippfisk, salted and dried cod, which was exported to Spain and Portugal for centuries. Kristiansund, the nearest town, is the capital of klippfisk and has a museum devoted to it.

The riding on and around the Atlantic Road is easy in technical terms but wonderful for the views. The road is flat and smooth, with gentle curves, but the wind can be ferocious, and spray from the sea makes the surface wet and salty. Traffic is heavy in summer, with tourists stopping on the bridges for photographs. The roads inland toward Eide and Molde follow fjords and pass through tunnels and small farms, with mountains on every side.

Eide and the villages along the route have shops and cafes, and Kristiansund, about twenty-two kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and hotels. Bring good rain gear, even in July, and stop at the viewpoints and fishing platforms built along the road to take it all in.
t.near puget theniers on the way back@43.9:
The upper Var valley around Puget-Théniers is a strange and beautiful corridor: a wide bed of grey gravel with the river braiding through it, steep wooded slopes on either side, and above them the bare limestone of the Pre-Alps catching the light. The N202 runs through it from Nice towards Digne, and for riders coming back from the Verdon it is the long, satisfying homeward leg, quick and open with the river beside you.

Puget-Théniers itself is a small town of under two thousand people, built where the Roudoule stream comes down to meet the Var. Its most famous son is Auguste Blanqui, the nineteenth-century revolutionary who spent much of his life in prison, and in the square stands a powerful bronze by Aristide Maillol, a woman with her hands bound behind her back, made in his honour. The town is also a stop on the narrow-gauge railway that runs from Nice to Digne, and on summer Sundays an old steam train puffs up the valley from here, which is a fine sight if you happen to be on the road alongside.

The water is the reason for the stop. The Var is cold even in high summer, fed by snowmelt from the Mercantour, and its gravel banks make natural beaches where you can wade in to the knees and feel it bite. Swim only in calm pools away from the main channel, because the river rises quickly after storms in the mountains, and never close to the dams and weirs downstream. The tributaries, the Roudoule and the Cians, have smaller, clearer pools in the gorges, and locals know their favourites.

Around here the riding gets serious if you leave the main road. Just upstream the Gorges de Daluis and, a little east, the Gorges du Cians cut through deep red rock, with tunnels, overhangs and narrow ledges where the road clings to the cliff, and they are among the most dramatic roads in the southern Alps. Climb them early in the day before the camper vans come, and watch for fallen stones after rain.

Puget-Théniers has cafés, a bakery and the basic services of a small town, and you should find fuel on the main road here, but stations are scarce up the side valleys. Carros, on the edge of the Nice plain, is the next large town, about thirty kilometres downstream, and from there the coast and the traffic begin again.
t.near aurlandsvangen@61.0,7.3:
At 1306 metres you are near the roof of Aurlandsfjellet, the high plateau that the Snow Road crosses between Aurland on the fjord and Lærdal to the north. It is a landscape of bare rock, small lakes, patches of old snow and wide open sky, scraped flat by the ice and left almost empty. Only a few hours before, if you came up from Aurland, you were among fruit trees and fjord water; up here the plants are lichen, moss and a few tough grasses, and the snowbanks along the road can still be taller than a person in early summer.

The road is the reason to come. Fylkesvei 243, known as Snøvegen, was built across the mountain as the main link between Aurland and Lærdal, and for decades it was the only way to drive between them until the Lærdal Tunnel opened beneath the mountain in 2000, the longest road tunnel in the world at more than 24 kilometres. Since then the old road has become a summer-only scenic route, usually opened once the snow is cleared in late May or June and closed again in autumn, often by October. Check before you go, because the season depends on the snow.

The climb from Aurland is the dramatic half: a long series of hairpins up from the fjord, past the Stegastein viewpoint, a wooden platform that juts out over the Aurlandsfjord, and then on up into the high country. The road is narrow, with passing places, low barriers or none, and buses and camper vans on it in summer, so take the hairpins carefully and be ready to wait. On the plateau the road straightens into a quiet track across the rock, and the descent to Lærdal is gentler, down a long valley with waterfalls.

The weather can change fast up here, and fog, wind and cold rain are common even in July, so pack warm gloves. There is nothing on the plateau except a couple of rest areas with views, so make your arrangements below. Lærdalsøyri, at the foot of the northern descent, has fuel and food, and Aurland and Flåm, on the fjord to the south, have more. Sogndal is the nearest larger town.
t.l rdals yri@61.1,7.5:
Lærdalsøyri is one of the best-preserved wooden towns in western Norway, a village of white and painted timber houses at the mouth of the Lærdal river, where it meets the inner Sognefjord. Its old quarter, known as Gamle Lærdalsøyri, has more than a hundred and fifty old buildings, from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, with narrow lanes between them, and it has been protected for its value. On a quiet evening it is one of the loveliest small places in the fjord country.

The town owes its life to its position. It sat at the western end of the old route over the mountains from eastern Norway, and goods travelling between Bergen and Oslo came down the Lærdal valley to the fjord here, where boats took them on. Markets were held here, and the town grew prosperous on trade. Today the same role is played by the E16, which comes through the long Lærdal Tunnel to the south and runs up the valley toward Filefjell and Oslo. The valley also holds the Borgund stave church, one of the finest medieval wooden churches in Norway, about half an hour up the road, and it is well worth the detour.

The river is famous for salmon. The Lærdalselva was once one of the most celebrated salmon rivers in Europe, visited by British anglers in the nineteenth century, and the Norwegian Wild Salmon Centre, in the village, tells that story with a window into the river. The valley is also unusually dry for western Norway, lying in the rain shadow of the mountains, and the fields are often green with irrigation in summer.

For riders, Lærdalsøyri is the hinge between two very different roads: the Snow Road over Aurlandsfjellet, which climbs straight out of the village to the south, and the E16 through the valley. It is also near the ferry from Fodnes to Mannheller, which crosses the Sognefjord toward Sogndal. The village has fuel, shops, cafes and places to stay, so it is a natural place to stop before or after the mountain. Wander through the old town, look at the carved doorways and the details on the houses, and sit for a moment by the river.
t.near f rde@61.4,5.9:
Moskog is not much more than a junction in the woods south of Førde, but it marks the western end of the Gaularfjellet route, where the E39 meets the road that climbs east over the mountains to Balestrand on the Sognefjord. Around it the country is green and rolling, with forests of pine and birch, lakes, small farms on cleared ground and steep hills rising behind. The river Gaula runs through the area and gives the route its name.

The interesting part of the ride lies to the east. Gaularfjellet takes you up from the valleys onto a high plateau and then down the far side in an extraordinary series of hairpins toward Balestrand, with views over the Vetlefjord and a viewing platform called Utsikten, a dramatic piece of architecture with a balcony hanging over the valley. On the way, waterfalls tumble beside the road, among them Likholefossen, where a footbridge and platform let you stand right next to the white water. The route is a summer road at its highest parts and can close in winter, so check conditions before planning a crossing in spring or autumn.

From Moskog the road east is calmer, following lakes and the Gaula valley through farmland and woods, with mostly flowing bends and a good surface. Traffic is modest, mostly local cars and a few tourists, and the scenery builds gradually. In the evening, when the light is low and the lakes are still, the valley is very lovely. In summer the meadows are full of flowers, and in autumn the birch turns gold.

Førde, about seven kilometres north, is the largest town in the area and the commercial centre of Sunnfjord, with a hospital, shopping centres, hotels, restaurants and plenty of fuel. It is a practical town rather than a charming one, but it has everything you might need. The Jølstra river runs through it on its way to the sea, and there is a traditional folk music festival in summer. Use Førde for supplies, then turn east at Moskog and enjoy the climb into the hills. Bring rain gear, because this is western Norway, where showers come and go all day.
t.near valldal@62.3,7.5:
Gudbrandsjuvet is a narrow gorge where the river Valldøla forces its way through a slot in the rock, only a few metres wide in places, with water that has polished the stone into smooth curves and potholes over thousands of years. It sits in the upper Valldalen, between the fjord village of Valldal and the climb to Trollstigen, and the scenic route has built a set of steel walkways and platforms that let you stand directly above the roaring water. Look down, and the force of it is startling.

According to a local legend, a man named Gudbrand escaped his pursuers by leaping across the gorge, which gave it its name. Whether or not anyone ever jumped, the gorge has been a place to stop for travellers on the route between Valldal and Romsdal for a long time. It is also one of the more successful examples of the modern architecture that Norway's National Tourist Routes have placed along the scenic roads: simple, angular and good at framing the view.

The road through Valldalen is part of the Geiranger to Trollstigen route, one of the most celebrated motorcycle roads in Norway. From the fjord at Valldal, famous for its strawberries, the road climbs gently up the valley past farms and woods, then gets steeper and more open beyond Gudbrandsjuvet, rising onto the high plateau and then dropping down the famous Trollstigen hairpins into Romsdalen. The surface is good, but traffic is heavy in high summer, with buses and camper vans, and the Trollstigen section is narrow with eleven hairpins and a steep drop. Trollstigen closes in winter, usually from autumn to late May or June.

Gudbrandsjuvet is a natural pause before or after the big climb. There is a cafe and a toilet at the site in summer. Valldal, back toward the fjord, has shops, cafes and fuel, and it is the place to eat strawberries in July. Molde and Åndalsnes are the larger towns beyond the mountains. Early in the morning, before the buses arrive, the gorge is quiet except for the water, and the light comes slanting down the valley. That is the best time to see it.
t.near heggenes@61.2,8.9:
Beitostølen is a ski resort with a long summer afterlife, sitting high on the edge of the Valdres valley at the point where farmland gives way to open mountain. The village is a collection of hotels, chalets, shops and lifts, and in summer it serves as the gateway to the Valdresflye, the high plateau road that crosses toward Jotunheimen, Norway's highest mountains. Heggenes and the rest of Øystre Slidre lie further down the valley, among farms, lakes and forests.

Valdres is one of Norway's most traditional valleys, known for its folk music, its old farms and its stave churches, of which there are six in the valley, more than in any other part of the country. The landscape is gentle and green, with lakes and rolling hills, and it has been a place of summer farming for centuries, with herders taking their animals up to the mountain pastures in summer. Some of those summer farms are still in use, and you can buy cheese, milk and other products from them along the roads.

The Valdresflye road, Fylkesvei 51, climbs from Beitostølen onto the high plateau, crossing open country of heather, lichen and small lakes, with views of the peaks of Jotunheimen to the north and west. The highest point is close to 1400 metres, and the road is closed in winter, usually from late autumn to spring, depending on the snow. The surface is good, with long sweeping bends and a few steeper sections, and traffic is moderate in summer. Conditions turn fast, and it can be cold and windy even in July. At the northern end, the road drops down toward Gjendesheim, starting point of the famous Besseggen ridge hike.

Below Beitostølen, the road through Valdres is a pleasant ride, with gentle curves, villages, lakes and farms. Few vehicles use it, apart from weekends and holidays. The best time is late summer and early autumn, when the colours change and the air is clear.

Beitostølen has fuel, food and somewhere to sleep, and it is the natural place to prepare for the plateau. Fagernes, further down the valley, is the main town of Valdres. Take warm clothes and enjoy the climb.
t.near sunndals ra@62.6,8.6:
The valley climbing south out of Sunndalsøra toward the Aursjøen reservoir is one of the starting points of the Aursjøvegen, a mountain road that is less a scenic route than an engineering track from the age of hydropower. It runs from the steep, green valleys of Sunndal up onto a high, bare plateau, past reservoirs, dams and tunnels, and then down the other side toward Lesja in the Gudbrandsdalen. It is narrow, partly gravel, and open only in summer, and for riders who like adventure it ranks among the most memorable roads in central Norway.

The road was built in the mid-twentieth century to serve the Aura hydroelectric scheme, which collects water from the high mountains and drops it down to a power station near Sunndalsøra, where it powers the aluminium works in the town. The landscape on top is rugged and wild, with lakes, rocky ridges and patches of snow well into summer, and there is a strong sense of being far from anywhere. Reindeer, both wild and herded, graze in the area, and the plateau is home to Arctic plants and birds.

The riding is demanding. The road climbs steeply with tight bends from the valley floor, the surface changes from asphalt to gravel and back, and there are single-lane sections, with passing places, where you meet cars, camper vans and the occasional bus. There are toll gates, and the road is usually open from June or July to September or October, depending on the snow, so check before you go. The weather on the plateau can be wild, with fog, rain and wind, and it can be cold even in midsummer.

The valley itself, at the bottom, is beautiful: steep, green and narrow, with waterfalls and rushing rivers, and old farms on the slopes. The Driva river, famous for salmon, flows through Sunndal to the fjord. The views from the road as it climbs back toward the valley are spectacular, with mountains rising over 1500 metres on both sides.

Sunndalsøra, a few kilometres north, has fuel, shops and cafes. There are few services on the road itself, so make sure you are prepared before you start.
t.sunndals ra@62.7,8.6:
Sunndalsøra is an industrial town in a spectacular setting, at the head of the Sunndalsfjord, where the steep valley of Sunndal opens out to the sea between mountains that rise more than 1500 metres on either side. It is dominated by the large aluminium plant of Hydro, one of the biggest and most modern in Europe, which has been the town's main employer since the mid-twentieth century and is powered by the hydroelectric stations in the mountains around it.

The town is a practical place, with shops, schools and housing for the workers, but the landscape around it is extraordinary. The valleys of Sunndal and Litldalen are steep and narrow, with waterfalls, rivers and old farms clinging to the slopes. To the east lies the Dovrefjell plateau, with its musk oxen and wild reindeer, and to the north the Trollheimen mountains, where the valley of Innerdalen is often called the most beautiful valley in Norway.

The Driva river, which flows through Sunndal to the fjord here, is among the most famous salmon rivers in Norway, and anglers come from far away to fish it in summer. Sunndalsøra also has a reputation for unusually warm winter weather, when warm, dry winds come down from the mountains and can push temperatures far above normal, although in summer the valley can be cool and rainy.

For riders, Sunndalsøra is a hub. The Aursjøvegen climbs from here into the mountains, a narrow, partly gravel road over the high plateau to Lesja, open only in summer. The main road through Sunndal follows the river up the valley toward Oppdal, with good surface, gentle curves and spectacular scenery, and the coastal road follows the fjord west toward Molde and Kristiansund. You will have the road mostly to yourself, except for the main road in summer.

Sunndalsøra has fuel, groceries and beds, which makes it the natural halt before or after the mountains. Take time to look at the mountains around the town, and if you have a few hours, ride up toward Innerdalen or the Aursjøvegen. The light in the valley in the evening, when the sun catches the peaks, is lovely.
t.near cagnes sur mer@43.6,7.2:
Love them or hate them, they are one of the landmarks of this coast, and they make an unmistakable meeting point for rides heading into the mountains.

The towns nearby have strong artistic and culinary connections. In Cagnes, Pierre-Auguste Renoir spent the last years of his life at Les Collettes, a house surrounded by olive trees, where he painted with brushes strapped to his arthritic hands; the house is now a museum. Above the modern town, Haut-de-Cagnes is a medieval hilltop village around a Grimaldi castle. Villeneuve-Loubet was the birthplace of Auguste Escoffier, the chef who codified modern French cuisine, and his family home is now a museum of culinary art.

The rides that start here head north into the Alps, to the Mercantour and the Col de Turini. Within half an hour, you can be climbing out of the coastal sprawl into a different world of gorges, perched villages and pine forests. The Var valley leads north towards the mountains, and roads branch off into narrow gorges like the Vésubie and the Tinée. The Col de Turini, at around 1,600 metres, is famous as a stage of the Monte Carlo Rally, with dozens of hairpins on each side, and the Mercantour roads climb even higher, to the Cime de la Bonette.

The coast itself is busy, with heavy traffic, especially in summer, and many roundabouts and traffic lights. Leave early, ideally at dawn, to avoid the worst of it. There are plenty of fuel stations, bakeries and cafés in the area, so you can stock up before heading into the mountains, where services are scarcer. In summer, the coast is hot and crowded; in spring and autumn, the light is clear and the mountain roads are quieter. Some high passes are closed by snow from late autumn to late spring.
t.near saint laurent du var@43.7,7.2:
Until 1860, the river at Saint-Laurent-du-Var marked an international frontier. On the west bank lay France; on the east bank lay the County of Nice, part of the Kingdom of Sardinia, and travellers along the coast had to cross the wide, shifting bed of the Var to pass from one to the other. For centuries there was no proper bridge, and the village made its living from the men who carried travellers across on their backs or guided them through the shallows. When Nice became French, the border vanished, but the river is still the dividing line between the town and the city.

Today Saint-Laurent is a busy suburb on the west bank, facing Nice's airport across the river mouth. It has a marina, a long pebble beach, the large Cap 3000 shopping centre and a small old village up the hill with a church and narrow streets. It is not especially beautiful, but it is lively and practical, with plenty of cafés and restaurants along the seafront.

The Var itself is a wild Alpine river, prone to sudden floods, and its broad gravel bed is now partly a nature reserve, home to herons and other birds. Following it north, the road leads into the mountains, and the gorges of the Vésubie, the Tinée and the upper Var all branch off within an hour. This is the way you will have come down if you are finishing a ride from the Col de Turini or the Mercantour, perhaps tired and dusty after a day of hairpins.

Coming back to the coast at the end of the day, expect a sudden shift from empty mountain roads to the dense traffic of the Nice agglomeration, with roundabouts, scooters and impatient drivers. Take it slowly. There are fuel stations and food everywhere, and the beachfront is a fine place to end the day, with the sun setting behind the Esterel and planes landing over the bay. In summer, the evenings stay warm and the beaches are busy until late; in winter, the coast is mild and quiet, and the mountains behind are often white with snow.
t.near antibes@43.6,7.1:
On 1 March 1815, Napoleon, having escaped from exile on Elba, landed on the beach at Golfe-Juan, a few kilometres west of Antibes, with a small band of loyal soldiers, and began his march to Paris. The route he followed through the mountains of Provence to Grenoble is now the Route Napoléon, one of the classic motorcycle roads of France, and Antibes is where rides along it begin and end.

Antibes is one of the most attractive towns on the Riviera. The old town, enclosed by ramparts, has narrow streets, a covered market and the Château Grimaldi, where Picasso worked for a few months in 1946 and which is now the Picasso Museum, with works he made here, full of Mediterranean light, fauns and fish. Below the walls, Port Vauban is one of the largest yacht harbours in Europe, with a quay of enormous superyachts, overlooked by the star-shaped Fort Carré. To the south, the Cap d'Antibes is a peninsula of luxury villas, pine trees and rocky coves, with a coastal path, and Juan-les-Pins is famous for its jazz festival.

The Route Napoléon, the N85, climbs north from Grasse through the Pre-Alps, via Castellane, Digne and Sisteron, to Grenoble, with long stretches of curves, mountain passes, gorges and old towns. It is a magnificent ride, with constantly changing scenery, and the road is generally well surfaced and wide enough to enjoy. On summer weekends, it can be busy with motorcyclists and tourists, and speed controls are frequent.

Coming back to the coast at the end of the day, the traffic around Antibes and Cannes can be heavy, especially in summer. Antibes has plenty of fuel stations, restaurants and cafés. Vallauris, just inland, is known for its pottery, which Picasso helped to revive after the war. The evening light on the old town walls, with the Alps behind and the sea in front, is a beautiful end to the day.
t.near cuneo on the way back@44.4,7.6:
Cuneo announces itself from a distance: a long, wedge-shaped town perched on a terrace where two Alpine rivers, the Stura di Demonte and the Gesso, cut deep beds on either side before joining just to the north. The name comes from that shape, cuneo meaning wedge. This stop lies just south-west of the town, on the open plain between Castelletto Stura and Beinette, with the Maritime Alps standing up as a wall along the southern horizon.

You come here on the way back from the high French roads, and the change is striking. After the Mercantour the plain feels almost absurdly flat, straight roads between maize and poplars, with the mountains receding in the mirrors. The riverbanks have been made into a large river park, with tracks and quiet places by the water. The rivers themselves are cold, fast and stony; a dip is possible in places in high summer, but treat it as a bracing paddle rather than a swim, and stay clear of the main current after rain.

Cuneo is a pleasant town to wander. Via Roma runs under long arcades, and Piazza Galimberti is one of those enormous Piedmontese squares that seem designed for a whole army to parade in. The local sweet is the cuneese al rum, a rum-filled chocolate praline sold in the old cafés. Chestnuts from the valleys turn up in everything in autumn.

From here the roads fan out. Valle Stura leads up to the Colle della Maddalena and France, a long gradual climb with a good surface and heavy trucks at times. Valle Vermenagna heads for the Tenda; check its status before relying on it, as the crossing has had long closures in recent years. Valle Gesso goes into the Alpi Marittime park and simply stops among the peaks.

You will not struggle for fuel, a meal or an espresso anywhere around Cuneo. Ride in at aperitivo hour and you will understand why people here are in no hurry.
t.near saint etienne de tinee on the way b:
High above the Tinée, south of Saint-Étienne, the country turns into great bare shoulders of grass and scree. This stop sits on that upland block between the Tinée and the Cians, under the mass of Mont Mounier, with the villages of Roubion, Beuil and Valberg scattered around its flanks. It is a long way from anywhere: the nearest proper towns are down in the Var valley, and the coast is a good hour and a half away.

The roads that cross this region are the reason to come. The D30 climbs from the Tinée through Roubion to the Col de la Couillole, all tight hairpins carved out of the mountainside with drops on the outside that make you concentrate. From Beuil, the Gorges du Cians run south, and the upper section is cut through deep red slate, the road squeezed under overhangs barely wider than a car. Few rides in the Alpes-Maritimes change colour quite so violently in so few kilometres.

Do not expect a beach. The water up here is snowmelt and spring water, mountain streams that run clear and icy over grey rock. On a hot afternoon a quick plunge of your hands and face is enough to reset you, and in calm spots a brave rider can sit in a pool for half a minute. Choose slack water away from the stream bed after storms, when levels rise quickly.

The nature is pure Mercantour edge. Chamois graze on the high slopes, marmots whistle from the boulder fields in summer, and larch forests turn gold in October. Sheep are moved up here in summer, so expect flocks and guard dogs on the road, and give both room.

Practicalities matter. Fuel is thin on the ground, so fill up in the valleys before climbing and do not count on the small villages. Beuil and Valberg have cafés and some shops in season. Roads above about 1,500 metres can be shut by snow from late autumn into spring, and evening storms in summer are common. Leave early, ride down slowly.
t.vence@43.7,7.1:
Vence is where the Riviera stops pretending to be the seaside and starts to become the mountains. The old town sits on a rocky spur about ten kilometres inland from the coast, still largely enclosed by its medieval walls, and behind it the land rises in steps of limestone, the baous, towards the high plateaus of the Préalpes. Finishing a ride here means ending among fountains, narrow lanes and terraces in the shade.

Artists made Vence famous in the twentieth century. Henri Matisse designed the Chapelle du Rosaire for the Dominican nuns, a small white building with blue and yellow stained glass and black line drawings on white tiles, which he considered his masterpiece. Marc Chagall lived in Vence for some years before moving to nearby Saint-Paul-de-Vence, and D. H. Lawrence died in the town in 1930. The Fondation Maeght, just outside Saint-Paul, is one of the best modern art collections in France.

The riding from here is superb. The D2 climbs north over the Col de Vence, a long series of bends up a bare limestone slope with views back over the coast, then crosses a wild plateau towards Coursegoules and Gréolières. The surface is generally good, but the road is narrow in places, and cyclists use it heavily. Watch for gravel in the corners after rain.

Saint-Paul next door is overrun in summer and lovelier seen from the road than squeezed through on foot. Vence is calmer. Walk in through the old gate to the Place du Peyra, where the fountain has been running for centuries, find a chair, and let the engine tick as it cools somewhere behind you. Fuel and food are no issue in town.
t.ramatuelle@43.2,6.6:
Above the beaches of Saint-Tropez, Ramatuelle coils around its hilltop like a snail shell, its houses forming a wall around the old village, with narrow lanes and arches leading up to the church. Below it, the long sweep of Pampelonne beach curves for kilometres along the bay, and the vineyards of the Côtes de Provence climb the slopes between.

The actor Gérard Philipe, one of the great stars of French cinema and theatre, loved Ramatuelle and is buried in the village cemetery. A theatre festival held every summer in an open-air amphitheatre was founded in his memory. The village is beautiful, but in July and August it is crowded, and parking is scarce.

The road over the hills from Ramatuelle to Gassin, the other hilltop village of the peninsula, passes the old windmills of Paillas, with views over the whole of the Saint-Tropez peninsula and the sea. It is a narrow, winding road through cork oak and pine, with a few tight bends and steep climbs. In summer, traffic is heavy, and the roads into Saint-Tropez can be blocked for hours.

At Cap Camarat, south of Pampelonne, a lighthouse stands on a headland above the sea, and the coastal path around the cape offers some of the most beautiful walking on the Riviera. The beaches below are clear and blue, ideal for a swim, but the crowds are heavy in summer.

Come in May, June or late September if you possibly can. The light is softer, the beach clubs half empty, and the hill road becomes the playground it should be rather than a car park with views. Fuel is easier down on the main roads towards La Croix-Valmer than in the village, and the cafés under the plane trees by the gate are worth an hour of anyone's day.
t.near finale ligure on the way back@44.2,:
Finale Ligure is a seaside town with two personalities. On the coast, Finale Marina is a classic Ligurian resort, with a long beach, a palm-lined promenade and colourful houses. A few hundred metres inland, Finalborgo is a medieval town enclosed by walls, with narrow streets, old churches and the ruins of Castel Gavone on the hill above. The two are linked by a short road, and it is worth visiting both.

Behind the town, limestone cliffs rise from the woods, and Finale has become one of the great climbing and mountain-biking centres of Europe. The crags are full of routes, and the trails through the hills attract riders from all over the world. On any given day, the town is full of people in climbing harnesses and muddy cycling gear.

The beach at Finale is long and sandy, and the sea is clear and calm in summer. There are public sections and private beach clubs, and the water is generally clean. Varigotti, a little east, is a former fishing village with pastel houses right on the beach, one of the prettiest spots on the Riviera.

The Via Aurelia, the old Roman coast road, runs through Finale, and it is a scenic but busy ride, with tunnels, bends and views over the sea. Inland, small roads climb into the hills, with tight bends and steep gradients, and the scenery changes quickly from coast to mountains.

For lunch, find a bakery in Finalborgo and ask for farinata, a thin chickpea pancake baked in a wood oven in great copper pans, eaten hot with black pepper. It costs little, weighs nothing in the stomach and keeps you sharp for the Aurelia's tunnels. Fuel is on the main road out of town.
t.borgio@44.2,8.3:
In the grottoes of Borgio Verezzi, the limestone has been stained by iron, copper and manganese, and the stalactites glow in shades of red, yellow and green, some of the most colourful caves in Italy. They were found in the 1930s and are now open on guided tours. It is a cool, otherworldly escape on a hot day.

Borgio is the lower village, on the coast between Finale Ligure and Pietra Ligure, and Verezzi sits high above, a cluster of stone hamlets clinging to the hillside with views over the sea. In summer, the small square of Verezzi hosts a theatre festival, with the sea glittering below the stage. It is an enchanting setting.

This stop marks the end of the ride from the Vésubie and Tinée valleys, down through the mountains to the coast, and it is a fitting place to finish. The roads from the mountains descend in tight bends through olive groves and pine woods, and the sea appears suddenly at the end of the valley.

The beach at Borgio is a mix of sand and pebbles, with clear water, and the sea is calm in summer. The towns along the coast are lively in the evenings, with restaurants, bars and gelato shops.

Dinner should be simple and local: trofie with pesto, which Liguria invented, and a bottle of oil made from the small Taggiasca olives to take home if the panniers allow. For fuel and late shopping, Pietra Ligure is two minutes along the coast.
t.near andalsnes@62.5,7.7:
Eleven hairpins stacked on a near-vertical wall of rock, with a waterfall thundering down beside them: that is Trollstigen, the Troll's Ladder, one of the most famous roads in the world. Opened in 1936 after eight years of construction, it climbs from the Isterdalen valley to a plateau at 858 metres, with steep gradients and bends so tight that buses and campervans must take them in several attempts. The Stigfossen waterfall plunges down beside the road, and on a misty day the whole scene looks like a set from a fairy tale.

At the top, a visitor centre designed by Norwegian architects, all glass, steel and concrete, has viewing platforms that hang over the edge of the cliff, with a view straight down the hairpins and the valley. The plateau is a stark world of rock, snowfields and meltwater lakes, even in summer.

Åndalsnes, at the foot of the road, sits at the head of the Romsdalsfjord, overlooked by Trollveggen, the Troll Wall, the tallest vertical rock face in Europe, a sheer cliff of more than a thousand metres. Climbers and BASE jumpers have made it famous.

South of Trollstigen, the road drops through the valley of Valldal, famous for its strawberries, to the Norddalsfjord, where a ferry crosses to the road for Geiranger, with its own set of hairpins, the Eagle Road, above one of the most beautiful fjords in Norway.

Trollstigen usually opens in late May and closes in October, snow permitting, and on summer days the queues of coaches and campervans on the hairpins can be long. Ride it early in the morning or in the long northern evening, when the light lingers until close to midnight in June. Fill the tank in Åndalsnes or Valldal; there is nothing on the mountain, and Norwegian prices reward planning.
t.near sambuco@44.4,7.1:
Sambuco is a tiny village in the Valle Stura, one of the Occitan valleys of Piedmont, on the road that climbs from Cuneo to the Colle della Maddalena, known to the French as the Col de Larche, and on into the Ubaye valley in France. It is a place of stone houses, wooden balconies and steep meadows, surrounded by mountains, where life has always been tied to pastures and flocks. The village has given its name to a local breed of sheep, the Sambucana, whose lamb is a prized speciality of the valley.

The road up the Valle Stura is a fine ride, following the river through a narrowing valley with forests, villages and rock walls. Below Sambuco stands the enormous Forte Albertino at Vinadio, a nineteenth-century fortress built by the Savoy kings to guard the valley against France, now open to visitors. Above Sambuco, the road climbs through Pietraporzio and Argentera to the pass at nearly two thousand metres, with wide hairpins and a landscape that becomes increasingly wild and alpine.

The road is popular with motorcyclists and is generally in good condition, but heavy goods traffic can be a nuisance, as it is a through route between Italy and France. The pass can be closed by snow in winter, and weather in the mountains can change quickly. Watch for cattle and sheep on the road in summer.

Sambuco has limited services, but the valley has fuel in the larger villages lower down, such as Demonte, and Cuneo has everything. Local trattorias serve hearty Piedmontese and Occitan food, including polenta, cheeses and lamb. Onward, the way crosses into France and continues towards the Mercantour, with its high passes and remote valleys.
t.near seillans@43.8,6.7:
Seillans clings to a hillside above the plain of Fayence, a perched village of ochre houses, narrow lanes and fountains, with a castle and a church at the top. It is one of the officially recognised most beautiful villages of France, and it has attracted artists for generations; the surrealist painter Max Ernst spent his last years here, and a small collection of his work can be seen in the village.

The view from the top of the village is magnificent, stretching over the plain towards the Lac de Saint-Cassien and the Esterel hills, with the Mediterranean shimmering beyond on clear days. Behind the village, the land rises towards the high plateaus of the Var, wild and empty, much of it used as a military training area.

The riding around Seillans is excellent. The roads that link the perched villages of the Pays de Fayence, Seillans, Fayence, Montauroux and others, are narrow and winding, with tight hairpins and great views. To the north, the roads climb towards Mons and the high plateaus, and eventually to the Gorges du Verdon, one of the great rides of Provence. The surfaces are generally good, but summer brings tourist traffic, and the heat can be intense. Watch for gravel on the corners and for cyclists on the climbs.

Seillans has a few cafés and restaurants, while fuel and supermarkets are found in Fayence and the plain below. A lunch on a village terrace, with a view over the plain, is a classic Provençal experience. After this stop the ride heads north-east towards the Col de Turini and the Mercantour, through some of the most spectacular mountain scenery in the south of France.
t.near roquebilliere@44.1,7.4:
Roquebillière has had to rebuild itself more than once. In 1926, a landslide swept down onto the old village, killing many of its inhabitants, and much of the population moved to a new site on the other side of the river. Then, in October 2020, Storm Alex unleashed catastrophic floods down the Vésubie valley, destroying roads, bridges and houses, and leaving scars that are still visible today. The resilience of the valley's people is remarkable, and the road has been rebuilt with new bridges and protections.

The Vésubie is one of the great valleys of the Alpes-Maritimes, cutting deep into the mountains north of Nice towards the Mercantour national park. Roquebillière sits in its middle section, surrounded by steep slopes of pine and chestnut, with high peaks rising beyond. The Templar church of Saint-Michel-du-Gast, by the river, is a remarkable Romanesque-Gothic building, and the old village has narrow lanes and stone houses.

The riding here is spectacular. The valley road climbs from the coast through gorges and villages, with tight curves and great views, and from nearby La Bollène-Vésubie, a road climbs to the Col de Turini, famous for the Monte Carlo Rally and its countless hairpins. To the north, Saint-Martin-Vésubie is the gateway to the Mercantour, with high mountain roads and trails. The surfaces are generally good, but watch for rockfall, gravel and roadworks, and allow time for the many bends.

Services in the valley are limited, so arrive with a full tank and check fuel availability before heading into the mountains. Roquebillière and Saint-Martin-Vésubie have cafés and restaurants, and the local cuisine is a mountain version of Niçois cooking, with ravioli, tourte de blettes and lamb.
