t.near vikersund@60.0,9.9:
Ski flyers have soared further at Vikersund than almost anywhere else. The giant hill above the village, Vikersundbakken, is one of the largest ski flying hills in the world and has seen several world records, with jumpers flying well over two hundred metres. Even in summer, the scale of the in-run and landing slope is astonishing, and the view from the top over the lake is spectacular.

Vikersund lies at the northern tip of Tyrifjorden, a large lake west of Oslo, surrounded by forested hills and farmland. The area is part of Modum, a municipality with a rich industrial past. A short ride north, at Åmot, the Blaafarveværket was once a major producer of cobalt blue pigment, exported around the world in the nineteenth century; the old works are now a museum and art gallery, with a beautiful setting by a waterfall.

As for the riding, it is pleasant and varied. Roads follow the shore of the lake, with gentle curves and views over the water, and climb into the hills, with forests and farms. Traffic is light, but the main roads can be busy on weekends. Speed limits are low and enforced, and wildlife can be a hazard. The weather can change quickly, and the lake can create mist in the mornings.

Vikersund has fuel, shops and cafés, making it a good place for a break. Try a Norwegian pastry or a light lunch before continuing towards the Atlantic coast, a long ride to the north-west through mountains and valleys.
t.near annot@44.1,6.7:
Annot sits in the valley of the Vaïre in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, a medieval village of tall stone houses huddled beneath a backdrop of extraordinary sandstone boulders. These are the Grès d'Annot, huge blocks of sandstone scattered through the chestnut woods above the village, some of them with houses built right into them. The rock gives its name to a geological formation that is studied by geologists from around the world.

The village has a well-preserved old quarter, with narrow lanes, archways and a fortified church. The Train des Pignes, a narrow-gauge railway running between Nice and Digne-les-Bains, stops here, and the line itself is a marvel of engineering, threading through gorges and over viaducts. On some summer weekends, a historic steam train runs on part of the route.

For riders, Annot is in the middle of superb country. The N202 runs along the valley of the Var to the south, with the dramatic Gorges de Daluis and the Gorges du Cians nearby, both carved through deep red rock and among the most spectacular roads in the southern Alps. To the north and west, the roads climb towards Colmars, the Col des Champs and the Verdon. Corners are endless, surfaces vary, and traffic is light outside July and August.

Annot has cafés, bakeries and restaurants, making it a good food stop. Fuel is available in the area, but stations are spread out in this mountainous region, so it is wise to fill up when you can, for example in Saint-André-les-Alpes or Puget-Théniers. Take time to wander the old village and climb up to the boulders for a view.
t.near draguignan@43.6,6.5:
Draguignan is a market town in the heart of the Var, set in a basin among wooded hills about thirty kilometres inland from the coast. It is a working town rather than a tourist resort, home to France's artillery school and a large military camp at Canjuers on the plateau to the north. The old town has narrow lanes, plane-shaded squares and a distinctive clock tower, and the Saturday market is one of the best in Provence.

Just outside town stands the Pierre de la Fée, a huge prehistoric dolmen, and the surrounding hills are dotted with perched villages like Flayosc, Tourtour and Lorgues. To the north, the land rises towards the Canjuers plateau and the Gorges du Verdon, one of the most spectacular canyons in Europe. Draguignan is a natural gateway to the gorges, and the roads that lead there are among the finest in France.

The riding from Draguignan is superb. Roads climb north through the hills and villages, with tight bends, steep gradients and views over the Var. The route towards Comps-sur-Artuby and the Verdon is a classic, and the corniche roads around the gorges are unforgettable. Surfaces are generally good, but the roads can be narrow, and summer traffic around the Verdon is heavy. Military vehicles are sometimes seen near Canjuers.

Draguignan has full services, including fuel, food and coffee. For a photo, the perched villages in the hills or the views from the roads north of town are rewarding. Summer heat can be intense, so start early and carry water.
t.near olivetta san michele@43.9,7.5:
Olivetta San Michele is a small Ligurian village in the valley of the Bevera, right on the border between Italy and France, a few kilometres up from Ventimiglia. The village clings to steep slopes covered with olive terraces, and its stone houses and church tower look much as they have for centuries. The French town of Sospel lies just upstream, across the border.

The Bevera valley has been a frontier for centuries, fought over by the counts of Savoy, the Republic of Genoa and France. Fortifications from different eras can be found in the hills, including forts built along the Maginot Line's alpine extension in the 1930s. The olive groves produce the small Taggiasca olives that are a speciality of western Liguria, and local oil is excellent.

As a start and fuel stop, Olivetta is close to Ventimiglia, which has plenty of services, and fuel is often cheaper on one side of the border than the other, so it pays to check. The roads from here are spectacular. The route up the Bevera to Sospel winds through a narrow gorge, then climbs to the Col de Brouis or the Col de Braus, both twisting passes with hairpins and views. Beyond Sospel lies the Col de Turini, famous from the Monte Carlo Rally.

Traffic is light on the mountain roads, but watch for cyclists, rally enthusiasts and local drivers who know every bend. Surfaces vary, and some roads are narrow. In summer, start early to avoid the heat; in winter, the high passes can be icy.
t.le cannet@43.6,7.0:
Le Cannet climbs the hills directly behind Cannes, and from its upper streets you look down over the rooftops of the city to the bay, the Lérins islands and the red Esterel mountains to the west. The old village at its heart, with narrow lanes, painted walls and small squares, still has a Provençal charm that the busy streets below have largely lost.

The painter Pierre Bonnard lived here for the last two decades of his life, in a villa called Le Bosquet, and painted the views from his windows again and again. The Musée Bonnard, in the town centre, is dedicated to his work and that of his contemporaries, and it is a lovely, quiet museum, well worth a visit if you have time.

As a start and fuel stop, Le Cannet is practical. There are service stations and shops in the town and along the main roads, and it is easy to fill up before heading into the hills. The roads north from here lead towards Mougins, Grasse and the Route Napoléon, or west towards the Esterel and the coast. Traffic can be heavy, especially in summer and during the Cannes Film Festival in May, so an early start is wise.

From Le Cannet, the transition from the coast to the mountains is rapid. Within half an hour, you can be climbing into the pre-Alps, with the Mediterranean shrinking behind you. Check your tyre pressures in the cool of the morning; by the time you reach the Route Napoléon the coast will be a blue haze far below.
t.near mandelieu la napoule@43.6,6.9:
Mandelieu-la-Napoule sits at the western end of the bay of Cannes, where the river Siagne meets the sea, and behind it rise two very different massifs. To the south-west, the Esterel is a jagged range of red volcanic rock, plunging into the sea along one of the most dramatic stretches of coast in France. To the north, the Tanneron is a softer range of hills famous for its mimosa, which blooms in brilliant yellow in late winter.

On the seafront stands the Château de la Napoule, a medieval fortress restored in the early twentieth century by the American artist Henry Clews and his wife Marie, who filled it with his strange, fantastical sculptures. Today it is a museum and art centre, with gardens overlooking the sea.

For riders, the Corniche de l'Esterel, running south-west along the coast towards Saint-Raphaël, is a classic, with tight bends, red cliffs and blue water below. The roads inland over the Esterel and the Tanneron are quieter, climbing through cork oak and pine forests with views over the coast. Surfaces are generally good, but traffic on the coast road can be heavy in summer. In dry weather, fire risk can close forest roads.

Fuel and food are plentiful in Mandelieu and Cannes. As a high point, the roads over the Tanneron or the Esterel offer views over the bay of Cannes and the Mediterranean, especially beautiful in the early morning or late evening.
t.near roquebilliere@44.0,7.2:
Roquebillière sits in the valley of the Vésubie, one of the deep valleys that cut into the Alpes-Maritimes north of Nice. The river rushes down from the high peaks near the Italian border, and the valley is steep, wooded and dramatic, with villages perched on the slopes and mountains rising on every side.

The village has a turbulent history. In 1926, after torrential rain, a landslide destroyed part of the old village, killing many people, and a new village was built on safer ground. In October 2020, Storm Alex brought devastating floods to the Vésubie valley, destroying roads, bridges and houses, and the scars are still visible. The valley has been rebuilding ever since, and the resilience of its people is remarkable. On the valley floor, the old church of Saint-Michel-du-Gast, built in the fifteenth century, survived both disasters.

For riders, the Vésubie valley is a gateway to some of the finest roads in the southern Alps. The road up the valley to Saint-Martin-Vésubie is winding and scenic, and from La Bollène-Vésubie, just above Roquebillière, the road climbs to the Col de Turini, famous from the Monte Carlo Rally. Surfaces vary, and some sections are still being repaired after the floods. Traffic is light, but watch for cyclists and rally fans.

Fuel options are limited in the valley, so fill up in Nice or the lower valley before heading up. Food is available in Roquebillière and Saint-Martin-Vésubie.
t.near fla@60.5,9.6:
Flå sits in the lower part of Hallingdal, one of the great valleys of southern Norway, where the river Hallingdalselva flows south into Lake Krøderen. Rv7, the main road from Oslo to Bergen over Hardangervidda, runs through the valley, and Flå is often the first stop for travellers heading west into the mountains.

The village is best known for its bear park, Bjørneparken, where brown bears, wolves, lynx and other Nordic animals live in large enclosures in the forest. It is a popular stop for families, and seeing a bear up close is a thrill. Wild bears still roam the forests of Vassfaret, a remote wilderness area east of Flå, once one of the last strongholds of the brown bear in southern Norway.

The valley here is narrow and forested, with steep slopes rising on both sides and the river rushing over rapids below. Further up the valley, around Gol and Geilo, the landscape opens up, and the road climbs to the high plateau of Hardangervidda, the largest mountain plateau in Europe. The views from the top are vast.

For riders, Rv7 through Hallingdal is a fine road, with gentle curves along the river and views of the valley and the mountains. Traffic can be heavy in summer and at holiday weekends, with caravans and camper vans. Speed limits are low and enforced, and speed cameras are common. Fuel and food are available in Flå. As a start and finish, Flå offers a good base for exploring Hallingdal and the mountains beyond.
t.near prestfoss@60.1,9.5:
Prestfoss is the main village of Sigdal, a long, green valley west of Drammen, where the river Simoa flows south between forested mountains. The village sits at a waterfall on the river, and around it the valley opens into farmland, with old wooden farmhouses, red barns and meadows.

Sigdal is closely associated with the painter Theodor Kittelsen, famous for his drawings and paintings of trolls, forest spirits and the dark, mysterious side of Norwegian folklore. He lived for some years in Sigdal, at a house called Lauvlia, near Prestfoss, which he designed and decorated himself. Today it is a museum, with his works, furniture and the atmosphere of the place where he lived and worked. Visiting it, you can almost feel the trolls lurking in the forest outside.

The valley also has the Sigdal Museum, an open-air collection of old farm buildings, and Eggedal, further up the valley, is the home of the painter Christian Skredsvig's farm, Hagan, also a museum. The landscape of Sigdal inspired several Norwegian painters of the nineteenth century.

For riders, Rv287 through Sigdal is a lovely road, with gentle curves along the river and views of the valley and the mountains. Traffic is light, especially outside the summer holidays. Speed limits are low and enforced. Fuel and food are available in Prestfoss. As a start, finish and photo stop, the valley, with its old farms and forested slopes, is classic Norwegian scenery.
t.near saint laurent du var@43.6,7.2:
Until 1860, the river at Saint-Laurent-du-Var marked an international frontier. On the west bank lay France; on the east bank lay the County of Nice, part of the Kingdom of Sardinia, and travellers along the coast had to cross the wide, shifting bed of the Var to pass from one to the other. For centuries there was no proper bridge, and the village made its living from the men who carried travellers across on their backs or guided them through the shallows. When Nice became French, the border vanished, but the river is still the dividing line between the town and the city.

Today Saint-Laurent is a busy suburb on the west bank, facing Nice's airport across the river mouth. It has a marina, a long pebble beach, the large Cap 3000 shopping centre and a small old village up the hill with a church and narrow streets. It is not especially beautiful, but it is lively and practical, with plenty of cafés and restaurants along the seafront.

The Var itself is a wild Alpine river, prone to sudden floods, and its broad gravel bed is now partly a nature reserve, home to herons and other birds. Following it north, the road leads into the mountains, and the gorges of the Vésubie, the Tinée and the upper Var all branch off within an hour. This is the way you will have come down if you are finishing a ride from the Col de Turini or the Mercantour, perhaps tired and dusty after a day of hairpins.

Coming back to the coast at the end of the day, expect a sudden shift from empty mountain roads to the dense traffic of the Nice agglomeration, with roundabouts, scooters and impatient drivers. Take it slowly. There are fuel stations and food everywhere, and the beachfront is a fine place to end the day, with the sun setting behind the Esterel and planes landing over the bay. In summer, the evenings stay warm and the beaches are busy until late; in winter, the coast is mild and quiet, and the mountains behind are often white with snow.
t.near mandelieu la napoule@43.5,6.9:
Mandelieu-la-Napoule sits at the western end of the bay of Cannes, where the river Siagne meets the sea, and behind it rise two very different massifs. To the south-west, the Esterel is a jagged range of red volcanic rock, plunging into the sea along one of the most dramatic stretches of coast in France. To the north, the Tanneron is a softer range of hills famous for its mimosa, which blooms in brilliant yellow in late winter.

On the seafront stands the Château de la Napoule, a medieval fortress restored in the early twentieth century by the American artist Henry Clews and his wife Marie, who filled it with his strange, fantastical sculptures. Today it is a museum and art centre, with gardens overlooking the sea.

For riders, the Corniche de l'Esterel, running south-west along the coast towards Saint-Raphaël, is a classic, with tight bends, red cliffs and blue water below. The roads inland over the Esterel and the Tanneron are quieter, climbing through cork oak and pine forests with views over the coast. Surfaces are generally good, but traffic on the coast road can be heavy in summer. In dry weather, fire risk can close forest roads.

Fuel and food are plentiful in Mandelieu and Cannes. As a high point, the roads over the Tanneron or the Esterel offer views over the bay of Cannes and the Mediterranean, especially beautiful in the early morning or late evening.
t.near eide@63.0,7.3:
The Atlantic Road was built to connect fishing villages on islands that had been linked only by boat, and it does so with a kind of reckless grace: a sequence of causeways, low bridges and short stretches of road that hop from skerry to skerry across the open edge of the Norwegian Sea. This point lies near Eide, on the mainland end of the route, between the fjord country and the coast, on the Romsdal peninsula between Molde and Kristiansund.

The Atlanterhavsvegen opened in 1989 after years of construction, often in brutal weather; workers faced twelve hurricane-force storms during the building. It is only about eight kilometres long, but it is one of the most photographed roads in the world, especially the Storseisundet bridge, which rises and curves so sharply that from some angles it seems to end in mid-air. On a calm summer day the sea is blue and glassy, with eider ducks and cormorants on the rocks. In autumn storms, waves crash over the road, and people drive out on purpose to watch.

The coast around here, Hustadvika, has a fearsome reputation among sailors, with shallow reefs and violent seas. Old fishing villages like Bud and the island community of Averøy survived on cod and herring, and the region is still known for klippfisk, salted and dried cod, which was exported to Spain and Portugal for centuries. Kristiansund, the nearest town, is the capital of klippfisk and has a museum devoted to it.

The riding on and around the Atlantic Road is easy in technical terms but wonderful for the views. The road is flat and smooth, with gentle curves, but the wind can be ferocious, and spray from the sea makes the surface wet and salty. Traffic is heavy in summer, with tourists stopping on the bridges for photographs. The roads inland toward Eide and Molde follow fjords and pass through tunnels and small farms, with mountains on every side.

Eide and the villages along the route have shops and cafes, and Kristiansund, about twenty-two kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and hotels. Bring good rain gear, even in July, and stop at the viewpoints and fishing platforms built along the road to take it all in.
t.near menton@43.8,7.5:
Menton is the last town in France before Italy, the finish of the Route des Grandes Alpes, and after seven hundred kilometres of mountains it feels like being tipped into a warm bath. The old town tumbles down a hill to the harbour in tones of ochre, apricot and cream, topped by the baroque Basilica of Saint Michael with its glowing facade. The climate is the mildest on the French Riviera, sheltered by the mountains behind, and the local lemons are famous, celebrated each February in the Fête du Citron, when huge sculptures made of fruit and flowers fill the gardens and people parade through the streets.

The town has a gentle, slightly faded elegance, a place where Victorian visitors came for their health and a gaggle of grand villas still look out over the water. Jean Cocteau, the writer and artist, decorated the registry office in the town hall, and a museum of his work stands on the seafront. A short walk away, the gardens of Garavan, planted with exotic trees and flowers, benefit from a warmth that few other places in France can match. The Italian border is just beyond, close enough to walk, and many people cross for lunch.

The final ride down the mountain is the real subject. Many riders arrive from the Col de la Bonette, at 2,715 metres the highest paved pass in France when including its extra loop, or from the Col de Vars, at 2,109 metres. The descent toward the coast winds through high pastures, then narrow gorges, then pine and chestnut forest, before finally dropping through olive groves and terraced hillsides toward the sea. Along the way, perched villages such as Sainte-Agnès, at about eight hundred metres the highest coastal village in Europe, cling to rocky crests above the bay, with narrow lanes and glorious views. The temperature climbs as the road falls, and a rider can go from a frosty morning to a hot afternoon in a few hours.

Practical matters are easy in a town of nearly thirty thousand. Fuel stations line the approach roads, and there are cafes and restaurants all along the seafront. Traffic along the coast is heavy in summer, and parking is tight, so look for a secure garage. Pastry shops sell tarte au citron, and the local speciality is socca, a thin chickpea pancake, or pissaladière, an onion tart. Treat yourself with a swim: it is the tradition at the end of this journey.
t.near balestrand@61.3,6.5:
Balestrand is a village on the north shore of the Sognefjord, and it has one of the best settings in Norway: a wide, calm stretch of the fjord with mountains reaching up on all sides, orchards at the water's edge and a quiet, old-fashioned atmosphere. It has fewer than eight hundred inhabitants, and in the nineteenth century it became a destination for British and German tourists, who came by steamer to stay in the large wooden hotels. The Kviknes Hotel, a grand dragon-style building from 1877, is still in operation, and the English church of St Olaf, built by an Englishwoman who married a local painter, stands nearby. Vik and Hermansverk are the nearest towns of any size.

The painter Hans Dahl made his home here and painted romantic scenes of fjords and farms, and Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany visited regularly, which brought more fame to the village. His statue of Fridtjof the Bold stands on a hill above the fjord, a gift from the Kaiser, while the legend of Fridtjof's saga is set around here. The lanes are lined with old wooden houses, apple trees and flowers, and the mood is peaceful.

The ride from Balestrand starts with a fjord road and then climbs into the Gaularfjellet, a mountain pass. The road follows the Sognefjord for a while, then turns inland, with a series of bends and a rise through birch forest to an open plateau. The surface is generally very good, and the gradient is moderate. On the way, waterfalls, such as Hellefossen and Likholefossen, spill over cliffs beside the road. In spring, meltwater makes them roar.

Fuel is available at a small station in the village, but supplies are limited, so it is safer to fill up in Vik or Sogndal. A ferry connects Balestrand with Hella and Dragsvik, which is an enjoyable way to cross the fjord. There are cafes and shops serving the usual coffee and cinnamon buns, and local fruit and cider are sold in summer. The best time to ride is June to September, when the days are long, and the village is an easy, relaxing place to begin.
t.near saint raphael@43.4,6.8:
Saint-Raphaël is the starting point of one of the most colourful roads in France, and the colour is its subject. The Esterel massif, a low range of volcanic rock behind the town, is made of red porphyry, which glows an almost unreal brick-red against the blue Mediterranean and the dark green of the pines. The town itself is a relaxed seaside resort of about thirty-five thousand people, with a promenade, a casino, a harbour and a handsome church in Neo-Byzantine style, Notre-Dame-de-la-Victoire, built in the nineteenth century.

History is thick here. Napoleon landed at Saint-Raphaël in October 1799, returning from Egypt, and left from the same shore for exile on Elba in 1814, so the town considers itself a footnote to imperial history. The neighbouring town, Fréjus, has Roman ruins, including an arena and an aqueduct, left from the days when it was a naval base of Julius Caesar. In the nineteenth century, the rise of the Riviera as a winter retreat brought writers and wealthy invalids, and Saint-Raphaël grew with them.

The Corniche d'Or, the Golden Corniche, runs southwest along the Esterel coast for about thirty kilometres to Théoule-sur-Mer, and it was built in the early twentieth century as one of the first tourist roads in France. The road clings to the cliffs, with the red rock on one side and the sea on the other, and it winds in and out of small coves, with views of rocks that rise from the water like carved sculptures. The bends are gentle and constant, the surface is good, and the pace is slow, because of the scenery and the traffic.

In July and August the Corniche can be clogged with cars, so ride early in the morning or in the shoulder seasons, and be careful about summer wildfires, which sometimes close the roads in the Esterel. Fuel, restaurants and bike shops are easy in Saint-Raphaël, so prepare there. The beaches along the coast are small and rocky, with clear water good for a swim, but the parking is limited. A plate of grilled fish and a chilled glass of Provence rosé in the old harbour will complete the picture.
t.near briancon@44.8,6.7:
Briançon calls itself the highest city in France, and at around 1,326 metres, it has a good case. It sits in the upper Durance valley in the Hautes-Alpes, where several rivers and several passes meet, and for centuries that made it both a trading post and a fortress. Roads climb from here to the Col du Galibier and the Lautaret in one direction, to the Col d'Izoard and the Queyras in another, and to Montgenèvre and Italy in a third. A rider arrives from any of them in much the same mood: pleased to be somewhere with a restaurant.

The old town, the Cité Vauban, sits on a hill above the modern town, enclosed by walls and ramparts. Louis XIV's great military engineer, Vauban, redesigned the defences in the late seventeenth century, and the result, with its forts, bastions and gates, is now on the UNESCO World Heritage list. The steep cobbled main street, the Grande Gargouille, has a stream running down the middle in a stone channel, and shops, bakeries and small restaurants line the sides. It is a pleasure to walk, though cobbles and riding boots are not natural friends.

The riding around Briançon is some of the best in the Alps. The road up toward the Lautaret and Galibier follows the Guisane valley in a long, steady climb, with larch forest, snow peaks and the dramatic scenery that cyclists crowd to see each summer in the Tour de France. The mountain passes here open in late spring or early summer, and the high ones close in winter, so check conditions before planning an early or late-season ride. Mornings are often clear, with cloud building in the afternoon and occasional thunderstorms.

As a stop, Briançon is excellent. With over eleven thousand inhabitants, it has fuel stations, supermarkets, bike shops, banks, hotels and plenty of cafes, and it is a natural place to refill both tank and stomach. Try the local cheeses and a tourte, or a hearty plate of gratin dauphinois, and drink a coffee on a sunny terrace. The air is clean and dry, and the sun is strong, which is why the town has long had a reputation as a place for health cures and recuperation.
t.near valldal@62.3,7.1:
Valldal is a small town at the head of the Norddalsfjord, in the green and orderly farmland that lies at the foot of the great Sunnmøre mountains, and it is the first proper settlement you reach after the long descent from the Trollstigen. Valldal is famous in Norway for its strawberries, which ripen in July in the long summer light and are sold in roadside stands, and the local people take a great deal of pride in them.

The fjord has a darker history. In 1934, a huge rockslide fell from the mountain above Tafjord, a neighbouring arm of the fjord, and the wave it created swept along the shore and killed dozens of people in the villages. The slopes above these fjords remain unstable, and the rock above is monitored today. A feeling of the scale of things, of vertical walls and deep water, is part of the experience of the place. Another part is the ferry between Eidsdal and Linge, which crosses the Norddalsfjord on the road to Geiranger, a short and pleasant crossing with fine views.

Riding here is some of the best in Norway. The road from the Trollstigen drops through forest and farmland, with wide bends and a long run down to the fjord, and from Valldal the climb to the Eagle's Road at Geiranger is a classic. The surface is mostly good, but the traffic in summer is heavy, with caravans and coaches, and the speed limits are low and strictly enforced. The weather is changeable, with rain common and mist hanging in the valleys, and the temperature can drop quickly with altitude. The Trollstigen and the Geiranger road are closed in winter, so check dates before planning.

It is a good place to refuel the bike and yourself, because the roads on either side are long and the next services are some way off. Stranda, sixteen kilometres away, is a larger town with more choices.

Eat strawberries in season, and cake and waffles year-round, and walk down to the quay to look up at the walls of rock. It is a quiet place that sits in the shadow of its famous neighbours.
t.near cargese@42.2,8.6:
Cargèse has two churches facing each other across a small valley, one Roman Catholic and one Greek Orthodox, and that tells you almost everything about the town. In 1676, a group of Greek families from the Mani peninsula in the Peloponnese, fleeing Ottoman rule, were given land on this stretch of the Corsican coast by the Republic of Genoa. They built their village, held to their rite and language for generations, and for a long time the Greeks and the Corsicans lived side by side without mixing. The two churches, one Latin and one Greek, stand on either side of the village, and the Greek church, with its icons and painted interior, is a delight.

The town sits on a small headland above the sea, on Corsica's west coast, north of Ajaccio and south of the great red cliffs of Piana. It has a population of about a thousand, a handful of cafes, a few restaurants, a pretty harbour and a long view across the Gulf of Sagone. Behind it rise the maquis-covered hills, thick with myrtle, rock rose and wild lavender, whose smell, on a warm evening, is a thing of wonder. A Genoese tower, built to watch for raiders, stands on the headland nearby.

The D81, which runs north from here toward Piana, Porto and the Calanques, is among the greatest coast roads in Europe. It twists above the sea, with the red granite cliffs of the Calanques plunging down to blue water, tunnels cut into the rock and views at every bend. The surface is generally good, but the road is narrow and winding, with sheer drops and few barriers, and in summer it is clogged with tour buses and campervans. Leave early, or ride in May or September when the light is clearer and the traffic lighter.

Be prepared for the Corsican weather, which can shift quickly, and for the wind, which on the exposed sections can push a loaded bike off line. In summer, wildfire is a risk and the maquis is tinder dry, so no smoking at the roadside.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Cargèse is a small place, so fill up in Ajaccio, around twenty-seven kilometres south, or check whether the local station is open, and do not run low before the long stretch to Porto. There are plenty of places to eat, and grilled fish with a chilled glass of local rosé is the thing to order.
t.near zonza@41.8,9.2:
The road from Porto-Vecchio to Zonza climbs out of the humid coast into another Corsica, one of chestnut and pine, granite and cold streams. Zonza lies at about eight hundred metres in the Alta Rocca, a small village of fewer than two thousand people scattered across a ridge, with the great granite needles of Bavella standing over it to the north. The coast is only twenty kilometres away, but the altitude, the air and the sense of space make it feel much further.

The Aiguilles de Bavella are a row of jagged granite pinnacles, bare and orange-brown in the late light, rising above the pass of the same name at around twelve hundred metres. They dominate the skyline for miles, and in the morning mist they appear and vanish like the spires of a drowned cathedral. The forests of laricio pine, the Corsican black pine, which grows tall and straight, cover the slopes, and the smell, resin and warm needles, is intoxicating. Wild mouflon, the shy mountain sheep of Corsica, live on the high ground, though you are more likely to see pigs and cows wandering on the road.

The riding is glorious. The road from Zonza to the pass is a narrow, winding climb through the forest, with tight bends, views over the valley and plenty of places to stop. The surface is generally good but uneven in places, and the road is often shared with free-roaming livestock, which have right of way in all but name. In summer, the traffic of campervans and hikers makes it slow, and in the early morning, it is magical. Weather in the mountains changes fast, so carry a waterproof.

The local food is the real treat. Corsican charcuterie, such as coppa, lonzu and figatellu, is cured in the mountain air, and a plate with a slice of brocciu, the fresh sheep's cheese, and a glass of local red is the perfect reward. Fire is the great danger here, and in dry summers the island is on high alert, so no smoking at the roadside.

Zonza has a few shops and restaurants and is the natural stop on this ride, but fuel is not something to count on, so the safest plan is to fill up in Porto-Vecchio, about twenty kilometres away.

t.near theoule sur mer@43.5,6.9:
Théoule-sur-Mer is a little town squeezed between the red rocks of the Esterel and the sea, and it looks like a painting from the early days of the French Riviera. The houses are pink and ochre, the harbour is small and crowded with boats, and the hills behind are covered with pines and cork oaks. A fortified château with round towers, dating from the fourteenth century and now used as the town hall, stands near the shore, and the old fishing quarter has narrow streets and small terraces. The population is only about thirteen hundred, though it swells in summer.

Just along the coast lies La Napoule, with a castle that was a ruin until 1918, when an American sculptor, Henry Clews, and his wife bought it and rebuilt it as a home and studio, filling it with his strange, brooding sculptures. It is now an arts foundation and open to visitors. Inland, the hills of the Tanneron are covered in mimosa trees, which flower bright yellow in January and February, and there is a mimosa route that runs through the forest in the depths of winter when the rest of Europe is grey.

At the end of the Corniche d'Or, the road changes character, passing from the wild Esterel into the busier coast of Cannes and Mandelieu. The final stretch is a sequence of bends and viewpoints, with small bays below where the water is clear enough to see the rocks on the bottom. Riders should be wary of tourists stepping out between parked cars, and the occasional scooter overtaking on the inside. Parking in summer is very difficult, so arrive early.

Théoule itself has a few shops, bakeries and cafés, but for fuel and larger stores, Mandelieu-la-Napoule, about four kilometres away, is the better bet. The beaches are small, rocky and lovely, and the sea is warm from July to September. The Esterel can burn in dry summers, so respect fire warnings and closures. The best time to be here is May or late September, when the weather is warm, the crowds are thin and the light on the red rocks is at its best. Order grilled sea bream, and watch the sun go down behind the headland.
t.near bedoin@44.2,5.3:
Bédoin is the village at the foot of Mont Ventoux, the white, bald summit that dominates Provence, and it is where the hardest and most famous approach starts. The mountain rises to 1,912 metres, and from far away it looks like it is covered in snow, though the whiteness is bare limestone scree. The ascent from Bédoin is about twenty-one kilometres, climbing through vineyards and cherry orchards and then through a dense forest of cedar and pine, before bursting out above the tree line at Chalet Reynard into a lunar landscape of pale stones, with a weather station and a radio mast on top. The Tour de France has crossed it many times, and the tiny memorial to the British cyclist Tom Simpson, who died near the summit in 1967, is a place of pilgrimage for cyclists.

Long before bikes, the poet Petrarch climbed Mont Ventoux in 1336 and wrote an account that many consider the first record of climbing a mountain for the sheer pleasure of the view. The wind has its own reputation, as the mistral, which blows down the Rhône valley, can gust here at over a hundred and fifty kilometres an hour, and the summit weather changes in minutes. The mountain is a biosphere reserve, with different climate zones from Mediterranean to alpine on its slopes, and it is rich in wild flowers and butterflies.

On a motorcycle, the climb is a delight: a steady, sinuous road with open bends and long views, though crowded with cyclists on summer mornings, so patience is needed on the lower slopes. The surface is generally good, and the upper part is exposed, with crosswinds and cold, so carry a warm layer even in July. The summit road is closed by snow from late autumn until spring, and sometimes at short notice, so check before you go. Bédoin, a village of about three thousand people, has fuel, cafés and bakeries, and Caromb and Mazan are close by with more.

The loop returns through the Gorges de la Nesque, a limestone canyon with a road cut into its walls and tunnels along the way, one of the great Provençal rides. Pack a picnic of local goat's cheese, bread and cherries, and sit above the gorge with your helmet off.
t.near eidfjord@60.4,7.2:
Eidfjord lies at the inner end of the Hardangerfjord, one of the longest fjords in Norway, and the village, with only a few hundred people, sits at the foot of steep cliffs, where waterfalls fall from the plateau above and the water below is dark green and still. The setting is dramatic. In the early morning, mist hangs on the fjord, and the mountains rise on every side, while orchards of apple and cherry trees on the lower slopes recall that the Hardanger region is Norway's fruit garden. In spring, when the trees blossom, the contrast with the snow on the peaks is striking.

Above the village lies the Hardangervidda, the largest mountain plateau in northern Europe, a wide, bare upland of lakes, bogs and rounded hills, which is home to the biggest herd of wild reindeer in the country. The road, Route 7, climbs from the fjord to the plateau through the Mabodalen valley, with a sequence of tunnels and hairpins and a view of Voringsfossen, a waterfall that drops about 180 metres in two stages into a deep gorge. The fall is one of the most visited in Norway, and the viewing platforms give a close look at the spray and the cliffs.

Eidfjord has a visitor centre, the Hardangervidda Nature Centre, with exhibits on the geology, wildlife and human history of the plateau, and a small hydroelectric industry nearby makes use of the water. The Hardanger Bridge, a suspension bridge that opened in 2013 and has a main span of about 1,310 metres, crosses the fjord just beyond the village, and the road across it is smooth, exposed and unforgettable. Wind can be strong on the bridge, so a firm grip is wise.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Eidfjord has a few services, but it is small, and pumps in rural Norway are often unmanned and take only cards. Ulvik and Granvin, the nearest villages, are also small, and the larger towns of Voss and Odda are about an hour away. Fill up beforehand, and keep a bank card with a PIN. Tolls on tunnels and bridges are charged automatically, and rental bikes usually have a tag. The riding season on the plateau runs from late May to October, and snow can fall in any month at height. Layers and waterproofs are essential, because the weather changes quickly.
